rows.historicalPrecedent: The Institute's namesake joined law and faith in one career. John Jay studied under King's College's 1763 plan, which set Grotius or Pufendorf in the fourth year. He became the first Chief Justice and in retirement served as president of the American Bible Society (1821–1827). In 1963 King's Birmingham letter showed that the Augustinian and Thomist distinction between just and unjust laws could still move American law.

sources.label: John Jay Institute, Our Beliefs (natural law and religious liberty)
John Jay Institute curriculum page, archived 23 Feb 2009 (Wayback Machine)

rows.notes: To be revised when the user attaches the John Jay Institute curriculum. The archived 2006–2009 module "Christianity, American Constitutionalism and Jurisprudence" read Coke, Selden, Hale and Blackstone, colonial charters and the founding documents. It also read Jay, Marshall, Kent and Story, and set James Fitzjames Stephen against J.S. Mill. "Modern Political Theory and Christian Thought" added Milton, Baxter, Wilberforce, Coleridge, Groen van Prinsterer, Kuyper, Leo XIII, John Courtney Murray, Reinhold Niebuhr, John Paul II and Richard John Neuhaus. The Institute's statement of beliefs calls religious freedom America's first freedom. The King letter is under copyright (King Estate) but is free to read at the King Institute. Cover was Jewish. His essay is included because it explains how a religious community's law lives alongside the state's, a theme Berman and Witte take up. civics-law-15 already reads Leo XIII against Dignitatis Humanae. Here the question is the jurisprudence of religious liberty.

rows.title: Responsive Talk: Serve-and-Return from Birth
rows.summary: The single most powerful language practice in infancy is ordinary conversation: noticing the baby's coos, gestures and gaze and answering them with words, faces and touch ("serve and return"). Narrate the day, name what the child looks at, pause for a reply, and read aloud from the first weeks. The AAP's 2024 literacy policy recommends shared reading from birth because it builds language and the parent-child bond together.
objectives: Parents narrate daily care (feeding, changing, walks) in full, rich sentences rather than baby talk alone
Follow the baby's gaze and name objects; wait for and answer every coo, babble and gesture
Read aloud daily from birth (board books, Mother Goose, psalms and poems), for the sound of language even before comprehension
Track CDC milestones at 2, 4, 6, 9 and 12 months (social smile, babbling, responding to name, first words) and raise concerns early
rows.historicalPrecedent: Quintilian (Institutio Oratoria I.1) insists that the nurse's speech be correct because the child's first impressions of language are the most lasting, and that the parents themselves be as well educated as possible. Locke (Thoughts §1) likewise holds that the "little, or almost insensible impressions on our tender infancies" have the most lasting consequences.

sources.label: AAP Policy (2024): Literacy Promotion, An Essential Component of Primary Care

CDC: Developmental Milestones (Learn the Signs. Act Early.)
Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria Book I ch. 1–3 (LacusCurtius)
Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education (Archive.org)

rows.notes: Reach Out and Read (reachoutandread.org) distributes books at well-child visits and is a good model for building a home library early.

rows.title: Infant Sleep, Feeding and First Foods
rows.summary: Establish the physical foundations: safe sleep, human milk where possible, vitamin D, and at about six months a varied introduction of iron-rich and whole foods, including early allergen introduction. Good sleep and nutrition in the first year support everything else in this track.
objectives: Safe sleep for every sleep: on the back, on a firm flat surface, in the parents' room but not the parents' bed, with no soft bedding (AAP 2022)
Aim for 12–16 hours of sleep per 24 hours from 4–12 months, including naps (AASM, endorsed by AAP)
Exclusive human milk for about six months if possible, continued through the first year; iron-fortified formula otherwise; vitamin D supplementation

Introduce complementary foods at about six months, with iron- and zinc-rich foods and early peanut and egg introduction per pediatric guidance (LEAP trial); avoid added sugars, ultra-processed foods and honey before age 1
Build a predictable daily rhythm of feeding, play, nap and bedtime, with a short bedtime ritual that includes a song and a prayer

sources.label: AAP: Safe Sleep
AAP Policy (2022): Sleep-Related Infant Deaths
AASM Consensus: Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations (2016)

Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 (ODPHP)

rows.notes: Medical specifics (allergen timing for high-risk infants, supplementation) should be decided with the child's pediatrician; this row gives the consensus defaults only.

rows.title: Floor Time, Tummy Time and First Movement
rows.summary: Babies need to be free on the floor, not strapped in seats. The WHO recommends interactive floor play several times a day and at least 30 minutes of tummy time spread across the day for infants who are not yet mobile, and no more than an hour at a time restrained in prams, high chairs or carriers.
objectives: At least 30 minutes of tummy time daily, in short sessions, from the first weeks
Daily unrestricted floor time on a safe surface to reach, roll, pivot, crawl and pull to stand
Offer graspable objects (rattles, wooden rings, cloth balls) for reaching, grasping and transferring hand to hand
Time outdoors every day in fair weather (pram walks, lying on a blanket under trees)

sources.label: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour and Sleep for Children under 5 (2019)
CDC: Developmental Milestones

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (Thoughts §§5–10, 30) summarizes the regimen for bodily health as "plenty of open air, exercise, and sleep, plain diet," and warns against coddling and overheating infants.

rows.title: Lullabies, Mother Goose and First Books (Read-Aloud from Birth)
rows.summary: Nursery rhymes are the infant's first poetry. Their strong meter, rhyme and alliteration train the ear for the sounds of English (phonological awareness) long before reading. Sing and chant Mother Goose daily, share sturdy picture books, and let the baby handle books.
objectives: Recite or sing several nursery rhymes every day, with bouncing, clapping and tickling games
Read short board books and picture books daily, pointing to and naming pictures
Keep a basket of books within the baby's reach
By 18–24 months the child fills in the last word of familiar rhymes

coreTexts.title: Divine Songs Attempted in Easy Language for the Use of Children
coreTexts.author: Isaac Watts

sources.label: AAP Policy (2024): Literacy Promotion
Reach Out and Read

rows.historicalPrecedent: Watts's Divine Songs (1715) was the most widely memorized children's verse in the English-speaking world through the 18th and early 19th centuries, alongside the Mother Goose collections first printed in London and Boston in the 1760s–1780s.

rows.title: Bilingual by Ear I: Spanish and Mandarin from Native Speakers
rows.summary: Infants can distinguish the sounds of every language, but between 6 and 12 months that ability narrows to the languages they hear from people. Kuhl, Tsao and Liu (2003) showed that 9-month-old American infants learned Mandarin phonetic contrasts from live native speakers but not from the same speakers on video or audio. The practice is therefore human and relational: Spanish- and Mandarin-speaking caregivers, relatives, nannies or playgroups, with consistent time in each language.
objectives: Arrange regular live exposure to native speakers of Spanish and of Mandarin, ideally several hours a week each, through a nanny, grandparent, au pair, playgroup or Saturday school
Use a consistent pattern (one-person-one-language, or set times and places for each language)
Caregivers sing lullabies and nursery rhymes and read picture books in their own language
Recorded songs support live exposure and do not replace it
By age 3 the child understands everyday commands and songs in both languages and begins to answer in them

sources.label: Kuhl, Tsao & Liu, PNAS 2003: Foreign-language experience in infancy
Harvard Center on the Developing Child: Serve and Return

rows.historicalPrecedent: Quintilian (I.1.12–14) advised that a Roman boy begin with Greek, heard from nurses and slaves, while Latin followed at home. Bilingual rearing by ear was the norm for the educated classes of antiquity. Montaigne was raised speaking only Latin with his tutors until age six.
rows.notes: Headland's collection gives English translations of Chinese nursery rhymes and is useful for parents. The caregiver should supply the Mandarin originals by ear. If native-speaker caregivers cannot be arranged, expect a slower start, and note it as a gap for the spanish and chinese tracks.

rows.title: Family Prayer from the Cradle
rows.summary: Faith is first caught and then taught. The child is carried to Sunday worship, blessed at bedtime, and hears grace at every meal and short prayers morning and night. By three the child makes the sign of the cross, folds hands, joins in the Our Father and a simple grace, and knows that the family prays together.
objectives: Bless the child at bedtime; sing a short hymn or Marian antiphon (for example the Salve Regina) as a lullaby
Keep grace before meals and short morning and night prayers every day, with the child present
Bring the child to Sunday Mass or worship every week from infancy
Set up a prayer corner at child height with a crucifix or cross, an icon or picture, and a candle for family prayer
By age 3 the child knows the Sign of the Cross, a simple grace, and the first lines of the Our Father and Hail Mary

coreTexts.title: Divine Songs Attempted in Easy Language for the Use of Children
coreTexts.author: Isaac Watts

curriculumOptions.name: Devotional Stories for Little Folks
curriculumOptions.notes: Short Catholic read-aloud stories for bedtime prayer.

curriculumOptions.name: The Jesus Storybook Bible (Sally Lloyd-Jones)
curriculumOptions.notes: Widely used evangelical story Bible for toddlers and preschoolers.

rows.notes: Catholic and Protestant note: Catholic families add Marian prayers, the Sign of the Cross and sacramentals (holy water, blessed candles), and bring infants to Mass. Many Protestant families keep "family worship" (Scripture, a psalm or hymn, and prayer). Both traditions agree on daily family prayer and weekly worship.

rows.title: Screens I: No Screens Before Two
rows.summary: Under two, children learn language and attention from people and real objects, not screens. The AAP discourages all screen media before 18 months except video-chatting with family, and the WHO recommends no sedentary screen time before age 2. This program adopts the stricter standard: no television, tablets or phones for the child before age 2, with video calls to grandparents as the one exception.
objectives: No television, tablet or phone viewing by the child before age 2, apart from live video chat with relatives
No background television. Adults keep phones away during feeding, play and reading
Replace screens with books, blocks, songs, outdoor time and conversation

sources.label: AAP Policy (2016, reaffirmed 2022): Media and Young Minds
WHO Guidelines for Children under 5 (2019)
Kuhl et al., PNAS 2003 (no language learning from video)

rows.title: Toddler Language: Rhymes, Finger Plays and Dialogic Reading
rows.summary: Toddlers' vocabularies explode when adults talk with them rather than at them. Use dialogic reading: ask the child to name, point, complete the rhyme and tell what happens next, then expand the child's words into full sentences. Add finger plays, action rhymes and short memorized verses. Expect the two-word phrases of age 2 to become the full sentences and short narratives of age 3.
objectives: Read aloud together at least 20–30 minutes a day, across several short sessions
Use dialogic reading prompts: completion ('Humpty Dumpty sat on a ___'), 'what' and 'where' questions, recall, and expansion
Memorize 20 or more nursery rhymes and finger plays by age 3
Introduce the first simple story picture books (Beatrix Potter) and illustrated word books
Check CDC milestones at 15, 18, 24 and 30 months, since language delay is the most common early concern

coreTexts.title: Orbis Pictus (The Visible World in Pictures)
coreTexts.author: Johann Amos Comenius

sources.label: CDC: Milestones by 2 Years
AAP Policy (2024): Literacy Promotion

rows.historicalPrecedent: Comenius's Orbis Pictus (1658), the first illustrated textbook for children, taught vocabulary by naming pictured objects in Latin and the vernacular, which is essentially the toddler word book. It was used in schools across Europe and colonial America for two centuries.

rows.title: Walking, Climbing and Outdoor Play
rows.summary: Once walking, children need at least three hours a day of physical activity of any intensity (WHO), much of it outdoors and self-directed: walking, climbing, carrying, running, digging and throwing. Locke's "hardiness" means plenty of fresh air, simple clothing, and permission to get cold, wet and dirty. It is still good advice.
objectives: 180 minutes or more of varied physical activity daily, spread through the day (WHO, ages 1–4)
Daily outdoor play in all but dangerous weather, dressed for the conditions
Walk rather than ride in a stroller when practical, lengthening walks gradually
Offer climbing, balancing and throwing challenges: low walls, logs, stairs, balls, a balance bike by age 2–3
Begin water familiarization with a parent (splashing, pouring, supported floating), and plan swim lessons from age 1 (AAP)

sources.label: WHO Guidelines for Children under 5 (2019)
AAP: Drowning Prevention and Water Safety
Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education §§5–10 (Archive.org)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (§9): children should "be much in the open air, and as little as may be by the fire, even in winter," and (§8) should learn to swim when of age. The Romans, he notes, ranked swimming with letters.

rows.title: Singing, Rhythm and Chant in the Home
rows.summary: Singing to and with children, keeping a steady beat, and moving to music build the ear, the voice and the child's sense of timing, which carries over into speech. Zhao and Kuhl (2016) found that 9-month-olds given a short course of social music play (waltz meter) showed stronger brain responses to timing in both music and speech. Keep an unaccompanied, in-tune adult voice at the center, with folk songs, hymns, chant and a few percussion instruments.
objectives: Sing to the child every day, unaccompanied, with a repertoire of folk songs, lullabies, hymns and simple chant
Bounce, clap, march and dance to steady beats in duple and triple meter
Give the child simple instruments: drum, rhythm sticks, shakers, a glockenspiel
By 4, the child sings short songs in tune within a small range and keeps a steady beat with the hands and feet
Include Spanish and Mandarin children's songs with the caregivers of those languages

curriculumOptions.name: Music Together (mixed-age family classes, 0–5)
curriculumOptions.notes: Research-informed parent-and-child classes; a good weekly anchor if one is local.

curriculumOptions.name: Kodály-inspired early childhood music (OAKE)
curriculumOptions.notes: Folk-song-first, singing-based approach that leads into the music track's formal Kodály/Ward sequence.

sources.label: Zhao & Kuhl, PNAS 2016: Musical intervention enhances infants' neural processing

rows.title: Toddler and Preschool Sleep, Meals and Daily Rhythm
rows.summary: Adequate sleep is associated with better attention, behavior, learning, memory and emotional regulation. Children 1–2 need 11–14 hours per 24 hours and children 3–5 need 10–13 hours (AASM, AAP-endorsed). Pair a fixed bedtime with shared family meals of whole foods, few added sugars and no ultra-processed snacks. A predictable daily rhythm is itself a form of habit training.
objectives: Sleep: 11–14 h (ages 1–2), 10–13 h (ages 3–5), 9–12 h (ages 6–12), including naps. Keep a consistent early bedtime and no screens in the hour before bed
Eat family meals together at the table at set times, with conversation and grace
Serve whole foods and full-fat dairy for toddlers, and avoid added sugars and ultra-processed foods (DGA 2025–2030)
The child helps set the table, pour, serve and clear, which is also practical-life training

sources.label: AASM Consensus: Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations
WHO Guidelines for Children under 5 (sleep recommendations)
Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 (ODPHP)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke's health regimen (§30) is "plenty of open air, exercise, and sleep, plain diet, no wine or strong drink, and very little or no physic." Charlotte Mason likewise gives the first part of Home Education to fresh air, food, sleep and regularity.

rows.title: Habit Training: Obedience, Order, Attention and Self-Control
rows.summary: Charlotte Mason called habit "ten natures," and Locke held that children learn by "indispensable practice," not rules. Train one habit at a time, gently and consistently, until it is automatic: prompt obedience, tidiness, attention, truthfulness, courtesy and waiting. The Dunedin study (Moffitt et al., 2011) found that childhood self-control predicted adult health, wealth and freedom from crime across the whole range of ability and background. Self-control is trainable, and play-based programs such as Tools of the Mind build it deliberately.
objectives: Work on one habit at a time for 4–6 weeks (for example, putting toys away, coming when called the first time), with calm consistency and no nagging
Build attention: short, complete tasks; narration (telling back a story just heard) begins around 5–6
Practice waiting and turn-taking through games (Simon Says, freeze-dance, board games)
Tell the truth always, and never reward a lie. Keep promises made to the child
Give real chores suited to age (sorting laundry, feeding pets, carrying groceries)

curriculumOptions.name: Tools of the Mind
curriculumOptions.notes: Vygotskian preschool/K program built around mature make-believe play and self-regulation. Adapt its games at home.

sources.label: Moffitt et al., PNAS 2011: Childhood self-control predicts health, wealth, and public safety

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke §66: "Children are not to be taught by rules... What you think necessary for them to do, settle in them by an indispensable practice." §67: manners are "rather to be learnt by example than rules."

rows.title: Practical Life and Fine Motor Skill
rows.summary: Montessori's "practical life" work (pouring, spooning, buttoning, sweeping, food preparation) builds concentration, independence and the hand control later needed for writing and drawing. Pair it with crayons, scissors, clay, bead-stringing, puzzles and blocks.
objectives: Child-sized tools for real work (pitcher, broom, cloth, butter knife) and time allowed to finish tasks without interruption
Dressing independently (buttons, zips, shoes) by 4–5
Fine motor progression: scribbling, then circles and crosses, then a tripod grasp and drawing people, then copying letters (5–6)
Daily construction play (unit blocks, puzzles), plus clay, scissors and paste

sources.label: CDC: Milestones by 3 Years

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (§§204–206) recommended gardening and woodworking as healthy recreations even for a gentleman's son, citing the ancients who "reconcile[d] manual labour with affairs of state."

rows.title: Early Numeracy Through Play
rows.summary: Number sense grows from everyday counting, comparing, sorting, patterning and games. Siegler and Ramani (2008) showed that four short sessions of a simple linear number board game (a 1–10 race game) eliminated the gap in number-line estimation between low- and middle-income preschoolers. Recognizing small quantities at a glance (subitizing) and grouping by five and ten prepare the child for formal arithmetic.
objectives: Count real things daily (stairs, spoons, steps), with one-to-one correspondence to 10 by 3–4 and to 20 or more by 5
Play linear number board games (Chutes and Ladders style), dice and dot-card games several times a week
Subitize quantities 1–5 and recognize 6–10 as "five and some more"
Sort, match, compare (more, less, same), measure with hands and cups, build patterns with blocks and beads
Use the language of shape and position (above, below, beside, between)

curriculumOptions.name: RightStart Mathematics Level A (2nd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Abacus- and game-based, strong on subitizing and grouping in fives. Use gently from about 5.

curriculumOptions.name: Junior Kindergarten (numbers strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: Two- or five-day plans for 4- and 5-year-olds that combine numbers, letters, prayer and read-alouds.

curriculumOptions.name: Singapore Math early-years materials
curriculumOptions.notes: Concrete, pictorial, abstract sequence. Early-years books lead into the mathematics track.

sources.label: Siegler & Ramani 2008: Playing linear numerical board games (PDF)

rows.title: Screens II: Limited, Co-Viewed and Purposeful (2–7)
rows.summary: After two, the AAP and WHO allow up to one hour a day of high-quality programming, watched together with a parent. Madigan et al. (2019) found that more screen time at 2 and 3 predicted poorer developmental screening scores a year or two later, and not the reverse. This program keeps entertainment screens well under the ceiling (a family film on weekends, video calls, occasional co-viewed nature or music programs) and keeps the rest of the day for play, books and people.
objectives: Write a family media plan: no screens in bedrooms, at meals or in the hour before bed
Keep entertainment screen time well under 1 hour a day, co-viewed and talked about
Do not use screens to pacify, reward or fill waiting time. Carry books and small toys instead
Parents model limits on their own phones

sources.label: AAP Policy: Media and Young Minds
AAP Family Media Plan (HealthyChildren.org)
Madigan et al., JAMA Pediatrics 2019: Screen time and developmental screening
WHO Guidelines for Children under 5 (2019)

rows.title: The Liturgical Year and the Catechesis of the Good Shepherd
rows.summary: From three, the child can live the Church year at home: Advent wreath and Jesse tree, Christmas crib, Lent, Holy Week and Easter, Marian feasts and name days, with the liturgical colors and the saints of the day. The Catechesis of the Good Shepherd (Cavalletti and Gobbi) is a Montessori-based atrium for ages 3–6 centered on the parable of the Good Shepherd, the Mass and the Holy Land. Godly Play is a Montessori-derived Protestant (Episcopal) alternative.
objectives: Keep the seasons at home, with colors, a prayer table, feast-day meals and saints' stories
Learn the Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be, grace and a morning offering by heart, with short Scripture verses and Psalm 23
Attend a Level I atrium (CGS) weekly if one is available, or set up a small home atrium
Hear the great Bible stories (Creation, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, the Nativity, the parables, the Passion and Resurrection)

curriculumOptions.name: Catechesis of the Good Shepherd (Level I atrium, ages 3–6)
curriculumOptions.notes: Parish-based Montessori catechesis. Parents can train as catechists.

curriculumOptions.name: The Religious Potential of the Child (Cavalletti), the CGS handbook for ages 3–6
curriculumOptions.notes: Read this before setting up a home atrium.

curriculumOptions.name: Godly Play
curriculumOptions.notes: Montessori-derived story-and-wonder method developed by an Episcopal priest (Jerome Berryman). Ecumenical in use.

rows.notes: Catholic and Protestant note: CGS is explicitly Catholic in its sacramental and Marian content, though it is used in some Anglican and Lutheran parishes. Godly Play is a Protestant adaptation that is lighter on sacraments. Families of either tradition can use the church year, Bible stories and memorized prayers.

rows.title: The Read-Aloud Canon: Fables, Fairy Tales, Verse and Nature Stories
rows.summary: Between three and six, read-alouds lengthen from picture books to chapter-length stories. Build a canon of old books with vivid language: Aesop, Grimm and Lang, Beatrix Potter, Stevenson's A Child's Garden of Verses, Burgess's animal stories, and the Hillsdale and AmblesideOnline preschool lists. The child should hear an hour or more a day, including one longer story told in installments.
objectives: Read aloud an hour or more daily, across sessions, including one ongoing chapter book from about age 4
Memorize and recite short poems (Stevenson, Mother Goose, psalms) and learn to say them clearly
The child retells (narrates) favorite stories and fables in order by 5–6
Know the core fables and fairy tales by name and moral (the Tortoise and the Hare, Cinderella, the Three Bears, and others)

coreTexts.title: The Burgess Animal Book for Children
coreTexts.author: Thornton W. Burgess

coreTexts.title: A Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales
coreTexts.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

curriculumOptions.name: AmblesideOnline Year 0 booklist
curriculumOptions.notes: Free Charlotte Mason read-aloud list for under-sixes. Christian, and widely used by Protestant and Catholic families.

curriculumOptions.name: Junior Kindergarten read-aloud program
curriculumOptions.notes: Weekly classic picture-book read-alouds with enrichment. Classical Christian.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (§156) recommends that the first book put in a child's hands be "some easy pleasant book," naming Aesop's Fables as the best, "which being stories apt to delight and entertain a child, may yet afford useful reflections to a grown man."

rows.title: Bilingual by Ear II: Songs, Stories and Play in Spanish and Mandarin
rows.summary: Keep up and deepen oral exposure. Native-speaker caregivers and playmates, picture books read aloud in each language, songs and rhymes, and games that require the child to speak. The aim by six is easy listening comprehension and conversational speech in both languages, so that formal reading and writing (Spanish at about 7, Chinese characters from about 7) builds on a spoken base.
objectives: Several hours a week of live interaction in each language (caregiver, playgroup, weekend language school, relatives)
A library of picture books in Spanish and in Mandarin, read aloud by fluent speakers
Sing 20 or more songs and rhymes in each language, and play games (store, cooking, hide-and-seek) conducted in them
Mandarin: hear and imitate the four tones through songs and rhymes. Pinyin and characters wait for the formal track
By 6, the child follows stories and holds simple conversations in both languages

curriculumOptions.name: Song School Spanish Book 1
curriculumOptions.notes: Chant- and song-based Spanish for early elementary. Use orally from about 5–6 as a bridge to the spanish track.

sources.label: Kuhl et al., PNAS 2003 (live vs. recorded exposure)

rows.notes: I could not verify a Mandarin early-childhood curriculum; the chinese-track agent should propose one. Audio and video are supplements. The research shows that live, social exposure drives early phonetic learning.

rows.title: Outdoor Hours, Nature Walks and Gross-Motor Skill
rows.summary: Charlotte Mason urged several hours a day out of doors for young children, and the WHO recommends at least three hours of activity a day for 3–4-year-olds, including an hour of energetic play. Go on daily walks and weekly nature rambles, learn to name local birds, trees and flowers, climb, run, ride a bike, and take swim lessons. This is the root of both the natural-science and physical-training tracks.
objectives: Three or more hours of activity daily, including 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous play (WHO, ages 3–4)
A weekly nature walk. By 6, name 20 or more local plants and animals and keep a simple picture nature notebook
Motor milestones: hop, skip, catch a bounced ball, pedal a bicycle, swim a short distance with support
Formal swim lessons (see physical-training-01) and supervised climbing, balancing and rough-and-tumble play

coreTexts.title: Home Education (Part II, Out-of-Door Life for the Children)
coreTexts.author: Charlotte M. Mason

sources.label: WHO Guidelines for Children under 5 (2019)
CDC: Milestones by 5 Years

rows.title: Readiness for Formal Schooling: Memory Work, Letters and Narration
rows.summary: This is the bridge into the formal curriculum. Quintilian argued against wasting the years before seven and said the child's memory is most retentive when young, but that early learning must be play and never drudgery. At 5–6 the child learns letter sounds and letter formation, recites memorized poems, prayers and catechism, narrates stories, counts past 100, and gets used to short daily "lessons" of 10–20 minutes. Formal reading, Latin and Spanish/Chinese literacy begin at 6–7 in their own tracks.
objectives: Knows all letter sounds, blends simple words, and forms letters with a correct pencil grip (hand-off to reading-phonics)
Recites 20 or more poems, the basic prayers, and short catechism answers from memory
Narrates a fable or story of several paragraphs in sequence after one hearing
Counts to 100, subitizes to 10, adds and subtracts within 10 with objects
Sits for short, complete lessons with full attention, and does chores independently

curriculumOptions.name: Junior Kindergarten and Kindergarten curriculum
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical Christian. Includes letters, numbers, prayer, recitation and read-alouds.

curriculumOptions.name: Kindergarten Enrichment (3rd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Read-aloud, art-card and poetry enrichment for 5–6-year-olds.

curriculumOptions.name: AmblesideOnline Year 0 (Charlotte Mason: no formal academics before 6)
curriculumOptions.notes: The gentler alternative. Delay formal lessons to 6 and keep to read-alouds, nature and habits.

coreTexts.title: McGuffey's Eclectic Primer and First Reader
coreTexts.author: William Holmes McGuffey

rows.historicalPrecedent: Quintilian I.1.15–20: some held that children should not learn letters before seven, but Quintilian (following Chrysippus) wanted no age to be idle, provided early learning is "an amusement." McGuffey's Primer and First Reader were the standard American entry into reading for five- and six-year-olds through the 19th century.

sources.label: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria Book I ch. 1–3 (LacusCurtius)

rows.notes: Start (family decision): gentle formal lessons begin at 5, meaning short daily phonics and number work in the Quintilian and Memoria Press manner. Full formal schooling begins at 6–7. There is a real disagreement to settle here. Quintilian and Memoria Press begin gentle formal lessons at 4–5, while Charlotte Mason and the Montessori tradition delay formal academics to about 6. For an accelerated program, gentle formal lessons from 5 with strict time limits fit best.

rows.title: Money Basics: Earning, Saving, Giving and Spending
rows.summary: Children form their basic money habits early, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Money as You Grow guide sets out age-appropriate milestones from age 3. Use real coins and three jars (Give, Save, Spend) with a small allowance or pay for extra jobs beyond ordinary family chores. Let the child tithe to the parish, save toward a wanted item, and make small spending choices that he can regret and learn from.
objectives: Name and count coins and bills and make change in play-store games
Divide money among Give, Save and Spend jars and explain why
Save for several weeks toward a chosen purchase (delayed gratification)
Understand that money comes from work and that things cost money

curriculumOptions.name: Money as You Grow (free parent guide by age band)
curriculumOptions.notes: Age-by-age milestones and activities; evidence-based and free.

sources.label: CFPB: Money as You Grow

rows.notes: Many Catholic and Protestant families teach the tithe (a tenth given first) from the start. Catholic practice speaks more broadly of supporting the Church "according to one's means." Either can be practiced with the Give jar.

rows.title: First Enterprise: The Lemonade Stand and Franklin's Way to Wealth
rows.summary: The child runs a real small business: a lemonade stand, a bake sale, eggs from the family hens, or a lawn service. He borrows start-up money from a parent at interest, buys supplies, sets a price, keeps a simple ledger, repays the loan and counts the profit. Alongside, he memorizes and discusses Poor Richard's maxims from Franklin's The Way to Wealth (1758) on industry, frugality and debt.
objectives: Plan, run and close out a small business with a written ledger of costs, revenue and profit
Explain costs, revenue, profit, loss, and interest on a loan in simple terms
Memorize ten Poor Richard maxims and apply them to real choices
Give a tithe or share of the profits and save the rest toward a goal

coreTexts.title: The Way to Wealth; or, Poor Richard Improved
coreTexts.author: Benjamin Franklin

curriculumOptions.name: Lemonade Day (free youth entrepreneurship program)
curriculumOptions.notes: A structured program that walks a child through budgeting, a loan and running a stand.

curriculumOptions.name: The Tuttle Twins books (e.g. The Miraculous Pencil)
curriculumOptions.notes: Picture-book introductions to free-market ideas (from Leonard Read, Bastiat and Hazlitt) for 5–11-year-olds.

curriculumOptions.name: Junior Achievement elementary programs
curriculumOptions.notes: Offered through schools and some homeschool groups; availability varies locally.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin wrote The Way to Wealth (1758) as the preface to the last Poor Richard's Almanack, gathering twenty-five years of maxims into one speech. It became one of the most reprinted American writings of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

rows.title: Whatever Happened to Penny Candy? Money, Inflation and the Business Cycle
rows.summary: Richard Maybury's "Uncle Eric" letters explain money, the dollar's history, inflation, interest rates and the business cycle in plain language, with examples from ancient Rome to the present. The student keeps a price journal (for example, the price of candy, gas and bread over the year) and compares prices today with those in old newspapers and catalogs.
objectives: Explain what money is and how commodity money differs from fiat money
Define inflation and explain why rising prices can come from an expanding money supply
Describe the boom-and-bust cycle in Maybury's terms
Keep a year-long price journal and graph the results

curriculumOptions.name: Whatever Happened to Penny Candy? with Study Guide
curriculumOptions.notes: The companion study guide adds questions and activities; Maybury writes from a libertarian, pro-sound-money standpoint.

rows.notes: Maybury's views on money and the Federal Reserve are those of the Austrian school. The later rows (economics-08 and -09) set them beside Keynesian and mainstream views.

rows.title: The Economic Way of Thinking: Bastiat and Hazlitt
rows.summary: Bastiat's "What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen" (the broken-window fallacy) and The Law (1850), and Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946), teach one lesson in many forms: judge a policy by its effects on all groups and over the long run, not only on one group now. The student learns scarcity, opportunity cost, supply and demand, prices as signals, comparative advantage, and the unintended consequences of price controls, tariffs, subsidies and minimum wages. A Christian economics course runs alongside.
objectives: Explain the broken-window fallacy and find a present-day example
Draw and explain supply and demand curves and the effect of a price ceiling
Define opportunity cost and comparative advantage with worked examples
Summarize Bastiat's argument in The Law about "legal plunder"
Write a short "seen and unseen" analysis of a current policy proposal

coreTexts.title: What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen (in Selected Essays on Political Economy)
coreTexts.author: Frédéric Bastiat

curriculumOptions.name: TAN Academy: An Introduction to Economics
curriculumOptions.notes: A video course with a workbook from a Catholic publisher.

curriculumOptions.name: Economics for Everybody (R. C. Sproul Jr.)
curriculumOptions.notes: A video course from a Reformed Protestant perspective; also sold by Roman Roads Press.

curriculumOptions.name: The Economics of Freedom (Bastiat essays, free)

rows.title: Personal Finance, Bookkeeping and Investing Basics
rows.summary: The household's economics. The course covers budgeting, a checking account, compound interest, credit and debt, insurance, taxes, and the difference between saving, investing and speculating. It introduces index funds, stocks and bonds, and a simulated portfolio. The student keeps his own books in double entry (see practical-arts-12), files a practice tax return, and reads Bogle's case for low-cost index investing. Graham's Intelligent Investor follows at the end of high school.
objectives: Build and live on a monthly budget for a real income (allowance, job or business)
Calculate compound interest and the true cost of a loan or credit-card balance
Explain stocks, bonds, index funds, diversification and risk
Run a paper portfolio for a year and write an evaluation
Read a simple balance sheet and income statement

coreTexts.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (10th Anniversary Ed.)
coreTexts.author: John C. Bogle

curriculumOptions.name: Personal Management Merit Badge
curriculumOptions.notes: A good checklist of budgeting, saving and investing tasks even outside a troop.

rows.notes: This row teaches general financial literacy. It is not individualized investment advice; families should consult a qualified advisor for real decisions.

rows.title: Adam Smith: The Theory of Moral Sentiments and The Wealth of Nations
rows.summary: Smith was a moral philosopher before he was an economist. The student first reads selections from The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) on sympathy, the impartial spectator and virtue. He then reads the heart of The Wealth of Nations (1776): the division of labor (the pin factory), the "invisible hand," natural price and market price, the mercantile system, and the duties of the sovereign (defense, justice, public works, education). Smith is read as the founders read him, in the year they declared independence.
objectives: Explain the division of labor and why it depends on the extent of the market
Summarize Smith's critique of mercantilism and his case for free trade
Explain the impartial spectator and the relation between self-interest and sympathy in Smith
Identify the three duties of the sovereign in Book V and Smith's limits on the market

coreTexts.title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
coreTexts.author: Adam Smith

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson wrote to his son-in-law in 1790: "In political oeconomy I think Smith's wealth of nations the best book extant." In the same letter he recommends Locke, Montesquieu (with cautions) and The Federalist for the science of government.

sources.label: Jefferson to Thomas Mann Randolph Jr., 30 May 1790 (Founders Online)

rows.title: Catholic Social Teaching on the Economy and Distributism
rows.summary: The Church's social encyclicals judge every economic system by the dignity of the person and the good of the family. Rerum Novarum (1891) covers private property, the just wage, workers' associations, and the rejection of socialism. Quadragesimo Anno (1931) covers subsidiarity and social justice. Centesimus Annus (1991) weighs the market economy after communism. Belloc's The Servile State and Chesterton's The Outline of Sanity argue for distributism, a society of widely held property: small farms, shops and family firms.
objectives: State Leo XIII's teaching on private property, the just wage and the rights of association
Define subsidiarity, solidarity and the universal destination of goods
Summarize Belloc's argument that capitalism and socialism both tend toward a "servile state"
Summarize John Paul II's qualified endorsement of the "business economy" and "free economy" in Centesimus Annus §42
Write an essay comparing distributism with the free-market arguments of Smith and Hayek

curriculumOptions.name: Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church (free)
curriculumOptions.publisher: Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace
curriculumOptions.notes: The official synthesis; use chapters 4 (principles) and 7 (economic life) as the reference text.

curriculumOptions.name: TAN Academy: An Introduction to Economics

rows.notes: A Catholic/Protestant note. Protestant readers approach the same questions through the Reformed idea of vocation and "sphere sovereignty" (Kuyper, Lectures on Calvinism) and Weber's thesis on the Protestant ethic. The Catholic encyclicals are more explicit about the just wage and the state's subsidiary role. Catholic thinkers themselves disagree about how far Centesimus Annus endorses market economies versus distributism.

rows.title: Classical Political Economy and Its Critics: Say, Ricardo, Mill and Marx
rows.summary: The nineteenth-century debate that shaped modern politics. Say's Treatise gives his "law of markets"; Jefferson recommended it alongside Smith as shorter and clearer. Ricardo's Principles gives comparative advantage, rent, and the labor theory of value. Mill's Principles of Political Economy is the Victorian synthesis, with its distinction between the laws of production and the laws of distribution. Marx's Communist Manifesto and selections from Capital are read critically as the great challenge to the whole tradition, and his errors about value, class and history are traced to their historical consequences.
objectives: State Say's law and Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage with a numerical example
Explain the labor theory of value and why the marginal revolution replaced it
Summarize Mill on production versus distribution and on the stationary state
Explain Marx's theory of surplus value and class struggle and give the main economic and moral objections to it

coreTexts.title: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation
coreTexts.author: David Ricardo

coreTexts.title: The Marx-Engels Reader (2nd ed.)
coreTexts.author: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels; Robert C. Tucker (ed.)

coreTexts.title: The National System of Political Economy
coreTexts.author: Friedrich List (trans. Sampson S. Lloyd)

curriculumOptions.name: Marxism, Socialism, and Communism (free online course)

rows.historicalPrecedent: In 1819, at thirteen, John Stuart Mill was taken by his father through "a complete course of political economy," with Ricardo's newly published Principles read and summarized on their daily walks. Mill describes it in his Autobiography, the classic account of an accelerated classical education. Jefferson wrote to John Norvell in 1807 that Smith's Wealth of Nations is the best book "unless Say's Political economy can be had, which treats the same subjects on the same principles, but in a shorter compass & more lucid manner."

sources.label: J. S. Mill, Autobiography (Project Gutenberg)
Jefferson to John Norvell, 11 June 1807 (Founders Online)
Hamilton, Final Version of the Report on the Subject of Manufactures, 5 December 1791 (Founders Online)

rows.notes: Three critics of the free-trade market are read against Smith and Ricardo. Friedrich List lived in Pennsylvania from 1825 to about 1832, wrote Outlines of American Political Economy (1827) for the American protectionists, and drew on Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) and the "American School" (Daniel Raymond, Mathew Carey, and Henry Clay's American System). His National System argues for protecting infant industries until a nation can compete, and should be read beside Hamilton's Report (linked under sources) as the founders' own alternative to laissez-faire. Marx is read critically through Tucker's Marx-Engels Reader, which contains the Manifesto and the key selections from Capital and can replace the separate texts above. Kropotkin's Conquest of Bread is an elective statement of anarchist communism, read as a critic of both the market and the state; the student should test its picture of voluntary cooperation against Aristotle on property (Politics II) and Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum (economics-07).

rows.title: Twentieth-Century Economics: Hayek, Röpke and Sowell
rows.summary: This course reads the twentieth-century arguments about planning, knowledge and the humane economy. Hayek's "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945) argues that prices convey dispersed knowledge no planner can gather, and The Road to Serfdom (1944) argues that central planning leads to tyranny. Röpke's A Humane Economy (1960) is the German ordoliberal and Christian case for a market "beyond supply and demand," rooted in family, property and community. Sowell's Basic Economics serves as a comprehensive, jargon-free reference. Keynes's ideas are presented fairly through the course lectures and the college principles course.
objectives: Explain Hayek's knowledge problem and its bearing on central planning
Summarize the argument of The Road to Serfdom and its reception
Explain Röpke's claim that the market depends on moral and social preconditions it cannot produce itself
Use Sowell's framework to analyze three current policy debates (housing, minimum wage, trade)

coreTexts.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
coreTexts.author: F. A. Hayek

coreTexts.title: The Road to Serfdom: Text and Documents, The Definitive Edition
coreTexts.author: F. A. Hayek

coreTexts.title: Basic Economics: A Common Sense Guide to the Economy
coreTexts.author: Thomas Sowell

curriculumOptions.name: Economics 101: The Principles of Free Market Economics (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Ten lectures by Gary Wolfram and Larry Arnn; covers Hayek's knowledge problem and Keynes.

rows.title: College Principles of Microeconomics and Macroeconomics
rows.summary: A college-level principles sequence, with calculus where helpful. Microeconomics covers consumer and producer theory, market structures, externalities, public goods and game theory. Macroeconomics covers national accounts, money and banking, the Federal Reserve, growth, unemployment and inflation, and fiscal and monetary policy, with Keynesian, monetarist and Austrian views presented fairly. Investing matures with Graham's The Intelligent Investor. The capstone is a policy paper that uses real data.
objectives: Solve standard micro problems (elasticity, consumer surplus, profit maximization, monopoly pricing)
Explain GDP, the money multiplier, and how the Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy
Compare Keynesian, monetarist and Austrian accounts of the business cycle
Apply Graham's margin-of-safety principle to evaluate a company's financial statements
Write a data-driven policy paper of 3,000 words

curriculumOptions.name: Principles of Microeconomics (free video course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok's rigorous, free principles course.

curriculumOptions.name: Economics 101 and Understanding Capitalism (free online courses)

rows.notes: A student who wants college credit can take CLEP Principles of Microeconomics and Macroeconomics after this course.

rows.title: Picture Study and First Drawing
rows.summary: This is Charlotte Mason's "picture study": look at one great painting at a time, closely and in silence, then describe it from memory. Six works by one artist each term, so the child comes to know Giotto, Fra Angelico, Raphael, Rembrandt, Millet and others as friends. Alongside this, daily free drawing and a first structured method for seeing basic shapes.
objectives: Study 18 or more masterworks a year (six per artist per term) and narrate each from memory
Recognize the works studied by title and artist
Draw daily from observation and imagination, using the five basic "elements of shape" (dot, circle, straight, curved and angle lines)
Handle crayons, colored pencils and watercolor crayons with control

curriculumOptions.name: Art Cards and Posters (by grade)
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded sets of masterwork prints for picture study.

curriculumOptions.name: Drawing with Children (Mona Brookes)
curriculumOptions.notes: The Monart method: shape-based observational drawing for 4-year-olds up to adults.

curriculumOptions.name: ARTistic Pursuits
curriculumOptions.notes: Christian homeschool art program combining art history, technique and picture study by grade.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Charlotte Mason's PNEU schools (from 1891) made picture study a weekly subject from age six. Comenius's Orbis Pictus (1658) had already made pictures the child's first textbook.

sources.label: Mason, Home Education (Project Gutenberg)

rows.title: Nature Journaling
rows.summary: The nature journal joins art and science. The student looks closely, draws what is actually there, labels it, and records date, place and weather. Weekly outings (Charlotte Mason's "nature walk") give subjects: leaves, birds, insects, clouds, seasonal change. The journal becomes a record of observation over years and trains the patience and accuracy needed for the drawing courses later in this track.
objectives: Make a dated nature-journal entry at least weekly, with drawing, labels and notes (what I see, what I wonder, what it reminds me of)
Draw 100 or more local species over five years, with growing accuracy of proportion and detail
Use colored pencil and then watercolor for field sketches
Use the Handbook of Nature-Study to research each specimen

curriculumOptions.name: Keeping a Nature Journal (3rd ed.), Clare Walker Leslie
curriculumOptions.notes: The classic month-by-month guide for families.

curriculumOptions.name: The Laws Guide to Nature Drawing and Journaling (John Muir Laws)
curriculumOptions.notes: Excellent technique book on birds, plants, landscapes and field watercolor. Suited to 10 and up. Free videos at johnmuirlaws.com.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Comstock's Handbook (1911) grew from the Cornell nature-study movement, which put field observation and drawing into American schools. Jefferson's weather and garden books, and the Lewis and Clark journals, are founding-era models.

rows.title: Penmanship to Calligraphy
rows.summary: Handwriting is the most used fine art. After print and cursive are secure in the grammar track, the student develops a beautiful and fast hand. That means a practical italic or cursive for daily use, and then the historical scripts as calligraphy: Roman capitals, uncial, Carolingian minuscule, blackletter, the English round hand of Bickham's Universal Penman, and American Spencerian. Copywork from Scripture, poetry and the Rules of Civility joins this row to the character and literature tracks.
objectives: Write a fluent, legible cursive or italic hand at speed for everyday use by 10
Learn broad-edge calligraphy with 3 or more historical hands (Roman capitals, Carolingian, italic)
Learn pointed-pen copperplate or Spencerian from the historical copybooks
Letter and illuminate a finished piece (a psalm, poem or the Declaration's preamble)

curriculumOptions.name: Aesop Cursive Copybook Set (and other MP copybooks)
curriculumOptions.notes: Copybook practice with classic texts, the bridge from cursive to a finished hand.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin, Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania (1749): "All should be taught to write a fair Hand, and swift, as that is useful to All." Washington copied his Rules of Civility as penmanship practice. Spencerian script was the standard American hand from about 1850 to 1925.

sources.label: Franklin, Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania (1749), Penn Archives

rows.notes: I could not verify a Getty-Dubay italic (Portland State) purchase link; it is a widely used italic option worth checking by hand.

rows.title: Drawing Fundamentals: Seeing, Line, Proportion and Value
rows.summary: This is systematic observational drawing: contour and blind-contour, negative space, sighting and measuring proportion, light and shadow (value), and texture. Betty Edwards's exercises teach students to draw what they see rather than what they "know," and Ruskin's Elements of Drawing (written as letters to beginners) trains patient, faithful looking.
objectives: Complete the core exercises of Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain (contour, negative space, sighting, value, self-portrait)
Work through Ruskin's first letter exercises (graded tones, shading a stone, drawing leaves and branches)
Draw still life, interiors and portraits from life with correct proportion and a full value range
Keep a sketchbook with daily drawing

coreTexts.title: The Elements of Drawing, in Three Letters to Beginners
coreTexts.author: John Ruskin

coreTexts.title: Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain (4th ed.)
coreTexts.author: Betty Edwards

curriculumOptions.name: Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain (Edwards)
curriculumOptions.notes: Best-selling observational drawing course. Its brain-hemisphere theory is dated, but the exercises work.

curriculumOptions.name: Creating Art
curriculumOptions.notes: Color theory, basic technique and early art history, with quizzes.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (Thoughts §161): once a boy writes well, he should "improve the use of it farther in drawing; a thing very useful to a gentleman in several occasions, but especially if he travel."

sources.label: Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education §161 (Archive.org)

rows.title: Watercolor and Color
rows.summary: Watercolor is portable, cheap and demanding, the traditional medium of travelers, naturalists and architects. The student learns washes, wet-in-wet, glazing, color mixing from a limited palette, and the color wheel, then paints landscapes and botanical studies from life. Ruskin's third letter, on color and composition, and Cennini's medieval handbook give the historical grounding.
objectives: Lay flat and graded washes and use wet-in-wet and glazing deliberately
Mix any observed color from a limited palette of three primaries plus earth colors
Complete 20 or more finished studies from life (landscape, botanical, architectural)
Read Ruskin's Letter III and selections of Cennini on pigments and procedure

coreTexts.title: The Elements of Drawing (Letter III, On Colour and Composition)
coreTexts.author: John Ruskin

coreTexts.title: The Book of the Art of Cennino Cennini (trans. Christiana Herringham)
coreTexts.author: Cennino Cennini

curriculumOptions.name: The Laws Guide to Nature Drawing and Journaling (watercolor chapters)
curriculumOptions.notes: Field watercolor technique, continuing the nature-journal strand.

curriculumOptions.name: ARTistic Pursuits (upper-grade books)
curriculumOptions.notes: Christian publisher. Graded media instruction including watercolor.

rows.title: Perspective and the Geometry of Seeing
rows.summary: Linear perspective, rediscovered by Brunelleschi and codified by Alberti and Leonardo, is geometry applied to seeing. The student learns one-, two- and three-point perspective, the horizon line and vanishing points, ellipses and cylinders, cast shadows and reflections, and then draws buildings and interiors from life. Read Leonardo's notes on perspective and light.
objectives: Construct one-, two- and three-point perspective drawings of boxes, rooms and streets
Draw circles in perspective (ellipses), arches and stairs correctly
Project cast shadows from sun and point light sources
Draw a building from life in accurate two-point perspective

coreTexts.title: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci (Part II, Linear Perspective; Part III, Light and Shade)
coreTexts.author: Leonardo da Vinci (trans. J. P. Richter)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin's 1749 Proposals called for "some of the first Principles of Perspective" alongside drawing "by Imitation of Prints."

sources.label: Franklin, Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania (1749)

rows.title: Sculpture and Modeling
rows.summary: Drawing is two-dimensional. Sculpture teaches the student to think in form and volume. Model in clay from life (reliefs, then heads and figures, following the academic method of Édouard Lanteri, who taught modeling in London), try carving in soap, wood or soft stone, and read Cellini's lively Autobiography for a Renaissance sculptor's world. Cast drawing later in the track builds on this work.
objectives: Model a relief (a leaf or rosette, then a copy of a classical relief) in clay
Model a portrait head from life at about half scale using Lanteri's measured method
Complete a small carving in wood or stone
Read Cellini's Autobiography (selections) and describe the lost-wax casting of the Perseus

coreTexts.title: Modelling: A Guide for Teachers and Students, Vol. I
coreTexts.author: Édouard Lanteri

coreTexts.title: The Autobiography of Benvenuto Cellini (trans. J. A. Symonds)
coreTexts.author: Benvenuto Cellini

rows.notes: Cellini's Autobiography contains violence and immoral episodes. Assign selections or read it at 14 or older.

rows.title: Art History I: Primary Sources, from Vasari to Ruskin
rows.summary: Study art history as the history track does history, from primary sources. Read Vasari's Lives (Giotto, Brunelleschi, Masaccio, Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo) as the founding text of the discipline, and Ruskin's Modern Painters and Stones of Venice as its great Victorian criticism. A good survey (Gombrich) supplies the chronology, and picture study continues at a more analytical level.
objectives: Read 10 or more of Vasari's Lives, including the prefaces, and explain Vasari's idea of the "rebirth" of the arts
Read selections of Ruskin (Modern Painters I on truth to nature, "The Nature of Gothic")
Place 100 or more major works in period, style and context, from ancient Greece to the 19th century
Write formal analyses of works seen in person at a museum

coreTexts.title: Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors and Architects, Vol. 1 (trans. de Vere)
coreTexts.author: Giorgio Vasari

curriculumOptions.name: A Classical History of Art
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical Christian survey with teacher guide and streaming lectures.

curriculumOptions.name: American Paintings (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free Hillsdale lecture course on American painting, tying art history to the history track.

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of Art (Gombrich)
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard one-volume narrative survey. Clear and humane.

rows.title: Architecture and the Classical Orders: Vitruvius and Palladio
rows.summary: Vitruvius's three requirements of good building (firmitas, utilitas, venustas: soundness, usefulness, beauty) and his account of the orders are the grammar of Western architecture. Learn to draw the Tuscan, Doric, Ionic, Corinthian and Composite orders from their modules. Read Palladio's Four Books, which Jefferson used to design Monticello and the University of Virginia, and study the classical buildings of the American founding (the Virginia Capitol, the U.S. Capitol, the White House).
objectives: Read Vitruvius Books I, III and IV and explain the orders, proportion and symmetry
Measure and draw the five orders in correct proportion from Palladio's plates
Analyze a Palladian villa and Jefferson's Monticello or Rotunda
Design and draw (plan, elevation, section) a small classical building

coreTexts.title: The Ten Books on Architecture (trans. M. H. Morgan)
coreTexts.author: Vitruvius

coreTexts.title: The Four Books of Architecture (Ware trans.)
coreTexts.author: Andrea Palladio

curriculumOptions.name: Institute of Classical Architecture & Art (courses and resources)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical drawing, orders and design courses (online and in person) for students and adults.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson owned several editions of Palladio (including Leoni's), modeled Monticello and the Rotunda on Palladian and Roman precedents, and based the Virginia State Capitol (1785–1788) on the Maison Carrée at Nîmes. Architecture was the one fine art he practiced seriously.

rows.title: Classical Drawing: The Bargue Plates and Cast Drawing
rows.summary: This is the academic method of the 19th-century ateliers. The student copies the Bargue lithographs (1866–1871) from outline to fully modeled value, then draws plaster casts of classical sculpture under controlled light, and finally the figure from life. This is the most rigorous training in accuracy and value available, and it is the foundation of today's atelier revival. Van Gogh taught himself from these plates.
objectives: Complete 10 or more Bargue plate copies at sight-size, from block-in to finished value
Complete 2 or more long cast drawings (for example a classical head or foot) in graphite or charcoal
Draw the figure from life in short and long poses if a supervised studio is available
Understand sight-size and comparative measurement methods

coreTexts.title: Exercices au fusain (Cours de dessin), 60 plates
coreTexts.author: Charles Bargue

curriculumOptions.name: Charles Bargue Drawing Course (ed. Gerald Ackerman)
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard modern reproduction of all 197 plates with commentary. The link is the publisher's home page, since I could not verify the product page.

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Drawing Atelier (Aristides)
curriculumOptions.notes: Atelier-method book with Bargue-style exercises and master drawings.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Bargue's Cours de dessin, produced with Jean-Léon Gérôme for Goupil & Cie (1866–1871), was used in French academies and ateliers. Van Gogh copied the whole set in 1880–1881 while teaching himself to draw.

rows.title: College: History of Art, Architecture and Sacred Art
rows.summary: A college survey and seminar on the Western tradition of art and architecture from the Parthenon to the 20th century, read through its own theorists and critics: Vitruvius, Vasari, Ruskin's Stones of Venice and The Two Paths, Cennini, and the Church's teaching on beauty and sacred art (John Paul II's Letter to Artists and Benedict XVI's address to artists in the Sistine Chapel). Museum study in person and a research paper complete it.
objectives: Trace architecture from the Greek temple through Roman, Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical to modernism, and argue its merits and losses
Read "The Nature of Gothic" (Stones of Venice II.6) and The Two Paths, and assess Ruskin's claim that art expresses a society's moral life
Read John Paul II's Letter to Artists and Benedict XVI's 2009 address on the "way of beauty"
Write a 3,000-word research paper on a building or artwork studied in person

coreTexts.title: Meeting with Artists in the Sistine Chapel
coreTexts.author: Pope Benedict XVI

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of Art (Gombrich), as the survey spine
curriculumOptions.notes: Pair with primary readings and museum visits.

curriculumOptions.name: A Classical History of Art (lectures)
curriculumOptions.notes: For review or if the high-school survey was skipped.

rows.notes: Catholic and Protestant note: Catholic teaching treats sacred images and beauty as a path to God (the via pulchritudinis), following the Second Council of Nicaea (787). The Reformed tradition was more cautious about images in worship, which is one reason Protestant architecture and painting took different forms, for example the Dutch Golden Age turn to landscape and genre painting. Both deserve study.

rows.title: Copywork & Penmanship
rows.summary: Daily, careful copying of short passages of Scripture, poetry and great prose, first in print and then in cursive. Copywork trains attention, spelling, punctuation and the feel of well-made sentences before the child is asked to compose.
objectives: Copy a 2–4 line passage daily with perfect accuracy and neat handwriting
Write fluent, legible cursive by about age 8
Notice and reproduce capitalization, punctuation and spelling in models

curriculumOptions.name: Copybook Cursive I–III (Scripture and poems)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical copybooks built on Scripture, poetry and proverbs.

curriculumOptions.name: Language of God, Level A (copywork and early language)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic early-grades language arts with copywork.

rows.historicalPrecedent: At about 14 to 16, George Washington copied the 110 "Rules of Civility & Decent Behaviour in Company and Conversation" into his school exercise book. This is the classic founding-era example of copywork as both penmanship and moral formation.

sources.label: Mount Vernon: The Rules of Civility

rows.title: Narration & Dictation
rows.summary: The child tells back in their own words what was read (oral narration, then written narration) and writes studied passages from dictation. Narration builds composition's raw material, ordered thought in sentences. Dictation fixes spelling and punctuation in memory.
objectives: Narrate a read-aloud passage orally in sequence, with detail, after one hearing
Write a 3–5 sentence narration independently by about age 8–9
Take dictation of a studied passage of 2–4 sentences without error

coreTexts.title: Home Education (Vol. 1), on narration and dictation
coreTexts.author: Charlotte M. Mason

curriculumOptions.name: Writing With Ease (Levels 1–4)
curriculumOptions.notes: Scripted narration and dictation from classic children's literature. The most turnkey option.

curriculumOptions.name: Language of God (Levels B–C)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic language arts with dictation and early composition. The link is Level A; later levels follow.

rows.title: First Grammar: Parts of Speech & the Sentence (Recitation)
rows.summary: The eight parts of speech, subject and predicate, the four kinds of sentences, capitalization and punctuation, learned by memorized definitions and oral recitation in grammar-stage style. This is coordinated with first Latin, which reinforces the same concepts.
objectives: Recite definitions of the eight parts of speech and identify them in sentences
Identify simple and complete subject and predicate
Punctuate declarative, interrogative, imperative and exclamatory sentences correctly

curriculumOptions.name: First Language Lessons for the Well-Trained Mind (Levels 1–4)
curriculumOptions.notes: Scripted oral lessons with poem memorization. Level 3–4 begins diagramming.

curriculumOptions.name: English Grammar Recitation I
curriculumOptions.notes: Catechism-style grammar recitation that repeats each year, tightly tied to Latin.

curriculumOptions.name: Well-Ordered Language (Level 1)
curriculumOptions.notes: Grammar through songs, chants and poetry, introducing diagramming gently.

rows.title: Grammar II: Systematic English Grammar (Shurley, Rod & Staff, Voyages)
rows.summary: A complete systematic grammar course: phrases and clauses, verb tenses and voice, pronoun case, agreement, and usage. Each lesson is applied immediately in short compositions. Choose one of three traditions.
objectives: Classify every word in a sentence by part of speech and function (parsing)
Identify phrases (prepositional, verbal) and clauses (independent, dependent)
Write a well-organized paragraph with a topic sentence and support

curriculumOptions.name: Shurley English (Levels 3–5)
curriculumOptions.notes: Question-and-answer "flow" chants for classifying sentences. Very effective for young children, though loud and repetitive.

curriculumOptions.name: Building Christian English (Grades 3–5)
curriculumOptions.notes: Mennonite, rigorous and thorough, with diagramming. Grades 6–8 books are near high-school level.

curriculumOptions.name: Voyages in English (Grades 3–5)
curriculumOptions.notes: Jesuit-published successor to the classic Catholic-school grammar series, with diagramming.

rows.title: Sentence Diagramming: Reed & Kellogg
rows.summary: Students learn the Reed–Kellogg diagram (1877), the visual syntax used in American schools for a century, from simple sentences through complex and compound-complex ones with verbals and clauses. Diagramming makes the logic of English sentences visible and prepares for Latin and Greek syntax.
objectives: Diagram simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences
Diagram participles, gerunds, infinitives, appositives and noun clauses
Diagram sentences from the Declaration and the Gettysburg Address

curriculumOptions.name: Well-Ordered Language (Levels 3–4)
curriculumOptions.notes: Modern classical program with full diagramming.

curriculumOptions.name: Building Christian English (Grades 6–7)
curriculumOptions.notes: Its diagramming is some of the most thorough available.

rows.title: Founding-Era Grammar: Lindley Murray & Harvey (Parsing, Syntax, Prosody)
rows.summary: The grammar the early Republic learned. Lindley Murray's English Grammar (1795), in its four parts (Orthography, Etymology, Syntax, Prosody), was the standard school grammar in America and Britain for half a century. It is paired with Harvey's English Grammar (1868), the McGuffey-era companion. Students parse sentences in full, correct false syntax, and learn punctuation and English prosody.
objectives: Parse any sentence fully in the 19th-century manner (part of speech, inflection, syntax rule)
Correct "false syntax" exercises by stating the violated rule
Master the rules of punctuation, and scan English verse (prosody)

coreTexts.title: English Grammar, Adapted to the Different Classes of Learners
coreTexts.author: Lindley Murray

curriculumOptions.name: English 7 for Young Catholics
curriculumOptions.notes: Traditional Catholic grammar and composition text to run alongside Murray.

curriculumOptions.name: Building Christian English (Grade 8)
curriculumOptions.notes: Completes grammar at a level that equals most high-school courses.

rows.historicalPrecedent: In his 1749 Proposals, Franklin asked that pupils be "taught the English Tongue by Grammar" and form their style on the best English authors. Murray's Grammar (first printed 1795) went through hundreds of American editions and became the grammar of the early-19th-century schoolroom.

sources.label: Franklin, Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania (1749), Penn Archives

rows.title: The Commonplace Book
rows.summary: A lifelong notebook of striking passages copied from one's reading and indexed by topic on John Locke's method. It is a store of quotations, arguments and models for writing and speaking, begun at 10 and kept through college. Jefferson's and Locke's own commonplace books are the models.
objectives: Keep a commonplace book with a Locke-style index, adding entries weekly from all subjects
Copy passages accurately with author, work and page
Use commonplace entries as material in essays and speeches

coreTexts.title: A New Method of Making Common-Place-Books
coreTexts.author: John Locke

coreTexts.title: Jefferson's Literary Commonplace Book
coreTexts.author: Thomas Jefferson, ed. Douglas L. Wilson

rows.historicalPrecedent: As a student and young lawyer (c. 1758–1772), Jefferson copied passages from Homer, Euripides, Cicero, Milton, Pope and Bolingbroke into his Literary Commonplace Book. It is the best surviving record of a Founder's self-education.

rows.title: Letter Writing on the Founders' Model
rows.summary: Students learn the forms of the letter (friendly, formal, business, condolence, thanks) and write real letters weekly by hand to grandparents, pen-pals, officials and authors. The models are the letters of the Founders and the classic letters of advice from father to son.
objectives: Write correctly formatted friendly, formal and business letters
Sustain a regular handwritten correspondence with at least one person for a year
Read and imitate letters of Adams, Jefferson and Franklin found on Founders Online

coreTexts.title: Letters to His Son
coreTexts.author: Philip Dormer Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield

coreTexts.title: Letter to Peter Carr, 10 August 1787 (a model letter of advice on education)
coreTexts.author: Thomas Jefferson

sources.label: Founders Online (National Archives)

rows.notes: Chesterfield's letters are brilliant on style and manners but worldly in morals. Johnson said they taught "the morals of a whore, and the manners of a dancing master." Read them selectively and discuss them.

rows.title: From Paragraph to Essay: Imitation & Franklin's Method
rows.summary: Students write multi-paragraph compositions by imitating model prose. Following Franklin, they take notes on an essay (the Spectator, Johnson, Lincoln), set it aside, rewrite it from the notes, and compare. Structured programs teach outlining, dress-ups of style, and the parts of the essay. The progymnasmata exercises run in parallel in the rhetoric track.
objectives: Outline a model essay and reconstruct it in their own words (Franklin's exercise)
Write a five-paragraph essay with thesis, ordered support and conclusion
Vary sentence openings and structures deliberately

coreTexts.title: Autobiography (Franklin on teaching himself to write from the Spectator)
coreTexts.author: Benjamin Franklin

curriculumOptions.name: The Lost Tools of Writing (Level I)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical invention, arrangement and elocution applied to the persuasive essay.

curriculumOptions.name: Structure and Style for Students
curriculumOptions.notes: Key-word outlines and stylistic techniques, taught by video. Very structured and effective for reluctant writers.

curriculumOptions.name: English 7 for Young Catholics (composition units)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic option that combines grammar review with composition.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin (Autobiography) took a volume of the Spectator, made short hints of each sentence, laid them by, and after some days tried to rewrite the papers "in any suitable words that should come to hand," then compared his version with the original and corrected his faults. He also turned the essays into verse and back to sharpen his vocabulary.

rows.title: Usage & Style I: Strunk and the Fowlers
rows.summary: Students learn the rules of plain, vigorous English: omit needless words, prefer the active voice and the concrete word, and avoid the common errors of usage. Revision becomes a habit through editing one's own and peers' essays against Strunk's rules and the Fowlers' examples.
objectives: Apply Strunk's elementary rules of usage and principles of composition in revision
Identify and correct common errors (dangling modifiers, faulty parallelism, vague pronouns)
Revise a draft to cut its length by a quarter without losing content

coreTexts.title: The King's English
coreTexts.author: H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler

rows.notes: The later Strunk & White editions (1959 onward) are copyrighted and widely available. The free 1918 text holds the core rules.

rows.title: The Essay: Expository & Persuasive Writing
rows.summary: Students write a full essay every week or two across genres (definition, comparison, cause and effect, literary analysis, and persuasion on a question of justice or policy), using classical invention (the topics) and the logic course's argument analysis. Timed essays prepare for exams.
objectives: Write 1,000–1,500-word expository and persuasive essays with a defensible thesis
Answer the strongest counter-argument fairly in every persuasive essay
Write a well-organized timed essay in 40 minutes

curriculumOptions.name: The Lost Tools of Writing (Levels II–III)
curriculumOptions.notes: Extends invention and arrangement into comparison, the judicial and the deliberative essay.

curriculumOptions.name: English Grammar & Composition (high-school course plan)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic classical homeschool course plan and tests for high-school composition.

curriculumOptions.name: Structure and Style for Students (Level C)
curriculumOptions.notes: High-school level of the IEW system, with essay models and critiques.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin's Proposals (1749) recommended that pupils write "Letters to each other, making Abstracts of what they read" and learn to express themselves "clearly, concisely, and naturally, without affected Words, or high-flown Phrases."

sources.label: Franklin, Proposals (1749), Archive.org

rows.title: The Research Paper
rows.summary: Students learn the research process: framing a question, finding and evaluating sources (especially primary sources), taking notes, outlining, drafting and documenting in Chicago style. They produce one substantial paper each year, for example on a founding-era question researched in Founders Online.
objectives: Formulate a research question and a working bibliography of primary and secondary sources
Write a 3,000–5,000-word research paper with Chicago/Turabian footnotes and bibliography
Defend the paper orally before a small panel

coreTexts.title: A Manual for Writers of Research Papers, Theses, and Dissertations (9th ed.)
coreTexts.author: Kate L. Turabian

curriculumOptions.name: They Say / I Say: The Moves That Matter in Academic Writing
curriculumOptions.notes: Short, practical guide to entering a scholarly conversation with templates for summarizing and responding to sources.

curriculumOptions.name: Founders Online (primary-source database)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free, searchable papers of Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Franklin, Hamilton, Madison and Jay, ideal for primary-source research.

rows.title: Usage & Style II: Fowler's Modern English Usage & Classic Prose
rows.summary: Advanced style. Students browse Fowler's Modern English Usage as a habit and study the sentence-level craft of clarity, cohesion, emphasis and concision (Williams). They learn the "classic style" of writers from Descartes to Jefferson (Thomas & Turner), and practise sustained imitation of masters such as Johnson, Burke, Lincoln and Newman.
objectives: Consult Fowler habitually and settle usage questions with reasons
Diagnose and revise prose for clarity, cohesion and emphasis (Williams's principles)
Write pastiches of three prose masters that a reader can recognize

coreTexts.title: A Dictionary of Modern English Usage (1st ed.)
coreTexts.author: H. W. Fowler

curriculumOptions.name: Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace (Joseph M. Williams & Joseph Bizup)
curriculumOptions.notes: The best modern treatment of sentence-level clarity, with graded exercises.

curriculumOptions.name: Clear and Simple as the Truth: Writing Classic Prose (Thomas & Turner)
curriculumOptions.notes: A philosophical account of "classic style" with many examples. Ideal for a strong 16-year-old.

rows.title: College Writing: Expository & Argumentative Prose; Politics and Language
rows.summary: A general-education college writing seminar. Students write sustained expository and argumentative essays across the disciplines (philosophy, history, science, law) under close editing, and study the ethics of language. Orwell's "Politics and the English Language" is the centerpiece, on how debased prose corrupts thought and is used to defend the indefensible.
objectives: Write argumentative essays of 2,500–5,000 words that meet college-seminar standards
Diagnose euphemism, jargon, and dead metaphor in political and academic prose (Orwell's six rules)
Produce a portfolio of revised essays, including one publishable op-ed and one scholarly paper

curriculumOptions.name: They Say / I Say (with readings)
curriculumOptions.notes: Standard college-composition text for argument with sources.

curriculumOptions.name: Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace
