curriculumOptions.notes: Continue the grammar-composition-13 exercises at college level.

curriculumOptions.name: The Lost Tools of Writing (advanced levels)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical option that keeps invention and arrangement rooted in the rhetorical tradition.

rows.title: Greek I: The Alphabet & First Words
rows.summary: A short, delightful first unit. The student learns to write and pronounce the 24 letters, diphthongs, breathings and accents, and reads and copies simple Koine words and verses (John 1:1, the Lord's Prayer). English derivatives link the new alphabet to words he already knows.
objectives: Write all 24 letters in upper and lower case in correct stroke order
Pronounce diphthongs, breathings and accents (choose Erasmian or restored Koine and stay consistent)
Read aloud John 1:1–5 and the Pater Noster in Greek
Transliterate Greek words and give 30+ English derivatives

curriculumOptions.name: The Greek Alphabet
curriculumOptions.notes: An 80-page letter-a-page workbook for grade 3 to adult. The fastest route.

curriculumOptions.name: Hey, Andrew! Teach Me Some Greek! (Levels 1–2)
curriculumOptions.notes: Gentle Biblical-Greek workbooks with an 8-level sequence that ends reading the Greek NT. Levels 1–2 are well below an accelerated 10-year-old, so move quickly.

curriculumOptions.name: Song School Greek
curriculumOptions.notes: Songs and games around Koine vocabulary. Leads into Greek for Children.

rows.historicalPrecedent: J. S. Mill began Greek at three (Autobiography). The English public schools and Boston Latin began Greek grammar after about three years of Latin. In 1789 Boston put "Greek Grammar" in the third of four classes, and in the 1880s Greek began in the Fourth Class alongside Caesar.

sources.label: J. S. Mill, Autobiography (Project Gutenberg)
Catalogue of the Boston Public Latin School (1886)

rows.notes: Sequence (family decision): Koine first (the Gospel of John), then Attic (Xenophon, Plato) and Homeric Greek.

rows.title: Greek II: Elementary Koine Greek
rows.summary: A first grammar in Koine Greek: the article, first and second declensions, present and future active verbs, and about 200 high-frequency New Testament words, with simple translation from the Gospels. The Latin background lets the student move faster than the book's stated grade level.
objectives: Decline the definite article and 1st/2nd-declension nouns and adjectives
Conjugate present, imperfect and future active indicative of ω-verbs and εἰμί
Translate simple Gospel sentences
Know the 200 most frequent NT words

curriculumOptions.name: Elementary Greek I–III (Christine Gatchell)
curriculumOptions.notes: Koine. Simple and substantial, and self-teachable for teens. Memoria's own path is Greek Alphabet, then Elementary Greek, then First Form Greek.

curriculumOptions.name: Greek for Children, Primer A
curriculumOptions.notes: Chant-based Koine with video and audio support.

curriculumOptions.name: Hey, Andrew! Teach Me Some Greek! (Levels 3–5)
curriculumOptions.notes: Continues the workbook series toward reading 1 John and the Gospels.

rows.title: Greek III: Full Grammar I (Attic or New Testament)
rows.summary: The first full grammar course. The family chooses the stream to lead with. The Attic stream uses Athenaze, a reading course set in 5th-century Athens, or First Form Greek (Memoria). The New Testament stream uses Machen's New Testament Greek for Beginners, the classic seminary grammar written by a Presbyterian scholar. Both streams cover the whole verb system in outline (aorist, perfect, middle and passive), the third declension, participles, and contract verbs.
objectives: Conjugate ω-verbs in all tenses and voices of the indicative, including first and second aorist
Decline 3rd-declension nouns and the participle
Translate connected adapted passages of 150–300 words
Build vocabulary to about 600 words (DCC Greek Core List)

curriculumOptions.name: Athenaze, Book I (3rd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: A reading-method Attic course. The story of the farmer Dikaiopolis gives way to adapted Herodotus and Thucydides in Book II. Widely used in high schools.

curriculumOptions.name: First Form Greek (and Second Form Greek)
curriculumOptions.notes: Grammar-first, in the same format as First Form Latin. Assumes two years of Latin, which this program provides.

curriculumOptions.name: New Testament Greek for Beginners (Machen)
curriculumOptions.notes: Terse and rigorous. It moves quickly to the Gospels and suits students who want the NT first. A free scan is on Archive.org.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Colonial schools taught Greek mainly through the Greek New Testament. Boston 1789 put "Greek Testament" in the top class, and Harvard 1642 required entrants to "decline perfectly the Paradigim's of Nounes and Verbes in the Greek tongue".

sources.label: New Englands First Fruits (1643)

rows.title: Greek IV: Full Grammar II (Intensive Attic)
rows.summary: Completion of classical Greek grammar: μι-verbs, the subjunctive and optative, conditions, indirect discourse, the uses of the participle, and the principal parts of the 100 most common irregular verbs. The texts are the rigorous college grammars. Crosby & Schaeffer was written for high-school Greek on the way to the Anabasis.
objectives: Conjugate μι-verbs and all moods including the optative
Classify and translate every type of condition and indirect discourse
Recite the principal parts of the 100 most important irregular verbs
Translate unadapted Xenophon with a vocabulary

coreTexts.title: An Introduction to Greek
coreTexts.author: H. Lamar Crosby & John N. Schaeffer

curriculumOptions.name: Greek: An Intensive Course (Hansen & Quinn)
curriculumOptions.notes: The most complete one-volume grammar, designed for the CUNY summer institute. Hard, but it leaves nothing out.

curriculumOptions.name: Athenaze, Book II
curriculumOptions.notes: Continues Book I into adapted Herodotus, Thucydides and Plato.

curriculumOptions.name: Crosby & Schaeffer, An Introduction to Greek
curriculumOptions.notes: Written for American high schools and built around the Anabasis vocabulary. Free.

rows.historicalPrecedent: White's First Greek Book (1896) and similar books prepared late-1800s American schoolboys to read "the first four books of Xenophon's Anabasis", which was then the standard college-entrance requirement in Greek.

rows.title: Koine Reading I: The Gospel of John
rows.summary: The easiest continuous Greek of real literary weight. The student reads John's Gospel through (with 1 John), using a reader's lexicon at first and then without. The simple syntax and small vocabulary build speed and confidence while he meets the Logos theology in its own words.
objectives: Read the whole Gospel of John in Greek
Read 1 John in Greek at sight by the end
Memorize John 1:1–14 in Greek
Compare three key verses in Greek, the Vulgate and the King James/Douay versions

curriculumOptions.name: A Graded Reader of Biblical Greek (Mounce)
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded NT passages with notes. A good bridge for self-study.

curriculumOptions.name: A Primer of Biblical Greek
curriculumOptions.notes: A Koine grammar and reader used in Memoria's upper sequence.

rows.historicalPrecedent: "Greek Testament" was the first Greek author in the Boston Latin School (1789) and at Harvard. New England's First Fruits describes students resolving the Greek Testament logically and grammatically.
rows.notes: Text-critical note: Protestants usually read the critical text (NA/UBS, SBLGNT) or the Textus Receptus behind the King James. Catholics use the same critical Greek text, and the Nova Vulgata was revised against it. The differences seldom matter at this level.

rows.title: Reference Grammars & Greek Prose Composition
rows.summary: The student learns to consult Goodwin (the 19th-century school standard) and Smyth (the comprehensive reference). He writes English-to-Greek sentences and short passages weekly from North & Hillard's Greek Prose Composition, which fixes accents, moods and particles.
objectives: Look up any construction in Smyth or Goodwin by section number
Complete the first 40 exercises of North & Hillard's Greek Prose Composition
Accent correctly any noun or verb form written

coreTexts.title: Greek Prose Composition for Schools
coreTexts.author: M. A. North & A. E. Hillard

curriculumOptions.name: Live online classes and tutors
curriculumOptions.notes: Live online classical language courses with expert teachers. Useful if a local tutor is not available.

rows.historicalPrecedent: English public schools (Eton, Rugby, Shrewsbury) required Greek prose and verse composition in the upper forms. Goodwin's grammar was the American college standard from the 1870s.
rows.notes: Done with a tutor (the family has tutors available): prose and verse composition need an expert to correct the student's exercises line by line.

rows.title: First Classical Readers: Aesop & Lucian
rows.summary: Short, witty classical prose. Aesop's fables in Greek come first, the traditional first Greek book. Lucian's True History, the ancestor of science fiction and of Swift, follows. Both give volume, humour and Attic idiom before the Anabasis.
objectives: Read 30+ Aesopic fables in Greek
Read True History Book I in Greek
Retell a fable in simple Greek (oral or written)
rows.historicalPrecedent: J. S. Mill: "Aesop's Fables, the first Greek book which I read. The Anabasis… was the second." Boston Latin's 1880s Fourth Class read "Lucian, Dialogues" alongside the Anabasis.

sources.label: J. S. Mill, Autobiography (Project Gutenberg)

rows.title: Xenophon: Anabasis (and Memorabilia)
rows.summary: The historic first Attic author, the counterpart of Caesar. The student reads Anabasis Books I–IV, the march of the Ten Thousand, with its lessons in leadership, improvised self-government and courage. Selections from the Memorabilia show Socrates through a soldier's eyes.
objectives: Read Anabasis I–IV (at least I and IV in full)
Read three chapters of the Memorabilia
Analyse Xenophon's portrait of leadership (Cyrus, Clearchus, Xenophon himself)

links.label: Goodwin & White school edition, Books I–IV (Archive.org)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson told Peter Carr (1785) to read "Xenophontis Hellenica, Xenophontis Anabasis" in the original and assigned the "Xenophontis Memorabilia" for morality. The Anabasis (Books I–IV) was the standard American college-entrance Greek text through the late 1800s.

sources.label: Jefferson to Peter Carr, 19 Aug 1785 (Wikisource)

rows.title: Koine Reading II: Luke–Acts
rows.summary: Luke writes the most literary Koine in the New Testament. The Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles bridge Koine and classical style. Paul's Areopagus speech (Acts 17) and his defences before Festus and Agrippa give rhetorical models.
objectives: Read Luke 1–2 and 15 and the Passion narrative in Greek
Read Acts 1–2, 9, 17 and 26–28 in Greek
Analyse the periodic prologue of Luke (1:1–4) as classical prose

coreTexts.title: Gospel of Luke & Acts of the Apostles
coreTexts.author: St. Luke

rows.title: Plato: Apology & Crito
rows.summary: Socrates on trial and in prison. The Apology and Crito are the first philosophical texts read in the original. The questions are the examined life, obedience to law and conscience, and the citizen's duty. Attic prose at its most natural.
objectives: Read the Apology and Crito complete in Greek
Memorize Apology 38a ("the unexamined life…") in Greek
Write an essay on the Laws' speech in the Crito and civil disobedience (compare King, Thoreau, Aquinas on unjust law)
rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson assigned "Plato's Socratic dialogues" to Peter Carr for morality (1785), though he later disparaged Plato's Republic. Socratic dialogues were standard reading in the colonial colleges and the English universities.

rows.title: Homer: Odyssey & Iliad
rows.summary: Homeric dialect and the dactylic hexameter. The student reads Odyssey Books I and IX–XII (Cyclops to Scylla) and Iliad I, VI (Hector and Andromache), and XXII–XXIV (the death of Hector and Priam's ransom). The rest is read in translation. Homer comes after Virgil in Latin, so the student can see what Virgil imitated.
objectives: Read about 2,500 lines of Homer in Greek
Scan and recite Homeric hexameter; memorize Iliad I.1–7 and Odyssey I.1–10
Know the main features of the Homeric dialect
Write a comparative essay on Achilles, Hector, Odysseus and Aeneas
rows.historicalPrecedent: Boston 1789, top class: "Greek Testament. Horace. Homer." Otis recalled that the "highest classes dipped into Xenophon and Homer." The 1880s Boston Latin Third Class read "Homer, Iliad." Harvard and Yale examined entrants on Greek grammar and the Greek Testament, and Homer followed in college.

rows.title: Herodotus: The Histories
rows.summary: The "Father of History" in Ionic Greek. The student reads Book I (Croesus and Solon, Cyrus) and the Persian War narratives (Thermopylae in Book VII, Salamis in Book VIII). Themes: liberty against despotism, fortune and hubris, and the Greek sense of law ("Law is king").
objectives: Read Herodotus I.1–94 (Croesus logos) in Greek
Read the Thermopylae narrative (VII.201–233) in Greek
Recognize Ionic dialect forms
Explain the Greek idea of freedom under law (Demaratus to Xerxes, VII.104)
rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson's reading plan for Carr (1785) begins ancient history "in the original" with "Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophontis Hellenica, Xenophontis Anabasis, Arrian…".

sources.label: Jefferson to Peter Carr, 19 Aug 1785 (Wikisource)

rows.title: Septuagint & the Greek Fathers
rows.summary: Biblical and patristic Greek. The student reads the Septuagint Genesis 1–11 and selected Psalms, the Old Testament the apostles quoted. He then reads Greek Fathers: St. John Chrysostom (a homily), St. Basil's Address to Young Men on Greek Literature (on how Christians should read the pagan classics), and the Nicene Creed in Greek.
objectives: Read LXX Genesis 1–3 and 6–9 and ten Psalms in Greek
Compare LXX, Hebrew and Vulgate readings of three key passages (e.g. Gen 1:2, Ps 22/21, Isa 7:14)
Read one Chrysostom homily and Basil's Address to Young Men (selections) in Greek
Recite the Nicene–Constantinopolitan Creed in Greek

coreTexts.title: Genesis 1–11: Septuagint and Vulgate with facing vocabulary
coreTexts.author: Geoffrey Steadman (ed.)

curriculumOptions.name: Septuaginta: A Reader's Edition
curriculumOptions.notes: Rahlfs–Hanhart text with running vocabulary. The best single tool for reading the LXX.

rows.notes: Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and the Fathers, received the LXX's wider canon, which includes the deuterocanonical books (Wisdom, Sirach, Maccabees, etc.). Protestants follow the shorter Hebrew canon and call these books the Apocrypha. Chrysostom and Basil are honoured by Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant readers.

rows.title: Attic Tragedy: Sophocles, Aeschylus & Euripides
rows.summary: The student reads one tragedy in Greek, Sophocles' Antigone, with selections from Euripides' Medea and the Oresteia, and the rest in translation. He learns the iambic trimeter, the choral lyric and the structure of tragedy. Antigone's clash of divine law and civic decree is the natural-law debate in dramatic form.
objectives: Read Sophocles' Antigone in Greek (dialogue complete, choral odes selectively)
Scan iambic trimeter
Memorize the "Ode to Man" (Antigone 332–375), at least its first strophe
Write an essay on Antigone and natural law (compare Aquinas and Martin Luther King)
rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson names "Euripides, Sophocles" among the poets Carr "will read at school" (1785). Tragedy was a set text in the English sixth forms and American colleges.

rows.title: College Greek: Thucydides, Plato & Reading at Sight
rows.summary: The hardest Attic prose and the core texts of political philosophy. Thucydides: the Archaeology, Pericles' Funeral Oration (II.35–46), the Plague, the Mytilene debate, the Corcyraean stasis (III.82–83) and the Melian Dialogue. Then Plato: Republic I and selections from the Phaedo or Gorgias. Sight-reading of the Greek New Testament and Xenophon becomes a daily habit.
objectives: Read the Funeral Oration, the Mytilene debate, the stasis at Corcyra and the Melian Dialogue in Greek
Read Republic I (or Gorgias) in Greek
Read any NT passage at sight
Write a paper connecting Thucydides on faction to Federalist No. 10
rows.historicalPrecedent: Thucydides was the second author on Jefferson's list for Carr. Hobbes translated him into English (1629) as a warning against democracy. The founders cited the Greek leagues and factions in the Federalist debates (Federalist 18–20).

rows.title: Hebrew I: Aleph-Bet, Vowel Points & First Words
rows.summary: Six to ten weeks on the writing system. The student learns the 22 consonants and final forms, the Masoretic vowel points, dagesh, shewa and syllabification, reading right to left aloud. He learns about 100 words and reads Genesis 1:1–5, the Shema (Deut 6:4–9) and Psalm 23 aloud.
objectives: Write and name all 22 letters and 5 final forms
Read pointed Hebrew aloud accurately, with correct syllable division
Read Genesis 1:1, the Shema and Psalm 23:1 aloud and know their meaning word by word
Learn about 100 high-frequency Biblical words

curriculumOptions.name: The First Hebrew Primer (Biblical Hebrew)
curriculumOptions.notes: A long-standing self-study primer built on Biblical passages. Clear, gentle and widely used by adult beginners and home learners. It is published for a Jewish audience and is non-confessional.

curriculumOptions.name: Aleph with Beth (free video course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Immersive, picture-based Biblical Hebrew lessons with no English grammar talk. A good companion for building the ear.

curriculumOptions.name: Hebrew for Christians (free online)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free alphabet, vowel and prayer pages. Useful for drill and reading practice.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Harvard's 1642 timetable (New England's First Fruits) set aside a weekday for "Hebrew, and the Easterne Tongues": Hebrew grammar in the first year, Chaldee (Aramaic) in the second and Syriac in the third. Hebrew was a required study at colonial Harvard and Yale.

sources.label: New Englands First Fruits (1643)

rows.title: Hebrew II: Grammar I (Nouns, Qal Verb, Syntax)
rows.summary: A standard seminary grammar at a steady pace. It covers nouns, the article, prepositions and pronominal suffixes, the construct chain, and the whole Qal stem of the strong verb (perfect, imperfect, wayyiqtol, imperative, infinitives, participles). Short verses are translated from the first weeks.
objectives: Parse any Qal strong verb form (stem, conjugation, person, gender, number, root)
Read construct chains and pronominal suffixes on nouns and prepositions
Understand the wayyiqtol narrative sequence
Know about 400 words (all words occurring 100+ times)

curriculumOptions.name: Basics of Biblical Hebrew Grammar (3rd ed.), Pratico & Van Pelt
curriculumOptions.notes: The most widely used US grammar, with a workbook, videos, charts and vocabulary cards. The best-supported option for home or self study.

curriculumOptions.name: Beginning Biblical Hebrew (Mark Futato)
curriculumOptions.notes: Compact, with readings from Ruth and Jonah built in. Fast, and suits a student who already has Latin and Greek.

curriculumOptions.name: A Practical Grammar for Classical Hebrew (2nd ed.), J. Weingreen
curriculumOptions.notes: The classic British grammar (Trinity College Dublin). Concise and traditional. Many Catholic seminaries used it.

rows.notes: Lambdin's Introduction to Biblical Hebrew (1971) is the rigorous alternative used at Harvard and many doctoral programs. It is excellent for a gifted student, but its exercises have no answer key without Williamson's Annotated Key.

rows.title: Hebrew III: Grammar II (Derived Stems, Weak Verbs) & Gesenius
rows.summary: Completion of the grammar: Niphal, Piel, Pual, Hiphil, Hophal and Hithpael, and the weak verb classes (I-guttural, III-he, hollow, geminate, I-nun, I-waw/yod). The student learns to use Gesenius as a reference, which is the Hebrew equivalent of Allen & Greenough or Smyth.
objectives: Parse any verb form in all seven major stems, including weak roots
Use the lexicon (BDB/HALOT or a reader's lexicon) to find roots from weak forms
Look up syntax in Gesenius' Hebrew Grammar by section number
Know about 800 words (all words occurring 50+ times)

coreTexts.title: Gesenius' Hebrew Grammar (Kautzsch–Cowley)
coreTexts.author: Wilhelm Gesenius, ed. E. Kautzsch, trans. A. E. Cowley

curriculumOptions.name: Basics of Biblical Hebrew Grammar (second half) + Workbook
curriculumOptions.notes: Continue the same text through the derived stems and weak verbs.

curriculumOptions.name: Graded Reader of Biblical Hebrew (Van Pelt & Pratico)
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded passages keyed to the grammar. The ideal bridge into unassisted reading.

rows.title: Reading I: Genesis 1–11
rows.summary: The first sustained reading. The chapters are Creation, the Fall, Cain and Abel, the Flood and Babel, all in simple narrative Hebrew. The student compares key words (bara', tohu wabohu, tselem, ruach) with the Septuagint and Vulgate and sees how translation shapes theology.
objectives: Read Genesis 1–4 and 6–9 in Hebrew with a reader's lexicon
Memorize Genesis 1:1–5 in Hebrew
Compare Gen 1:1–3 and 1:26–27 in Hebrew, LXX and Vulgate

coreTexts.title: Genesis 1–11: Septuagint and Vulgate with facing vocabulary
coreTexts.author: Geoffrey Steadman

curriculumOptions.name: A Reader's Hebrew Bible (2nd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Full Hebrew OT with footnoted glosses for words occurring fewer than 100 times.

curriculumOptions.name: Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia: A Reader's Edition
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard scholarly BHS text with glosses and parsing of difficult verbs.

rows.title: Reading II: Ruth & Jonah
rows.summary: Two complete short books of classical Hebrew prose. Ruth deals with hesed (covenant loyalty), kinship law and the line of David. Jonah deals with mercy for the nations and has a psalm embedded in the narrative. Each is read whole and fast, in a few weeks.
objectives: Read the whole of Ruth and Jonah in Hebrew
Trace the word hesed through Ruth and explain its range
Read Jonah 2 as a first taste of Hebrew poetry

curriculumOptions.name: Beginning Biblical Hebrew (Futato), Ruth and Jonah readings
curriculumOptions.notes: Futato's grammar builds its readings around these books.

rows.title: Reading III: The Psalms
rows.summary: Hebrew poetry: parallelism, terseness, chiasm and acrostics. The student reads about 25 Psalms (1, 2, 8, 19, 22, 23, 51, 90, 110, 119 in part, 139 and the Hallel 113–118). They are the prayer book of Israel and the Church, sung in Latin in the Office and quoted throughout the New Testament.
objectives: Read about 25 Psalms in Hebrew and classify their parallelism
Memorize Psalm 1 or 23 in Hebrew
Compare Ps 22 (21 in LXX/Vulgate) in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and explain the numbering difference
rows.notes: Psalm numbering differs. Catholic liturgical books traditionally follow the Greek/Latin numbering (usually one lower from Ps 10 to 147), while Protestant and Jewish Bibles follow the Hebrew. Teach both.

rows.title: Reading IV: Isaiah & the Prophets
rows.summary: Elevated prophetic poetry and prose. The student reads Isaiah 1, 6, 7:10–17, 9:1–7, 11, 40, 52:13–53:12 and 61, with Micah 6:8 and Amos 5. Much of the vocabulary is new and the syntax is more demanding. These chapters shape Handel's Messiah, the abolitionists and Martin Luther King's rhetoric.
objectives: Read ten selected chapters of Isaiah in Hebrew
Discuss the translation question of Isaiah 7:14 ('almah / parthenos / virgo) from the texts themselves
Memorize Isaiah 40:1–8 or Micah 6:8 in Hebrew
rows.notes: Christian (Catholic and Protestant) and Jewish readings of Isaiah 7 and 53 differ sharply. Present the texts and the main interpretations fairly.

rows.title: Tools & Texts: Sefaria, BHS, and the Vulgate–Septuagint Question
rows.summary: A standing unit on the scholar's tools and the history of the text. The tools are Sefaria (free Hebrew with Jewish commentary), the Westminster Leningrad Codex, BHS and its apparatus, and readers' Bibles. The history covers the Masoretic Text, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, Jerome's Vulgate made "from the Hebrew truth" (Hebraica veritas), and the Reformation and Catholic returns to the original languages.
objectives: Navigate Sefaria and look up a verse with Rashi's commentary
Read a BHS page and explain the Masoretic notes and critical apparatus in outline
Explain why Jerome translated the OT from Hebrew and how the Vulgate relates to the MT and LXX
Summarize Pius XII's Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943) on original-language study
rows.notes: A Catholic note. Jerome translated most of the Old Testament directly from the Hebrew, and Trent declared the Vulgate "authentic" for doctrine. Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943) urged Catholic scholars to work from the original languages, and the Nova Vulgata (1979) revised Jerome's Latin against the Hebrew and Greek. A Protestant note. The Reformers' ad fontes ("back to the sources") made the Hebrew and Greek texts the final authority (Westminster Confession I.8), and so Hebrew was required of ministers and taught at Harvard and Yale.

rows.title: Optional: Modern Hebrew Exposure
rows.summary: A short, optional unit on Israeli pronunciation, everyday vocabulary and unpointed script. Reading modern headlines and speaking a little show Hebrew as a living language, and unpointed text builds the fluency needed for rabbinic and modern texts.
objectives: Read short unpointed modern texts (signs, headlines)
Hold a two-minute conversation of greetings and basics
Know the main pronunciation differences between Biblical (Tiberian) reading and Israeli Hebrew

curriculumOptions.name: EKS Publishing, Modern Hebrew titles
curriculumOptions.notes: The same publisher as the First Hebrew Primer. It has a Modern Hebrew line.

rows.title: College Hebrew: Sight Reading & the Trilingual Bible
rows.summary: The capstone. The student reads Hebrew narrative (the Joseph story, Genesis 37–50, and 1–2 Samuel selections, David and Saul) at sight or near-sight. He does a "trilingual" study of key passages in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, in the manner of the Complutensian Polyglot and the colonial colleges. He also gets a first taste of Biblical Aramaic (Daniel 2:4–7:28).
objectives: Read Genesis 37–50 in Hebrew with minimal lexicon use
Read 1 Samuel 16–17 in Hebrew
Read Daniel 2:4–13 in Aramaic with a grammar
Produce an annotated comparison of one passage in Hebrew, LXX Greek and Vulgate Latin
rows.historicalPrecedent: Harvard (1642) taught Hebrew, Chaldee (Aramaic) and Syriac across the three years. At Yale, President Ezra Stiles (1778–1795) "obliged all the Freshmen to study Hebrew". His first commencement address (1781) was delivered in Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic, and the valedictorians of 1785 and 1792 spoke in Hebrew. The Yale arms (adopted 1746) carry the Hebrew words Urim v'Thummim, rendered in Latin as "Lux et Veritas".

sources.label: New Englands First Fruits (1643)
Coat of arms of Yale University (Wikipedia)
Ezra Stiles (Wikipedia)

rows.title: First Stories of the Past: Bible Narratives, Aesop & the Nation's Words
rows.summary: The doorway into history is the story heard aloud. The child hears Bible narratives (Creation to the Exodus, David, Daniel; the life of Christ), Aesop's fables, family stories told by grandparents, and short hero tales. He also memorizes the Pledge of Allegiance and the preamble of the Declaration of Independence. The aim is a love of "true stories" and the first sense that the past is real, ordered, and full of people worth imitating.
objectives: Retell in order a Bible narrative or hero story heard the day before (narration)
Recite the Pledge and the Declaration's preamble ("We hold these truths…") from memory
Distinguish "long ago" from "now", and "a true story" from "a fable"
Begin a family timeline (grandparents, parents, child)

curriculumOptions.name: Stories of Great Americans for Little Americans
curriculumOptions.notes: Edward Eggleston's 1895 hero stories, re-edited with a guide. Good read-aloud at 6–7.

curriculumOptions.name: Child's Bible History
curriculumOptions.notes: The classic short Catholic Bible history (Knecht), useful as the spine for Bible narratives.

curriculumOptions.name: Our Lady of Victory: early-grade history (America My Country)
curriculumOptions.notes: Traditional Catholic program; its first-grade history is a simple workbook on flag, founders, Pilgrims and pioneers.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Colonial and 19th-century children met history first through Scripture, the catechism, fables and the school reader. The McGuffey Readers mixed Bible stories, fables and short patriotic pieces, and children memorized the Declaration and Washington's words for exhibitions and declamation days.
rows.notes: Catholic families may prefer the Douay-Rheims or RSV-CE and a Catholic Bible history (Knecht); Protestant families the KJV or ESV and a Bible storybook such as Egermeier or Hurlbut. The narratives read are the same.

rows.title: Maps, Timelines & the Book of Centuries
rows.summary: This is the running "skeleton" of the whole history track. A wall timeline goes up in the schoolroom, the child learns map work, and a Book of Centuries is started: a hand-kept notebook with one spread per century, into which the child draws and dates people, events, buildings and inventions as he meets them. Memory work pins about 100–160 key dates and events in place by age 10. Everything later hangs on this frame.
objectives: Place the major eras (Creation/Patriarchs, Egypt, Israel, Greece, Rome, Christ, Middle Ages, Renaissance, Reformation, Exploration, America) in order
Memorize a timeline of about 100–160 events with dates
Locate the Mediterranean, Fertile Crescent, Greece, Italy, Holy Land, British Isles, France, Spain and the thirteen colonies on a blank map
Keep a Book of Centuries, adding an entry for every person or event studied

coreTexts.title: A Child's History of the World
coreTexts.author: V.M. Hillyer

curriculumOptions.name: Timeline Program (160 events)
curriculumOptions.notes: Timeline cards, composition book and drill for the five eras. A clean backbone for the memorized timeline.

curriculumOptions.name: History Flashcards & Self-Paced courses
curriculumOptions.notes: Five card sets (OT & Egypt → 1815 to Present), 32 events each, sung and drilled. Can be used without the online course.

curriculumOptions.name: History Timeline Template
curriculumOptions.notes: A free printable timeline template from CHC. Pair it with saints' feast days.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Chronology was taught as a discipline in the 18th and 19th centuries: "chronology and geography are the two eyes of history" was a schoolroom maxim. Charlotte Mason's Book of Centuries (late 19th c.) and the wall charts of Priestley's "Chart of Biography" (1765) are the direct ancestors of this practice.
rows.notes: The Book of Centuries is kept from about 7 through 16, so the child who reads Thucydides at 13 already has a page waiting for 431 BC.

rows.title: Cycle 1 · The Ancient World: Egypt, Israel, Greece & Rome
rows.summary: The first narrative year covers the ancient world through its great men and deeds. Haaren & Poland's Famous Men of Greece and Famous Men of Rome (in the Memoria Press editions) give 30 lives each: Lycurgus, Solon, Leonidas, Pericles, Alexander, Horatius, Cincinnatus, Scipio, Caesar, Constantine. Guerber and Hillyer fill in Egypt and Israel. The Boys' and Girls' Plutarch is read aloud as the child's first taste of the ancient source itself.
objectives: Narrate the lives of about 20 Greek and Roman worthies and state the virtue or vice each shows
Place Egypt, Israel, Persia, Greece and Rome on the timeline and on a map
Hear Plutarch retold and name the difference between a "life" and a "history"
Recite short famous sayings (Leonidas, Horatius, Caesar's "veni, vidi, vici")

coreTexts.title: Famous Men of Greece
coreTexts.author: John H. Haaren & Addison B. Poland

coreTexts.title: Famous Men of Rome
coreTexts.author: John H. Haaren & Addison B. Poland

curriculumOptions.name: Famous Men of Greece Set / Famous Men of Rome Set
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard classical-school edition, with student and teacher guides, maps, drills and videos. Greece set is at /famous-men-greece/.

curriculumOptions.name: Old Testament & Ancient Egypt / New Testament, Greece & Rome
curriculumOptions.notes: Sung timeline cards plus an online course. Covers biblical history in the context of all history. The companion NT, Greece & Rome cards are at /new-testament-greece-rome-flashcards.html.

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of Civilization, Vol. 1: The Ancient World
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic narrative spine for the elementary years, with activity book and audio. Softer than Famous Men but more complete.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Haaren & Poland wrote the Famous Men series (1904) for the New York public schools on the old principle that the young learn history best through biography. Plutarch was the most widely read ancient author among the American founders. Hamilton, Adams, Jefferson and Franklin all cite him, and Mill read Langhorne's Plutarch "with great delight" as a small boy.

sources.label: J.S. Mill, Autobiography (1873), ch. 1

rows.notes: The Famous Men books are by Haaren & Poland, not Guerber. Guerber's Story of the Greeks and Story of the Romans are the companion narratives.

rows.title: Cycle 1 · The Middle Ages: Christendom, Kings & Saints
rows.summary: The second narrative year runs from the fall of Rome to the eve of the Renaissance, again through lives. Famous Men of the Middle Ages gives Alaric, Clovis, St. Benedict, Charlemagne, Alfred, William the Conqueror, Barbarossa, St. Louis and Joan of Arc. The early chapters of Marshall's Our Island Story give England's story from the Romans to the Wars of the Roses. Saints' lives and the Crusades are told as the living heart of Christendom.
objectives: Narrate the lives of about 20 medieval figures (kings, saints, popes, knights)
Explain in a child's terms what a monastery, a castle, a manor, a cathedral and a crusade were
Retell the story of Alfred, Charlemagne, William I, Magna Carta and St. Louis
Add the medieval centuries to the Book of Centuries

coreTexts.title: Famous Men of the Middle Ages
coreTexts.author: John H. Haaren & Addison B. Poland

coreTexts.title: The Story of the Middle Ages
coreTexts.author: Samuel B. Harding

curriculumOptions.name: Famous Men of the Middle Ages Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Text, student and teacher guides, maps and drill.

curriculumOptions.name: Middle Ages, Renaissance & Reformation
curriculumOptions.notes: Timeline cards and self-paced course, written from a Reformed perspective.

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of Civilization, Vol. 2: The Medieval World
curriculumOptions.notes: A Catholic narrative of Christendom for children.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Our Island Story (1905) was the history every British child of the Empire era grew up on, and it was reissued in 2005 after a public campaign. In 19th-century schools the Middle Ages came to children through Scott, Froissart "for boys" and lives of the saints and kings.
rows.notes: Catholic and Protestant tellings differ mainly in emphasis: the papacy, monasticism and the Crusades on one side, Wycliffe and "forerunners of the Reformation" on the other. Reading Famous Men as the spine keeps the child on the shared ground of persons and deeds.

rows.title: Cycle 1 · Early Modern: Renaissance, Reformation & the Age of Exploration
rows.summary: The third narrative unit covers Gutenberg, Columbus, Michelangelo, Luther and Loyola, Elizabeth, Drake and the Armada, and Galileo, and runs on to Louis XIV and Peter the Great. Our Island Story continues through the Tudors and Stuarts. Columbus's own account of the first landfall is read aloud, the child's first "explorer's primary source".
objectives: Narrate the lives of the great explorers, artists, reformers and monarchs
Tell the story of the Reformation and the Catholic Reformation fairly, naming Luther, Calvin, Henry VIII, More, Loyola, Teresa and Trent
Trace the voyages of Columbus, da Gama, Magellan and Cartier on a map
Hear extracts of Columbus's journal read aloud and narrate them

coreTexts.title: A Child's History of the World (later chapters)
coreTexts.author: V.M. Hillyer

curriculumOptions.name: Famous Men of Modern Times Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Continues the Famous Men lives from the Renaissance to the 19th century.

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of Civilization, Vol. 3: The Making of the Modern World
curriculumOptions.notes: A Catholic account of the Renaissance, Reformation, Catholic Reformation and exploration.

curriculumOptions.name: Middle Ages, Renaissance & Reformation
curriculumOptions.notes: Its second half covers this period from a Reformed perspective.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Nineteenth-century Anglo-American schoolbooks (Marshall, Goodrich's "Peter Parley", the McGuffey Readers) told this period as a drama of discovery and liberty, and Catholic schoolbooks as the story of the Church's renewal and missions. This program tells both.
rows.notes: Neutral note: Catholics generally present the Reformation as a rupture, with Trent, Loyola and Teresa as the true reform. Protestants present it as the recovery of the Gospel. At this age, tell each figure's story in his own terms and save the argument for Cycles 2 and 3.

rows.title: Cycle 1 · The American Story: Colonies, Founding & Nation
rows.summary: The last narrative year tells America's story from the Norsemen and Columbus through Jamestown, Plymouth, the Revolution, the Constitution, the frontier, the Civil War and into the 20th century. It uses H.E. Marshall's This Country of Ours and Guerber. The child memorizes the Declaration's preamble and the Gettysburg Address, learns the presidents, and hears Washington's and Lincoln's own words.
objectives: Narrate the founding of Virginia, Plymouth, Massachusetts Bay, Maryland and Pennsylvania
Tell the story of the Revolution, the Declaration and the Constitution in order
Recite the Declaration's preamble and the Gettysburg Address
Name the presidents in order through Lincoln, and the major wars through WWII

coreTexts.title: The Story of the Thirteen Colonies
coreTexts.author: H.A. Guerber

curriculumOptions.name: The Hillsdale K-12 American History & Civics Curriculum (1776 Curriculum)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free K-12 lesson plans organized by era, from the Hillsdale network of classical charter schools. Primary-source based even in the lower grades.

curriculumOptions.name: From Sea to Shining Sea (CHC Grade 5)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic Textbook Project narrative of North America to the early 20th century.

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of the Thirteen Colonies & the Great Republic Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Guerber's two American volumes with guides.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Hillsdale K-12 Program Guide and the Barney Charter School Initiative put American history in the early grades as a story of founding principles and founders, read partly in the founders' own words. That approach descends from the McGuffey Readers and the 19th-century "declamation" of the Declaration and Washington's Farewell.

sources.label: Hillsdale K-12: Curriculum Overview

rows.title: Sources I: The Ancient Near East & Israel (Scripture, Hammurabi, Josephus)
rows.summary: The second cycle starts where history starts, with Mesopotamia, Egypt and Israel, now read in the sources. The student reads Genesis 12–50, Exodus, Joshua–Kings in selection, Daniel and Maccabees. Beside them come the Code of Hammurabi and Near Eastern texts from the Ancient History Sourcebook, with excerpts from Josephus's Antiquities to see how an ancient historian retold the same events. Guerber's Story of the Chosen People is the guide.
objectives: Read the Code of Hammurabi and compare it with the Mosaic law (Exodus 20–23)
Trace the history of Israel from Abraham to the Maccabees on the timeline
Write a one-page narration comparing a biblical account with Josephus's retelling
Identify what kind of source a text is (law code, chronicle, prophecy, royal inscription)

coreTexts.title: The Story of the Chosen People
coreTexts.author: H.A. Guerber

curriculumOptions.name: The Book of the Ancient World Set (Dorothy Mills)
curriculumOptions.notes: Mills's 1920s narrative of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia and Israel, with a study guide, and quotes the sources often.

curriculumOptions.name: Christ the King, Lord of History
curriculumOptions.notes: Anne Carroll's Catholic world history, ancient to modern. Serves as a spine for all of Cycle 2 (also sold by Seton).

curriculumOptions.name: Old Testament & Ancient Egypt
curriculumOptions.notes: Reformed classical course that keeps sacred and secular history together.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Rollin's Ancient History (1730–38) opened with Egypt, Assyria and the Hebrews. It was the standard ancient history of 18th-century schools and gentlemen's libraries on both sides of the Atlantic, and the young J.S. Mill read it. Colonial college students read the Old Testament as the oldest history of the world.

sources.label: Rollin, Ancient History, Vol. 1 (Gutenberg)

rows.notes: Catholic Bibles include 1–2 Maccabees, which are essential for the Hellenistic period. Protestant readers can find them in the KJV Apocrypha.

rows.title: Sources II: Greece in Herodotus, Plutarch & Xenophon
rows.summary: Greek history is read in the Greeks' own words. The student reads Herodotus in selection (Croesus and Solon, Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis), Plutarch's Lives of Lycurgus, Solon, Themistocles, Aristides, Pericles and Alexander, and passages of Xenophon's Anabasis, with Guerber or Mills as the guide. Narration moves to written summaries, and the child begins to ask "how does Herodotus know this?"
objectives: Read about 150 pages of Herodotus in selection and narrate the Persian Wars
Read five Plutarch Lives and write a character sketch of each statesman
Compare Sparta and Athens using Plutarch's Lycurgus and Solon
Distinguish eyewitness report, hearsay and legend in Herodotus

curriculumOptions.name: The Book of the Ancient Greeks Set (Dorothy Mills)
curriculumOptions.notes: A narrative guide that quotes Herodotus, Thucydides and Plutarch at length, plus a student guide.

curriculumOptions.name: Athens and Sparta (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free video lectures. Watch them with a parent at this age, then again at 13.

curriculumOptions.name: New Testament, Greece & Rome
curriculumOptions.notes: Timeline cards and course for Greece and Rome, with the New Testament woven in.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson told his nephew Peter Carr (1785) to read ancient history "in the original" in this order: Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon's Hellenica and Anabasis, Quintus Curtius, Justin. This row is the English-language first pass at that list.

sources.label: Jefferson to Peter Carr, 19 Aug 1785 (Founders Online)

rows.title: Sources III: Rome in Livy, Plutarch & Caesar
rows.summary: Roman history is read in the sources. The student reads Livy Book I (Romulus to the Tarquins, Lucretia and the founding of the Republic), Plutarch's Romans (Numa, Publicola, Coriolanus, Fabius, Cato the Elder, the Gracchi, Marius, Cicero, Caesar, Brutus) and Caesar's Gallic War Books I and IV–V in English. Guerber is the guide. The student meets the Roman idea of virtus and the problem of how republics fall.
objectives: Read Livy Book I entire and narrate the founding and the expulsion of the kings
Read six Roman Lives and write a comparison of two (Plutarch's own method)
Read Caesar on the Helvetians and the invasion of Britain, and map the campaigns
Explain in a paragraph why the Republic fell, citing at least two sources

coreTexts.title: De Bello Gallico and Other Commentaries
coreTexts.author: Julius Caesar (tr. McDevitte & Bohn)

curriculumOptions.name: The Book of the Ancient Romans Set (Dorothy Mills)
curriculumOptions.notes: Narrative guide built around quotations from Livy, Plutarch and Caesar.

curriculumOptions.name: The Rise and Fall of the Roman Republic (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free lectures. The American founders' preoccupation with the Roman Republic is the subtext.

curriculumOptions.name: Mother of Divine Grace: 6th-grade syllabus (The Old World and America)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic program using Furlong's The Old World and America (TAN) with historical fiction.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Livy and Caesar were grammar-school Latin authors from Boston Latin to Eton. Here they are read first in English, so the Latin track (Caesar at about 11.5, Livy at about 14) meets familiar ground. The founders drew their pseudonyms from these pages: Publius, Cato, Brutus, Cincinnatus.

rows.title: Sources IV: The Early Church (Acts, Pliny, the Martyrs & Eusebius)
rows.summary: The birth and spread of Christianity is read as history. The student reads the Acts of the Apostles whole, Tacitus and Pliny on the Christians, the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, and selections from Eusebius's Church History (the apostles' successors, the persecutions, Constantine). He learns to use a Christian source and a pagan source side by side.
objectives: Read Acts entire and map Paul's journeys
Compare Pliny's letter to Trajan with the Martyrdom of Polycarp as sources on persecution
Narrate Eusebius's account of Constantine's conversion and the Edict of Milan
Explain why Eusebius is called "the Father of Church History"

coreTexts.title: Pliny the Younger: Letter to Trajan on the Christians
The Martyrdom of Polycarp; The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity

curriculumOptions.name: History of the Early Church Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Guided readings in early Church history for the middle grades, from a broadly Christian perspective.

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of the Church: Her Founding, Mission and Progress
curriculumOptions.notes: Classic Catholic school history of the Church. MODG uses it in 8th grade.

curriculumOptions.name: Ancient Christianity (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free lectures on the first centuries, good for the parent or an advanced 11-year-old.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Eusebius's Church History was a standard text in the colonial colleges and the Jesuit colleges alike. The Ratio Studiorum and Harvard's early course both treated sacred history as part of history proper.
rows.notes: Catholic and Protestant readers agree on the facts of the first three centuries but read them differently. Catholics stress apostolic succession and the Roman primacy that Eusebius and Irenaeus record. Protestants stress the primitive Church as a pattern for reform. Point out the passages each side cites.

rows.title: Sources V: Medieval Christendom (Bede, Einhard, Roland, Magna Carta, Joinville)
rows.summary: The Middle Ages are read in their chronicles and charters: Bede on Augustine of Canterbury, Caedmon and Whitby; Einhard's Life of Charlemagne; the Song of Roland with Einhard's two-line account of Roncevaux beside it; Urban II at Clermont; Magna Carta; and Joinville's Life of St. Louis. Each source comes with a short guide, and the student starts writing one-page source reports (who wrote it, when, why, and what it tells us).
objectives: Read Einhard's Life of Charlemagne entire
Compare the Song of Roland with Einhard's report of Roncevaux (legend vs. chronicle)
Read Magna Carta and summarize five clauses in plain English
Write four one-page source reports (author, date, purpose, reliability, content)

coreTexts.title: Urban II: Speech at Clermont (five versions)
Memoirs of the Lord of Joinville (Life of St. Louis)

curriculumOptions.name: Light to the Nations, Part 1: The History of Christian Civilization
curriculumOptions.notes: Well-written Catholic 7th-grade text from Christ to the eve of the Enlightenment. Serves as the guide for rows 10–12.

curriculumOptions.name: A History of Medieval Europe Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical narrative with a student guide. It can also serve as the spine in Cycle 3.

curriculumOptions.name: Middle Ages, Renaissance & Reformation
curriculumOptions.notes: Reformed classical option. Pair it with the sources above.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Magna Carta was the founders' touchstone. Its chapter 39 ("no free man shall be taken or imprisoned… except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land") passes through Coke into the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. Bede was read in the English grammar schools and by King Alfred's own order.

rows.title: Sources VI: Renaissance, Reformation & Catholic Reform (Documents from Both Sides)
rows.summary: The 16th century is read in the words of the men who made it, and from both sides. Luther's Ninety-Five Theses and Calvin's Reply to Sadoleto are read beside the decrees of the Council of Trent (on Scripture and Tradition, and on Justification). Erasmus's Praise of Folly and More's Utopia come in selection, along with the Act of Supremacy and Elizabeth's Armada speech. The student's task is to state each side's case so fairly that its own adherents would accept it.
objectives: Read the 95 Theses and the Trent decree on justification, and summarize each in one paragraph
Write a two-column comparison of Catholic and Protestant positions on Scripture, grace and the Church, citing the documents
Narrate the English Reformation from Henry VIII to Elizabeth, using the Act of Supremacy
Explain the Catholic Reformation (Trent, the Jesuits, Teresa of Avila) as a response and a renewal

coreTexts.title: Canons and Decrees of the Council of Trent

curriculumOptions.name: Renaissance & Reformation Times Set (Dorothy Mills)
curriculumOptions.notes: Mills's narrative with a guide. Even-handed in tone.

curriculumOptions.name: The Old World and America
curriculumOptions.notes: Fr. Furlong's classic Catholic world history for the middle grades, used by MODG.

curriculumOptions.name: Middle Ages, Renaissance & Reformation
curriculumOptions.notes: Presents the Reformation from a Reformed perspective. Use it beside the Trent decrees.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Colonial American colleges were Protestant foundations, and Reformation history was taught as the origin of their liberties. The Jesuit colleges of the Ratio Studiorum taught the same events as the Church's reform. Reading both sets of documents is the fairer inheritance of each.
rows.notes: Neutral note: this is the row where Catholic and Protestant accounts diverge most. Read the Theses and Trent in full, not just summaries of them. Catholics will add Loyola's Spiritual Exercises and Teresa, Protestants the Augsburg Confession and Calvin's Institutes. The theology track (theology-19) handles the doctrine; this row handles the events.

rows.title: Sources VII: Exploration & Colonial America (Columbus, Bradford, Mayflower, Winthrop)
rows.summary: The founding of the Americas is read in its sources. Columbus's letters on the first voyage open the unit. Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation is read in large part, with the Mayflower Compact, Winthrop's "A Model of Christian Charity" ("a city upon a hill"), and the colonial charters in the Avalon Project. The Catholic colonies (New Spain, New France, Maryland) and the missions are treated as fully as the Puritan ones.
objectives: Read Columbus's letter on the first voyage and describe what he saw and what he sought
Read Bradford Book I and chapters of Book II; narrate the Pilgrims' reasons for leaving
Explain the Mayflower Compact as self-government by covenant
Compare the religious purposes of Plymouth, Massachusetts Bay, Maryland and New France

coreTexts.title: Modern History Sourcebook: Colonial North America

curriculumOptions.name: America's Catholic Heritage
curriculumOptions.notes: The Catholic side of the American story (missions, Maryland, Carroll).

curriculumOptions.name: Christ and the Americas
curriculumOptions.notes: Anne Carroll's Catholic history of the Americas for high school. Usable early by strong readers, and used by MODG.

curriculumOptions.name: The Hillsdale 1776 Curriculum (Colonial unit)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free primary-source lesson plans on the colonial era.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Bradford's manuscript was treated as a national relic, and Winthrop's "city upon a hill" became a fixed phrase of American rhetoric from Kennedy to Reagan. The Mayflower Compact was read in 19th-century schools as the seed of American self-government.

rows.title: Sources VIII: The Founding & the Republic in Documents
rows.summary: A guided first reading of the American founding documents, as a bridge into Cycle 3. It covers the Declaration entire, the Constitution and Bill of Rights, Washington's Farewell Address, the Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural, and short passages of the Federalist (Nos. 1, 10, 51). McClay's Land of Hope or a comparable narrative is the guide. The goal is command of the documents' structure and principal arguments before the seminars at 15–16.
objectives: Outline the Declaration (preamble, grievances, conclusion) and memorize its second paragraph
Summarize each Article of the Constitution and each of the first ten Amendments
Read Washington's Farewell and list his warnings (faction, foreign entanglement, religion and morality)
Read Lincoln's two great speeches and explain how he appeals to the Declaration

coreTexts.title: The Constitution of the United States

curriculumOptions.name: The Great American Story (free online course, on Land of Hope)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free lectures by Wilfred McClay on his narrative. The book is below.

curriculumOptions.name: Land of Hope: Young Reader's Edition, Vol. 1
curriculumOptions.notes: The best recent single narrative of American history, adapted for middle-school readers.

curriculumOptions.name: A Concise History of the American Republic Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Morison, Commager and Leuchtenburg with MP guides. More demanding, and can carry into Cycle 3.

curriculumOptions.name: The Story of Civilization, Vol. 4: The History of the United States
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic narrative of the United States.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Nineteenth-century American schoolchildren declaimed Washington's Farewell and the Declaration each year. Lincoln said in 1861, "I have never had a feeling politically that did not spring from the sentiments embodied in the Declaration of Independence."

rows.title: Seminar: Ancient Greece — Herodotus & Thucydides
rows.summary: This is the first rigorous seminar. The student reads Herodotus substantially (Books I, VI–IX) and Thucydides nearly whole: the Archaeology, the causes of the war, Pericles' Funeral Oration, the plague, Mytilene, the Corcyraean stasis, the Melian Dialogue and Sicily. Xenophon's Hellenica is optional. The student meets the invention of history: inquiry (historia) versus Thucydides' "possession for all time." Weekly Socratic discussion and four argumentative essays.
objectives: Read about 1,200 pages of Herodotus and Thucydides
Contrast the two historians' method, sources and view of causation in a 1,500-word essay
Analyze the Funeral Oration and the Melian Dialogue as statements of Athenian self-understanding
Draw lessons for republics (stasis, empire, demagoguery) and test them against the founders' use of Greek history

coreTexts.title: The History of the Peloponnesian War
coreTexts.author: Thucydides (tr. Crawley)

curriculumOptions.name: The Landmark Herodotus / The Landmark Thucydides (ed. Strassler)
curriculumOptions.notes: The best student editions, with maps on every other page, running dates and appendices. Landmark Herodotus is at /the-landmark-herodotus-the-histories-herodotus/f1e630dd0f8b614d.

curriculumOptions.name: Mother of Divine Grace: Ancient History & Literature
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic high-school syllabus reading Herodotus, Polybius and Plutarch with Warren Carroll's Founding of Christendom as the spine, with paper topics.

curriculumOptions.name: Athens and Sparta (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale's free lectures on the Greek city-states and the Peloponnesian War.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson's 1785 reading plan for Peter Carr begins "Herodotus. Thucydides." Thomas Arnold of Rugby edited Thucydides (1830–35) and made him central to the Sixth Form. Hobbes's first published work was his translation of Thucydides (1629), made as a warning against democracy.

sources.label: Jefferson to Peter Carr, 19 Aug 1785

rows.title: Seminar: The Roman Republic — Polybius, Livy & Sallust
rows.summary: The rise and fall of the Republic in its historians. The student reads Polybius Books I, III and VI (the mixed constitution, the founders' favorite ancient text on government) and Livy Books I–V and XXI–XXII (Hannibal). Sallust's Catiline and Jugurtha supply the moralist's view of decline. Essays pair ancient analysis with American application, for example Polybius VI against Federalist 47–51 and John Adams's Defence.
objectives: Explain Polybius's theory of the cycle of constitutions and the mixed constitution
Read Livy on the Second Punic War and assess Hannibal and Fabius as leaders
Analyze Sallust's thesis that wealth and ambition corrupted Rome
Write a 2,000-word essay on Polybius VI and the American separation of powers

coreTexts.author: Sallust

coreTexts.title: Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius
coreTexts.author: Niccolò Machiavelli

curriculumOptions.name: The Rise and Fall of the Roman Republic (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures by Hillsdale faculty that pair well with the Polybius–Livy–Sallust sequence.

curriculumOptions.name: Mother of Divine Grace: Ancient History & Literature
curriculumOptions.notes: Its Rome weeks use Polybius and Livy's Early History of Rome and War with Hannibal.

curriculumOptions.name: Challenge II–III (Classical Conversations)
curriculumOptions.notes: A Protestant community-based high-school program that reads Western history and literature in seminar. Adapt its reading list to these sources.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Polybius VI was the ancient text the framers cited on mixed government. John Adams's Defence of the Constitutions (1787) quotes it at length. Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy was read by Adams and Jefferson. Livy and Sallust were the standard historians in the upper forms of Boston Latin, Eton and the colonial colleges.

rows.title: Seminar: Imperial Rome & Judea — Tacitus, Suetonius & Josephus
rows.summary: The Principate read in its historians: Tacitus's Agricola, Annals I–IV (Tiberius) and XV (the fire and the Christians under Nero); Suetonius on Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula and Nero; and Josephus's Jewish War on the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Tacitus's prose portrait of tyranny and flattery is the central lesson for a future statesman. Josephus connects Roman and sacred history.
objectives: Read the Agricola and Annals I–IV, XV, and analyze Tacitus's portrait of Tiberius
Compare Tacitus and Suetonius as sources for the same emperor
Read Jewish War Books V–VI and assess Josephus's reliability and loyalties
Write an essay on how liberty is lost under a republican facade, using Tacitus

coreTexts.title: The Lives of the Twelve Caesars
coreTexts.author: Suetonius

curriculumOptions.name: The Wars of the Jews Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Josephus with a student and teacher guide.

curriculumOptions.name: Pilgrimage, Vol. 1: A History of Western Civilization
curriculumOptions.notes: A Catholic high-school survey from antiquity to the High Middle Ages. Use it as the narrative frame for rows 15–20.

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books 101 (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale's survey of the ancient-to-medieval great books.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Tacitus was the Whig historian par excellence. Jefferson called him the first writer in the world, and Gordon's translation (1728–31) with its Discourses was a Revolutionary-era handbook against tyranny. Gibbon's Decline and Fall begins where Tacitus leaves off.

rows.title: Seminar: Late Antiquity & the Early Church — Eusebius & Augustine's City of God
rows.summary: The Christianization of the Empire and the Christian theology of history. The student reads Eusebius's Church History (Books I–III, VIII–X) and Life of Constantine in selection. He reads Augustine's City of God Books I–V, XIV.28, and XIX in excerpt, where Augustine answers the pagan charge that Christianity caused Rome's fall and founds the Western philosophy of history. Gibbon chapters 15–16 are read as the Enlightenment counter-reading.
objectives: Read about 400 pages of Eusebius and 250 pages of the City of God
Explain Augustine's "two cities" and his account of Rome's greatness and fall
Compare Eusebius's providential reading of Constantine with Augustine's more reserved view
Write an essay weighing Gibbon's ch. 15–16 against Eusebius and Augustine

coreTexts.title: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (Vol. 1)
coreTexts.author: Edward Gibbon

coreTexts.title: Ancient History Sourcebook: Late Antiquity; Christian Origins

curriculumOptions.name: City of God Set
curriculumOptions.notes: A guided abridgment for high school.

curriculumOptions.name: Ancient Christianity (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale faculty lectures on the Fathers, councils and Constantine.

curriculumOptions.name: Church History: A History of the Catholic Church to 1940 (Laux)
curriculumOptions.notes: Fr. John Laux's standard Catholic high-school Church history, strong on the patristic age.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Gibbon's Decline and Fall (1776–89) was read by the founding generation as it appeared, and the young J.S. Mill read it in the 1810s. Augustine's City of God was part of the arts and theology curriculum from the Carolingian schools to the Jesuit colleges.
rows.notes: Gibbon's chapters 15–16 are deliberately ironic about the early Church. Reading them against Eusebius and Augustine is an exercise in detecting a historian's bias, not an endorsement.

rows.title: Seminar: The Making of Christendom — Gregory of Tours, Bede, Einhard & the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
rows.summary: How barbarian kingdoms became Christendom. The student reads Gregory of Tours's History of the Franks (Clovis, Brunhild, the bishop-historian's world), Bede's Ecclesiastical History whole, Einhard's Charlemagne again with Notker for contrast, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle from Alfred to the Conquest. Dawson's The Making of Europe is the interpretive frame. The question: what made a "Christian civilization"?
objectives: Read Bede entire and about 200 pages of Gregory of Tours
Compare a monastic historian (Bede) with a court biographer (Einhard) and an annalist (the Chronicle)
Trace the conversion of the English and the Franks on a map
Write an essay on Dawson's thesis that religion is the key to cultural history, tested against these sources

coreTexts.title: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
coreTexts.author: Bede

coreTexts.title: Early Lives of Charlemagne (Einhard and the Monk of St Gall)
coreTexts.author: ed. A.J. Grant

curriculumOptions.name: Mother of Divine Grace: Medieval European History & Literature
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic high-school syllabus using Warren Carroll's History of Christendom volumes, Churchill's History of the English-Speaking Peoples and primary sources.

curriculumOptions.name: A History of Medieval Europe Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical narrative with a guide for the high-school medieval year.

curriculumOptions.name: The Days of Christendom (two-volume set)
curriculumOptions.notes: Seton's Catholic high-school world history.

rows.historicalPrecedent: King Alfred had Bede translated into English for his people. Hume's History of England and the 19th-century Whig historians (Stubbs, Freeman) all begin from Bede and the Chronicle. Thomas Jefferson studied Anglo-Saxon because he believed English liberty was Saxon in origin.

rows.title: Seminar: Church, Empire & Crusade — Gregory VII, Unam Sanctam, Villehardouin, Joinville & Froissart
rows.summary: The High and late Middle Ages in their documents and chronicles. The student reads the Investiture Contest (Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae and Henry IV's letters), Boniface VIII's Unam Sanctam, and Urban II and the Crusade chronicles. Villehardouin tells the Fourth Crusade and the sack of Constantinople, Joinville the life and crusade of St. Louis, and Froissart the Hundred Years' War and chivalry. The theme is the relation of spiritual and temporal power, the root of the Western idea of limited government.
objectives: Read the Gregory VII–Henry IV exchange and Unam Sanctam, and state each side's claim
Read Villehardouin and Joinville entire and compare two crusaders as witnesses
Read Froissart on Crécy, Poitiers and the Peasants' Revolt
Write a 2,000-word essay on church and state from Gelasius to Unam Sanctam, and its legacy for the First Amendment

coreTexts.author: Jean Froissart

curriculumOptions.name: Mother of Divine Grace: Medieval European History & Literature
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic syllabus. Carroll's volumes are strongly pro-papal, so balance them with the imperial documents.

curriculumOptions.name: Religion and the Rise of Western Culture (Dawson)
curriculumOptions.notes: Dawson's Gifford Lectures, the best interpretive companion to this seminar.

curriculumOptions.name: Western Heritage (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale's core course from Genesis to Locke. Its medieval lectures fit here.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Boy's Froissart (Lanier, 1879) was a favorite prize-book in Victorian and American schools. Froissart and Joinville were read as manuals of chivalry, and Scott drew on Froissart for his novels. Ages 14–15 can read the full Johnes translation.

sources.label: The Boy's Froissart (Archive.org)

rows.notes: Neutral note: Catholic readers see the Investiture Contest as the Church's liberation from lay control. Protestant and secular readers often see papal overreach. Both traditions credit the struggle with producing the Western distinction between Church and state.

rows.title: Seminar: English Constitutional History — Magna Carta to Burke
rows.summary: The inheritance the American colonists claimed. The student reads Magna Carta closely with Coke's commentary (Second Institute), the Petition of Right (1628), the 1689 Bill of Rights, and selections from Clarendon's History of the Rebellion. Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France closes the course as the classic defense of the "inheritance" view. Hume's and Macaulay's Histories of England are read in extended selections as models of narrative and as partisan (Tory and Whig) interpretations to be weighed critically.
objectives: Trace chapter 39 of Magna Carta through Coke, the Petition of Right and the Bill of Rights into the U.S. Bill of Rights
Read Clarendon on the outbreak of the Civil War and Macaulay on 1688, and compare their politics
Read Burke's Reflections in substantial part and summarize his argument on prescription and reform
Write a 2,500-word essay on whether the American Revolution was a conservative revolution, citing these sources

coreTexts.title: Second Part of the Institutes of the Laws of England (Magna Carta commentary)

coreTexts.title: The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England

rows.historicalPrecedent: Coke's Institutes were how the colonial lawyers (Adams, Jefferson, Otis, Wilson) learned English liberty. Hume's History was the standard English history of the age, and Jefferson warned that it was "so plausible & pleasing" that it disguised Tory principles (to John Norvell, 1807). J.S. Mill read Hume, Robertson and Gibbon as a boy.

rows.title: Seminar: Renaissance, Reformation & Counter-Reformation
rows.summary: The 16th century revisited at seminar depth. The student reads Machiavelli's Prince, More's Utopia and Erasmus as the Renaissance humanist debate, then the Reformation documents at length: Luther's 95 Theses and Freedom of a Christian, Calvin's Reply to Sadoleto, and the Augsburg Confession. On the Catholic side come Trent's decrees on Scripture, Justification and the Sacraments and Loyola's Spiritual Exercises (the Rules for Thinking with the Church). The English Reformation is read through More's trial and the Act of Supremacy. Dawson's The Dividing of Christendom frames the whole.
objectives: Read Luther and Trent on justification side by side and write a fair summary of each that its adherents would accept
Analyze The Prince against Erasmus's Education of a Christian Prince or More's Utopia
Explain the political consequences of the Reformation (cuius regio, the wars of religion, toleration)
Write a 2,500-word essay on the Reformation's legacy for liberty and conscience, using both Catholic and Protestant sources

rows.historicalPrecedent: The founding generation's political theology (toleration, conscience, covenant) grew directly out of Reformation history, which Protestant colleges taught as the origin of liberty. The Jesuit colleges of the Ratio Studiorum, where John Carroll was educated (St. Omer), taught the same era as the Catholic Reformation.
rows.notes: Neutral note: present both communions' own best self-understanding. On justification, compare the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (Catholic–Lutheran) as a coda for advanced students.

rows.title: Seminar: Colonial & Revolutionary America — the Founders in Their Own Words
rows.summary: The American Revolution read almost entirely in primary sources from Founders Online and the Avalon Project: the colonial charters, the Stamp Act resolves, Paine's Common Sense, Adams's Thoughts on Government and his Diary, the Declaration with Jefferson's rough draft, Washington's letters and his Circular to the States (1783), and the Articles of Confederation. The course ends with the Constitutional Convention and the ratification debate (Federalist and Anti-Federalist). This is the heart of forming a "modern founding father."
objectives: Read Common Sense entire and Adams's Thoughts on Government, and compare their plans of government
Compare Jefferson's rough draft of the Declaration with the adopted text, and explain Congress's changes
Read 20 Washington letters (incl. the 1783 Circular and the Newburgh period) and write a character study
Read Federalist 1, 10, 39, 47–51, 70, 78 and two Anti-Federalist replies; write a 2,500-word essay on the ratification debate

rows.title: Seminar: The Early Republic, the Sectional Crisis & the Civil War
rows.summary: From Washington's Farewell to Lincoln's Second Inaugural, in the words of the actors. The student reads Tocqueville's Democracy in America (Vol. I selections) and Webster's Second Reply to Hayne against Calhoun (the Exposition tradition and the Oregon Bill speech). He reads Douglass's Narrative and "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?", the Lincoln–Douglas debates, the House Divided and Cooper Union speeches, and the Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural. The key question is the meaning of the Declaration's equality principle.
objectives: Read Douglass's Narrative entire and his Fourth of July oration
Stage a debate reproducing Webster vs. Calhoun on union and nullification
Read at least three of the seven Lincoln–Douglas debates and write a judgment between the two on popular sovereignty
Write a 2,500-word essay on Lincoln's interpretation of the Declaration, from the Peoria speech to Gettysburg

rows.title: Seminar: Nineteenth-Century Europe & Britain — Revolution, Reaction & Reform
rows.summary: Europe from 1789 to 1914 in its documents and its interpreters. The student reads the French Revolution documents (the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Terror), then Carlyle and Burke as contrasting witnesses. Then come the Congress of Vienna and the Conservative Order, 1848, and the Communist Manifesto read critically. Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum and Pius IX's Quanta Cura give the Catholic response to modernity. For Britain, Bagehot's English Constitution and the Reform Acts from the 19th-century Britain sourcebook complete the course.
objectives: Compare the French Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) with the American Declaration
Read the Communist Manifesto and Rerum Novarum, and write a comparison of their accounts of labor and property
Explain the British way of reform (1832, 1867) using Bagehot's "dignified" and "efficient" parts
Trace nationalism from Napoleon to German and Italian unification using the sourcebook

coreTexts.title: Modern History Sourcebook: French Revolution; Conservative Order; 1848; 19C Britain; Socialism; 19C Religion

curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale's critical introduction to Marx and his heirs, for the Manifesto week.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Victorian schoolboys at Rugby and Eton read their Macaulay, Carlyle and Burke. Arnold of Rugby, as Regius Professor of Modern History (1841), urged that modern history be taught with the same seriousness as ancient. Mill's Autobiography records the effect of Carlyle's French Revolution on his generation.

rows.title: Seminar: The World Wars — Churchill, the Popes & the Documents
rows.summary: The two world wars in the words of statesmen and witnesses. For World War I the student reads Benedict XV's Ad Beatissimi (1914) and Wilson's Fourteen Points, with documents from the sourcebook. For the interwar crisis come Pius XI's Mit brennender Sorge (against Nazism) and Divini Redemptoris (against Communism), both 1937, and the Nazism and Holocaust documents. For World War II the student reads Churchill's great speeches of 1940 and the Atlantic Charter. Churchill is studied as a model statesman-historian.
objectives: Read and deliver one of Churchill's 1940 speeches, and analyze its rhetoric
Read Mit brennender Sorge and Divini Redemptoris, and state the Church's case against both totalitarianisms
Compare the Fourteen Points and the Atlantic Charter as statements of war aims
Write a 2,500-word essay on statesmanship in 1938–40, drawing on Churchill's speeches and the diplomatic documents

rows.historicalPrecedent: Churchill was himself a historian (Marlborough, The World Crisis, The Second World War, A History of the English-Speaking Peoples) who formed his style on Gibbon and Macaulay, read at Bangalore as a young officer. His career is the best modern case of what this track aims at: a statesman formed by history.

rows.title: Seminar: Totalitarianism, the Cold War & Civil Rights
rows.summary: The second half of the 20th century. The student reads Solzhenitsyn's Gulag Archipelago (abridged) and his Harvard address "A World Split Apart," Kennan's Long Telegram, and Churchill's "Sinews of Peace" (the Iron Curtain), with documents from the Avalon Cold War collection. For civil rights he reads King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which argues from Augustine and Aquinas, as the fulfillment of the Declaration–Lincoln–Douglass argument. John Paul II's Centesimus Annus (1991) is the Catholic reading of 1989.
objectives: Read the one-volume Gulag Archipelago and write on how ideology licenses terror
Analyze Kennan's Long Telegram and Churchill's Fulton speech as the founding documents of containment
Read King's Letter entire and trace his use of natural law (Augustine, Aquinas) and the Declaration
Write a 2,500-word essay on Solzhenitsyn's Harvard address as a critique of both East and West

rows.historicalPrecedent: King wrote the Letter in the tradition of the Declaration and of Lincoln. He quotes Augustine ("an unjust law is no law at all") and Aquinas. Hillsdale's American Heritage course places the civil-rights movement in that same line of argument from the founding.
rows.notes: The Birmingham Letter is still under copyright (King Estate). TAH publishes excerpts, and the full text is widely reprinted in anthologies.

rows.title: Historiography: How History Is Written — Rollin, Hume, Gibbon, Macaulay, Acton, Dawson & Johnson
rows.summary: The capstone of the high-school cycle is reading the historians as historians. It starts with Rollin's pious-classical Ancient History (the founders' schoolbook), then Hume's skeptical Tory History of England, Gibbon's ironic Decline and Fall, Macaulay's Whig History, and Acton's inaugural Lecture on the Study of History. Dawson's Catholic cultural history and Paul Johnson's popular narrative represent the 20th century. The student learns to detect bias, weigh evidence, understand providential, Whig, Marxist and cultural interpretations, and articulate a Christian view of history that is neither naive nor cynical.
objectives: Read a long passage of each historian and identify his method, sources and assumptions
Compare Hume and Macaulay on the Stuarts, and Gibbon and Dawson on the rise of Christianity
Explain Acton's maxims on the historian's moral judgment
Write a 3,000-word historiographical essay on one event as told by three historians

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson warned against Hume's partisan charm and recommended correcting him (to Norvell, 1807). Acton's Cambridge lecture (1895) defined the Victorian ideal of the historian as judge. Hillsdale's core curriculum treats the reading of great historians as part of liberal education, not merely a professional skill.

rows.title: College: Western Heritage I — From Genesis to the High Middle Ages
rows.summary: This course follows Hillsdale College's Western Heritage core: the formation of the West from Israel, Greece and Rome through Christendom, read in primary texts. At college level the student returns to sources read at 12–15 with more maturity. The readings are Genesis and Exodus, Thucydides, Plato's Apology, Aristotle's Politics I, Cicero, Augustine's Confessions and City of God, Benedict's Rule, Magna Carta, and Aquinas on law. Seminar discussion and a 4,000-word research paper using sources in the original language where possible (Latin/Greek).
objectives: Synthesize Jerusalem, Athens and Rome as the sources of Western civilization in a research paper
Read at least one historical source in Latin or Greek (e.g. Livy, Caesar, Thucydides) alongside the translation
Lead a seminar discussion on a primary text
Take the Hillsdale Western Heritage lecture series and pass a comprehensive oral exam on it
