rows.historicalPrecedent: The colonial colleges (Harvard, Yale, William & Mary, King's, the College of New Jersey) taught ancient history through the classical authors themselves in the original. Hillsdale's Western Heritage sequence is the modern descendant, required of every student.
rows.notes: Hankins's Golden Thread (Encounter Books, 2025) is the narrative spine for the course. A Harvard historian of the Renaissance and the classical tradition, he traces how the Greek, Roman and Judeo-Christian threads were woven together from classical Greece through Christendom to the Renaissance. Read it chapter by chapter alongside the primary sources. Allen Guelzo's Volume II continues the story in history-30.

rows.title: College: Western Heritage II — From the Renaissance to the Modern World
rows.summary: The second half of the Western Heritage core covers the Renaissance, Reformation, scientific revolution, Enlightenment, the English, American and French revolutions, liberalism and its critics, and the totalitarian century. The primary texts include Machiavelli, Luther and Trent, Hobbes and Locke, Burke and Paine, Tocqueville, Marx, Leo XIII, Churchill and Solzhenitsyn. There is a seminar and a 4,000-word research paper.
objectives: Write a research paper on a modern Western turning point, using at least ten primary sources
Defend in oral examination a thesis about modernity's debt to, and break from, Christendom
Relate the English, American and French revolutions to each other through their founding documents

The student makes a documentary study of the whole of American history: the founding principles, their challenge in slavery and the Civil War, the Progressive critique of the founding (Wilson, Croly), the New Deal, and the recovery of constitutionalism. The course reads Constitution 101 and the Federalist in full, Tocqueville Vol. II, and the Teaching American History core documents, and ends in a thesis on an American statesman.

Compare the founders' constitutionalism with the Progressive critique, using primary sources

rows.title: College Seminar: Church History from Pentecost to the Present
rows.summary: A college-level seminar on the history of Christianity. It covers the apostolic and patristic Church, the councils, monasticism, the papacy and empire, the schism of 1054, the mendicants and universities, the Reformation and Catholic Reform, the missions, the Church under revolution and totalitarianism, and Vatican I and II. It is read in documents (Eusebius, conciliar decrees, papal bulls, Reformation confessions, encyclicals) with a Catholic and a Protestant narrative side by side, so the student can explain where and why the traditions' histories diverge.

The aim is joy, pronunciation and memory. Translation is kept to a minimum.

Chant first-conjugation verb endings and first- and second-declension noun endings

curriculumOptions.notes: The most playful option, with songs, stories and a video teacher. Book 2 leads into Latin for Children. Book 1 alone is enough for an accelerated 7-year-old.

In colonial Boston the first-year books were Cheever's Accidence, a small Nomenclator (vocabulary) and Corderius's Colloquies (H. G. Otis's recollection of the early 1770s). J. S. Mill began Latin "in my eighth year".

rows.title: Latin IV: Grammar Completion (Syntax & the Subjunctive)
rows.summary: This year completes the whole of Latin grammar: participles, infinitives and indirect statement, the subjunctive and its uses (purpose, result, cum-clauses, indirect question, conditions), gerunds and gerundives, and deponent verbs. Choose one main text. The three options stand for three pedagogies: the Catholic Jesuit grammar-translation approach (Henle), the university compressed course (Wheelock), and the natural or reading method (Ørberg). Many families pair Ørberg with one of the others.

curriculumOptions.name: Henle Latin, First Year (with Memoria Press guides)
curriculumOptions.publisher: Memoria Press / Loyola Press (Robert J. Henle, S.J.)
curriculumOptions.notes: The 1945 Jesuit series that descends from the Ratio Studiorum. Its exercises mix Roman, American and Christian content. Memoria's Third and Fourth Form cover the same syntax for younger students. Also sold by Christianbook (https://www.christianbook.com/henle-latin-1-text-first-year/robert-henle/9780829410266/pd/646687).

curriculumOptions.name: Wheelock's Latin (7th ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard US college text, with every chapter built on real sentences from Cicero, Virgil and others. Too dense for most 10-year-olds unless paced over two years.

curriculumOptions.name: Lingua Latina per se Illustrata, Pars I: Familia Romana
curriculumOptions.notes: The whole book is in Latin, and grammar is learned from context. It builds real reading fluency and pairs well with Henle or Wheelock for explicit grammar. Pars II (Roma Aeterna) moves into Livy, Virgil and Cicero.

curriculumOptions.name: North American Cambridge Latin Course (Units 1–4)
curriculumOptions.notes: A story-based reading course set in Pompeii, Roman Britain and Rome. Rich in culture but slower on forms. Best used as a supplementary reader, not as the main grammar here.

curriculumOptions.name: Ossa Latinitatis Sola: The Mere Bones of Latin (Latinitatis Corpus I)
curriculumOptions.publisher: Catholic University of America Press (Reginald Foster & Daniel McCarthy)
curriculumOptions.notes: The method of Fr. Reginald Foster, O.C.D., papal Latinist 1969–2009, set out in 105 "encounters" over three "Experiences" and read from real Latin of every age, pagan and Christian, from the start. It is written for adults, so a parent works through it alongside the child or it is used from about 12 as a second pass after Henle or Wheelock. Fr. McCarthy's site (https://thelatinlanguage.org/ossa/) has readings, errata and course listings. The Liturgy Institute (London) teaches two-week online and in-person courses straight from the book, with Pooley's Ossa Ostensa workbook; they admit adults (18+), so they suit a parent learning ahead of the child (https://liturgyinstitute.org/la411/). Ossium Carnes Multae (latin-11) continues the method.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Jesuit Ratio Studiorum (1599) set out three grammar classes (lower, middle and upper) before Humanities and Rhetoric. Henle's four-year series is its twentieth-century American heir.
rows.notes: A Catholic/Protestant difference: Henle's reading content is openly Catholic (saints, the Church, Christian Rome). Protestant classical schools (Classical Conversations Challenge, for example) also use Henle widely and simply read past the confessional material.

rows.title: Graded Readers: Fabulae Faciles, Corderius, Erasmus & Eutropius
rows.summary: Wide, easy, connected reading alongside grammar completion. Ritchie's Fabulae Faciles tells the stories of Perseus, Hercules, the Argonauts and Ulysses in simplified Latin. Corderius's and Erasmus's Colloquies are the school dialogues colonial boys actually read. Eutropius's Breviarium gives the whole of Roman history in plain classical prose. The goal is volume and speed.
objectives: Read Fabulae Faciles through, about 60 pages of Latin
Read 20+ of Corderius's and several of Erasmus's Colloquies, and act out one aloud
Read Eutropius Books I–II (kings and early Republic) as a historical reader
Sustain 15 minutes of reading without stopping to parse every word

coreTexts.title: Ritchie's Fabulae Faciles: A First Latin Reader
coreTexts.author: Francis Ritchie (ed. J. C. Kirtland)

links.label: Steadman edition with facing vocabulary (free PDF)

coreTexts.title: Colloquiorum Centuria Selecta (Corderius's school colloquies, Willymot ed.)
coreTexts.author: Mathurin Cordier

curriculumOptions.name: Lingua Latina, Familia Romana (reading supplement)
curriculumOptions.notes: If Ørberg was not the main text in latin-04, use it here as the extensive reader.

curriculumOptions.name: Latin Alive! (Books 1–3)
curriculumOptions.notes: Upper-school course with many adapted readings from real authors.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boston Latin School, 1789: "Corderius's Colloquies — Latin and English… Aesop's Fables — Latin and English… Eutropius". Otis also recalled "Clarke's Introduction" and "making Latin" from Garretson's Exercises in the fourth year. Erasmus's Colloquies were read in English and colonial grammar schools from Milton's day onward.

sources.label: Catalogue of the Boston Public Latin School (1886)

rows.title: Reference Grammars: Bennett, Allen & Greenough, Gildersleeve
rows.summary: The student learns to use a full scholarly reference grammar, the habit of the nineteenth-century schoolboy. Bennett is compact enough for daily use. Allen & Greenough is the standard American citation grammar ("A&G §419"). Gildersleeve & Lodge serves the advanced student and composition. From here on, every commentary note is looked up.
objectives: Find any construction in Bennett or A&G by index and section number
Explain a syntax point by citing its grammar section
Read the grammar's sections on prosody (dactylic hexameter) before starting Ovid

coreTexts.title: Allen and Greenough's New Latin Grammar
coreTexts.author: J. H. Allen & J. B. Greenough

curriculumOptions.name: Henle Latin Grammar
curriculumOptions.publisher: Loyola Press (sold by Memoria Press, Christianbook)
curriculumOptions.notes: The 250-page reference that goes with all four years of Henle. The friendliest bridge to A&G.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Eton, Westminster and the American academies taught from a single grammar learned by heart: Lily's grammar, later the Eton Latin Grammar in England, and Ward's revision of Lily in Boston. By the late 1800s Allen & Greenough, Bennett and Gildersleeve were the standard American school and college grammars.

rows.title: Caesar & Nepos: First Real Authors
rows.summary: The traditional first unadapted author. The student reads Caesar's Gallic War (Books I–IV with the Helvetian campaign) and Nepos's Lives (Hannibal, Themistocles, Atticus). The prose is clear, military and political, and it trains accurate construing. It also opens discussion of ambition, command and the fall of the Republic.
objectives: Read at least Bellum Gallicum I and selections from II–VII in Latin
Read three of Nepos's Lives, including Hannibal
Construe periodic sentences with ablative absolutes and indirect speech
Write a one-page English essay judging Caesar as a commander and a statesman

links.label: Steadman, College Caesar (free PDF with facing vocabulary)
Dickinson College Commentaries, Life of Hannibal

curriculumOptions.name: Henle Latin, Second Year (Caesar)
curriculumOptions.notes: Caesar with a steady grammar review and composition.

curriculumOptions.name: Caesar: Selections from De Bello Gallico (Mueller)
curriculumOptions.notes: The classic Mueller school edition with running vocabulary.

curriculumOptions.name: Dickinson College Commentaries, Caesar and Nepos
curriculumOptions.notes: Free and scholarly, with audio and vocabulary lists. Enough on its own for a strong self-directed student.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boston 1789, third class: "Caesar's Commentaries. Tully's Epistles, or Offices. Ovid's Metamorphoses. Virgil." In the Boston Latin course of the 1880s the Fifth Class read "Nepos; Justin" and the Fourth Class "Caesar, De Bello Gallico". Caesar remained the standard college-entrance author well into the 1900s.

sources.label: Catalogue of the Boston Public Latin School (1886)

rows.title: Latin Composition I: Bradley's Arnold & North and Hillard
rows.summary: "Making Latin": English-to-Latin prose composition done weekly across two to three years. The student starts with single sentences on one construction at a time (Bradley's Arnold) and moves to connected passages in the style of Caesar and Cicero (North & Hillard). Nothing else fixes grammar so permanently.
objectives: Complete the exercises of Bradley's Arnold Parts I–II
Write a correct 100-word Latin paragraph in the style of Caesar
Choose the right idiom for purpose, result, indirect speech and conditions
Keep a personal phrase-book of Ciceronian idioms collected from reading

coreTexts.title: A Practical Introduction to Latin Prose Composition (Bradley's Arnold)
coreTexts.author: Thomas Kerchever Arnold, rev. George Granville Bradley

coreTexts.title: Latin Prose Composition for the Middle Forms of Schools
coreTexts.author: M. A. North & A. E. Hillard

curriculumOptions.name: Henle Latin (composition exercises, Years 1–3)
curriculumOptions.notes: Henle builds English-to-Latin exercises into every unit, so it can stand in for Arnold for younger students.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The 1789 Boston course prescribes "The making of Latin, from Garretson's Exercises" in the second class and "The making of Latin from King's History of the Heathen Gods" in the third. Bradley's Arnold and North & Hillard were the standard English public-school (Eton, Rugby, Marlborough) and American prep-school composition books c. 1880–1950.
rows.notes: Done with a tutor (the family has tutors available): prose and verse composition need an expert to correct the student's exercises line by line. The "Arnold" of Bradley's Arnold is Thomas Kerchever Arnold, not Thomas Arnold of Rugby. Bradley was Master of Marlborough and later Dean of Westminster. Answer keys were restricted to teachers, so a Latinist tutor to correct proses is highly desirable.

rows.title: Ovid: Metamorphoses & Tristia (First Latin Verse)
rows.summary: The first Latin poetry. The student reads selected myths from the Metamorphoses (Creation and Flood, Daedalus and Icarus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Baucis and Philemon, Apollo and Daphne) and some of Ovid's exile elegies, the Tristia. He learns to scan the dactylic hexameter and the elegiac couplet aloud. Ovid is the mythological dictionary of all later Western art and poetry.
objectives: Scan and read aloud dactylic hexameter and elegiac couplets fluently
Read about 600–800 lines of the Metamorphoses in Latin
Memorize and recite the opening of the Metamorphoses (I.1–20)
Trace three Ovidian myths into later English poetry or painting

curriculumOptions.name: Steadman, Ovid selections (free PDF with facing vocabulary)
curriculumOptions.notes: Pharr-format pages with vocabulary and notes on the same page. Free PDF or cheap paperback.

curriculumOptions.name: Lingua Latina Pars II, Roma Aeterna (poetry chapters)
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes Ovid excerpts in its natural-method progression.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boston's early course had "Ovid de Tristibus" and the Metamorphoses. In 1789, "Ovid's Metamorphoses" was set in the third class. Boston Latin in the 1880s read the Metamorphoses in the Fourth Class alongside Caesar.

rows.title: Ecclesiastical Latin I: Vulgate, Hymns, Mass & the Hours
rows.summary: Latin as the living language of the Church. The student reads the Vulgate (Genesis 1–11, Gospel of John, Psalms), the great hymns (Veni Creator, Pange Lingua, Dies Irae, Stabat Mater), the Ordinary of the Mass, and Vespers and Compline. He learns where medieval Latin differs from classical usage. Prayer and grammar reinforce each other.
objectives: Read the Vulgate Genesis 1–3 and John 1 without a translation
Follow the Latin Mass (Ordinary) and Compline in Latin with understanding
Memorize and sing or recite four great Latin hymns
List the main differences of ecclesiastical and medieval Latin (quod/quia clauses, vocabulary, orthography)

coreTexts.title: Nova Vulgata (official Latin Bible of the Catholic Church)
coreTexts.author: Holy See

coreTexts.title: Divinum Officium (Breviary and Missal texts in Latin)
coreTexts.author: Various

curriculumOptions.name: Lingua Angelica I & II
curriculumOptions.notes: Translation course built on the great Latin hymns and prayers, with recordings.

curriculumOptions.name: Selections from the Vulgate
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded Bible passages in Latin with notes.

curriculumOptions.name: A Primer of Ecclesiastical Latin (John F. Collins)
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard seminary grammar of Church Latin, drawn from the Vulgate and the liturgy. A good second pass for an older student.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boston 1789 included "Selectae e Veteri Testamento Historiae" (Latin Bible stories) in the second class. The Ratio Studiorum assumed daily liturgical Latin for all students.
rows.notes: Catholic and Protestant readers differ here. For Catholics the Vulgate was declared the authentic Latin text by the Council of Trent, and the Nova Vulgata (1979) is the current official edition. Protestants value the Vulgate historically but treat the Hebrew and Greek as the sole authoritative texts. Both traditions read it as the Bible of Western Christendom for a thousand years.

rows.title: Cicero: Orations, Letters, De Amicitia & De Officiis
rows.summary: "Tully", the model of Latin prose and of republican statesmanship. The student reads the First Catilinarian and Pro Archia (the defence of liberal letters), a selection of letters, and De Amicitia and De Senectute. He finishes with De Officiis Book I, the moral handbook of the founders' generation, which Boston boys read as "Tully's Offices".
objectives: Read In Catilinam I and Pro Archia in full
Read 15–20 letters to Atticus and to friends
Read De Amicitia and De Officiis Book I (all or large parts)
Memorize and declaim "Quo usque tandem" (Cat. I.1–2)
Analyse the structure of a Ciceronian period and a classical oration (exordium to peroratio)

coreTexts.title: Tusculanae Disputationes (selections, esp. Books I and V)
coreTexts.author: Cicero

curriculumOptions.name: Henle Latin, Third Year (Cicero)
curriculumOptions.notes: The Catilinarians and Pro Archia with Henle's grammar and composition apparatus.

curriculumOptions.name: Wheelock's Latin Reader (2nd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Cicero, Livy, Ovid, Catullus, Pliny, Martial, the Vulgate and more, with notes keyed to Wheelock.

curriculumOptions.name: Dickinson College Commentaries, Cicero
curriculumOptions.notes: Free annotated selections from the Verrines, De Imperio and Philippics.

curriculumOptions.name: Ossium Carnes Multae: The Bones' Meats Abundant (Cicero's letters, Latinitatis Corpus II)
curriculumOptions.publisher: Catholic University of America Press (Reginald Foster & Daniel McCarthy)
curriculumOptions.notes: The second volume of Foster's method (see latin-04), reading complete letters of Cicero. For families who began with Ossa Latinitatis Sola.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Harvard's 1642 admission rule: "When any Scholar is able to understand Tully, or such like classicall Latine Author extempore… Let him then and not before be capable of admission." Boston 1789: "Tully's Epistles, or Offices" (third class) and "Tully's Orations" (fourth class). Jefferson recommended "Cicero's philosophies" for morality to his nephew Peter Carr (1785). King's College (Columbia) read the Tusculan Disputations in the fourth year, and Yale examined its Berkeley Scholars on them in 1780 (see the founding lists).

sources.label: New Englands First Fruits (1643), Harvard rules
Jefferson to Peter Carr, 19 Aug 1785 (Wikisource)

rows.title: Virgil: The Aeneid (and Eclogues)
rows.summary: The summit of the school course. The student reads Aeneid Books I, II, IV and VI in full, the rest selectively and the rest in translation, plus Eclogues I and IV. Pietas, duty, founding a nation and the cost of empire make this the founding father's epic. Large passages are memorized.
objectives: Read Aeneid I, II, IV and VI in Latin (about 3,000 lines)
Scan and read hexameter aloud with expression at sight
Memorize at least 100 lines (e.g. I.1–33, VI.847–853)
Write an essay on pietas in Aeneas compared with Achilles or Odysseus
Read Eclogue IV and know its place in Christian reception (the "Messianic" eclogue)

curriculumOptions.name: Henle Latin, Fourth Year (Virgil)
curriculumOptions.notes: Aeneid selections with the Henle apparatus. Closes the Jesuit four-year cycle.

curriculumOptions.name: Vergil's Aeneid: Selected Readings from Books 1, 2, 4 and 6
curriculumOptions.notes: A student reader of the most-taught books.

curriculumOptions.name: Dickinson College Commentaries, Aeneid
curriculumOptions.notes: Free full-scale commentary with audio. Excellent for independent study.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Harvard's 1642 admission rule named Tully (Cicero); Virgil was added to the requirement by the 1655 laws. In Boston 1789 the upper classes read Virgil, and Otis recalled "the first books of the Aeneid". In the 1880s the Boston Latin Fourth Class read Aeneid I–II and the Third Class Aeneid III–V and the Eclogues. Jefferson listed Virgil first among the poets Carr "will read at school".
rows.notes: Pronunciation: introduce restored classical pronunciation here, so the quantities and meter of Virgil's hexameter can be heard. Ecclesiastical pronunciation remains the default for Church Latin.

rows.title: Roman Historians: Livy & Sallust
rows.summary: Roman history in Roman words. Livy's Preface and Book I (the kings, Lucretia, the founding of liberty) and selections from the Hannibalic war (Books XXI–XXII). Sallust's Bellum Catilinae is read as a study of republican decay beside Cicero's speeches. These were the founders' handbooks on virtue, faction and liberty.
objectives: Read Livy's Praefatio and large parts of Book I in Latin
Read Sallust's Bellum Catilinae (chapters 1–13 and the Caesar–Cato debate, 51–54)
Compare Sallust's Catiline with Cicero's in an essay
Draw three lessons on republican virtue that Adams or Jefferson drew from Roman history

curriculumOptions.name: Lingua Latina Pars II, Roma Aeterna
curriculumOptions.notes: Its later chapters are lightly adapted Livy, a good lead-in to the unadapted text.

curriculumOptions.name: Steadman Livy & Sallust editions
curriculumOptions.notes: Free PDFs with facing vocabulary and notes. Low-cost paperbacks.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Boston Latin course of the 1880s set "Sallust, Catiline" in the Third Class. Jefferson told Carr (1785) to read history "in the original and not in translations", and planned for him to move from the Greek historians to "Roman history".

rows.title: Horace: Odes, Satires & Epistles (with the Ars Poetica)
rows.summary: The poet of the golden mean, contentment and friendship, and the most quoted Latin author in eighteenth-century English letters. The student reads selected Odes (I.9, I.11, II.3, II.10, III.1–6 "Roman Odes", III.30), two Satires and the Ars Poetica. He learns the lyric metres (Alcaic, Sapphic, Asclepiad) and builds a stock of tags for conversation and writing.
objectives: Read 25–30 Odes and scan the Alcaic, Sapphic and Asclepiad metres
Read the Ars Poetica and summarize its precepts on poetry
Memorize five Odes (e.g. I.11 "carpe diem", III.2 "dulce et decorum", III.30 "exegi monumentum")
Imitate one Horatian ode in English verse

curriculumOptions.name: Wheelock's Latin Reader
curriculumOptions.notes: Contains Horace and Catullus selections with notes.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Horace was set in Boston's highest class in 1789 ("Greek Testament. Horace. Homer."). Jefferson names Horace among the school poets. Eton and Westminster boys memorized Horace in bulk and composed Latin lyric verse on his model.

rows.title: Latin Composition II: Advanced Prose & Verse
rows.summary: The capstone of "making Latin". The student writes continuous Ciceronian prose from English originals (a Federalist paragraph, a Burke passage, a Washington letter) and composes Latin elegiacs and hexameters with a Gradus ad Parnassum. The aim is to write a Latin letter, speech or dedication with confidence.
objectives: Complete North & Hillard's continuous-prose passages (Part II)
Render a 250-word English passage into periodic Ciceronian Latin
Compose 12 correct elegiac couplets on a set theme
Write and deliver a short Latin oration (3–5 minutes)

coreTexts.title: Latin Prose Composition for the Middle Forms of Schools
coreTexts.author: M. A. North & A. E. Hillard

coreTexts.title: A Practical Introduction to Latin Prose Composition (Bradley's Arnold), Part III
coreTexts.author: T. K. Arnold, rev. G. G. Bradley

curriculumOptions.name: Live online classes and tutors
curriculumOptions.notes: Live online classical language courses with expert teachers. Useful if a local tutor is not available.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boston 1789, highest class: "Gradus ad Parnassum. The making of Latin continued." English public schools (Eton, Rugby, Shrewsbury) made Latin verse composition the crown of the Sixth Form. Harvard 1642 required candidates to "make and speake true Latine in Verse and Prose".
rows.notes: Done with a tutor (the family has tutors available): prose and verse composition need an expert to correct the student's exercises line by line. A tutor able to correct Latin proses is almost essential. Consider an online Latin prose-composition tutor or a university classicist.

rows.title: Ecclesiastical Latin II: Augustine, Bede & Aquinas
rows.summary: Patristic and medieval Latin prose. The student reads selections from Augustine's Confessions (Book I and the conversion in Book VIII) and Bede's Ecclesiastical History (Caedmon, Gregory and the Angles). He then turns to Thomas Aquinas: the Eucharistic hymns (Pange Lingua, Adoro Te) and the scholastic article form of the Summa (e.g. I q.2 a.3, the Five Ways). He learns how Christian Latin reshaped classical prose.
objectives: Read Confessions I and VIII in Latin
Read Bede HE IV.24 (Caedmon) and II.1 (Gregory and the English slaves)
Read and outline three articles of the Summa Theologiae in Latin (objections, sed contra, respondeo, replies)
Memorize Adoro Te Devote or Pange Lingua

curriculumOptions.name: Steadman, Medieval Latin (free PDF)
curriculumOptions.notes: A graded medieval anthology with facing vocabulary.

curriculumOptions.name: A Primer of Ecclesiastical Latin (Collins)
curriculumOptions.notes: Use as the grammar of reference for Church-Latin idiom.

rows.notes: Augustine is a shared Father for Catholics and Protestants (Luther was an Augustinian friar, and Calvin quotes him constantly). Aquinas is the Common Doctor of the Catholic Church. Many Reformed scholastics also read him. Present both receptions briefly.

rows.title: College Latin I: Lucretius & Tacitus
rows.summary: College-level reading of the two hardest "pagan" authors, with a commentary. Lucretius's De Rerum Natura (Books I and III) is Epicurean physics and the ancestor of modern materialism that Jefferson admired. Tacitus's Agricola and Annals I and XV show tyranny, flattery and liberty under the emperors.
objectives: Read De Rerum Natura I and III in Latin and give a Christian and classical critique of Epicureanism
Read the Agricola complete and selections from Annals I, IV and XV
Analyse Tacitean style (brevity, inconcinnity, sententiae)
Write a Latin summary (argumentum) of each book read
rows.historicalPrecedent: Tacitus was a staple of colonial college reading and a favourite of Jefferson and the Whig opposition, as the historian of liberty lost. Colonial colleges read Latin authors through all four years, with Latin as the language of disputations and commencement theses.
rows.notes: Lucretius should be read with a teacher. His denial of providence and of the soul's immortality is the classical counter-position that Christian authors (Lactantius, Augustine, Aquinas) answer.

rows.title: College Latin II: Augustine & Aquinas in Full, Reading at Sight
rows.summary: The finishing course. The student reads the whole of the Confessions in Latin and a sequence of Summa questions (e.g. on law, I-II qq.90–97, which is foundational for natural-law political thought). He reads selections of Neo-Latin (Erasmus, Thomas More's Utopia, Grotius) and practises daily sight-reading of unseen passages from any period. The test is the Harvard standard of reading Tully (and, from 1655, Virgil) "ex tempore".
objectives: Read Confessions I–X in Latin
Read Summa Theologiae I-II qq.90–97 (the Treatise on Law) in Latin
Translate an unseen passage of Cicero, Livy or Virgil at sight with minimal help
Read a Neo-Latin political text (More, Erasmus's Institutio Principis Christiani, or Grotius)
rows.historicalPrecedent: Harvard, 1642: admission required reading "Tully, or such like classicall Latine Author extempore". Graduates then defended Latin theses in public. Colonial college libraries and curricula (Harvard, Yale, William & Mary, King's) assumed Latin as a working language for theology, law and natural philosophy. Jefferson's Latin let him read Grotius, Pufendorf and Coke's Latin sources directly.

sources.label: New Englands First Fruits (1643)

rows.title: Fables, Fairy Tales & First Stories
rows.summary: Daily read-aloud and narration from the oldest stories in the tradition: Aesop, Grimm, Andersen, Andrew Lang's fairy books, Beatrix Potter and Kipling's Just So Stories. The fable teaches the moral imagination, and the fairy tale teaches that the world is enchanted, perilous and just. Both supply the stock of allusion that later literature assumes.
objectives: Narrate (retell aloud) a fable or fairy tale in sequence with its key details
State the moral of an Aesop fable in one sentence and apply it to a real situation
Recognize stock characters and patterns (the youngest son, the trickster, the three trials)
Sit attentively through 20–30 minutes of read-aloud of an unabridged text

coreTexts.title: Grimms' Fairy Tales
coreTexts.author: Jacob & Wilhelm Grimm (trans. Edgar Taylor & Marian Edwardes)

coreTexts.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit (and the other Potter tales)
coreTexts.author: Beatrix Potter

curriculumOptions.name: The Blue Fairy Book Set (3rd grade literature guide)
curriculumOptions.notes: Selections from Lang with vocabulary, comprehension and narration questions. Also see their Tales from Beatrix Potter set for 2nd grade.

curriculumOptions.name: Classic Children's Literature (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Parent-facing lectures on why and how to read fairy tales and children's classics. Useful teacher formation.

curriculumOptions.name: Primary Literature (Grades 3–4) Course Plan
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic course plan with tests. An accelerated student can begin it around 6–7.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Aesop was the first reading book of English and colonial grammar schools. Locke's Some Thoughts Concerning Education (1693) recommends Aesop for a child's first reading after the primer, and Aesop was among the handful of books the boy Lincoln read and re-read on the Indiana frontier.
rows.notes: Read unabridged versions. Grimm and Andersen contain frightening episodes; that is part of their moral force. Lang's color fairy books continue through 12 volumes for eager readers.

rows.title: Classic Children's Novels (Read-Aloud)
rows.summary: The first full-length novels, read aloud and then re-read independently. They are the Victorian and Edwardian children's classics: The Wind in the Willows, Heidi, Alice, Pinocchio, Winnie-the-Pooh and George MacDonald's fairy novels. Their prose is rich and their moral worlds are serious, and they build the attention span for long narrative.
objectives: Follow a chapter book across several weeks, recalling characters and earlier events
Narrate a chapter orally and draw a scene from it
Discuss a character's choice (e.g. Toad's boasting, Pinocchio's lies) in terms of virtue and vice
Begin reading shorter chapters independently by age 7–8

coreTexts.title: At the Back of the North Wind
coreTexts.author: George MacDonald

curriculumOptions.name: Heidi Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Text with student and teacher guides. Also available as a Wind in the Willows set and a Winnie-the-Pooh set.

curriculumOptions.name: The Wind in the Willows Set
curriculumOptions.notes: MP places it in 7th grade for independent study. Here it is a read-aloud first and a guided re-read later.

curriculumOptions.name: Literature (Treasure Trove series and read-alouds)
curriculumOptions.notes: Gentle Catholic literature guides for the primary grades.

rows.notes: Kingsley's Water-Babies contains 19th-century anti-Catholic and ethnic jibes. Read it selectively or save it for later with discussion. MacDonald (a Scottish Congregationalist) was the writer Lewis called his "master". His universalist leanings do not surface in these children's books.

rows.title: Pilgrim's Progress, Narnia & the Christian Imagination
rows.summary: Christian allegory and fantasy for young readers. The course reads Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress in a children's retelling, Lewis's seven Chronicles of Narnia, and MacDonald's Curdie books. The child learns to read a story on two levels (literal and allegorical), which is the foundation for Spenser, Dante and Bunyan in full later.
objectives: Identify allegorical figures (Christian, Evangelist, Giant Despair; Aslan) and what they signify
Retell the journey structure of Pilgrim's Progress from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City
Read all seven Narnia books, at least the later ones independently
Connect episodes to Scripture stories already known

coreTexts.title: The Pilgrim's Progress in Words of One Syllable
coreTexts.author: John Bunyan, adapted by Lucy Aikin

coreTexts.title: The Chronicles of Narnia (7 vols., box set)
coreTexts.author: C. S. Lewis

curriculumOptions.name: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Student and teacher guides for the first Narnia book.

curriculumOptions.name: Dangerous Journey Set (Pilgrim's Progress retold)
curriculumOptions.notes: Uses Dangerous Journey, an illustrated abridgement in Bunyan's own words, with a study guide.

curriculumOptions.name: Little Pilgrim's Progress (Illustrated Edition)
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard evangelical children's retelling, with Joe Sutphin's illustrations.

rows.notes: Catholic/Protestant note. Bunyan was a Puritan Baptist preacher, and the allegory reflects Reformed conversion theology (justification received as a crisis, the burden falling off at the Cross). Catholic readers have long loved the book, and Chesterton and Knox both admired it. A Catholic teacher may point out that the pilgrimage also images the lifelong cooperation of grace and works. Lewis was an Anglican whose "mere Christianity" is shared ground for both traditions.

rows.title: Greek & Norse Myths for Children
rows.summary: The gods and heroes of Greece and the North, read in the classic children's versions. The D'Aulaires' books are the modern standard, and Hawthorne's and Kingsley's Victorian retellings supply richer prose. Myth is the grammar of Western allusion. Without it, Milton, Shakespeare and the poets cannot be read.
objectives: Name the Olympians, their attributes and their Roman names
Retell the labors of Heracles and the stories of Perseus, Theseus and Jason
Recognize mythological allusions in everyday language (panic, echo, Achilles' heel)
Contrast the Greek gods with the God of Scripture

rows.notes: Hawthorne's retellings are "Victorianized" (Pandora is a small child, for example). Read the D'Aulaires for the myths as the Greeks told them and Hawthorne for the English prose.

rows.title: Homer, Virgil & the Heroes for Young Readers
rows.summary: The whole story of Troy, the return of Odysseus, Aeneas' voyage to Italy and the quest for the Golden Fleece, in the prose retellings by Alfred J. Church, Padraic Colum and Andrew Lang that generations of schoolchildren read. This prepares the student for Homer and Virgil entire at 12–13 and for Latin reading of the Aeneid.
objectives: Narrate the Trojan War from the Judgment of Paris to the fall of the city
Trace Odysseus' voyage episode by episode and map it
Compare Achilles, Hector, Odysseus and Aeneas as types of heroism (wrath, duty, cunning, piety)
Memorize the opening invocation of the Iliad or Odyssey in English

rows.historicalPrecedent: Victorian and American schoolchildren met Homer through Church's retellings (widely used in 19th- and early 20th-century schools) before construing Homer in Greek. The colonial colleges required Virgil for admission, so the story had to be known by about 12.

rows.title: Tales from Shakespeare & Spenser
rows.summary: A bridge to Shakespeare and the Renaissance. The student reads the Lambs' prose Tales from Shakespeare and Jean Lang's Faerie Queene stories, and memorizes short passages in Shakespeare's own words, following Ken Ludwig's method. The plots and people become familiar years before the plays are studied.
objectives: Retell the plots of at least eight plays (e.g. The Tempest, Midsummer, Macbeth, Lear)
Memorize and recite three short Shakespeare passages (e.g. "I know a bank where the wild thyme blows")
Retell the Redcrosse Knight's quest from Faerie Queene Book I
Watch or attend one live or filmed family-friendly production

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Lambs wrote the Tales (1807) expressly as an introduction to Shakespeare for young readers, and nineteenth-century schoolrooms and nurseries used it that way. Selections from Shakespeare also filled the McGuffey Fifth and Sixth Readers.

rows.title: McGuffey's Readers & the 19th-Century Schoolbook Canon
rows.summary: The anthologies that formed American readers from 1836 into the twentieth century. McGuffey's Fourth to Sixth Eclectic Readers excerpt Shakespeare, Milton, Addison, Johnson, Irving, Scott, Dickens, Webster and the Bible, each with vocabulary and rules for reading aloud. Bingham's Columbian Orator is the declamation book on which Frederick Douglass taught himself. The student reads selections aloud, answers McGuffey's questions, and meets a hundred authors in miniature.
objectives: Read aloud with correct articulation, inflection and emphasis, following McGuffey's rules
Complete the questions and definitions for weekly lessons in the Fourth and Fifth Readers
Keep a commonplace book of memorable sentences from the selections
Identify at least 30 authors the Readers introduce and note which to read in full later

curriculumOptions.name: McGuffey's Eclectic Readers (free, self-directed)
curriculumOptions.notes: The Readers are their own curriculum, with questions and definitions after each lesson. Use them for oral reading 3–4 days a week.

curriculumOptions.name: Recitation program
curriculumOptions.notes: A modern analogue that pairs recitation of poems and passages with the literature year.

rows.historicalPrecedent: McGuffey's Readers sold an estimated 120 million copies between 1836 and 1960. The Fifth and Sixth Readers were in effect the literature course of the American common school. In his Narrative (1845), Douglass records buying The Columbian Orator at about 12 and learning from its dialogues and speeches the arguments against slavery.
rows.notes: The Readers' Protestant moral framing (and occasional anti-Catholic asides in older selections) should be read with discussion. Their literary selections are superb.

rows.title: Legends: Robin Hood & King Arthur
rows.summary: Medieval legend in the great American retellings by Howard Pyle and Sidney Lanier. Pyle's Robin Hood comes first, then his four-volume Arthurian cycle and Lanier's Boy's King Arthur (Malory abridged in Malory's own words), with Pyle's novels of chivalry. This is the school of knighthood as a moral ideal: courtesy, loyalty, largesse and the Grail quest. It prepares for Malory, Spenser and Tennyson later.
objectives: Narrate the major Arthurian episodes (the sword in the stone, the Round Table, the Grail, the fall of Camelot)
Explain the code of chivalry and where knights keep or betray it
Read Malory's own prose (via Lanier) and note archaic words and style
Write a short narrative imitating Pyle's archaic style

rows.title: Adventure, Shipwreck & Quest Novels
rows.summary: The great adventure novels read independently: Treasure Island, Robinson Crusoe, The Swiss Family Robinson, Kidnapped, The Jungle Book, Captains Courageous and Tolkien's The Hobbit. They teach courage, providence, self-reliance and resourcefulness, and they build reading stamina for 300-page books.
objectives: Read at least five full-length novels independently, keeping a reading log
Write a one-paragraph narrative summary and a one-paragraph character sketch for each
Discuss providence and repentance in Robinson Crusoe
Compare Bilbo's and Jim Hawkins' growth in courage

rows.historicalPrecedent: Rousseau's Emile (1762) made Robinson Crusoe the one book a boy should have, and it was a staple of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century boyhood reading. Franklin and Lincoln both read Defoe.

rows.title: What the Founders & Lincoln Read
rows.summary: A unit built on the actual boyhood reading of Franklin, Washington's generation and Lincoln. It covers the King James Bible, Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress in full, Plutarch's Lives, Weems' Life of Washington, Franklin's Autobiography, Robinson Crusoe and Addison's Cato. The student reads the books that formed the men who founded and preserved the republic, and learns why those men valued them.
objectives: Read Pilgrim's Progress (Part I) complete in Bunyan's text
Read at least six of Plutarch's Lives (Lycurgus, Solon, Themistocles, Cato the Younger, Cicero, Caesar)
Read Franklin's Autobiography Part I, noting the books Franklin names and his method of imitating the Spectator
Distinguish legend (Weems' cherry tree) from history, and explain why Weems wrote as he did
Memorize a speech from Addison's Cato (e.g. "'Tis not in mortals to command success")

curriculumOptions.notes: A gentler Plutarch-derived reader if the White edition is too dense. It pairs with the history track.

curriculumOptions.name: Mother of Divine Grace syllabi
curriculumOptions.notes: MODG schedules Franklin's Autobiography and Plutarch in its history and literature years.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin's Autobiography lists his boyhood books: Pilgrim's Progress, Burton's historical collections, Plutarch's Lives ("in which I read abundantly"), Defoe's Essay upon Projects and Mather's Essays to Do Good. He learned to write by rewriting Spectator essays from memory. Herndon's biography records that the young Lincoln read the Bible, Aesop, Pilgrim's Progress, Robinson Crusoe and Weems' Life of Washington; Lincoln later recalled Weems in his 1861 Trenton address. Washington had Addison's Cato performed for the army at Valley Forge, and Nathan Hale's and Patrick Henry's famous lines echo it.

sources.label: Franklin, Autobiography (Gutenberg)
Herndon & Weik, Abraham Lincoln: The True Story of a Great Life, vol. 1

rows.notes: Catholic/Protestant note. The KJV was the Bible of the Founders and of English literature, and it is read here for its literary and historical influence. Catholic families will use the Douay-Rheims (Challoner) for devotion and doctrine (see the theology track). The two share much of their English diction, because the KJV translators consulted the Rheims New Testament.

rows.title: Dickens, Scott & the Historical Romance
rows.summary: Nineteenth-century historical romance and first Dickens. The course reads A Christmas Carol, Scott's Ivanhoe and The Talisman, Stevenson's Black Arrow, Cooper's Last of the Mohicans, Dumas' Three Musketeers and Orczy's Scarlet Pimpernel. It pairs with medieval and early-modern history, and it trains the student in long, richly described Victorian prose.
objectives: Read Scott's Ivanhoe complete and explain its picture of Saxon, Norman and Jew under Richard I
Analyze Scrooge's conversion as a moral structure (past, present, future; repentance and amendment)
Write a comparison essay between two historical novels and the history they fictionalize
Identify the conventions of romance (disguise, tournament, rescue, recognition)

rows.notes: Scott's Ivanhoe contains period prejudices (and an idealized Rebecca that answers them). The Three Musketeers depicts Richelieu unflatteringly and the musketeers' morals loosely; read it with discussion.

rows.title: American Classics for Young Readers
rows.summary: American boyhood and girlhood classics alongside American history. The course reads Irving's Sleepy Hollow, Twain's Tom Sawyer and The Prince and the Pauper, Alcott's Little Women and London's The Call of the Wild, plus two twentieth-century Newbery novels of the Revolution and the early republic (Johnny Tremain; Carry On, Mr. Bowditch).
objectives: Read five American novels independently and discuss their pictures of American character
Identify Twain's humor and satire, and Irving's gentle Gothic
Connect Johnny Tremain to the history of Boston 1773–1775
Write a book review with a thesis statement

rows.title: Shakespeare I: The Comedies
rows.summary: The first plays read in full: A Midsummer Night's Dream, then Twelfth Night, As You Like It, Much Ado About Nothing and The Comedy of Errors. The student reads aloud in parts, memorizes speeches, and stages scenes. Comedy teaches the conventions of Shakespeare's stage and verse (blank verse, prose, song) in the most forgiving form.
objectives: Read three comedies complete, aloud in parts
Memorize and perform at least 40 lines per play, with attention to meter and sense
Distinguish verse from prose speeches and explain why a character shifts between them
Stage one scene for family or co-op, with blocking and simple costume

rows.historicalPrecedent: Declaiming Shakespeare was a staple of 19th-century schoolrooms (the McGuffey Readers and the "Speakers"). Lincoln read and recited Shakespeare all his life and wrote to the actor James Hackett in 1863 that "some of Shakespeare's plays I have never read; while others I have gone over perhaps as frequently as any unprofessional reader."
rows.notes: The Folger texts are free online with line numbers and are ideal for marking up. Buy the Folger paperbacks or MP editions for annotation.

rows.title: Great Expectations, Gulliver & Kim
rows.summary: The transition from children's classics to adult novels. The course reads Dickens's Great Expectations and Oliver Twist, Swift's Gulliver's Travels (all four voyages, the satire now understood), Kipling's Kim, Doyle's Hound of the Baskervilles and Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues. Students begin the formal literary essay.
objectives: Read Great Expectations complete and trace Pip's moral education (pride, ingratitude, repentance)
Explain the targets of Swift's satire in each of Gulliver's four voyages
Write a 3–5 paragraph analytical essay with thesis, textual evidence and conclusion
Identify narrator, point of view and irony

rows.title: Shakespeare II: The Histories & Roman Plays
rows.summary: Shakespeare on kingship, rebellion, war and the republic: Julius Caesar, Henry V, Richard II and Henry IV Part 1. These are the plays a future statesman most needs. The course gives close attention to the great political speeches (Brutus and Antony in the Forum; Henry at Harfleur and Agincourt; Gaunt's "This royal throne of kings") and memorizes one full speech per play.
objectives: Read four history/Roman plays complete
Analyze Antony's funeral oration as rhetoric (ethos, pathos, irony, repetition)
Trace the legitimacy question from Richard II to Henry V (the Henriad)
Memorize and declaim one full speech per play (e.g. St. Crispin's Day, Friends Romans countrymen)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Julius Caesar was among the most-declaimed plays in 19th-century American schools, and its Forum speeches appear in the McGuffey Sixth Reader. John Adams and Jefferson both quoted Shakespeare freely, and on their 1786 visit to Stratford they paid homage at his birthplace.

rows.title: Ancient Epic & Tragedy in Translation
rows.summary: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey and Virgil's Aeneid complete in verse translation. With them come Aeschylus' Oresteia, Sophocles' Theban plays, Euripides' Medea and selections from Ovid's Metamorphoses. This is the foundation of the Western literary tradition, read slowly with seminar discussion. It runs parallel to Latin Aeneid reading and precedes Greek.
objectives: Read the Iliad, Odyssey and Aeneid complete in a verse translation
Explain the epic conventions (invocation, in medias res, catalogue, epic simile, descent to the underworld)
Analyze the tragic hero, hamartia, and the chorus with reference to Aristotle's Poetics
Write a 1,000-word seminar essay comparing Achilles, Odysseus and Aeneas
Memorize the proem of each epic (in English; in Latin for the Aeneid)

curriculumOptions.notes: Kolbe pairs the Iliad with Herodotus and the Aeneid with Livy. Its Roman course is at /products/course-plans-tests-core-ancient-roman-literature-10.

curriculumOptions.notes: Wes Callihan's video great-books course (The Epics; Drama and Lyric; etc.), from a classical Christian perspective.

Hillsdale free course: The Odyssey

rows.historicalPrecedent: Colonial college admission (Harvard, Yale, King's, William & Mary) required the ability to read Virgil and Cicero and to construe the Greek New Testament. Homer in Greek followed in the first college years. J. S. Mill's Autobiography records that Pope's Iliad was the first English poem he loved as a small boy, read alongside the Greek he had begun at three. Jefferson told Peter Carr (1785) to read Homer, Virgil and the Greek tragedians in the original.
rows.notes: Translation choice: Fagles (vigorous, contemporary) or Lattimore (line-for-line, closest to the Greek) for seminar work, and Pope and Dryden as English poems in their own right (see poetry-10). Read Homer in Greek later (Greek track).

rows.title: Shakespeare III: The Great Tragedies
rows.summary: Macbeth, Hamlet, King Lear and Othello, with Romeo and Juliet as the lyric prelude. The student reads each play twice (once for story, once for language), studies the soliloquies closely, and reads a critical edition's essays. The tragedies are the summit of English dramatic poetry and a school in the anatomy of sin, conscience, providence and grace.
objectives: Read five tragedies complete, with at least one read twice in an annotated edition
Explicate a soliloquy line by line (e.g. "To be, or not to be"; "Tomorrow, and tomorrow")
Write a 1,500-word critical essay on a tragedy with engagement of one critic
Memorize and perform a soliloquy of 20+ lines
Discuss Shakespeare's religious world (Catholic recusancy, Protestant England) as critics debate it

curriculumOptions.name: Macbeth, Hamlet & King Lear Sets

curriculumOptions.name: Ignatius Critical Editions (ed. Joseph Pearce)

curriculumOptions.name: Shakespeare: Hamlet and The Tempest (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Prof. Stephen Smith, seven lectures. It pairs Hamlet here with The Tempest in Shakespeare IV.

rows.notes: Catholic/Protestant note. Whether Shakespeare was a crypto-Catholic (Pearce, Asquith) or a conforming Protestant is disputed. Read Hamlet's Purgatory ghost and Lear's world of grace with both readings in view. The texts support fruitful discussion either way.

rows.title: The Christian Middle Ages: Augustine, Beowulf, Dante, Chaucer
rows.summary: The literary achievement of Christendom. The course reads Augustine's Confessions as spiritual autobiography, Beowulf and Sir Gawain as heroic and chivalric poetry, Dante's Divine Comedy complete (or Inferno and Purgatorio with Paradiso selections), the fuller reading of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales in modern verse translation, the morality play Everyman and Malory's Morte d'Arthur. It pairs with the Old English units and medieval history.
objectives: Read the Confessions (Books I–X) and trace the structure of conversion
Read the Inferno and Purgatorio complete, and map Dante's moral architecture

Read the Canterbury Tales in modern verse translation: the General Prologue and at least eight tales (e.g. Knight's, Man of Law's, Wife of Bath's, Clerk's, Franklin's, Pardoner's, Second Nun's, and the Parson's Prologue with the Retraction), leaving the Nun's Priest's Tale for old-english-05
Compare the heroic ideal in Beowulf with the Christian knight in Gawain
Trace the pilgrimage frame and the "quiting" of tale against tale across the Canterbury Tales

coreTexts.author: Geoffrey Chaucer

curriculumOptions.notes: Two semesters on medieval and early Renaissance literature, "from pagan glory through Christian chivalry … to the interior pilgrimage of the soul".

curriculumOptions.notes: MP studies the whole Comedy in 10th grade. The Canterbury Tales set is at /eighth/canterbury-tales-set/.

rows.notes: Catholic/Protestant note. Dante's Purgatorio and his placing of popes in Hell have been read as both supremely Catholic and proto-reformist. Dante is an orthodox Catholic poet who distinguishes the office of the papacy from the sins of individual popes. Longfellow, a Unitarian, translated him out of admiration, and the Comedy is shared ground. Chaucer's pardoner and friars show the lay criticism of clerical abuse that preceded the Reformation. Read the Confessions again in the theology track; here the focus is its art. Chaucer split: this row carries the fuller reading of the Canterbury Tales, in modern verse translation. The original Middle English (the General Prologue and the Nun's Priest's Tale, read aloud with glosses and the opening lines memorized) is taught in old-english-05 at 16, so those selections are not assigned in Middle English here. The bawdy fabliaux (Miller's, Reeve's, Merchant's) are left out at this age.

rows.title: English Literature I: The Renaissance & Seventeenth Century
rows.summary: Spenser's Faerie Queene Book I, Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, Bacon's Essays and the King James Bible as English prose, then Milton's Paradise Lost complete. The prose of Walton, Browne and Bunyan round out the term. This is the age in which English became a great literary language. The metaphysical poets (Donne, Herbert) are read alongside in the poetry track.
objectives: Read Faerie Queene Book I and interpret its allegory of holiness
Read Paradise Lost complete (12 books) and discuss Milton's theodicy and his Satan
Imitate one of Bacon's essays in form and length
Memorize the opening 26 lines of Paradise Lost

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Core is Spenser, Bacon (whom the founders read for counsel on statecraft) and Paradise Lost complete. Catholic/Protestant note. Milton was a Puritan republican whose De Doctrina Christiana held heterodox views (anti-trinitarian leanings, mortalism) that most Protestants also reject. Paradise Lost itself is broadly orthodox in its narrative and is read by both traditions as the great English Christian epic; Lewis's Preface is the classic defense. Spenser's Book I is Protestant allegory: Duessa and Archimago figure the Roman Church. Note this plainly, as a historical fact of Elizabethan polemic.

rows.title: English Literature II: The Augustan Age
rows.summary: Restoration and eighteenth-century literature, the age the Founders read and imitated. The course covers Dryden, Pope's Rape of the Lock and Essay on Man, Swift's satire, Addison and Steele's Spectator, Johnson's Rasselas, Goldsmith's Vicar of Wakefield, and Boswell's Life of Johnson, the greatest biography in English. Its concerns are wit, balance, the heroic couplet and the periodical essay.
objectives: Read Boswell's Life of Johnson (abridged or selections of 300+ pages) and keep a commonplace of Johnson's sayings
Imitate a Spectator essay by Franklin's method (notes, then rewrite, then compare)
Analyze Swift's irony in A Modest Proposal
Explicate a passage of Pope's heroic couplets
