curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic anthology survey "from the author of Beowulf to Chesterton" with longer works.

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry & Prose Book Two (Elizabethan to Neoclassical)
curriculumOptions.notes: Covers Dryden and Pope among others.

rows.historicalPrecedent: This was the living literature of the founding generation. Franklin taught himself to write from the Spectator. Jefferson's 1771 reading list for Robert Skipwith includes Pope, Swift, Addison, Goldsmith, Johnson and Sterne. Washington's favorite play was Addison's Cato, and Adams quoted Pope's Essay on Man in his letters.
rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. The core (Pope's Essay on Man, Swift, the Spectator and Boswell) is what the founding generation itself read and imitated.

rows.title: English Literature III: Austen, Scott & the Romantics
rows.summary: The novel of manners and the Romantic revolution. The course reads Austen's Pride and Prejudice, Emma and Persuasion; Scott's Waverley and The Heart of Mid-Lothian; Mary Shelley's Frankenstein; and the prose criticism of the Romantic poets (Coleridge's Biographia Literaria, Wordsworth's Prelude). The poetry itself (Wordsworth, Coleridge, Keats) is studied in the poetry track.
objectives: Read Pride and Prejudice and Persuasion (and Emma if chosen) and analyze Austen's irony and her moral vocabulary (principle, amiable, sense)
Explain the Romantic shift in the idea of the poet and of nature, using the Prelude (and the Biographia if chosen)
If Frankenstein is chosen, read it as a response to Paradise Lost and to Enlightenment science
Write a 2,000-word comparative essay (e.g. Austen's Elizabeth and Anne Elliot)

coreTexts.title: The Prelude, or Growth of a Poet's Mind
coreTexts.author: William Wordsworth

curriculumOptions.name: Pride & Prejudice Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Third-edition student and teacher guides.

curriculumOptions.name: The Young Jane Austen: Northanger Abbey (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on Austen's early parody. Add Northanger Abbey as a fourth novel if used.

curriculumOptions.name: British Literature Course Plan
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic British survey.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Scott's Waverley is core because Scott was the most widely read novelist of the nineteenth-century schoolroom, and the Prelude because it is the poet's own account of his formation.

rows.title: English Literature IV: The Victorian Novel
rows.summary: The great Victorian novels of the 1840s–60s. The course reads Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre, Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights, Dickens's David Copperfield, A Tale of Two Cities and Bleak House, Thackeray's Vanity Fair and Gaskell's North and South. It covers the "condition of England" question, the Victorian conscience, and the novel at the height of its social and moral ambition.
objectives: Read the three core novels (Bleak House complete) and two electives
Analyze how Victorian novels treat class, industry, law and religion
Compare Jane Eyre's passion and the moral frame that judges it with Heathcliff's (if Wuthering Heights is chosen) or Becky Sharp's (if Vanity Fair is chosen)
Present a 15-minute seminar introduction on one novel

curriculumOptions.name: Jane Eyre Set / Wuthering Heights Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Wuthering Heights set is at /ninth/wuthering-heights-set/.

curriculumOptions.name: A Tale of Two Cities Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Pairs with the French Revolution in history and Burke in civics.

curriculumOptions.name: English 12 (British Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic British survey with longer works.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Bleak House (law and the Chancery courts) and A Tale of Two Cities (revolution, read with Burke) are core for a future statesman; Jane Eyre is the core novel of conscience.

rows.title: English Literature V: High Victorians & the Oxford Movement
rows.summary: The later Victorian achievement. The course reads George Eliot's Middlemarch (the greatest English novel, by many judgments), Trollope's Barsetshire novels, Hardy's Mayor of Casterbridge, Tennyson's Idylls of the King, and Newman's Apologia, Idea of a University and Loss and Gain. It traces faith and doubt, the Oxford Movement, and the English idea of a gentleman and a liberal education.
objectives: Read Middlemarch complete and analyze its narrator and its ethic of "unhistoric acts"
Read Newman's Idea of a University (Discourses V–VII) and state his definition of liberal knowledge
Compare Hardy's fatalism with Eliot's humanism and Newman's faith
Write a 2,500-word research essay using at least two secondary sources

coreTexts.title: Loss and Gain: The Story of a Convert (elective)
coreTexts.author: John Henry Newman

curriculumOptions.name: British Literature Course Plan
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic British survey. Add Newman in full.

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry Book III: The Romantic to the Victorian Age (set)
curriculumOptions.notes: Anthology and guide for the Victorian poets read alongside.

curriculumOptions.name: English 12 (British Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic anthology survey.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives (The Warden and Barchester Towers may be taken as a pair). Newman's Apologia and Idea of a University are core because they define the liberal education this program aims at. Catholic/Protestant note. Newman (now St. John Henry Newman) left the Church of England for Rome in 1845. The Apologia is his defense of that conversion against Charles Kingsley, and Loss and Gain fictionalizes it. Protestant readers can read him as the great apologist for dogmatic Christianity against liberalism, a cause shared across traditions. George Eliot had lost her evangelical faith; Middlemarch is the humanist counterpoint.

rows.title: English Literature VI: Conrad, Chesterton & the Catholic Revival
rows.summary: Literature of the turn of the twentieth century. The course reads Conrad's Heart of Darkness and Lord Jim; Chesterton's Orthodoxy, The Everlasting Man, The Man Who Was Thursday and the Father Brown stories; Belloc's The Path to Rome; and Eliot's The Waste Land as the modernist crisis to which the Catholic revival answered. Kipling's Kim (read earlier) is revisited as imperial literature.
objectives: Analyze Conrad's frame narration and moral ambiguity
Summarize the argument of Orthodoxy chapter by chapter
Read The Waste Land with notes and identify its sources (Dante, Shakespeare, the Upanishads, the Grail)
Write an essay setting Chesterton's paradox against Conrad's darkness

curriculumOptions.name: Modern Era Literature 12
curriculumOptions.notes: Kolbe's 12th-grade modern literature course.

curriculumOptions.name: English 12 (British Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Its anthology ends with the Catholic literary revival (Chesterton, Belloc, Waugh, Greene).

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Mature content: a parent should read Heart of Darkness (racial language and atrocity) and The Waste Land (the loveless seduction in section III) first and discuss them with the student. Achebe's critique of Conrad is worth reading alongside it at this age.

rows.title: English Literature VII: The Inklings, Waugh, Greene, Orwell & Eliot
rows.summary: Mid-twentieth-century British literature. The course reads Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings; Lewis's Till We Have Faces, Out of the Silent Planet and The Screwtape Letters; Waugh's Brideshead Revisited; Greene's The Power and the Glory; Orwell's Animal Farm and 1984; and Eliot's Four Quartets. It sets the Christian imagination against totalitarianism and the secular age.
objectives: Read The Lord of the Rings complete and discuss its theology of providence, pity and the Ring
Compare the Catholic novels of Waugh and Greene (grace working through sinful men)
Analyze Orwell's treatment of language and power, with "Politics and the English Language"
Explicate one of the Four Quartets (here if chosen, otherwise in poetry-12)

curriculumOptions.name: The Lord of the Rings (MP guides)
curriculumOptions.notes: Study guides for each volume.

curriculumOptions.name: Totalitarian Novels (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on Orwell and other anti-totalitarian fiction.

curriculumOptions.name: An Introduction to C. S. Lewis: Writings and Significance (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Nine-week course on Lewis's fiction and apologetics.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Four Quartets is also studied in poetry-12, and Lewis's fiction may be taken up as electives or as free reading. Mature content: a parent should read Brideshead Revisited, The Power and the Glory and 1984 first and discuss them with the student. Brideshead and The Power and the Glory depict adultery, alcoholism and a sinful priest, in the service of a Catholic account of grace; 1984 has sexual content and scenes of torture. They are placed at 15.5–16 and read with discussion. Catholic/Protestant note: Tolkien was Catholic and Lewis Anglican. Their long friendship, and Lewis's refusal to "go further" to Rome, is itself a good discussion topic.

rows.title: Shakespeare IV: Romances, Sonnets & Full Production
rows.summary: The late romances (The Tempest, The Winter's Tale) with The Merchant of Venice and the Sonnets. The capstone is a full student production of one play, in which the student directs, acts or both, or else a public recitation of 200+ memorized lines. Themes are forgiveness, grace, mercy and justice, and the reconciliation of generations.
objectives: Read The Tempest and The Winter's Tale and analyze the pattern of loss, repentance and restoration
Analyze Portia's "quality of mercy" speech alongside Shylock's claim of justice
Write a production concept (cuts, setting, casting) with justification from the text
Mount or take a principal part in a staged production, or give a 200-line recital

coreTexts.title: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (elective)
coreTexts.author: William Shakespeare

curriculumOptions.name: Shakespeare: Hamlet and The Tempest (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Contrasts Hamlet's tragedy with Prospero's happiness.

curriculumOptions.name: Shakespeare's Romances / Merchant of Venice Set
curriculumOptions.notes: The Merchant of Venice set is at /ninth/merchant-of-venice-set/.

curriculumOptions.name: Challenge III (Poetry and Shakespeare strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: Five plays a year with a Christian commentary, plus a student poetry anthology.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 1 of the electives. The Sonnets are also studied in poetry-09, and the Complete Works serves when the production is of a play not read here. The Merchant of Venice raises anti-Judaism directly. Read it with that history in view.

rows.title: American Literature I: Founding to the American Renaissance
rows.summary: American letters from Franklin to Melville. The course reads Franklin's Autobiography complete, Irving's Sketch-Book, Cooper's Deerslayer, Poe's tales and poems, Hawthorne's Scarlet Letter, Melville's Moby-Dick, Emerson's Essays, Thoreau's Walden and "Civil Disobedience", and Douglass's Narrative. The questions are what is American about American literature, and how Puritan, Enlightenment and Romantic strands interweave.
objectives: Read Moby-Dick complete and discuss its cosmology, its Ahab and its Ishmael
Contrast Hawthorne's Puritan conscience with Emerson's self-reliance
Analyze Douglass's Narrative as rhetoric and as an argument from natural rights
Write a thesis-driven essay on an American Renaissance text

coreTexts.title: The Works of Edgar Allan Poe, Vol. 1 (tales) (elective)
coreTexts.author: Edgar Allan Poe

coreTexts.title: Walden, and On the Duty of Civil Disobedience (elective)
coreTexts.author: Henry David Thoreau

coreTexts.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
coreTexts.author: Frederick Douglass

curriculumOptions.name: English 11 (American Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic American literature survey.

curriculumOptions.name: Challenge I (American literature strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: About 21 American books with persuasive-essay writing, including sermons and speeches.

curriculumOptions.name: Scarlet Letter Set / Moby-Dick
curriculumOptions.notes: MP also offers a Moby-Dick text and guides (/literature-and-poetry/moby-dick/).

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Franklin, Hawthorne, Melville, Emerson and Douglass are core; Thoreau's "Civil Disobedience" is short enough to read even if Walden is not chosen. Emerson and Thoreau are Transcendentalists who left orthodox Christianity. Read them as the American Romantic counter-tradition, with Hawthorne and Melville as their skeptics. The Gutenberg Scarlet Letter (25344) includes "The Custom-House" introduction.

rows.title: American Literature II: Realism & the Poets (1865–1920)
rows.summary: Post-Civil War American literature. The course reads Twain's Huckleberry Finn, the two great American poets Dickinson and Whitman, Henry James's Daisy Miller and The Portrait of a Lady, Crane's Red Badge of Courage, Cather's My Ántonia, and Frost's early books. American English finds its own voice in the vernacular (Huck), the lyric (Dickinson) and the long line (Whitman).
objectives: Read Huckleberry Finn complete and analyze Huck's crisis of conscience (chapter 31)
Explicate five Dickinson poems and five sections of Song of Myself
Contrast Cather's frontier with James's international theme (if a James novel is chosen)
Write a comparative essay on American realism and naturalism

coreTexts.title: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete
coreTexts.author: Emily Dickinson

coreTexts.title: The Portrait of a Lady, Vol. 1 (elective)
coreTexts.author: Henry James

curriculumOptions.name: Mark Twain: Tom Sawyer, Huckleberry Finn & Short Stories (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Nine lectures by Hillsdale faculty.

curriculumOptions.name: English 11 (American Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic American survey.

curriculumOptions.name: Challenge I (American literature strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: American literature with persuasive essays.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Frost's North of Boston is also read in poetry-12, so choose it here only if that row has not yet been taken. Huckleberry Finn uses racial slurs as part of its satire of slavery. Teach it; do not bowdlerize it. Mature content: a parent should read Whitman's "Children of Adam" section of Leaves of Grass first and discuss it, or assign Song of Myself and the Lincoln elegies without it.

rows.title: American Literature III: Modern & Southern Fiction
rows.summary: Twentieth-century American fiction. The course reads Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby, Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises and The Old Man and the Sea, Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury, Cather's Death Comes for the Archbishop, Flannery O'Connor's stories, Walker Percy's The Moviegoer and Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird. It follows the Lost Generation and the Southern renaissance, and the Catholic novelists' answer to modern alienation.
objectives: Analyze Gatsby's narrator and the American dream as myth
Read five O'Connor stories and explain her "moment of grace" through violence
Compare Hemingway's code hero with Percy's searching Binx Bolling
Write a 2,500-word research essay on one author

coreTexts.title: The Old Man and the Sea
coreTexts.author: Ernest Hemingway

curriculumOptions.name: The Great Gatsby Set / To Kill a Mockingbird Set
curriculumOptions.notes: The Mockingbird set is at /ninth/to-kill-a-mockingbird-set/.

curriculumOptions.name: Modern Era Literature 12
curriculumOptions.notes: Kolbe's modern literature course, with Catholic framing for the modern novel.

curriculumOptions.name: English 11 (American Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic American survey.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 2 of the electives. Mature content: a parent should read The Sun Also Rises and The Sound and the Fury first and discuss them with the student. They are adult books (promiscuity, heavy drinking, suicide, and in Faulkner a disordered family and incestuous obsession) and are placed at 15.5–16 for that reason; The Great Gatsby (adultery, a killing) and The Moviegoer (casual affairs) deserve the same parental reading. Gutenberg's Hemingway, Faulkner and Fitzgerald texts are public domain in the U.S. only (1925–1929 publications). O'Connor and Percy were Catholic converts or cradle Catholics writing for a "hostile audience". Their essays (Mystery and Manners; The Message in the Bottle) make good companion reading. The Fountainhead is read as a critical elective at 15.5–16, for its hold on ambitious young readers and on American politics. Howard Roark's integrity and refusal to compromise his work are admirable; Rand's Objectivism, which makes rational selfishness a virtue and altruism a vice, is set against Aristotle's magnanimous man and his account of friendship (philosophy-07), and against Christian charity and humility (theology-14, character-virtue-09). The student should write on whether Roark is a great-souled man or a proud one. The novel includes a violent sexual encounter that Rand presents approvingly; a parent should read it first.

rows.title: The European Novel in Translation
rows.summary: The Continental novels that English readers treat as their own. The course reads Cervantes' Don Quixote, Manzoni's The Betrothed (the great Catholic novel), Hugo's Les Misérables, Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov, Tolstoy's War and Peace, Sienkiewicz's Quo Vadis and Undset's Kristin Lavransdatter. Students learn to judge translations and to read the novel as moral philosophy.
objectives: Read the three core novels complete and one elective
Discuss the Grand Inquisitor chapter as a seminar text
Compare Manzoni's providence with Cervantes' idealism, or with Tolstoy's philosophy of history if War and Peace is chosen
Compare two translations of one passage and judge their fidelity and style

curriculumOptions.name: World Literature / Honors World Literature
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic world-literature course. An honors version is also offered.

curriculumOptions.name: Modern Era Literature 12
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes modern European fiction.

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books 102: Renaissance to Modern (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes Dostoevsky among its authors.

rows.notes: Core texts are required; choose 1 of the electives. Only one is asked because each core novel (Don Quixote, The Betrothed, The Brothers Karamazov) runs 700–1,000 pages. Mature content: a parent should read Kristin Lavransdatter (premarital sex and adultery, frankly told) and Crime and Punishment (murder, prostitution) first and discuss them with the student; the same applies to the Karamazov household's sensuality and patricide. The Gutenberg Karamazov and Crime and Punishment are Constance Garnett's translations. For seminar work, consider buying Pevear & Volokhonsky.

rows.title: Great Books Seminar I: Antiquity & the Bible
rows.summary: A college-level Socratic seminar on the ancient foundations, modeled on the freshman years of St. John's College and Thomas Aquinas College and on Hillsdale's Great Books 101. It re-reads Homer in full, and adds Hesiod, Herodotus and Thucydides, Plato's Republic, Aristotle's Ethics, Lucretius and Virgil, with Genesis, Exodus and Job as literature. Texts are read in Greek or Latin where the language tracks allow.
objectives: Lead and participate in two-hour seminars on primary texts with no secondary sources
Write a 3,000-word seminar paper and defend it orally (St. John's "don rag" / oral examination)
Read at least one work (e.g. Iliad I or Aeneid I) in the original language
Trace the dialogue between Athens and Jerusalem across the term

coreTexts.title: The Iliad of Homer (trans. Richmond Lattimore)
coreTexts.author: Homer

coreTexts.title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
coreTexts.author: Hesiod (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

coreTexts.title: The History of the Peloponnesian War
coreTexts.author: Thucydides (trans. Richard Crawley)

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books 101: Ancient to Medieval (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: 11-week lecture course (Homer, Sophocles, Virgil, Augustine, Dante, Chaucer) mirroring Hillsdale's required core.

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books Reading List (freshman & sophomore years)
curriculumOptions.notes: The canonical all-seminar curriculum. The freshman year is Greek.

curriculumOptions.name: Syllabus (Freshman year)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic great-books curriculum ordered toward theology, with Aristotle and Euclid at its center.

sources.label: Hillsdale College: Classical Liberal Arts Core

rows.historicalPrecedent: The colonial college course of study was largely this list read in the original. Harvard's seventeenth- and eighteenth-century course included Greek and Hebrew Scripture, the Greek poets and orators, Aristotelian logic and ethics, and Cicero. J. S. Mill had read Herodotus, Xenophon and six dialogues of Plato in Greek by age 8, and Thucydides and Aristotle's Rhetoric by 12.
rows.notes: Plato, Aristotle and Scripture stay in this seminar as works of literature, because St. John's College and Thomas Aquinas College read them that way: as dialogues, arguments and narratives to be discussed whole around a table. Philosophical and theological depth comes in the philosophy track (philosophy-05) and the theology track (theology-15). This seminar reads them as literature and conversation; coordinate so works are not read twice at the same depth.

rows.title: Great Books Seminar II: Christendom to the Modern Age
rows.summary: A second college seminar, from Dante complete through Cervantes, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Milton, Pascal, Goethe and Dostoevsky, on the model of Hillsdale's Great Books 102 and the St. John's junior year. It closes the literature track with the student able to read, discuss and write about any major work of the Western canon at the level of a strong college junior.
objectives: Read the Paradiso complete, and write on the unity of the Comedy
Discuss Montaigne's and Pascal's rival accounts of the self
Write and defend a senior-style essay (5,000 words) on a text of the student's choosing
Present a public lecture or a seminar-leader's opening question to an audience

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books 102: Renaissance to Modern (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Shakespeare, Milton, Dostoevsky, Austen, Twain and more.

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books Reading List (junior & senior years)
curriculumOptions.notes: The junior and senior years cover the modern authors.

curriculumOptions.name: Syllabus (Junior & Senior years)
curriculumOptions.notes: TAC's upper years pair modern literature with St. Thomas.

rows.notes: Several texts here were first read at 13–16. The seminar re-reads them at college depth, which is the classical principle of returning to the same great works at each stage.

rows.title: Puzzles, Games & First Reasoning
rows.summary: Grid deduction puzzles, riddles, strategy games (chess, checkers) and "what follows?" talk at the table build the habit of reasoning step by step before any formal terminology. Children learn to hold several clues in mind, rule out possibilities and explain why an answer must be true.
objectives: Solve grid-style deduction puzzles by recording and eliminating possibilities
Explain an answer aloud with "because" and "therefore"
Distinguish a guess from a conclusion that must follow from clues
Play strategy games while thinking two moves ahead

curriculumOptions.name: Mind Benders (Levels 1–4, plus Verbal)
curriculumOptions.notes: Best-selling deductive grid puzzles, graded by level. Short, self-checking, and good for 10–15 minutes a day. The Verbal book is read aloud to children who are not yet fluent readers.

rows.notes: Keep this playful and short. Chess is the classic companion to this unit. Parents can model reasoning aloud: "If it rained, the grass is wet; the grass is dry; so..."

rows.title: Informal Logic: Fallacies & Good Arguments
rows.summary: Students learn to recognize the common informal fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, red herring, begging the question, false dilemma, slippery slope, and others) in advertisements, speeches, and everyday argument. This is the natural entry point to the "logic stage" of the trivium, and it makes children alert, charitable critics of what they hear.
objectives: Name, define, and give an original example of about 25–35 informal fallacies
Identify fallacies in ads, cartoons, political speeches and editorials
Distinguish relevance, presumption and clarity fallacies
Restate an opponent's argument fairly before criticizing it

curriculumOptions.name: The Art of Argument (Revised Edition)
curriculumOptions.notes: Teaches 28 informal fallacies with dialogues and many real-world ad examples. It has a teacher's edition and a video course, and is aimed at middle school and up.

curriculumOptions.name: The Fallacy Detective (38 lessons)
curriculumOptions.notes: Light, cartoon-rich lessons from a Christian homeschool family, nominally ages 12 and up. Strong readers can do it at 10. It is short enough to finish in a semester.

rows.notes: You can use both: Fallacy Detective at 9–10 and Art of Argument at 10–11. Keep a family "fallacy jar" for the ones you catch at dinner.

rows.title: Traditional Logic I: Terms, Propositions & the Syllogism
rows.summary: This is the core of formal Aristotelian logic: the three acts of the mind (simple apprehension, judgment, reasoning), the four categorical propositions (A, E, I, O), the square of opposition, equivalence (conversion, obversion, contraposition), and the rules for the validity of the categorical syllogism. It is the logic that Western schools taught from the medieval universities through the 19th century.
objectives: Classify propositions by quantity and quality (A, E, I, O)
Use the square of opposition to infer truth values
Convert, obvert and contrapose propositions correctly
Determine mood and figure, and test syllogisms against the seven rules of validity

curriculumOptions.name: Traditional Logic I Complete Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Textbook, workbook, quizzes and tests, a key, and instructional video by Martin Cothran. It is designed for grade 7 and up and takes about one semester.

curriculumOptions.name: The Discovery of Deduction
curriculumOptions.notes: Categorical logic taught through Socratic dialogue, with more history of logic than Cothran. It is written for grade 8 and up and has a video course.

curriculumOptions.name: Introductory Logic
curriculumOptions.notes: The Canon Logic series used in classical Christian (ACCS) schools. It covers terms, propositions and syllogisms, and leads into Canon's Intermediate Logic.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Jesuit Ratio Studiorum (1599) and English grammar schools alike assumed a boy would enter university already able to dispute in syllogisms. Harvard's first course of study, described in New England's First Fruits (1643), put logic in the first year.

rows.title: Traditional Logic II & Socratic Logic
rows.summary: This course extends categorical logic to enthymemes, sorites, hypothetical and disjunctive syllogisms, and dilemmas, and applies it to real arguments. Kreeft's Socratic Logic is the reference text: it is the most complete Aristotelian logic in print, written with wit and dialogue, and many exercises come from the great books.
objectives: Reduce enthymemes to full syllogisms by supplying the missing premise
Analyze hypothetical, disjunctive and conjunctive syllogisms and dilemmas
Translate ordinary-language arguments into logical form
Define terms by genus and specific difference and test definitions

coreTexts.title: Socratic Logic: A Logic Text using Socratic Method, Platonic Questions, and Aristotelian Principles (ed. 3.1)
coreTexts.author: Peter Kreeft

curriculumOptions.name: Traditional Logic II Complete Set
curriculumOptions.notes: The direct sequel to Traditional Logic I, covering advanced syllogistic forms.

curriculumOptions.name: Socratic Logic (self-study with a tutor or parent)
curriculumOptions.notes: College-level but readable. Use its exercises selectively at 12–13 and return to it as a reference through high school.

rows.title: Material Logic & the Liberal Arts of the Trivium
rows.summary: Formal logic concerns the shape of reasoning. Material logic concerns its content: the categories and predicables, definition and division, and the modes of knowing and of argumentation (demonstration, dialectic, rhetoric, poetics). Sister Miriam Joseph's The Trivium joins logic, grammar and rhetoric in one Catholic, Aristotelian-Thomist philosophy of language.
objectives: Name and apply Aristotle's ten categories and the five predicables
Distinguish demonstrative, dialectical, rhetorical and poetic argument
Build definitions and divisions that are neither too broad nor too narrow
Explain how grammar, logic and rhetoric correspond to thought, reality and communication

coreTexts.title: The Trivium: The Liberal Arts of Logic, Grammar, and Rhetoric
coreTexts.author: Sister Miriam Joseph, C.S.C.

curriculumOptions.name: Material Logic Complete Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Modes of being, knowledge and argumentation. A one- or two-semester follow-up to Traditional Logic.

curriculumOptions.name: The Trivium (with The Trivium Companion)
curriculumOptions.notes: Written for freshmen at Saint Mary's College (Notre Dame) in the 1930s–40s. Dense but beautiful, and best read slowly with a tutor.

rows.title: The Logic Masters: Watts, Jevons & Joseph
rows.summary: The student reads the textbooks that formed earlier generations of statesmen and scholars. Isaac Watts's Logick (1724) was the standard logic at the colonial colleges; Jevons's Elementary Lessons in Logic (1870) served Victorian schools; and H.W.B. Joseph's Oxford Introduction to Logic (1906) is the fullest traditional treatment in English. Watts also teaches the practical "right use of reason": judgment, prejudice, and method in study.
objectives: Read and summarize Watts's four parts (perception, judgment, reasoning, method)
Work Jevons's exercises, including his introduction to induction
Compare how three centuries of textbooks define the syllogism and fallacies
Write a short essay on a "prejudice" of judgment in the manner of Watts

coreTexts.title: Logick: or, The Right Use of Reason in the Enquiry after Truth
coreTexts.author: Isaac Watts

coreTexts.title: Elementary Lessons in Logic: Deductive and Inductive
coreTexts.author: W. Stanley Jevons

rows.historicalPrecedent: Watts's Logick went through dozens of editions and was the standard logic at Harvard, Yale and Oxford through much of the 18th century, so many of the Founders' teachers learned from it. Jevons's Lessons was the usual English school and university text in the late 19th century.
rows.notes: This is a reading unit, not a drill course. Assign selected chapters, have the student narrate them, and compare them with Memoria Press or Kreeft.

rows.title: Symbolic Logic: Truth Tables, Proofs & Boolean Reasoning
rows.summary: Modern propositional and predicate logic covers symbolization, truth tables, validity and consistency, formal proofs (natural deduction), truth trees, and quantifiers. It links Aristotle to Boole, Frege and computer science, and prepares the student for mathematics proofs, programming and analytic philosophy.
objectives: Symbolize English sentences with connectives and quantifiers
Build truth tables to test validity, equivalence and consistency
Construct natural-deduction proofs using the standard rules of inference
Explain the relation of Boolean algebra to logic gates and circuits

coreTexts.title: forall x: Calgary. An Introduction to Formal Logic
coreTexts.author: P.D. Magnus, Tim Button, et al.

curriculumOptions.name: Intermediate Logic (Mastering Propositional Arguments)
curriculumOptions.notes: Truth tables, formal proofs, truth trees and argument analysis, with DVD lessons by James Nance. For grade 8 and up, and the most accessible option for home study.

curriculumOptions.name: A Concise Introduction to Logic (14th ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: The most widely used college intro text, covering informal, categorical, propositional and predicate logic and induction. It is suitable for dual-credit rigor at 15–16.

curriculumOptions.name: forall x: Calgary
curriculumOptions.notes: A free, rigorous open textbook with solutions. Good for a mathematically minded student.

rows.title: College Seminar: Aristotle's Organon, Induction & Scientific Method
rows.summary: The student reads Aristotle's own logical works (Categories, On Interpretation, and selections from the Prior Analytics) with a tutor, as at Thomas Aquinas College and St. John's College. The seminar then follows the argument about method: Bacon's Novum Organum and Mill's System of Logic on induction and the canons of experimental inquiry.
objectives: Read the Categories and On Interpretation closely and explain the key distinctions
Reconstruct Aristotle's proofs of the valid moods in the Prior Analytics
Compare Aristotelian demonstration with Baconian and Millian induction
Apply Mill's methods of agreement and difference to a real causal question

coreTexts.title: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
coreTexts.author: John Stuart Mill

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Logic and Rhetoric (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Ten lectures modeled on the logic and rhetoric core course that every Hillsdale student takes. A good capstone overview alongside the primary texts.

curriculumOptions.name: Thomas Aquinas College syllabus (logic tutorial, freshman year)
curriculumOptions.notes: A model reading list for pacing the Organon in seminar.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Aristotle's Organon was the backbone of the medieval arts degree and remained in the curriculum at Oxford and the colonial colleges. J.S. Mill, whose father had him study logic as a boy, wrote the System of Logic that became the standard 19th-century account of induction.

rows.title: Number Talk, Counting & Finger Patterns
rows.summary: Number sense starts in the home language long before school. Parents who count stairs, grapes and buttons aloud, name small quantities ("two shoes"), and use comparison words (more, fewer, bigger) give children a measurably larger early number vocabulary, and early math knowledge is one of the strongest predictors of later school achievement.
objectives: Hear counting and quantity words in daily routines (meals, stairs, dressing)
Recognize one, two, three objects at a glance (subitizing)
Recite counting songs and rhymes and begin one-to-one counting by about 3
Use comparison words (more, less, same, big, small)

curriculumOptions.name: DREME Family Math resources
curriculumOptions.notes: Free, research-based activities for everyday number talk with babies and toddlers.

sources.label: Levine et al. (2010), What counts in the development of young children's number knowledge?
Duncan et al. (2007), School readiness and later achievement

rows.notes: Keep it conversational and joyful. No worksheets or screens are needed at this age; the evidence favors adult talk about quantity during ordinary life.

rows.title: Pattern, Shape & Spatial Play
rows.summary: Block building, puzzles, pattern blocks, tangrams and sorting games develop the spatial reasoning and patterning that underlie geometry and algebra. Preschoolers' skill at copying block structures predicts their early mathematics, and linear number board games (like Chutes and Ladders) improve number-line understanding.
objectives: Sort and classify by color, shape and size
Copy and extend simple patterns (AB, ABB, ABC)
Build and copy block structures and complete jigsaw puzzles
Play linear number board games, counting spaces aloud

sources.label: Verdine et al. (2014), Deconstructing Building Blocks (Child Development)
Siegler & Ramani (2008), Playing linear numerical board games
AAP (2018), The Power of Play

rows.notes: Use unit blocks, pattern blocks, tangrams and simple board games. Name shapes and positions (above, beside, inside).

rows.title: Montessori Materials & Concrete Number
rows.summary: Montessori-style concrete materials (number rods, sandpaper numerals, spindle boxes, golden bead place-value materials) let children handle quantity before they write symbols. Add cooking, measuring, money and calendar play. By 6 the child should count reliably past 100, understand "ten and some more," and compose and decompose small numbers.
objectives: Match numerals to quantities 0–10, then to 100
Compose and decompose numbers to 10 (number bonds) with objects
Explore place value with bead or block materials (units, tens, hundreds)
Measure in the kitchen and handle coins

curriculumOptions.name: Association Montessori Internationale
curriculumOptions.notes: Source for authentic Montessori training and materials guidance.

curriculumOptions.name: Numbers books & Counting with Numbers (preschool)
curriculumOptions.notes: Gentle classical preschool workbooks. Use them sparingly, alongside hands-on materials.

sources.label: Lillard & Else-Quest (2006), Evaluating Montessori Education (Science)
Lillard et al. (2017), Montessori Preschool Elevates and Equalizes Child Outcomes

rows.title: Arithmetic I: Number Bonds, Place Value & Math Facts
rows.summary: Formal arithmetic on the Singapore (concrete–pictorial–abstract) model that Hillsdale K-12 uses: numbers to 1,000, addition and subtraction with regrouping, the beginnings of multiplication, money, time and measurement. Addition and subtraction facts are memorized to automaticity through daily oral drill.
objectives: Master addition and subtraction facts to 20 with instant recall
Understand place value to 1,000 and regroup confidently
Solve one- and two-step word problems with bar models
Tell time, count money and measure length

coreTexts.title: Ray's New Primary Arithmetic for Young Learners
coreTexts.author: Joseph Ray

curriculumOptions.name: Dimensions Math PK–5 (or Primary Mathematics 2022)
curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale K-12's math spine. Strong conceptual foundation with bar-model problem solving.

curriculumOptions.name: RightStart Mathematics
curriculumOptions.notes: Abacus-based, very hands-on. Excellent for mental math and a natural next step after Montessori.

curriculumOptions.name: Rod & Staff Grade 3 Math (as sold in Memoria Press core)
curriculumOptions.notes: Traditional drill-heavy arithmetic (Mennonite author). Rigorous facts practice.

curriculumOptions.name: Math for Young Catholics
curriculumOptions.notes: Seton's own elementary series (grade 1 shown; later grades on the same site). A Catholic option, not a requirement.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Nineteenth-century American schools began with Ray's arithmetic series (from the 1830s), a McGuffey-era companion used by millions. Colonial children learned "cyphering" from manuals such as Nicolas Pike's New and Complete System of Arithmetic (1788), the first widely used American arithmetic.

sources.label: Hillsdale K-12 Curriculum Overview (Singapore Math sequence)

rows.title: Mental Arithmetic & Fact Mastery (Ray's Intellectual Arithmetic)
rows.summary: Daily oral work in the Pestalozzi–Colburn tradition. Children solve problems "in the head" and explain their reasoning aloud, then memorize the multiplication and division tables through 12×12. This is the nineteenth-century "intellectual arithmetic" that trained quick, confident calculators, and it also trains articulate reasoning.
objectives: Recall all multiplication and division facts through 12×12 instantly
Solve multi-step word problems mentally and explain the steps aloud
Compute with fractions of simple quantities mentally

curriculumOptions.name: Multiplication & Division Flashcards
curriculumOptions.notes: Simple daily drill.

curriculumOptions.name: Rod & Staff Speed Drill Packet
curriculumOptions.notes: Timed fact sheets.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Warren Colburn's First Lessons in Intellectual Arithmetic (1821) and Ray's Intellectual Arithmetic made oral mental arithmetic a standard daily exercise in American common schools through the 1800s.
rows.notes: 10–15 minutes daily, run in parallel with the written arithmetic course.

rows.title: Arithmetic II: Multiplication, Fractions, Decimals & Problem Solving
rows.summary: Long multiplication and division, fractions, decimals, percent, ratio, area and volume, and multi-step problems. Pair a solid core text with a harder problem-solving strand (Beast Academy) so that capable children are stretched rather than merely drilled. Ray's Practical Arithmetic provides the classic applications to commerce: interest, measures and business.
objectives: Multiply and divide multi-digit numbers accurately with standard algorithms
Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and decimals
Solve ratio, percent and rate problems with bar models
Compute area, perimeter and volume of basic figures

curriculumOptions.name: Beast Academy (levels 2–5)
curriculumOptions.notes: Comic-guided, challenging problem solving for gifted students. Pairs well with Singapore.

curriculumOptions.name: Dimensions Math 3–5
curriculumOptions.notes: Continues the Hillsdale K-12 sequence.

curriculumOptions.name: Saxon Math (5/4–8/7)
curriculumOptions.notes: Incremental spiral review, used widely by Catholic programs (Mother of Divine Grace, Seton) and classical homeschools. Less conceptual than Singapore.

curriculumOptions.name: Math Mammoth
curriculumOptions.notes: Inexpensive, mastery-based, self-teaching worktexts. A good independent option.

curriculumOptions.name: Math for Young Catholics
curriculumOptions.notes: Seton's own elementary series (grade 1 shown; later grades on the same site). A Catholic option, not a requirement.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Pike's Arithmetic (1788) and later Ray's Practical Arithmetic were used to teach the "rule of three," interest, exchange and mensuration. That was the practical mathematics a merchant or planter of the founding generation needed.

sources.label: Pike, A New and Complete System of Arithmetic (1797 ed.)

rows.title: Pre-Algebra & Higher Arithmetic
rows.summary: The bridge from arithmetic to algebra: integers and negative numbers, exponents, primes and factorization, variables and simple equations, ratio and proportion, and an introduction to geometric reasoning. AoPS Prealgebra teaches by posing problems before explaining. Ray's Higher Arithmetic shows how far the nineteenth century carried pure arithmetic (roots, progressions, mensuration).
objectives: Work fluently with integers, exponents, and prime factorization
Solve linear equations in one variable and translate words into expressions
Reason with ratio, rate and percent in multi-step problems
Explain why arithmetic rules work, not just how

curriculumOptions.name: Prealgebra
curriculumOptions.notes: First choice for strong students. Discovery-based and demanding.

curriculumOptions.name: Memoria Pre-Algebra
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical-school sequence with lesson plans.

curriculumOptions.name: Dimensions Math 6–8
curriculumOptions.notes: Continues Hillsdale's Singapore sequence into pre-algebra.

rows.title: Number Theory & Competition Math I: MATHCOUNTS
rows.summary: Divisibility, primes, GCD/LCM, modular arithmetic and number bases, learned through contest problems. MATHCOUNTS (grades 6–8) gives an accelerated student a team, deadlines and a scoreboard. It builds speed and the habit of attacking unfamiliar problems.
objectives: Use divisibility rules, prime factorization, GCD and LCM in problems
Compute in modular arithmetic and convert between number bases
Compete in MATHCOUNTS at school/chapter level

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Number Theory
curriculumOptions.notes: Standard text for strong middle schoolers.

curriculumOptions.name: MATHCOUNTS Competition Program
curriculumOptions.notes: National middle-school competition. Free problem archives.

coreTexts.title: Essays on the Theory of Numbers
coreTexts.author: Richard Dedekind

rows.notes: Standard for every student (family decision), not optional enrichment. Save Dedekind for later rereading (mathematics-21). It is listed here as the classic foundation of the number concept.

rows.title: Algebra I
rows.summary: Linear equations and inequalities, systems, functions and graphs, polynomials and factoring, radicals, and quadratics. Choose a rigorous text: AoPS for the mathematically gifted, Jacobs for a clear and engaging standard course. Dolciani's mid-century Structure and Method, now out of print but available used, is the traditional rigorous alternative.
objectives: Solve and graph linear equations, inequalities and systems
Factor polynomials and solve quadratics by factoring, completing the square and formula
Understand functions and read graphs
Write clear algebraic justifications for each step

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Algebra
curriculumOptions.notes: Covers Algebra I and much of Algebra II. Best for strong students.

curriculumOptions.name: Elementary Algebra (Harold Jacobs)
curriculumOptions.notes: Jacobs's classic, clear and witty text. Master Books is an evangelical publisher, but the math content is standard.

curriculumOptions.name: Memoria Algebra I
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical-school course with lesson plans and video support.

curriculumOptions.name: Algebra 1 / Honors Algebra 1 (online)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic online school course catalog, for live or self-paced instruction.

curriculumOptions.name: Saxon-based course syllabi
curriculumOptions.notes: MODG publishes Saxon Algebra 1/2, Algebra I, Algebra II and Advanced Math syllabi. A Catholic option, not a requirement.

rows.title: Euclid's Elements I: Books I–IV & Demonstrative Geometry
rows.summary: Geometry learned from the source. Students read, construct (compass and straightedge) and recite the propositions of Euclid Books I–IV, from the definitions and postulates through the Pythagorean theorem and the constructions of polygons. Byrne's colored 1847 edition helps visual learners, and a modern text (Jacobs, Kiselev or AoPS) supplies exercises and coordinate connections. This is the course where the student learns what a proof is.
objectives: State definitions, postulates and common notions and use them in demonstrations
Construct and demonstrate Books I–IV propositions at the board from memory
Prove the Pythagorean theorem (I.47) and its converse
Solve modern geometry problems on congruence, similarity, area and circles

coreTexts.title: The First Six Books of the Elements of Euclid (colored diagrams)
coreTexts.author: Oliver Byrne

coreTexts.title: The First Six Books of the Elements of Euclid
coreTexts.author: John Casey

curriculumOptions.name: Euclid's Elements (Densmore ed., Heath trans.)
curriculumOptions.notes: All thirteen books in one volume, the edition used at St. John's College. A companion "Book One with Questions for Discussion" is also available.

curriculumOptions.name: Geometry: Seeing, Doing, Understanding (Harold Jacobs)
curriculumOptions.notes: Best-loved modern proof-based high-school geometry. Evangelical publisher, standard math.

curriculumOptions.name: Kiselev's Geometry, Book I: Planimetry
curriculumOptions.notes: Kiselev's classic Russian gymnasium text, adapted by A. Givental. Rigorous and elegant.

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Geometry
curriculumOptions.notes: Problem-heavy. Best for competition-bound students.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Euclid was the core of geometry at Harvard, Yale and William & Mary, and at Eton and Rugby, into the 1800s. Hillsdale K-12 still teaches "Euclid's principles, constructions and proofs throughout" its geometry course. Jefferson in retirement wrote that he had given up newspapers "for Newton & Euclid."

sources.label: Jefferson to John Adams, 21 Jan. 1812 (Founders Online)
Hillsdale K-12 Curriculum Overview

rows.notes: Plato's Meno (the slave-boy geometry lesson) makes an ideal companion reading.

rows.title: Algebra II & Gelfand's Algebra
rows.summary: Polynomial, rational, exponential and logarithmic functions, complex numbers, sequences and series, and conic sections. Gelfand and Shen's Algebra, written for the Moscow correspondence school, adds the elegant problem-driven perspective of the Russian tradition.
objectives: Analyze polynomial, rational, exponential and logarithmic functions
Work with complex numbers and the binomial theorem
Sum arithmetic and geometric series and use induction informally

coreTexts.title: Algebra
coreTexts.author: I. M. Gelfand and A. Shen

curriculumOptions.notes: Demanding. Covers AMC/AIME-level algebra.

curriculumOptions.name: Memoria Algebra II
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical-school sequence.

curriculumOptions.name: Honors Algebra 2/Trig (online)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic online option.

curriculumOptions.name: Saxon-based course syllabi
curriculumOptions.notes: MODG publishes Saxon Algebra 1/2, Algebra I, Algebra II and Advanced Math syllabi. A Catholic option, not a requirement.

rows.notes: Foerster's Algebra and Trigonometry (Pearson/Prentice Hall) is a widely praised traditional alternative, but no current publisher page was verified.

rows.title: Euclid's Elements II: Books V–VI, Nicomachus & Archimedes
rows.summary: Eudoxus's theory of proportion (Book V) and similar figures (Book VI). This is the ancient answer to incommensurable magnitudes and the root of the real numbers. Read beside Nicomachus's Introduction to Arithmetic (the medieval quadrivium's arithmetic) and Archimedes's Measurement of a Circle and On the Equilibrium of Planes, which show Greek geometry applied to measurement and mechanics.
objectives: Follow Euclid's definition of same ratio (V, Def. 5) and prove key proportion theorems
Demonstrate Book VI similarity theorems
Reproduce Archimedes's bounds for π from inscribed and circumscribed polygons
Explain the Pythagorean/Nicomachean classification of numbers

coreTexts.title: The First Six Books of the Elements of Euclid
coreTexts.author: Oliver Byrne

coreTexts.title: Introduction to Arithmetic
coreTexts.author: Nicomachus of Gerasa (trans. M. L. D'Ooge)

curriculumOptions.name: Euclid's Elements (Densmore ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Continue in the same edition.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Nicomachus's Arithmetic, through Boethius's Latin adaptation, was the standard arithmetic of the medieval quadrivium. Archimedes's works were core reading for the mathematicians of the Scientific Revolution.
rows.notes: No verified free edition of D'Ooge's Nicomachus translation was found. It is included in Great Books of the Western World vol. 11.

rows.title: Precalculus & Trigonometry (with Gelfand's Trigonometry and Method of Coordinates)
rows.summary: Trigonometric functions and identities, the unit circle, vectors, polar coordinates, complex numbers in polar form, matrices, and limits as a preview of calculus. Gelfand's short books, Trigonometry, Functions and Graphs, and The Method of Coordinates, teach the student to think geometrically about algebra.
objectives: Solve triangles with the laws of sines and cosines
Prove and apply trigonometric identities
Graph and transform functions and use polar and parametric coordinates
Use vectors and matrices for basic geometric problems

coreTexts.title: Trigonometry
coreTexts.author: I. M. Gelfand and M. Saul

coreTexts.title: The Method of Coordinates
coreTexts.author: I. M. Gelfand, E. G. Glagoleva, A. A. Kirillov

coreTexts.title: Functions and Graphs
coreTexts.author: I. M. Gelfand, E. G. Glagoleva, E. E. Shnol

curriculumOptions.name: Precalculus
curriculumOptions.notes: Rigorous, with complex numbers and linear algebra previews.

curriculumOptions.name: Precalculus Lesson Plans
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical-school scheduling support.

curriculumOptions.name: Saxon-based course syllabi
curriculumOptions.notes: MODG publishes Saxon Algebra 1/2, Algebra I, Algebra II and Advanced Math syllabi. A Catholic option, not a requirement.

rows.title: Competition Math II: AMC 10/12 & AIME
rows.summary: A standing problem-solving seminar alongside the main sequence. Students prepare for the American Mathematics Competitions (AMC 10/12) and the AIME, working through algebra, combinatorics, number theory and geometry problems well beyond the textbook. The aim is resourcefulness, not trophies.
objectives: Sit the AMC 10/12 annually and qualify for the AIME
Write up complete solutions to olympiad-style problems
Build a personal toolkit of problem-solving strategies

curriculumOptions.name: American Mathematics Competitions
curriculumOptions.notes: AMC 8/10/12, AIME, USAMO pathway.

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Counting & Probability
curriculumOptions.notes: Core AMC combinatorics text.

rows.notes: Standard for every student (family decision), not optional enrichment.

rows.title: Practical Mathematics: Surveying, Navigation & Measurement
rows.summary: The founders' applied mathematics. Students survey a field with chain (or tape), compass and a homemade theodolite, compute areas by triangulation, plot the plat, and learn celestial navigation basics (latitude from the sun or Polaris). This is trigonometry made concrete, as Washington learned it at 16.
objectives: Measure distances and angles and compute unknown sides by trigonometry
Survey and plat a real parcel of land, computing its area
Determine latitude by sun or Polaris sighting
rows.historicalPrecedent: George Washington taught himself surveying from geometry and trigonometry texts and was commissioned county surveyor of Culpeper in 1749 at 17. Jefferson and Franklin both prized practical mathematics for surveying, astronomy and invention.

sources.label: Mount Vernon: Surveying (Washington's career)

rows.notes: Pairs naturally with practical-arts and natural-science astronomy units.

rows.title: Counting, Probability & Statistics
rows.summary: Combinatorics and probability (permutations, combinations, expected value, conditional probability), then descriptive and inferential statistics: distributions, sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and regression. The civic aim is to read polls, studies and economic data critically.
objectives: Count arrangements and selections and compute probabilities
Summarize data and interpret distributions
Construct confidence intervals and conduct basic hypothesis tests
Critique misleading statistics in news and policy debates

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Counting & Probability
curriculumOptions.notes: Rigorous probability foundation.

curriculumOptions.name: OpenIntro Statistics
curriculumOptions.notes: Free, high-quality introductory statistics (AP level).

curriculumOptions.name: Introductory Statistics 2e
curriculumOptions.notes: Free alternative.

rows.title: Proof Writing: How to Prove It
rows.summary: A bridge from Euclidean demonstration to modern proof. Students study logic, sets, relations, functions, and induction, and write proofs in clear mathematical prose. This prepares them for Spivak-style calculus and for college analysis.
objectives: Write direct, contrapositive, contradiction and induction proofs
Use quantifiers, sets, relations and functions precisely
Critique and revise proofs for rigor and clarity

coreTexts.title: How to Prove It: A Structured Approach
coreTexts.author: Daniel J. Velleman

rows.title: Calculus (with Thompson, Newton & a Modern Text)
rows.summary: Single-variable calculus to AP BC level and beyond: limits, derivatives, integrals, the fundamental theorem, series, and differential equations. Begin with Thompson's Calculus Made Easy ("What one fool can do, another can"). Then take a full course in Stewart (standard), Spivak (honors and proof-based) or Apostol. Read Newton's own lemmas on first and last ratios from the Principia to see where the ideas came from.
objectives: Differentiate and integrate elementary functions and apply them to motion, area and optimization
State and prove the fundamental theorem of calculus
Work with sequences, series and Taylor polynomials
Read Newton's Principia Book I, Section 1 (first and last ratios) with understanding

coreTexts.title: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy (Principia), Book I §1
coreTexts.author: Isaac Newton, trans. Andrew Motte

curriculumOptions.name: Calculus, 4th ed. (Michael Spivak)
curriculumOptions.notes: The honors choice. Proof-based and beautiful. Take after proof writing.

curriculumOptions.name: Calculus, Vol. 1 (Tom Apostol)
curriculumOptions.notes: Rigorous, integral-first, with linear algebra. Excellent for the mathematically inclined.

curriculumOptions.name: Stewart Calculus
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard AP/college text, with abundant exercises.

curriculumOptions.name: Calculus
curriculumOptions.notes: Rigorous, concise alternative.

curriculumOptions.name: Honors Calculus / AP Calculus AB (online)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic online option.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Newton's natural philosophy was taught at colonial colleges from the 1720s. Isaac Greenwood, Harvard's first Hollis Professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy (1727), and his successor John Winthrop brought Newtonian fluxions into American teaching.

rows.title: Linear Algebra
rows.summary: Vectors, matrices, linear systems, vector spaces, linear maps, determinants, eigenvalues and inner products. Strang's MIT course gives the computational and applied view. Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right gives the proof-based, structural view.
objectives: Solve linear systems and interpret them geometrically
Prove basic theorems about vector spaces and linear maps
Compute and apply eigenvalues, eigenvectors and orthogonal projections

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Linear Algebra (Gilbert Strang) + MIT 18.06
curriculumOptions.notes: Free video lectures. The book is at https://math.mit.edu/~gs/linearalgebra/.

curriculumOptions.name: Linear Algebra Done Right (Sheldon Axler)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free PDF. Proof-based second course.

rows.title: Multivariable Calculus & Introduction to Real Analysis
rows.summary: Partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus (Green, Stokes, divergence theorems), then a first rigorous course in analysis: the real numbers, sequences, continuity, differentiation and Riemann integration proved from the ground up.
objectives: Compute multiple and line integrals and apply the vector calculus theorems
Construct epsilon-delta proofs about limits and continuity
Prove the main theorems of single-variable analysis (IVT, MVT, FTC)

curriculumOptions.name: MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus
curriculumOptions.notes: Free full course.

curriculumOptions.name: Vector Calculus, Linear Algebra, and Differential Forms (Hubbard & Hubbard)
curriculumOptions.notes: Unified rigorous treatment, for the strongest students.

curriculumOptions.name: Understanding Analysis (Stephen Abbott)
curriculumOptions.notes: The most readable first analysis text.

rows.title: College Tutorial: The Great Mathematical Books (St. John's Model)
rows.summary: A St. John's College–style mathematics tutorial. Students read the originals and demonstrate them at the board: Ptolemy's Almagest (chord tables and planetary models), Apollonius's Conics, Descartes's Geometry (the birth of analytic geometry), Newton's Principia, Lobachevsky's non-Euclidean Geometrical Researches, and Dedekind's essays on continuity and number. The aim is to understand how mathematics was discovered and what its first principles are.
objectives: Demonstrate selected propositions of Apollonius and Ptolemy
Reconstruct Descartes's solution of Pappus's problem
Follow Lobachevsky's construction of a geometry without the parallel postulate
Explain Dedekind's construction of the real numbers by cuts

coreTexts.title: The Geometry of René Descartes (Smith & Latham trans.)
coreTexts.author: René Descartes

coreTexts.title: Geometrical Researches on the Theory of Parallels
