coreTexts.title: Essays on the Theory of Numbers
coreTexts.author: Richard Dedekind

curriculumOptions.name: Conics: Books I–IV (Apollonius)
curriculumOptions.notes: Taliaferro translation used in the St. John's tutorial.

curriculumOptions.name: The Almagest: Introduction to the Mathematics of the Heavens (Ptolemy)
curriculumOptions.notes: Selections prepared for tutorial use.

curriculumOptions.name: Newton's Principia: The Central Argument
curriculumOptions.notes: Densmore's guided translation.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Colonial colleges taught arithmetic, geometry and astronomy (Harvard from 1640s; Isaac Greenwood's and John Winthrop's Hollis professorship from 1727/1738). St. John's College has preserved a great-books mathematics tutorial since 1937, and Thomas Aquinas College's curriculum likewise reads Euclid, Ptolemy, Apollonius and Descartes.

sources.label: St. John's College Great Books Reading List
Thomas Aquinas College: Why We Study Mathematics

rows.title: Singing and Solfège: Kodály Foundations
rows.summary: Formal music begins with the voice. The Kodály approach teaches pitch through movable-do solfège and hand signs, rhythm through spoken syllables, and repertoire through the child's own folk songs, moving from sound to sign to symbol. By eight the child sings in tune, keeps a steady beat, and reads simple melodies in stick notation and on the staff.
objectives: Sing 50 or more folk songs, rounds and singing games in tune with a light head voice
Use Curwen hand signs and solfège for the pentatonic scale (s-m, l, d-r), then the full diatonic scale
Read and clap quarter, eighth and half notes and rests with rhythm syllables
Sing simple two-part rounds and ostinati

curriculumOptions.name: Kodály-certified teachers and programs (OAKE)
curriculumOptions.notes: Find a Kodály-trained teacher or children's choir. Materials are folk-song based.

curriculumOptions.name: British Kodály Academy (courses and resources)
curriculumOptions.notes: UK counterpart, with good parent and teacher courses.

curriculumOptions.name: Discovering Art & Music in the Younger Years, Vol. 1
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical Christian introduction to great works of art and music for the early grades.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Zoltán Kodály's method became the basis of Hungarian national music education after 1945. Its roots are older: Guido of Arezzo's syllables (ut-re-mi, c. 1025) and John Curwen's tonic sol-fa and hand signs (England, 1840s–1870s), which taught millions of Victorian children to sing at sight.

rows.title: The Ward Method: Chant-Based Musicianship
rows.summary: Justine Ward's method, developed from about 1910 with Fr. Thomas Shields of the Catholic University of America in response to Pius X's call for the restoration of Gregorian chant, trains children's voices, ear, rhythm and sight reading (numbered notation and then staff) and leads them into singing the chant of the liturgy. It is the Catholic alternative or complement to Kodály, and both use movable do.
objectives: Develop a pure, light vocal tone through Ward's daily vocal exercises
Sight-sing in number notation and then staff notation, and take melodic dictation
Conduct and feel free "chironomic" chant rhythm (arsis and thesis)
Sing the ordinary chants of a simple Mass (for example Mass XVIII) and common Latin hymns (Adoro te, Salve Regina)

curriculumOptions.name: Ward Method (teacher training and contacts)
curriculumOptions.notes: CMAA keeps the Ward Method alive through courses and a list of certified teachers.

curriculumOptions.name: Kodály continuation (OAKE)
curriculumOptions.notes: The non-liturgical path, continuing the music-01 sequence.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Pius X, Tra le sollecitudini (1903), called for the use of Gregorian chant by the people to be restored. Ward's method was taught in thousands of American Catholic schools in the 1920s–1950s and in Europe.

sources.label: Pius X, Tra le sollecitudini (1903), English (Adoremus)

rows.title: Instrument I: Piano or Violin Foundations
rows.summary: Begin a primary instrument at 6–7 with a good private teacher: piano for harmony and keyboard literacy, or violin for ear and ensemble playing. Daily practice (15–30 minutes, rising with age) builds diligence as much as skill. Aim to reach about ABRSM/RCM Grade 3 by 10.
objectives: Practice daily with a written practice plan kept by the student and checked by a parent
Piano: five-finger positions to hands-together playing, scales and arpeggios in keys to 2 sharps and flats, Grade 1–3 repertoire (Bach Anna Magdalena, Clementi sonatinas)
Violin: posture, bow hold, first position, Suzuki Books 1–3 or equivalent
Perform in a recital two or more times a year

curriculumOptions.name: Suzuki Method
curriculumOptions.notes: Ear-first "mother-tongue" method with a parent in lessons. Strong for violin from 4–6. Add note reading early.

curriculumOptions.name: Piano Adventures
curriculumOptions.notes: The most widely used reading-based piano method. Pair with a private teacher.

curriculumOptions.name: Hoffman Academy (online piano)
curriculumOptions.notes: Low-cost video piano lessons with solfège and ear training. A bridge where no teacher is available.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson played the violin for much of his life, and Franklin invented the glass armonica. Locke (§197), by contrast, thought music took too much time for a gentleman to gain "but a moderate skill" in it. This program sides with the ancients and Jefferson.

sources.label: Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education §197 (Archive.org)

rows.title: Recorder and Reading Music
rows.summary: The soprano recorder is a cheap, portable first melodic instrument that makes staff reading concrete. Alongside it, the student learns the rudiments of notation: the staff and clefs, note and rest values, meter, key signatures to one sharp or flat, and basic musical terms. Combined with singing, this gives the student full musical literacy for early grades.
objectives: Play a one-octave diatonic range on soprano recorder (B-A-G first), reading from the staff
Play 30 or more folk tunes, hymn melodies and simple duets
Name notes on treble and bass staves, and read and write simple and compound meters
Know basic Italian tempo and dynamic markings

curriculumOptions.name: Reading Music: Introduction to Music Theory
curriculumOptions.notes: Rhythm, meter and notation text, workbook and teacher guide for the grammar years.

curriculumOptions.name: musictheory.net (free lessons and drills)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free note-reading, key and interval drills. Use as daily practice.

rows.notes: I did not verify a specific recorder method book. Most Kodály and Orff classroom recorder methods work well.

rows.title: Hymnody: The Catholic and Protestant Hymn Traditions
rows.summary: Memorize one great hymn a month (text and tune) across five years, covering the Latin office hymns of Ambrose and Aquinas, the Lutheran chorale, the metrical psalms, Watts and Wesley, the Victorian hymn writers, and American spirituals. Hymns are among the best poetry most children memorize and the shared song of Christian worship. Learn to sing the parts once voices allow.
objectives: Memorize 60 or more hymns (text and tune), including the major Latin, Lutheran, English and American hymns
Know the author, era and tradition of each hymn and the meter name (Common, Long, 8.7.8.7)
Sing hymns in parts (soprano/alto, then tenor/bass) from a hymnal
Compare a psalm with Watts's paraphrase of it

coreTexts.title: The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament
coreTexts.author: Isaac Watts

curriculumOptions.name: Adoremus Hymnal (2nd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic hymnal with Latin chant, the great English hymns and the Mass ordinaries.

curriculumOptions.name: Cantus Christi 2020: Psalter & Hymnal
curriculumOptions.notes: Reformed psalter-hymnal used by many classical Christian schools, with metrical psalms and hymns in parts.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Bay Psalm Book (1640) was the first book printed in British North America. Watts's Psalms and Hymns and the Wesleys' hymns were the most sung texts in 18th- and 19th-century America.
rows.notes: Catholic and Protestant note: Catholic practice gives pride of place to Gregorian chant and Latin hymns in the liturgy (Sacrosanctum Concilium 116) and also uses vernacular hymns. The Reformed tradition emphasizes metrical psalm-singing, and Lutheran and Anglican/Methodist traditions center on the chorale and the English hymn. Many great hymns are shared by both, and either hymnal serves.

rows.title: Music Appreciation I: Composers and the Orchestra
rows.summary: Listen closely to one composer a term (Charlotte Mason's "composer study"), with a short biography, the instruments of the orchestra, and the main forms (fugue, sonata, symphony, concerto, opera, mass). Go to live concerts. The aim is familiarity and love: the child knows Bach, Handel, Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as well as he knows the heroes of his history books.
objectives: Study 12 or more major composers from Palestrina to Dvořák, and recognize their best-known works by ear
Identify the instruments and sections of the orchestra by sight and sound
Attend 4 or more live concerts or services with sacred music a year
Narrate a composer's life and describe a listened-to work in simple musical vocabulary

coreTexts.title: The World's Great Men of Music: Story-Lives of Master Musicians
coreTexts.author: Harriette Brower

curriculumOptions.name: Music Appreciation I Set (book and audio)
curriculumOptions.notes: Twenty-six canonical works set in historical context.

curriculumOptions.name: Zeezok Music Appreciation (composer biographies)
curriculumOptions.notes: Nondenominational Christian publisher. Uses Opal Wheeler's classic composer biographies with activity books.

rows.title: Gregorian Chant and the Liber Usualis
rows.summary: Learn to read square notation on the four-line staff (neumes, clefs, the Solesmes rhythmic signs) and to sing the chant of the Mass and Office: the Ordinaries (Kyriale), seasonal antiphons, sequences (Victimae paschali, Veni Sancte Spiritus), office hymns and psalm tones. Chant is the foundation of Western music and its Latin reinforces the Latin track. The student should end able to sing a simple sung Mass and Vespers.
objectives: Read square notation in do and fa clefs, and sing neumes (podatus, clivis, torculus, porrectus, and others) correctly
Sing the eight psalm tones and chant a psalm with its antiphon
Sing three or more Mass Ordinaries (e.g. I, VIII, XI, XVIII) and the four seasonal Marian antiphons
Translate and explain the Latin texts sung

coreTexts.title: The Parish Book of Chant (2nd ed.)
coreTexts.author: Church Music Association of America

curriculumOptions.name: The Parish Book of Chant and CMAA resources
curriculumOptions.notes: Free chant books, summer Sacred Music Colloquium, and training in chant and polyphony.

curriculumOptions.name: Early Sacred Music: From the Temple Through the Middle Ages
curriculumOptions.notes: History-oriented course on psalmody, chant and early polyphony. Complements singing practice.

sources.label: Vatican II, Sacrosanctum Concilium (§116, chant's pride of place)

rows.notes: Protestant families can take this as music history and Latin, or substitute psalm chanting (Anglican chant) using a psalter. The Liber Usualis is large, so the Parish Book of Chant is the practical student book.

rows.title: Music Theory I: Graded Rudiments (ABRSM Grades 1–5)
rows.summary: A structured theory sequence through the graded exam syllabi: all major and minor keys and scales, intervals, triads and their inversions, cadences, simple and compound time, transposition, the C clefs, ornaments, instruments and terms. Sitting the ABRSM Grade 5 theory exam (or RCM equivalent) by about 12 gives an external benchmark.
objectives: Write all major and minor (harmonic and melodic) scales and key signatures
Name and write all intervals and triads, and recognize perfect, imperfect, plagal and interrupted cadences
Transpose a melody by an interval and between clefs
Pass ABRSM Grade 5 theory or RCM Level 6–8 theory

curriculumOptions.name: ABRSM Music Theory graded exams
curriculumOptions.notes: The UK/international standard. Grade 5 theory is traditionally required before higher practical grades.

curriculumOptions.name: Royal Conservatory Certificate Program (theory levels)
curriculumOptions.notes: North American equivalent, with practical and theory levels coordinated.

curriculumOptions.name: musictheory.net
curriculumOptions.notes: Free lessons and exercises for self-study and drill.

rows.title: Instrument II: Graded Repertoire and Performance
rows.summary: Continue the primary instrument through graded exams (to about Grade 6–7 by 14), with serious repertoire across periods (Bach inventions, Classical sonatas, Romantic character pieces, or for violin Vivaldi and Bach concertos). Add chamber music or orchestra and accompany hymns or choir, so that the instrument serves the community.
objectives: Pass graded practical exams in sequence (ABRSM or RCM) to about Grade 6–7
Learn and perform 6 or more substantial pieces a year from contrasting periods
Play in a chamber group, orchestra or church ensemble, or accompany congregational hymns
Sight-read at two grades below the performance level

curriculumOptions.name: ABRSM practical graded exams
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded repertoire lists and sight-reading standards.

curriculumOptions.name: RCM Certificate Program
curriculumOptions.notes: North American graded curriculum and exams.

curriculumOptions.name: Suzuki Method (continuing books)
curriculumOptions.notes: For violin students continuing in Suzuki studios. Add orchestra.

rows.title: The Choral Tradition: Polyphony and the Choir
rows.summary: Sing in a serious choir (a parish schola, cathedral or Anglican choir school, or community youth choir) and learn the great a cappella repertoire of the Renaissance: Palestrina, Victoria, Byrd, Tallis, Josquin, alongside Bach chorales and English anthems. Choral singing trains sight reading, blend, Latin diction, and the discipline of rehearsal and service.
objectives: Sing weekly in a choir with a liturgical or classical repertoire for three or more years
Sight-sing a part in four-voice polyphony and hold it against other parts
Learn 20 or more motets and anthems (for example Palestrina's Sicut cervus, Byrd's Ave verum, Tallis's If ye love me, Victoria's O magnum mysterium)
Earn choir awards or take a section-leader role

coreTexts.title: Music in the History of the Western Church
coreTexts.author: Edward Dickinson

curriculumOptions.name: Church Music Association of America (chant and polyphony training)
curriculumOptions.notes: Resources and courses for Catholic scholas singing chant and Renaissance polyphony.

curriculumOptions.name: RSCM Voice for Life
curriculumOptions.notes: Anglican choir-training scheme with graded awards, used in parish and cathedral choirs worldwide.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Cathedral choir schools (e.g., Westminster Abbey, King's College Cambridge, the Sistine Chapel) trained boys in singing, Latin and grammar together for centuries. Many English grammar and public schools grew from them.

rows.title: Music Theory II: Harmony and Species Counterpoint
rows.summary: The grammar of Western art music: four-part chorale harmony (voice leading, diatonic and chromatic chords, modulation, non-chord tones), figured bass, and Fux's five species of counterpoint. Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum (1725) taught Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. Harmonizing Bach chorales is the traditional proof of mastery.
objectives: Write two- and three-voice counterpoint in all five species (Fux)
Harmonize a melody or figured bass in four parts with correct voice leading, including secondary dominants and modulation to related keys
Analyze Bach chorales and Classical sonata expositions with Roman numerals
Reach ABRSM Grade 6–8 theory or Advanced Placement Music Theory level

coreTexts.title: The Study of Counterpoint (from Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum)
coreTexts.author: Johann Joseph Fux; trans. Alfred Mann

curriculumOptions.name: Open Music Theory (free open textbook)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free, college-level. Covers counterpoint, harmony, form and post-tonal theory.

curriculumOptions.name: ABRSM Grades 6–8 theory
curriculumOptions.notes: External benchmark in harmony, figured bass and analysis.

rows.title: Music History II: The Western Tradition from Chant to the Moderns
rows.summary: A chronological survey of Western music tied to the history track: Greek theory and chant, the Notre Dame school and Ars Nova, Renaissance polyphony, Baroque, Classical, Romantic and the 20th century, with listening, score study and primary-source readings (composers' letters and treatises). Include American music: the Bay Psalm Book, shape-note singing, Gottschalk, Ives, Copland and the spiritual.
objectives: Identify the style period of an unfamiliar work by ear and explain why

Know the major genres and landmark works of each period (Machaut's Messe, Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass, Monteverdi's Orfeo, Bach's St Matthew Passion, Mozart's Requiem, Beethoven's Ninth, and others)
Read 10 or more primary sources (Guido of Arezzo, Luther on music, Mozart's letters, Wagner, Stravinsky)
Write a research essay on a composer or work

coreTexts.title: Music in the History of the Western Church
coreTexts.author: Edward Dickinson

curriculumOptions.name: The History of Classical Music: Pythagoras through Beethoven (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free Hillsdale lecture course. Continue with Part 2, Chopin through Gershwin.

curriculumOptions.name: The History of Classical Music: Chopin through Gershwin (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Second half of the Hillsdale survey.

curriculumOptions.name: Discovering Music (2nd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Upper-school survey of Western music history with listening.

rows.title: Composition Basics
rows.summary: This course puts theory to work. The student writes hymn tunes and harmonizations for texts from the poetry track, chant-style psalm settings, simple binary and ternary piano pieces, a theme and variations, and a short motet or anthem for the choir, and hears the pieces performed. Notation software makes scores clean and playable.
objectives: Compose and harmonize 4 or more hymn tunes in four parts for existing or original texts
Write a binary- or ternary-form keyboard piece and a set of variations
Set a Latin or English text as a short motet for the choir, and rehearse it with singers
Produce clean scores with notation software

curriculumOptions.name: MuseScore (free notation software)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free, full-featured notation and playback.

curriculumOptions.name: Open Music Theory (form and composition chapters)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free material on phrase, form and model composition.

rows.title: College: Music as a Liberal Art, from Boethius to the Western Canon
rows.summary: A college seminar on music as the quadrivial art of number in time. Read Plato (Republic III, Timaeus), Aristotle (Politics VIII), Augustine's De musica, Boethius's De institutione musica (musica mundana, humana, instrumentalis) and the treatises and documents in Strunk's Source Readings, through Zarlino, Rameau and the Romantics. Pair the reading with advanced harmony and analysis of major works, and ask what music does to the soul and to the city.
objectives: Read Boethius Book I in full and explain the Pythagorean ratios of the consonances and the threefold division of music
Trace the idea of music's ethical power from Plato to Pius X and Benedict XVI
Complete a harmony-and-analysis sequence equivalent to two college semesters (chromatic harmony, form, analysis of a sonata movement and a fugue)
Write a seminar paper on music and moral formation

coreTexts.title: Fundamentals of Music (De institutione musica), trans. Calvin M. Bower
coreTexts.author: Boethius

coreTexts.title: Strunk's Source Readings in Music History (rev. ed.)
coreTexts.author: Oliver Strunk; Leo Treitler (gen. ed.)

curriculumOptions.name: Hillsdale College, The History of Classical Music (Pythagoras through Beethoven)
curriculumOptions.notes: Its opening lectures on Pythagoras and ancient theory fit this seminar.

curriculumOptions.name: Open Music Theory (college harmony and form)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free text for the harmony-and-analysis half of the course.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boethius's De institutione musica was the standard music text of the medieval quadrivium at Paris, Oxford and every cathedral school for nearly a thousand years.

rows.title: Outdoor Exploration & Sensory Nature Play
rows.summary: Daily unstructured time outdoors (grass, water, mud, sand, leaves, wind, weather) with an adult who names what the child sees and wonders aloud. Contact with nature in childhood is associated with better attention, mood, physical activity and motor development. Free play is the foundation of scientific curiosity.
objectives: Spend time outdoors every day in all reasonable weather
Handle natural materials and observe animals, plants and weather with an adult naming them
Ask and be asked "what do you notice?" and "what do you wonder?"

sources.label: Chawla (2015), Benefits of Nature Contact for Children
AAP (2018), The Power of Play

rows.notes: Supervise water play closely. Teach "look, don't touch" for unknown plants, fungi and insects.

rows.title: Gardening & Caring for Animals
rows.summary: A child-sized garden plot, seeds sprouting on the windowsill, and responsibility for a pet or backyard animals (chickens, fish, a caterpillar-to-butterfly kit). These teach life cycles, patience, cause and effect, and stewardship, and give children real work that matters.
objectives: Plant, water and harvest a simple crop (beans, radishes, sunflowers)
Observe a life cycle (butterfly, frog, chick) from start to finish
Feed and care for an animal on a daily routine

curriculumOptions.name: Onions in My Boots: Basic Gardening for Young Sprouts
curriculumOptions.notes: Simple, faith-friendly children's gardening guide.

sources.label: Chawla (2015), Benefits of Nature Contact for Children

rows.title: Collecting, Sky-Watching & First Experiments
rows.summary: Collections of rocks, shells, leaves and feathers, sorted and labeled. Watching the moon change and finding the Big Dipper. Simple kitchen experiments (sink/float, melting, magnets, shadows) where the child predicts before trying. This is the seed of the scientific method: notice, guess, test, tell.
objectives: Build and sort a nature collection by observable properties
Track the moon's phases for a month on a simple chart
Make a prediction before a simple experiment and describe the result

curriculumOptions.name: Behold and See K: Exploring Nature with Stories, Activities, and Nature Walks
curriculumOptions.notes: Gentle Catholic kindergarten nature program.

curriculumOptions.name: Kindergarten Supplemental Science Enrichment Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Read-aloud science picture books for the classical kindergarten.

rows.title: Nature Study I: Comstock, Burgess & the Nature Journal
rows.summary: Charlotte Mason–style nature study. There is a weekly nature walk, and the child keeps a nature journal of dated, labeled drawings of birds, trees, flowers, insects and weather. Comstock's Handbook of Nature Study guides the parent. Burgess's Bird Book and Animal Book are read aloud as living books that name and describe North American wildlife.
objectives: Identify 25 local birds, 15 trees and common wildflowers by sight
Keep a weekly illustrated nature journal with dates, places and observations
Narrate a Burgess chapter and connect it to animals seen outdoors

coreTexts.title: The Burgess Bird Book for Children
coreTexts.author: Thornton W. Burgess

coreTexts.title: The Burgess Animal Book for Children
coreTexts.author: Thornton W. Burgess

curriculumOptions.name: The Book of Birds Set & My Nature Journal
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical nature-study units. Pair with My Nature Journal (https://www.memoriapress.com/curriculum/science/my-nature-journal/).

curriculumOptions.name: Behold and See 3: Beginning Science
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic elementary science with a nature-study flavor.

curriculumOptions.name: REAL Science Odyssey: Biology 1
curriculumOptions.notes: Hands-on secular elementary life science with lab sheets.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Cornell nature-study movement (Liberty Hyde Bailey, Anna Comstock), active from the 1890s, put nature study into American schools. Charlotte Mason's Parents' Union Schools in England made the nature notebook a daily habit.

rows.title: Naked-Eye Astronomy & Earth Science
rows.summary: Learn the constellations, the motions of the sun, moon and planets, the seasons, and how to find north by Polaris, using only the eyes and a star chart. Earth science covers rocks and minerals, weather observation and recording, and landforms. The sky is where natural philosophy began, and these observations prepare for Ptolemy and Kepler later.
objectives: Identify 15+ constellations and 5 bright stars through the seasons
Explain day/night, the seasons and the moon's phases with a model
Keep a weather log and classify common rocks and minerals

curriculumOptions.name: Book of Astronomy Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Constellations and star stories in the classical core.

curriculumOptions.name: REAL Science Odyssey: Earth & Environment 1
curriculumOptions.notes: Hands-on elementary earth science.

curriculumOptions.name: Apologia Astronomy (Young Explorer series)
curriculumOptions.notes: Popular Christian elementary astronomy. It is written from a young-earth creationist perspective (see notes on natural-science-12).

rows.notes: A planisphere and a pair of 7×50 or 10×50 binoculars are the only equipment needed.

rows.title: Nature Study II: Fabre's Insects & Naturalist Observation
rows.summary: Jean-Henri Fabre, the great French naturalist whom Darwin called "an inimitable observer," shows how patient watching becomes science. Children read Fabre's Book of Insects and The Life of the Spider, keep live insects for observation, and write naturalist's field notes. Fabre's Story-Book of Science introduces everyday physics and chemistry through dialogue.
objectives: Observe and record the behavior of a living insect over several weeks
Write field notes with measurements, sketches and questions
Narrate Fabre chapters and distinguish observation from inference

coreTexts.title: Fabre's Book of Insects
coreTexts.author: Jean-Henri Fabre (retold by Mrs. Rodolph Stawell)

curriculumOptions.name: The Book of Insects Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical insect study with drawing and memory work.

curriculumOptions.name: Handbook of Nature Study (print)
curriculumOptions.notes: A print copy of Comstock as the parent's reference.

curriculumOptions.name: Behold and See 5
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic upper-elementary science.

rows.title: Physical Science by Experiment: Faraday's Candle
rows.summary: A year of hands-on physical science covering matter, heat, light, sound, simple machines, magnetism and electricity. Every lesson has an experiment and a written lab report (question, hypothesis, procedure, data, conclusion). The crown is Faraday's Chemical History of a Candle, his 1860 Christmas lectures for children, performed as a series of real demonstrations.
objectives: Write a complete lab report with controlled variables and measured data
Perform Faraday's candle demonstrations and explain combustion
Explain simple machines, heat transfer, and basic circuits

coreTexts.title: The Chemical History of a Candle
coreTexts.author: Michael Faraday

curriculumOptions.name: Physical Science (Novare)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical Christian, mastery-based. The Memoria Press recommendation for grade 8 (https://www.memoriapress.com/curriculum/science/novare-physical-science/).

curriculumOptions.name: REAL Science Odyssey: Chemistry 1 / Physics 1
curriculumOptions.notes: Lab-heavy secular option.

curriculumOptions.name: Intro to Physics and Chemistry (online)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic online option.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Faraday gave the Candle lectures at the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people in 1848 and 1860. Hillsdale K-12 names Faraday among the scientists studied in the middle grades.

sources.label: Hillsdale K-12 Curriculum Overview

rows.title: Programming I: From Scratch to Python
rows.summary: Computational thinking for the future inventor. Begin with Scratch's block programming (loops, events, variables) through games and animations. Then move to Python and write real programs: calculators, text games, data from science experiments, and small automations. The student learns to break problems into steps, debug patiently, and make tools.
objectives: Build interactive Scratch projects using loops, conditionals and variables
Write Python programs with functions, lists, dictionaries and files
Use Python to record and graph data from a science experiment

curriculumOptions.name: Scratch
curriculumOptions.notes: Free. Ideal first language at 10.

curriculumOptions.name: Python Crash Course, 3rd ed. (Eric Matthes)
curriculumOptions.notes: Project-based introduction, good for a motivated 11–12 year old.

curriculumOptions.name: Think Python, 3rd ed. (Allen Downey)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free online. More conceptual, teaches thinking like a computer scientist.

curriculumOptions.name: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python (Al Sweigart)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free online. Practical scripts for real tasks.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boole's Laws of Thought (1854) joined logic and algebra, and his algebra later became the basis of digital circuits. The founders' ideal of the practical inventor (Franklin's stove and lightning rod, Jefferson's polygraph and plow) is today served by programming.
rows.notes: Keep screen time purposeful and bounded. Programming is making, not consuming.

rows.title: Life Science & Linnaean Classification
rows.summary: Cells and the microscope, the classification of living things, plants, animals, ecology and the basics of heredity. Students learn binomial nomenclature from its inventor, Linnaeus, a devout naturalist who saw classification as reading the order of creation. They prepare microscope slides and dissect a flower.
objectives: Use a compound microscope and prepare wet-mount slides
Classify organisms using kingdom-to-species taxonomy and binomial names
Dissect a flower and label its parts and describe plant and animal cells

curriculumOptions.name: Life Science (Novare)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical Christian middle-school life science.

curriculumOptions.name: Life Science
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic middle-school option.

curriculumOptions.name: REAL Science Odyssey: Biology Level 2
curriculumOptions.notes: Rigorous secular middle-school biology with labs.

rows.notes: Latin students can read Linnaeus's genus and species descriptions directly (links well with the Latin track).

rows.title: Electronics & Making: Franklin's Workshop
rows.summary: Hands-on electricity and engineering in Franklin's tradition. Students repeat Franklin's Leyden-jar and static experiments, then build circuits on a breadboard (resistors, capacitors, LEDs, transistors, logic gates), solder a small project, and program an Arduino microcontroller to sense and act on the world.
objectives: Measure voltage, current and resistance and apply Ohm's law
Build and debug breadboard circuits and solder a working kit
Program an Arduino to read a sensor and control an output
Read Franklin's letters on electricity and reproduce a safe static experiment

coreTexts.title: Experiments and Observations on Electricity, made at Philadelphia in America
coreTexts.author: Benjamin Franklin

coreTexts.title: The Kite Experiment (Franklin to Collinson, Oct. 1752)
coreTexts.author: Benjamin Franklin

curriculumOptions.name: Make: Electronics, 3rd ed. (Charles Platt)
curriculumOptions.notes: Learning by discovery with matching component packs.

curriculumOptions.name: Arduino Starter Kit
curriculumOptions.notes: Official kit with a project book of 15 builds.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin's electrical experiments (1746–1752), published in London as Experiments and Observations on Electricity, made him the most famous American scientist in Europe and won him the Royal Society's Copley Medal (1753).
rows.notes: Never attempt the kite experiment. Franklin was lucky, and others were killed repeating it. Teach mains-voltage safety explicitly.

rows.title: Human Anatomy, Physiology & First Aid
rows.summary: The body's systems (skeletal, muscular, circulatory, respiratory, digestive, nervous, endocrine, reproductive) studied with models, drawings and dissection. The course is paired with certified first aid and CPR training. A future leader should be able to act calmly in an emergency and care for his own health.
objectives: Name and explain the function of the major organs and systems
Draw and label the skeleton, heart and major vessels from memory
Earn a first-aid/CPR/AED certification

coreTexts.title: Anatomy of the Human Body (Gray's Anatomy)
coreTexts.author: Henry Gray

curriculumOptions.name: First Aid / CPR / AED classes
curriculumOptions.notes: Certification course. Required.

curriculumOptions.name: First Aid Merit Badge
curriculumOptions.notes: Structured requirements that work well in a troop or family setting.

curriculumOptions.name: Behold and See 4: Human Anatomy and Health
curriculumOptions.notes: A gentler Catholic introduction. Use it as a younger-sibling or review text.

curriculumOptions.name: Apologia Anatomy and Physiology
curriculumOptions.notes: Popular Christian option (young-earth perspective).

rows.title: Biology: Cells, Heredity & Evolution (Mendel, Darwin, Humani Generis)
rows.summary: A full lab biology course covering biochemistry, the cell, genetics, molecular biology, evolution, ecology and the diversity of life. Students read Mendel's pea paper (by an Augustinian friar), the first edition of Darwin's Origin of Species read critically as an argument, and Pius XII's encyclical Humani Generis on what Catholic teaching permits and forbids in evolutionary theory.
objectives: Carry out lab work (microscopy, dissection, a Mendelian cross, DNA extraction)
Solve monohybrid and dihybrid genetics problems and explain Mendel's reasoning from his data
Outline Darwin's argument and distinguish its empirical claims from philosophical extrapolations
State the Catholic position in Humani Generis and compare other Christian positions fairly

coreTexts.title: On the Origin of Species (1st ed.)
coreTexts.author: Charles Darwin

curriculumOptions.name: General Biology, 2nd ed. (Novare)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical Christian, mastery-based. Also sold by Memoria Press. Advanced Biology follows.

curriculumOptions.name: Exploring Creation with Biology, 3rd ed.
curriculumOptions.notes: Widely used homeschool biology with strong labs. It teaches from a young-earth creationist perspective.

curriculumOptions.name: Biology with Lab / Honors Biology (online)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic online course.

curriculumOptions.name: Biology 2e (Campbell-level alternative)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free college-level text comparable in scope to Campbell Biology. Use it for AP-level depth.

curriculumOptions.name: Selections from Darwin's Origin of Species: The Shape of the Argument
curriculumOptions.notes: Guided reading of Darwin's argument.

rows.notes: Neutral note on differing views. Catholic teaching (Humani Generis, 1950; later papal statements) allows scientific inquiry into the evolution of the human body from pre-existing matter. It holds that each human soul is directly created by God and rejects polygenism and materialist philosophy. Many Protestants hold the same view, while others (e.g., Apologia, Answers in Genesis) hold young-earth creationism. Present the evidence and the arguments honestly, and let parents decide the emphasis. Campbell Biology (Pearson) is the standard AP/college text if a print textbook is preferred. The Selfish Gene is an elective and a critical reading for the end of the course (13+): it is the classic popular statement of the gene's-eye view of evolution and of kin selection, and the student should separate its genuine science from Dawkins's reductionist and materialist gloss ("survival machines"), which Humani Generis and theology-14 answer. Jurassic Park is a light elective for 13+, a thriller about cloning dinosaurs from ancient DNA. Read it for the ethics of science: Ian Malcolm's chaos-theory warnings against the hubris of doing whatever technology makes possible. Parents should know it has thriller violence and some profanity.

rows.title: Conceptual Physics & Galileo's Two New Sciences
rows.summary: Algebra-based physics with understanding before formulas (Hillsdale K-12's ninth-grade course): motion, forces, momentum, energy, gravity, fluids, heat, waves, electricity, magnetism, light and the atom. Students read Galileo's Two New Sciences (Third Day, on naturally accelerated motion) and repeat his inclined-plane experiment, then Feynman's Six Easy Pieces for the modern picture.
objectives: Explain Newton's laws, conservation of momentum and energy conceptually and with algebra
Repeat Galileo's inclined-plane experiment and derive the odd-number rule from data
Explain wave behavior, simple circuits and the basic structure of the atom

rows.title: Chemistry: Lavoisier, Dalton & the Laboratory
rows.summary: A full lab chemistry course covering measurement, atomic structure, the periodic table, bonding, stoichiometry, gases, solutions, acids and bases, thermochemistry, kinetics and equilibrium. Students read the founding documents: Lavoisier's Elementary Treatise (1789), which overthrew phlogiston and established conservation of mass, and Dalton's New System (1808), with its atomic theory and weights. A lab notebook is kept to professional standards.
objectives: Perform quantitative labs (titration, gas laws, calorimetry) with error analysis
Solve stoichiometry, gas-law and equilibrium problems
Reconstruct Lavoisier's argument against phlogiston and Dalton's case for atoms

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson followed Lavoisier's new chemistry closely while minister in Paris. Joseph Priestley, discoverer of oxygen, emigrated to Pennsylvania in 1794 and corresponded with Jefferson and Adams.

rows.title: Astronomy: Ptolemy, Copernicus, Kepler & Galileo
rows.summary: The St. John's approach to the Scientific Revolution. Students work through the geocentric models of Ptolemy's Almagest, Copernicus's heliocentric alternative (Book I of De Revolutionibus), Kepler's discovery of elliptical orbits in the Astronomia Nova, and Galileo's telescopic discoveries in the Starry Messenger. They make their own observations with a small telescope and ask what counts as evidence for a cosmology.
objectives: Model retrograde motion with epicycles and with a heliocentric system
Follow Kepler's reasoning to the ellipse and state his three laws
Observe Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus and record them as Galileo did
Assess the Galileo affair historically and fairly

rows.historicalPrecedent: John Winthrop, Hollis Professor at Harvard (1738–1779), observed the 1761 and 1769 transits of Venus and taught Newtonian astronomy to John Adams's generation. Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia praises David Rittenhouse's orrery as proof of American genius.

rows.title: Programming II: Algorithms & Data Structures
rows.summary: From programmer to computer scientist: Harvard's CS50 (C, Python, SQL, web), then algorithms and data structures (sorting, searching, recursion, graphs, dynamic programming, complexity) practiced through the USA Computing Olympiad. Strong students read CLRS and SICP. They build a substantial project, such as a tool, a simulation or a scientific-data pipeline.
objectives: Complete CS50x with a final project
Implement and analyze core algorithms and data structures (Big-O)
Compete in USACO Bronze/Silver or equivalent

rows.summary: Mechanics, then electricity and magnetism, with calculus (AP Physics C level; Halliday's Fundamentals). The primary sources are Newton's Principia (Definitions, Axioms and the Laws of Motion, Book I sections on central forces, and Book III's System of the World with the General Scholium) and the Opticks (prism experiments, which students repeat). Requires concurrent calculus (mathematics-18).
objectives: Solve mechanics and E&M problems using derivatives and integrals
Derive Kepler's laws from the inverse-square law (with guidance)
Repeat Newton's experimentum crucis with prisms and explain it
Read the General Scholium and discuss Newton's natural theology

rows.historicalPrecedent: Newtonian natural philosophy entered colonial colleges in the 1720s–40s through Isaac Greenwood and John Winthrop at Harvard and William Small at William & Mary. Jefferson said Small "fixed the destinies of my life" by teaching him mathematics and natural philosophy.

rows.title: Philosophy of Science & the Catholic Contribution (Duhem, Jaki)
rows.summary: What is a scientific theory, and what can it prove? Students read Pierre Duhem, a Catholic physicist and historian who discovered the medieval roots of mechanics (Buridan, Oresme) and analyzed the structure of physical theory. They read Stanley Jaki, Benedictine priest and physicist, on why science was "stillborn" in other cultures and was born alive in Christian Europe. Then they compare Bacon's induction, Popper's falsification and Kuhn's paradigms.
objectives: Explain the Duhem thesis on testing hypotheses and the aim of physical theory
Summarize Jaki's argument about the Christian origins of science and its critics
Distinguish scientific, philosophical and theological claims in a given debate

rows.title: College Seminar: Natural Philosophy & Laboratory (St. John's / TAC Model)
rows.summary: A great-books natural philosophy seminar joined to a laboratory, modeled on the St. John's College laboratory and the Thomas Aquinas College natural science sequence. Students read Aristotle's Physics (the nature of motion and cause), Archimedes on floating bodies, Galileo, Newton, Lavoisier, Faraday's Experimental Researches in Electricity, Maxwell's Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, Mendel, and Einstein on relativity. Classic experiments are repeated at the bench. The goal is to see how modern science follows from, and departs from, Aristotelian natural philosophy.
objectives: Discuss Aristotle's definitions of nature, motion and cause in seminar
Repeat Faraday's induction experiments and follow Maxwell's path to the field equations
Write a senior essay on a question in natural philosophy

rows.historicalPrecedent: Harvard's John Winthrop lectured on natural philosophy with experimental apparatus and wrote on earthquakes (1755) and comets (1759). Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia (1785) is itself a founder's work of natural history, covering climate, minerals, fossils and a rebuttal of Buffon's theory of American degeneracy.

rows.title: College Computer Science: SICP & the Theory of Computation
rows.summary: The capstone of the computing strand, and a course in thinking rather than in tools. Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs teaches abstraction, recursion, higher-order procedures, state and interpreters: how a language itself is built. The theory of computation (automata, formal languages, computability, and complexity including P vs NP) then asks what can be computed at all. Students read Turing's founding papers as primary sources: the 1936 paper on computable numbers and the 1950 "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", which opens the philosophical question of machine minds.
objectives: Work through SICP chapters 1–4, including writing a metacircular evaluator (an interpreter for Scheme in Scheme)
Prove results about finite automata, regular and context-free languages, and Turing machines
Explain the halting problem and reproduce Turing's diagonal argument
Define the classes P and NP and explain what NP-completeness means
Write a seminar essay on Turing's 1950 paper in the light of Aristotle and Aquinas on intellect

rows.historicalPrecedent: Leibniz, a hero of 18th-century learning, dreamed of a calculus ratiocinator that would settle disputes by calculation. Babbage and Ada Lovelace's Analytical Engine (1830s–40s) made the dream mechanical. Turing's 1936 paper answered Hilbert's decision problem and defined the modern computer in the same stroke.
rows.notes: Added by family decision as the college-level completion of the programming strand. The texts are copyrighted but freely available from the authors or their institutions. Turing's 1950 paper pairs well with the philosophy of mind in philosophy-14 and with Aquinas on the immateriality of the intellect.

rows.title: Old English Grammar: Sounds, Inflections & First Sentences
rows.summary: Pronunciation (æ, þ, ð, the palatal c and g), the case system (a light version of Latin's), strong and weak nouns and adjectives, strong verb classes and word order. Baker's free Old English Aerobics exercises give daily drill. The student's Latin and knowledge of English cognates make this go quickly.
objectives: Pronounce Old English correctly and read aloud from the Anglo-Saxon Lord's Prayer
Decline strong and weak nouns and adjectives and the demonstratives se/sēo/þæt
Recognize the seven strong verb classes and conjugate weak verbs
Translate simple prose sentences with a glossary

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson championed Anglo-Saxon as the root of English liberty and common law. He wrote "An Essay towards Facilitating Instruction in the Anglo-Saxon and Modern Dialects of the English Language", printed "for the use of the University of Virginia". Sweet's Primer and Reader were the standard Victorian university texts.

rows.title: Old English Prose: Ælfric's Colloquy, Bede's Cædmon & the Chronicle
rows.summary: Easy, humane prose. Ælfric's Colloquy is a schoolroom dialogue of monk, ploughman, fisherman and merchant, written to teach Latin, with an Old English gloss. It is the English cousin of Corderius. The Old English Bede's story of Cædmon comes next, then Chronicle entries (Cynewulf and Cyneheard, 755; William the Conqueror, 1087) that show loyalty, kingship and law.
objectives: Read Ælfric's Colloquy in Old English (and compare the Latin)
Read the Old English Bede's account of Cædmon
Read two Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entries (755 and 1087) in Old English
Explain the comitatus ideal of lord and retainer from the Cynewulf and Cyneheard episode

rows.title: Old English Poetry: Cædmon's Hymn, The Dream of the Rood, The Wanderer, The Seafarer
rows.summary: Alliterative verse: the half-line, stress, alliteration and kennings. The student reads Cædmon's Hymn (the first English poem), The Dream of the Rood (Christ as warrior-king), and the elegies The Wanderer and The Seafarer on exile, transience and the heavenly home. The Battle of Maldon, the last stand of Byrhtnoth, is added for courage. Each poem is read aloud.
objectives: Scan Old English alliterative lines (stress and alliteration)
Read The Dream of the Rood and The Wanderer complete in Old English
Read selections of The Seafarer and The Battle of Maldon (lines 309–319, "Hige sceal þē heardra")
Memorize and recite Cædmon's Hymn
Write an original poem in modern English alliterative verse
rows.notes: Tolkien wrote a verse-drama sequel to Maldon, The Homecoming of Beorhtnoth Beorhthelm's Son (1953). It makes a good companion to the Maldon reading (https://www.tolkienestate.com/scholarship/thomas-honegger-the-homecoming-of-beorhtnoth-beorhthelms-son/). The Dream of the Rood is a shared Christian devotional classic. Its cross-veneration imagery fits Catholic and Orthodox piety naturally, and Protestants read it as a poem of Christ's victory.

rows.title: Beowulf in Old English (with Tolkien)
rows.summary: The student reads the great epic in excerpts in the original: the opening (1–52), Grendel's attack and the fight (702–836), Grendel's mother's mere (1345–1382), and the dragon and Beowulf's death (2711–2820 and 3137–3182). The whole poem is read in translation. Tolkien's 1936 lecture, "Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics", guides the interpretation. It transformed the poem's study by treating the monsters as the point.
objectives: Read about 400 lines of Beowulf in Old English
Memorize and perform the opening lines ("Hwæt! Wē Gār-Dena in geār-dagum…")
Read Tolkien's "The Monsters and the Critics" and summarize its argument
Compare Beowulf with Achilles and Aeneas as heroic ideals, and with Christian virtue

rows.title: Bridge to Middle English: Chaucer in the Original
rows.summary: A short bridge from Old to Middle English. The unit covers the loss of inflections, the French and Latin influx, and the Great Vowel Shift in outline. The student reads Chaucer's General Prologue and the Nun's Priest's Tale aloud in Middle English. The Canterbury Tales are thus heard as Chaucer wrote them, and the whole history of English becomes visible.
objectives: Pronounce Chaucer's Middle English and read the first 42 lines of the General Prologue aloud from memory
Read the General Prologue and the Nun's Priest's Tale in Middle English with glosses
Trace five words from Old English through Middle English to modern English
Explain in outline the Norman Conquest's effect on English vocabulary and grammar

The fuller literary reading of Chaucer is in the literature survey (literature-18). This unit overlaps with the literature track. Coordinate so that the full Canterbury Tales (in modern translation or the original) is read there, and pronunciation and language history are taught here.

rows.title: Wonder & Big Questions at Home
rows.summary: Young children ask philosophical questions without prompting: What is real? Is it fair? Why is there something? Parents cultivate this by taking the questions seriously, asking "What do you think? Why?" and discussing picture books and fables that raise questions of friendship, courage, fairness and truth. Nothing is taught formally. The aim is the habit of wondering aloud and giving reasons.
objectives: Ask and answer "why" questions and give a reason for an opinion
Listen to another child's view and say whether they agree and why
Discuss the moral of a fable or picture book
Notice puzzles (e.g. "Is a copy of my toy my toy?") with delight rather than frustration

rows.notes: Evidence on "philosophy for children" (P4C) is mixed. A 2015 Education Endowment Foundation trial found about two months' extra progress in reading and maths, but a larger follow-up trial found no measurable gain. Treat this as formation of the habit of reasoned conversation, not as a test-score intervention.

rows.title: Philosophy for Kids: Socratic Conversation
rows.summary: A weekly guided conversation on the classic questions of values, knowledge, reality and reasoning, framed as short puzzles. Parent or tutor leads by the Socratic method: define the term, test the definition with counterexamples, refine it. This prepares the child to meet Socrates himself.
objectives: Propose and test definitions (e.g. of courage, friendship, justice) with counterexamples
Distinguish opinion, belief and knowledge in simple cases
Keep a philosophy notebook of questions and tentative answers
Conduct a short Socratic dialogue with a sibling or parent

rows.title: Socrates: Euthyphro, Apology, Crito, Phaedo
rows.summary: Students read Plato's four dialogues on the trial and death of Socrates: piety (Euthyphro), the philosopher's defense of his life (Apology), justice and the laws (Crito), and the immortality of the soul (Phaedo). Kreeft's Philosophy 101 by Socrates uses the Apology as a guided introduction to what philosophy is.
objectives: Trace the Euthyphro dilemma and state its significance for ethics and theology
Summarize Socrates' defense and his claim that the unexamined life is not worth living
Evaluate the Laws' argument in the Crito for obeying the city
Reconstruct at least two arguments for immortality in the Phaedo

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Video lectures to accompany the reading. Choose the Socrates and Plato lectures here.

rows.title: How to Read a Book & Aristotle for Everybody
rows.summary: Mortimer Adler, architect of the Great Books movement, teaches two things. How to Read a Book covers the levels of reading (elementary, inspectional, analytical, syntopical) that the rest of this program assumes. Aristotle for Everybody introduces Aristotle's common-sense philosophy of nature, action, happiness and knowledge in plain English.
objectives: Apply Adler's rules of analytical reading (classify, outline, find terms and propositions, criticize)
Write a structural outline and a one-paragraph summary of a philosophical work
Explain Aristotle's four causes, his view of happiness, and his distinction between wants and needs
Begin a commonplace book of key passages from the great books

rows.notes: Adler was raised Jewish, became an Aristotelian and a friend of the Thomist revival, and late in life was received first as an Episcopalian and then into the Catholic Church. He is a fitting guide for a program that joins the Great Books to the Catholic intellectual tradition.

rows.title: Plato's Republic & Meno
rows.summary: The Meno asks whether virtue can be taught and introduces recollection and the difference between knowledge and true opinion. The Republic asks what justice is and whether the just life is happier. Its answer includes the tripartite soul, the city in speech, the education of guardians, the philosopher-king, the divided line, the cave, and the decline of regimes. It is the founding text of Western political philosophy and of the theory of education itself.
objectives: Reconstruct the slave-boy demonstration and the Meno's paradox of inquiry
Summarize the definitions of justice in Book I and Socrates' refutations
Explain the tripartite soul and its parallel in the city
Interpret the sun, line and cave, and apply them to the program's own aims
Evaluate Plato's account of the decline from aristocracy to tyranny against American history

curriculumOptions.notes: Student and teacher guides for a full-year high-school reading.

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books 101: Ancient to Medieval (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale's Great Books lectures, including Plato.

rows.historicalPrecedent: J.S. Mill read several Platonic dialogues in Greek before age 8. Jefferson, by contrast, disliked the Republic, and the tension between the founders' Lockean politics and classical political philosophy is itself a seminar topic.

rows.title: The Stoics: Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius & Seneca
rows.summary: Roman Stoicism covers what is and is not in our power, virtue as the only true good, duty, self-command and providence. It shaped Roman statesmen, early Christian moralists, and the founders, who read Cicero and Seneca as moral philosophy. Students read Epictetus's Enchiridion and selected Discourses, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's Letters, with attention to where Stoicism anticipates Christian ethics and where it diverges.
objectives: Explain the dichotomy of control and apply it in a personal journal
Compare Marcus Aurelius's private notes on duty with his public role as emperor
Read ten of Seneca's letters and summarize their teaching on time, death, friendship and wealth
Contrast Stoic apatheia with Christian charity and the theological virtues

coreTexts.title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Encheiridion
coreTexts.author: Epictetus (trans. George Long)

coreTexts.title: Tusculan Disputations (Books I, II and V at least)
coreTexts.author: Cicero (trans. C. D. Yonge)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson's 1771 reading list for Robert Skipwith put Epictetus, Seneca, Cicero's moral works and Marcus Aurelius under moral philosophy, and Washington loved Addison's Cato, a Stoic hero play. Cicero's Tusculan Disputations, his Roman digest of Stoic and Platonic teaching on death, pain, the passions and whether virtue suffices for happiness, was a colonial-college text: King's College (Columbia) set it in the fourth year, and Yale's Berkeley Scholar examinations of 1780 tested candidates on it with Horace and Homer.

rows.title: Aristotle: Nicomachean Ethics & Politics
rows.summary: This is the foundation of the ethics of virtue and of political science. The Ethics covers happiness as activity of soul in accordance with virtue, the mean, habituation, voluntary action, justice, prudence, friendship and contemplation. The Politics covers man as the political animal, the household, the classification of regimes, citizenship, the mixed regime (polity), and education for leisure. Together they are the natural-law and statesmanship core of a founder's formation.
objectives: Define happiness, virtue and the mean, with examples from one's own life
Explain how virtue is acquired by habituation and why character is formed young
Summarize Aristotle's six regimes and his case for the mixed regime
Compare Aristotle's polity with the constitutional design of the Federalist
Write a seminar paper on friendship (Ethics VIII–IX) or on education (Politics VII–VIII)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson named Aristotle among the sources of "the harmonizing sentiments of the day" behind the Declaration, together with Cicero, Locke and Sidney (letter to Henry Lee, 1825). The Ethics and Politics were core texts at the colonial colleges and Oxford.

rows.title: The Christian Synthesis: Augustine, Boethius & Aquinas
rows.summary: The course traces how Christian thinkers took up Greek and Roman philosophy. Readings are Augustine's City of God (the two cities, providence and history, the critique of Roman virtue); Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (fortune, happiness, evil, providence and free will, among the most-read books of the Middle Ages); and Aquinas on faith and reason, the existence of God, the soul, and natural law.
objectives: Summarize Augustine's two loves and two cities and apply them to the fall of Rome
Explain Lady Philosophy's arguments on fortune, the highest good, and divine foreknowledge
State Aquinas's distinction between truths of reason and truths of revelation (ST I q.1)
Outline the five ways (ST I q.2 a.3) and one objection and reply for each

rows.historicalPrecedent: King Alfred translated Boethius into Old English, and Chaucer and Queen Elizabeth I also translated him, so a founder-in-training is in good company. See the old-english track.

rows.title: Early Modern Philosophy: Descartes, Locke, Hume & Kant
rows.summary: This is the modern "turn to the subject" in theory of knowledge: Descartes' methodical doubt and cogito; Locke's empiricism (Essay, Book II), the mind that more than any other shaped the founders; Hume's skepticism about causation, the self and miracles; and Kant's attempted synthesis and his ethics of duty and autonomy. Kreeft's Socrates Meets… dialogues give a realist critique of each.
objectives: Reconstruct Descartes' path from doubt to the cogito to God in Meditations I–III
Explain Locke's ideas of sensation and reflection and his critique of innate ideas
State Hume's problem of induction and his argument against miracles, and answer them
Explain Kant's categorical imperative in its first two formulations
Evaluate each thinker from the standpoint of Aristotelian-Thomist realism

curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on modern authors.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke's Essay entered the Yale and Harvard curricula in the 18th century and was standard reading for the founding generation. Jefferson counted Locke, Bacon and Newton as his "trinity of the three greatest men".

rows.title: Political Philosophy of the Founding and Its Critics: Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Burke, Tocqueville
rows.summary: The modern political tradition is read against the classical and Christian one: Machiavelli's break with the ethics of rule, Hobbes's state of nature and Leviathan, Locke's Second Treatise (natural rights, consent, property, revolution), which is the philosophical vocabulary of the Declaration, Rousseau's general will, Burke's Reflections on prudence, prescription and tradition, and Tocqueville's diagnosis of democracy in America (voluntary associations, religion, soft despotism).
objectives: Compare the state of nature in Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau
Trace Locke's language in the Declaration of Independence
Explain Burke's critique of abstract rights and his defense of prudence and prescription
Summarize Tocqueville on religion, associations, and the danger of soft despotism
Write a seminar paper judging one modern theory by Aristotle's Politics or by natural law

curriculumOptions.notes: A Socratic cross-examination of The Prince.

curriculumOptions.notes: Survey lectures for context.

rows.notes: This row overlaps with civics-law. Tocqueville is treated here as a thinker, and his institutional history belongs there. Catholic readers note Locke's and Hobbes's departure from Thomist natural law; Protestant readers often stress Locke's roots in Reformed resistance theory. Both lines of interpretation are worth presenting.

rows.title: J.S. Mill: Liberty, Utility & an Extraordinary Education
rows.summary: John Stuart Mill is both a model and a warning for this program. His Autobiography describes the most famous accelerated education in history (Greek at three, Latin at eight, logic and political economy before his teens) and the mental crisis at twenty that showed him what his father's purely analytic schooling had left out: feeling, poetry and faith. On Liberty and Utilitarianism are read closely and critically as the charter of modern liberalism.
objectives: Summarize Mill's education and his account of his crisis and recovery through Wordsworth
State the harm principle and test it against hard cases (speech, drugs, family, religion)
Explain Mill's "higher and lower pleasures" and the standard objections to utilitarianism
Compare Mill's liberty with Aristotle's and Aquinas's view of law as a teacher of virtue
Write an essay on what this program should learn and avoid from Mill's upbringing
rows.historicalPrecedent: James Mill educated his son at home on a deliberately accelerated classical and analytic plan, which is the model this program adapts. The younger Mill judged that it formed his intellect but starved his affections, and this program's poetry, music, faith and friendship tracks answer that defect.
rows.notes: Mill was not a Protestant theologian. He was raised by his father without any religion, called himself one who had never had religious belief, and late in life allowed only a limited "religion of humanity" or theism (see Three Essays on Religion). Read him as a brilliant secular liberal to be understood before he is criticized.

rows.title: Critics of Modernity: Marx, Nietzsche & Kierkegaard
rows.summary: Three 19th-century thinkers attack the bourgeois, rationalist, and nominally Christian world from different directions. Marx offers historical materialism and class struggle, Nietzsche the death of God, the will to power and the genealogy of morals, and Kierkegaard a Christian's protest against "Christendom" and the crowd in the name of the individual before God. They are read critically as the sources of 20th-century revolutions and of much contemporary thought.
objectives: Summarize the Communist Manifesto's theory of history and assess it against 20th-century results
Explain Nietzsche's master and slave moralities and his critique of Christianity, then answer it
Explain Kierkegaard's stages (aesthetic, ethical, religious) and his idea of the "single individual"
Identify each thinker's influence on present-day politics and culture

coreTexts.title: Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (trans. L.M. Hollander)
coreTexts.author: Søren Kierkegaard

curriculumOptions.name: Marxism, Socialism, and Communism (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on Marx's thought and its historical outcomes.

rows.notes: Kreeft's Socrates Meets Marx and Socrates Meets Kierkegaard (Ignatius) continue the series from philosophy-09. Kierkegaard was a Lutheran whose attack on the Danish state church is often read with sympathy by Catholics and Protestants alike.

rows.title: College Seminar: 20th-Century Christian Philosophy (Pieper, Maritain, Gilson, MacIntyre, Fides et Ratio)
rows.summary: This seminar reads the 20th-century recovery of classical and Thomist philosophy in answer to modernity. Pieper defends leisure and contemplation as the basis of culture; Maritain gives a Thomist introduction to philosophy; Gilson argues that there is a "Christian philosophy"; and MacIntyre diagnoses the collapse of moral discourse after the Enlightenment and argues for a return to the virtues. John Paul II's Fides et Ratio (1998) states the Church's charter for the partnership of faith and reason.
objectives: Explain Pieper's distinction between leisure and idleness and its meaning for education
Summarize MacIntyre's account of the failure of the Enlightenment project and his concept of a practice
Discuss Gilson's thesis on Christian philosophy and its critics
Outline Fides et Ratio's account of the relation of philosophy to theology
Write a seminar paper applying MacIntyre or Pieper to the design of this program

coreTexts.title: Leisure: The Basis of Culture (with The Philosophical Act)
coreTexts.author: Josef Pieper

coreTexts.author: Alasdair MacIntyre

coreTexts.author: Neil Postman

rows.notes: Pieper, Maritain, Gilson and MacIntyre were all Catholic, MacIntyre having entered the Church in the early 1980s. Protestant counterparts worth adding are C.S. Lewis's The Abolition of Man (see theology-18) and, for advanced students, Alvin Plantinga's work on faith and reason. John Senior, founder of the Integrated Humanities Program at the University of Kansas, is the classic Catholic case for the kind of education this program attempts: nursery rhymes, fairy tales and "gymnastic" (music and the body) before the great books, then a list of a "thousand good books" as the soil in which the Great Books can grow. The student reads him as the philosophy of his own schooling and tests it against Pieper and MacIntyre. Senior's two books, and Postman's The End of Education, are also recommended reading for parents, ideally before the child starts school. Postman writes as a secular humanist; his "end" means both purpose and death, and his claim that schools need a unifying "narrative" (a god to serve) is read as an elective, set beside Senior's answer that the narrative is the Christian one.

rows.title: College Seminar: Metaphysics & the Great Conversation
rows.summary: This is a Great Books seminar in the manner of Thomas Aquinas College and St. John's College. It reads Aristotle's Metaphysics (Books I, IV, VII, XII) on being, substance, first principles and the unmoved mover, alongside Aquinas's commentary tradition and selected modern responses. The student then returns to earlier texts with more maturity, since each great book is meant to be read more than once.
objectives: Explain the principle of non-contradiction (Metaphysics IV) and its defense
Distinguish substance and accident, act and potency, matter and form
Reconstruct Aristotle's argument for the unmoved mover (Metaphysics XII)
Lead a 90-minute seminar with an opening question and sustained follow-up

rows.historicalPrecedent: Aristotle's Metaphysics, read with Aquinas's commentary, was the summit of the medieval arts course and remains the center of the Thomas Aquinas College curriculum.

rows.title: Natural Law I: From Antigone to Aquinas, the Law of Nations and the Founders
rows.summary: The natural-law tradition is read as one argument running from the Greeks to the Declaration. Antigone appeals to the unwritten laws of the gods against Creon's decree. Aristotle distinguishes natural from legal justice (Ethics V.7) and cites Antigone for a "common law" of nature (Rhetoric I.13). Cicero defines true law as right reason in agreement with nature (Republic III, Laws I). Aquinas's Treatise on Law (Summa I-II qq. 90–97) gives the classic synthesis. The early moderns (Suárez, Hooker, Grotius, Pufendorf and Burlamaqui) turn it into a science of rights and of the law of nations, and the founders took it from them into the Declaration and James Wilson's law lectures. Budziszewski's Written on the Heart is the guide, and Lewis's Abolition of Man shows the same moral law across cultures.
objectives: Explain Antigone's appeal to the unwritten laws and Aristotle's use of it in Rhetoric I.13
Distinguish natural from legal justice (Ethics V.7) and state Cicero's definition of true law
State Aquinas's four kinds of law and the first precept of practical reason (ST I-II q.94 a.2)
Explain how human law derives from natural law by conclusion and by determination (q.95 a.2), and why an unjust law does not bind in conscience (q.96 a.4)
Trace the move from natural law to natural rights through Suárez, Grotius's Prolegomena, Pufendorf and Burlamaqui
Show how the Declaration's "Laws of Nature and of Nature's God" and Wilson's lecture "Of the Law of Nature" draw on this tradition
Match the precepts in Lewis's appendix ("Illustrations of the Tao") to the Decalogue and to Aquinas q.94

curriculumOptions.notes: Essays and lectures on natural law and the free society. Acton is an ecumenical institute founded by a Catholic priest.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The founders learned natural law as a college subject. King's College's 1763 plan put Grotius or Pufendorf in the fourth year, and John Jay (class of 1764) studied under it. Witherspoon's Princeton lectures sent Madison's generation to Grotius, Pufendorf and Burlamaqui, and Burlamaqui entered the Harvard course in the Revolutionary era. In 1790–91 James Wilson, a signer of the Declaration and the Constitution and a Supreme Court justice, gave his law lectures at the College of Philadelphia with President Washington in the audience at the first one. He grounded American law in the law of nature, which he held to be the law of God.

rows.notes: To be revised when the user attaches the John Jay Institute curriculum. Publicly, the John Jay Institute (Langhorne, PA; founded 2005 by the Rev. Alan R. Crippen II) lists "Natural Law" as one of five three-week seminar modules in its post-college Fellows Program. An archived 2006–2009 description of the module, then titled "Natural Law and Public Moral Discourse," names Sophocles, Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Aquinas, Calvin, Hooker, C.S. Lewis and J. Budziszewski, with Kant, Mill, Nietzsche and Peter Singer as challengers. Its aim was to find common moral ground with opponents on politics, technology, sexuality and human life. This row follows that sequence and adds the early-modern jurists the founders read. The current syllabus, editions and page assignments are not public. civics-law-09 reads Cicero and Aquinas at 13–14, and here they are reread as philosophy. A Catholic/Protestant note: Calvin (Institutes II.8.1, on the law "engraved on every heart") and Hooker give the Reformed and Anglican doctrine of natural law. Budziszewski, an evangelical who entered the Catholic Church in 2004, writes for both readerships.

rows.title: College Seminar: The Natural Law Revival and Its Critics (Maritain, Grisez, Finnis, George, Budziszewski, Feser; Hume and Hart)
rows.summary: After the totalitarian regimes of the 20th century, philosophers and jurists revived natural law. The seminar reads Maritain's Man and the State on natural law and human rights, and Grisez's 1965 commentary on ST I-II q.94 a.2, which launched the "new natural law theory". It then reads that theory's full statement in Finnis's Natural Law and Natural Rights (basic goods and practical reasonableness) and its public application in Robert George's In Defense of Natural Law. Budziszewski's What We Can't Not Know explains conscience and our evasions of it. Feser's Aquinas answers from the older Aristotelian-Thomist side. The critics get a full hearing: Hume's is-ought problem and H.L.A. Hart's legal positivism, including his "minimum content of natural law".
objectives: State Hume's is-ought objection and reconstruct both the new-natural-law reply (Grisez, Finnis) and the Aristotelian-Thomist reply (Feser)
List Finnis's basic goods and requirements of practical reasonableness and apply them to a legal question
Explain Maritain's account of knowledge of natural law "by inclination" and how it grounds human rights
Summarize Hart's separation of law and morals and his "minimum content of natural law", and give a natural-law answer
Write a seminar paper on a live public controversy that argues from natural law to a reader who rejects it

curriculumOptions.notes: An annual conference of lectures on natural law, theology and economics. It is ecumenical and suits a mature 18-year-old attending with a parent.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The revival had a public purpose from the start. Maritain wrote the introduction to UNESCO's 1948 symposium on the philosophical grounds of human rights, the background to the Universal Declaration. There he observed that nations could agree on a list of rights while disagreeing about why they hold. The Hart–Fuller debate of 1958 over Nazi-era statutes made the natural-law-versus-positivism question a standard part of legal education.
rows.notes: To be revised when the user attaches the John Jay Institute curriculum. The Institute's archived "Natural Law and Public Moral Discourse" module paired Lewis and Budziszewski with challengers including Peter Singer. Singer's Practical Ethics can be added here as a contemporary utilitarian foil. Budziszewski defends the older Thomist view of natural law and Finnis and George the "new natural law". Feser is sharply critical of the new theory, and the disagreement is itself a good seminar question. Grisez's 1965 article is copyrighted but free on Notre Dame's repository.

rows.title: Learning to Swim and Water Safety
rows.summary: Drowning is a leading cause of death among young children. The AAP recommends swim lessons for most children from age 1, together with barriers, constant supervision and life jackets, since no lesson makes a child "drown-proof." By 4–8 the child should move through formal learn-to-swim levels to water competency: entering deep water, surfacing, floating, turning, swimming 25 yards and exiting.
objectives: Progress through Red Cross Learn-to-Swim Levels 1–3 or an equivalent (breath control, floats, glides, front crawl, treading water)
Achieve water competency: jump into deep water, return to the surface, float or tread for one minute, turn, swim 25 yards, exit
Learn water-safety rules, including life jackets in boats and "reach or throw, don't go"

curriculumOptions.name: Learn-to-Swim (Levels 1–6)
curriculumOptions.notes: Six-level progression offered at most community pools.

curriculumOptions.name: USA Swimming clubs (competitive pathway after basic competency)
curriculumOptions.notes: Club swimming builds stroke technique and endurance from about 7–8.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (Thoughts §8): swimming "saves many a man's life; and the Romans thought it so necessary, that they ranked it with letters." Franklin taught himself to swim as a boy, once swam the Thames from Chelsea to Blackfriars, and wrote a letter of swimming advice to Oliver Neave that was widely reprinted.

rows.title: Tumbling, Gymnastics and Calisthenics Foundations
rows.summary: Gymnastics develops strength relative to body weight, flexibility, balance, spatial awareness and courage. These are the foundation for every later sport and combat art. Take recreational gymnastics or tumbling classes and do a short daily calisthenics routine at home (bear crawls, hollow holds, push-ups, pull-up progressions, handstands against a wall).
objectives: Forward and backward rolls, cartwheel, bridge, handstand against a wall (30 seconds)
Hang from a bar 30 seconds or more, and progress to one or more strict pull-ups by 10
Balance-beam walking, jumping and landing with control
Ten minutes of daily calisthenics as a habit (paired with morning prayer or before lessons)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Greek education joined gymnastike to mousike. In America, Charles Beck introduced German Turnen gymnastics at George Bancroft's Round Hill School (Northampton, Mass., 1825), one of the first school gymnasiums in the country.

rows.title: Walking, Running and Field Games
rows.summary: Daily vigorous activity (the CDC and WHO recommend 60 minutes or more for school-age children) through long walks, running games, tag, relays and field days. Jefferson prescribed two hours of walking a day for his nephew. Build aerobic base gradually. Short sprints and play come first, and steady running distances are added from about 9–10.
objectives: Sixty minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, much of it outdoors
Family hikes of 3–5 miles by age 8, and 8–10 miles by 10
Run a mile continuously by 8, and a 5K by 10–11 if interested
Learn to throw, catch and kick well through playground and field games
rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson to Peter Carr (1785): "Give about two of them, every day, to exercise; for health must not be sacrificed to learning... Walking is the best possible exercise. Habituate yourself to walk very far." He also judged ball games "too violent for the body" and to "stamp no character on the mind," a view later schools like Rugby rejected.

rows.summary: The student learns to be at home in the wilderness: pack and walk a trail, pitch a tent, build and put out a fire, cook outdoors, purify water, use a knife and axe safely, tie the essential knots, read a map and compass, and give first aid. Advance from family day hikes to overnight and multi-day backpacking trips, ideally through a scouting-type program with the patrol method and rank advancement.
objectives: Master 10 knots and lashings, knife and axe safety, fire building (including in wet weather), and Leave No Trace
Navigate a 5-mile cross-country course with map and compass by 12
Complete a 3-night backpacking trip carrying his own gear by 13
Earn first-aid certification and know wilderness responses to cold, heat, sprains and bleeding

rows.historicalPrecedent: Washington was a trained surveyor who worked in the Virginia backcountry at 16–17. Nessmuk and Dan Beard's woodcraft books formed the generation that founded American Scouting (1910).

rows.title: Archery
rows.summary: Archery teaches concentration, breath control, consistency and strict range discipline. Begin with a light recurve bow in a certified program that teaches range commands and whistle signals, then progress to scored target rounds. Roger Ascham, tutor to Elizabeth I, wrote the first English book on it.
objectives: Learn and obey range safety commands without exception
Master the steps of the shot (stance, nock, set, draw, anchor, aim, release, follow-through)
Shoot consistent groups at 10–18 meters, and complete a scored round
Read selections of Ascham's Toxophilus on archery as a gentleman's exercise
