curriculumOptions.name: National Archery in the Schools Program (NASP)
curriculumOptions.notes: School- and co-op-based program for grades 4–12 with standardized equipment and tournaments.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Ascham's Toxophilus (1545), dedicated to Henry VIII, defended archery as honest recreation and national defense for English youth. Ascham's The Scholemaster (1570) is a founding text of English humanist pedagogy.

rows.title: Horsemanship
rows.summary: Riding was the essential skill of the founding-era gentleman and remains a school of patience, courage and responsibility for another creature. Learn riding and stable management together, including grooming, tacking up, feeding and the horse's health, through Pony Club ratings or 4-H horse projects. Read Xenophon's On Horsemanship, which is still sound on gentle handling.
objectives: Groom, tack and care for a horse independently
Ride at walk, trot and canter with a secure, balanced seat, and jump small fences or ride trails
Earn successive Pony Club ratings (D levels through C) or complete 4-H horse project years
Read Xenophon's On Horsemanship and compare it with modern practice

curriculumOptions.notes: Rated progression in riding and horse management (the "unmounted" knowledge is excellent).

curriculumOptions.name: 4-H Horse Project
curriculumOptions.notes: Lower-cost, county-based option in rural areas.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (§198) notes that riding the great horse was thought a necessary part of a gentleman's breeding. Washington was reckoned the finest horseman of his age. Jefferson, contrarily, warned his nephew that reliance on the horse weakens the body and urged walking instead.

rows.title: Firearm Safety, Hunter Education and Marksmanship
rows.summary: This course proceeds in stages. Safety comes first ("Stop! Don't touch. Run away. Tell a grown-up" for young children), then formal hunter-education certification, then supervised marksmanship with air rifle and .22 rimfire in a club or junior program. It teaches respect for lethal tools, precision, breath and trigger control, and the lawful responsibilities of a citizen.
objectives: Ages 8–9: know and practice the child firearm-safety rules; never handle a firearm without an adult
Ages 10–12: pass a state hunter-education course (four rules of firearm safety, ethics, game laws, first aid)
Ages 12–15: shoot supervised air rifle or .22 in a junior club, and earn marksmanship qualifications
Clean, store and transport firearms lawfully and safely

curriculumOptions.name: Eddie Eagle GunSafe Program (pre-K to grade 4)
curriculumOptions.notes: Accident-prevention program only, with no firearm handling.

curriculumOptions.name: Hunter Education
curriculumOptions.notes: State-administered certification, required for a first hunting license in most states.

curriculumOptions.name: CMP Youth Programs (junior air rifle, marksmanship)
curriculumOptions.notes: Congressionally chartered. Junior three-position air rifle and clinics.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson to Peter Carr (1785): "As to the species of exercise, I advise the gun. While this gives a moderate exercise to the body, it gives boldness, enterprize, and independance to the mind... Let your gun therefore be the constant companion of your walks."

sources.label: Jefferson to Peter Carr, 19 Aug. 1785 (Founders Online)

rows.notes: Firearm safety and marksmanship are standard. Hunting itself is optional: hunter education is kept as the standard safety certification whether or not the family hunts. Laws vary by state. Secure storage is non-negotiable at every age.

rows.title: Team Sport: Soccer, Baseball, Rugby and Lacrosse
rows.summary: Team sport teaches what individual training cannot: subordinating oneself to a common good, obeying a captain and later leading as one, losing well, and playing hard within rules. Play at least one team sport a year, sample widely before 12 (avoid early single-sport specialization), and choose one or two to pursue seriously in the teens, ideally with a captaincy.
objectives: Play one or more seasons a year of a team sport from 8, trying several sports before 12
Learn the rules, positions and basic tactics of the chosen sports
Show sportsmanship (no cheating, gracious in loss and victory) and accept coaching
Serve as captain or assistant coach of a younger team by 15–16

curriculumOptions.name: US Youth Soccer
curriculumOptions.notes: Recreational through competitive club soccer.

curriculumOptions.name: Little League Baseball and Softball
curriculumOptions.notes: Local leagues, ages 4–16.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Thomas Arnold's Rugby School (1828–1842), portrayed in Tom Brown's School Days, made team games a school of "muscular Christianity." The ideal spread through the English public schools and then American prep schools and colleges.

rows.title: Advanced Swimming, Lifesaving and Open Water
rows.summary: This course builds on basic water competency: all four competitive strokes, endurance, open-water skills (currents, cold water, swimming in clothes), and rescue. It culminates in a lifeguard certification at 15, a qualification that is both a life skill and a form of service.
objectives: Complete Red Cross Levels 4–6 or swim-club equivalents (freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly)
Swim 1,000 yards or more continuously, and one mile by 14
Learn open-water safety and basic reaching, throwing and rowing rescues
Earn Lifeguarding certification at 15 (minimum age for the Red Cross course)

curriculumOptions.name: Swimming and lifeguarding courses
curriculumOptions.notes: Levels 4–6, then the Lifeguarding course.

curriculumOptions.name: USA Swimming clubs
curriculumOptions.notes: For stroke technique and competitive endurance.

rows.title: Wrestling and Grappling
rows.summary: Grappling under good coaching teaches physical courage, composure under pressure, humility and the ability to defend oneself and others without striking. Wrestle folkstyle through a school or club, with judo or Brazilian jiu-jitsu as alternatives or complements. Grappling gives the self-defense and character benefits of combat sport with far less risk of head injury than striking arts.
objectives: Wrestle a full season or more each year with sound technique in takedowns, escapes, reversals and pins
Learn basic self-defense escapes and control holds (judo or jiu-jitsu) as a complement to wrestling
Show self-control in anger, respect for opponents, and willingness to lose and learn

coreTexts.title: Laws (Book VII, on wrestling and gymnastic training)
coreTexts.author: Plato (trans. Benjamin Jowett)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (§199) preferred wrestling to fencing for a gentleman's son: "I had much rather mine should be a good wrestler than an ordinary fencer." Plato, himself a wrestler, prescribes wrestling in the Laws as training for war. Abraham Lincoln's frontier wrestling record is famous.

sources.label: Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education §199 (Archive.org)

rows.notes: Boxing is deliberately excluded (family decision), because of the risk of head injury. No USA Wrestling URL could be verified (the site refused automated checks), so none is listed. Local school and club programs are the usual route.

rows.title: Fencing
rows.summary: Fencing is the gentleman's combat art of the 17th and 18th centuries, now an Olympic sport. It sharpens reflexes, footwork, tactical thinking ("physical chess") and courtesy (the salute, the acknowledgment of touches). Train foil first, then épée or sabre, in a club affiliated with the national governing body, and read the classic 18th-century manual.
objectives: Master en garde, advance, retreat, lunge, parries 4 and 6, and the basic riposte
Fence bouts under the rules of foil, and later épée or sabre, and referee a bout
Compete in local and regional youth tournaments if desired
Read selections of Angelo's School of Fencing and compare classical and modern technique

curriculumOptions.name: USA Fencing member clubs
curriculumOptions.notes: National governing body. Use its club finder and youth tournament circuit.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke (§§198–199) records that fencing and riding were "looked upon so necessary parts of breeding" that omitting them would be thought a great fault. Angelo's London academy and treatise (1763) trained generations of Georgian gentlemen.

rows.title: Strength Training and Conditioning
rows.summary: The AAP's 2020 clinical report finds supervised resistance training safe and beneficial for children and adolescents. It improves strength, bone density, body composition, injury resistance and confidence when technique comes first and loads progress gradually. Move from bodyweight work to barbell basics (squat, deadlift, press, bench press, power clean) under qualified coaching, and build a habit that lasts a lifetime.
objectives: Learn and demonstrate correct technique in the main barbell lifts with an empty bar before loading
Follow a written progressive program 2–3 days a week, with a training log
Meet conditioning standards by 16: 10+ pull-ups, 40+ push-ups, a sub-8-minute mile, and a bodyweight squat and 1.5× bodyweight deadlift (with coaching)
Understand the basics of recovery, sleep and nutrition for training

coreTexts.title: Starting Strength: Basic Barbell Training (3rd ed.)
coreTexts.author: Mark Rippetoe

sources.label: AAP Clinical Report (2020): Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents
Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education §1 (Archive.org)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Locke opens his treatise with "a sound mind in a sound body" (Juvenal's mens sana in corpore sano). Jefferson told Carr "a strong body makes the mind strong." The 19th-century "muscular Christianity" of Kingsley and Hughes made physical vigor a Christian duty.

rows.title: Nursery Rhymes, Mother Goose & Lullabies
rows.summary: Sing and say nursery rhymes, lullabies and finger-plays with the child every day from birth. Rhyme, alliteration and strong meter train the ear to hear the sound-structure of words. That phonological awareness predicts later reading. It also gives the child a first inheritance of English verse before formal schooling.
objectives: Birth–2: hear lullabies and bouncing rhymes daily (lap games, clapping to the beat)
2–4: join in on rhyming words and complete familiar couplets
4–6: recite 30+ Mother Goose rhymes; clap syllables; produce rhymes for a given word
Associate verse with affection and play (sung at bedtime, in the car, at work)

curriculumOptions.name: A Children's Anthology of Poems & Lullabies
curriculumOptions.notes: A read-aloud anthology for the nursery years.

curriculumOptions.name: Junior Kindergarten Recitation
curriculumOptions.notes: A structured daily recitation of rhymes, prayers and short poems for ages 4–5.

sources.label: Bryant, Bradley, Maclean & Crossland (1989), Nursery rhymes, phonological skills and reading, J Child Lang
AAP (2024), Literacy Promotion: An Essential Component of Primary Care Pediatric Practice (policy statement)

rows.notes: Evidence: Bryant et al. found that 3-year-olds' knowledge of nursery rhymes predicted later phonological awareness and early reading, even after controlling for IQ and social background. The AAP recommends daily reading, rhyming, singing and talking from infancy. Sing rather than recite where possible. For bilingual households, do the same in Spanish and Chinese (see the language tracks).

rows.title: Children's Verse & First Memorization
rows.summary: The first formal memory work in verse. The child learns a short poem each week from Stevenson's A Child's Garden of Verses, Milne, de la Mare, Eugene Field, Lear and Belloc, recites it with clear diction, and keeps a poetry notebook with each poem copied out and illustrated. Poems are chosen for strong rhythm and rhyme and for a child's world seen truthfully.
objectives: Memorize 30–40 short poems (4–20 lines) in two years and keep them in review
Recite with clear articulation, natural pauses and eye contact
Copy each poem in the poetry notebook (pairs with handwriting and copywork)
Hear and clap the beat of a line; identify rhyming words

coreTexts.title: Peacock Pie: A Book of Rhymes
coreTexts.author: Walter de la Mare

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry for the Primary Stage (anthology)
curriculumOptions.notes: A graded anthology used with MP's 1st–2nd grade literature and recitation programs.

curriculumOptions.name: The Harp and Laurel Wreath
curriculumOptions.notes: Poems graded by stage (grammar, dialectic, rhetoric) with dictation passages. The anthology behind Mother of Divine Grace's memory work, usable from here to 14.

curriculumOptions.name: 1st Grade Recitation
curriculumOptions.notes: Daily recitation cards and schedule. Continues through 7th grade.

rows.title: The Great Anthologies: Memorization & Recitation
rows.summary: Longer and greater poems learned by heart from the classic school anthologies: Andrew Lang's Blue Poetry Book, Palgrave's Golden Treasury and Favorite Poems Old and New. The student learns the lyrics every educated English speaker once knew (Blake, Wordsworth, Tennyson, Longfellow, Shakespeare's songs) and begins to hear the differences among meters.
objectives: Memorize 25+ lyric poems of 12–40 lines (total 600+ lines) and review them on a rotating schedule
Recite a poem before an audience with appropriate expression, pace and volume
Tell iambic from trochaic and anapestic rhythm by ear
Name the poet and approximate century of each memorized poem

coreTexts.title: Songs of Innocence and of Experience
coreTexts.author: William Blake

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry for the Grammar Stage Set (3rd ed.)
curriculumOptions.notes: Anthology with teacher guide covering meter, rhyme and imagery, for grades 3–6.

curriculumOptions.name: The Harp and Laurel Wreath
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes Catholic devotional poems (Hopkins, Southwell, Thompson) alongside the standard canon.

curriculumOptions.name: 4th Grade Recitation
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded recitation schedule. Accelerated versions exist for 3rd–6th.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Palgrave's Golden Treasury (1861) was for a century the standard gift and school anthology in Britain and America. Memorization of poetry "by heart" was a daily staple of 19th-century schools from the dame school to Eton, where boys learned and "said" set passages of English and Latin verse.

rows.title: Ballads & Narrative Verse
rows.summary: The ballad tradition and the great narrative poems. The course reads the Child Ballads and Percy's Reliques (Sir Patrick Spens, Chevy Chase, the Robin Hood ballads), Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome, Scott's Lady of the Lake, Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Longfellow's Evangeline and Hiawatha, and Browning's Pied Piper. Narrative verse carries a young reader through long poems by the power of story. The ballad stanza is also the first form the student will write.
objectives: Memorize one long narrative poem (Horatius, 70 stanzas; or the Rime, Part I)
Identify the ballad stanza (4-3-4-3 stresses, abcb rhyme), refrain and incremental repetition
Compose an original ballad of 8+ stanzas on a historical or family subject
Read aloud a narrative poem with dramatic variation of voice

coreTexts.title: The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, Vol. 1
coreTexts.author: Francis James Child (ed.)

coreTexts.title: Reliques of Ancient English Poetry, Vol. 1
coreTexts.author: Thomas Percy (ed.)

coreTexts.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
coreTexts.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

coreTexts.title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin, and Other Poems
coreTexts.author: Robert Browning

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry & Short Stories for the Logic Stage Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes ballads and narrative poems with analysis of form.

curriculumOptions.name: 5th Grade Recitation
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded recitation that continues memory work alongside the ballads.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Macaulay's "Horatius" was among the most-recited poems in Victorian and Edwardian schools; as a Harrow boy, Churchill won a prize for reciting 1,200 lines of the Lays without error. Longfellow's narrative poems filled American readers and school exhibitions.

rows.title: Declamation & Public Recitation
rows.summary: The nineteenth-century art of declamation: speaking a memorized poem or speech before an audience with trained voice, posture and gesture. Texts come from the Columbian Orator, McGuffey's Sixth Reader, Shakespeare's speeches, Macaulay, Kipling and the great patriotic verse. The student performs at a public "exhibition" each term. This is the bridge from poetry to rhetoric.
objectives: Declaim a memorized piece of 40–100 lines each term before an audience
Apply McGuffey's rules of articulation, inflection, accent, emphasis and pause
Mark a text for breath, emphasis and pause before memorizing it
Recite Kipling's "If—" and one Shakespeare speech from the literature track

coreTexts.title: McGuffey's Sixth Eclectic Reader (with rules for elocution)
coreTexts.author: William Holmes McGuffey

coreTexts.title: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (speeches)
coreTexts.author: William Shakespeare

curriculumOptions.name: 7th Grade Recitation
curriculumOptions.notes: The last of MP's graded recitation programs. Add a public exhibition each term.

curriculumOptions.name: The Columbian Orator (free)
curriculumOptions.notes: Bingham's own "Rules for Eloquence" preface plus 80+ pieces to declaim. It is its own course.

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry Out Loud (national recitation contest)
curriculumOptions.publisher: National Endowment for the Arts and state arts agencies (administered by Mid Atlantic Arts)
curriculumOptions.notes: The national recitation contest, running from school or group rounds through state finals to a national final. Open to students in grades 9–12; homeschoolers enter through a local school or a homeschool group registered with the state coordinator. Poems must come from its online anthology. Enter once the student is doing high-school work (about 12–13 here), and keep competing through 16.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Declamation was a fixture of Anglo-American schooling from the colonial Latin schools through the 1800s: weekly "speaking" of memorized pieces, and public exhibitions at term's end. Bingham's Columbian Orator (1797) went through dozens of editions. Douglass bought it at about 12 and credited it with his rhetoric of freedom. McGuffey's Fifth and Sixth Readers open with rules of elocution.

sources.label: Poetry Out Loud: Rules & Eligibility

rows.notes: Coordinate with the rhetoric track, which takes up the delivery canon (actio) formally. The student's tutor or verse mentor should hear each piece before the exhibition and coach breath, pace and emphasis; the evaluation criteria in Poetry Out Loud's Teacher's Guide make a useful shared rubric.

rows.title: Psalms & Hymnody as Poetry
rows.summary: The Psalms are the oldest poetry the student will memorize. The unit studies Hebrew parallelism (read further in the Hebrew track), the psalms in the KJV and Douay-Rheims, and the English metrical psalm (Bay Psalm Book, Watts). It then turns to the great hymn-writers as poets: Watts, the Wesleys, Newton and Cowper (Olney Hymns), Keble, and Caswall's translations of the Latin breviary hymns. These are English verse forms (common meter, long meter) that the student will sing and write.
objectives: Memorize Psalms 1, 23, 51, 90 and 121 (in a Bible translation) and one metrical psalm
Identify synonymous, antithetic and synthetic parallelism in Hebrew poetry
Scan hymn meters (common meter 8.6.8.6, long meter 8.8.8.8) and match texts to tunes
Write a metrical paraphrase of a short psalm in common meter

coreTexts.title: The Book of Psalms (King James Version)
The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament
coreTexts.author: Isaac Watts

coreTexts.title: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists
coreTexts.author: John & Charles Wesley

curriculumOptions.name: Copybook Cursive, Scripture & Poems
curriculumOptions.notes: Copywork of Scripture and poems. Useful for fixing psalms in memory.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Bay Psalm Book (1640) was the first book printed in British North America. Watts's Psalms and Divine Songs were among the most-memorized texts of colonial and early-republic childhood, and Franklin printed Watts's Psalms in 1729. Psalm-singing and hymn memorization were universal in 18th- and 19th-century schools and homes, Catholic and Protestant.
rows.notes: Catholic/Protestant note. Protestant English hymnody (Watts, Wesley, Newton) and the Catholic Latin hymn tradition (Aquinas's Adoro te devote, Pange lingua; Caswall and Newman as translators) are both treated as English poetry. Catholic Psalter numbering (Vulgate/Douay) differs by one from the Hebrew/KJV for most of Psalms 10–147. Note which numbering is in use when memorizing.

rows.title: Prosody & Scansion
rows.summary: The formal study of English meter. The student learns stress and syllable, the feet (iamb, trochee, anapest, dactyl, spondee), line lengths (trimeter to hexameter), caesura and enjambment, substitution, and rhyme and its kinds. Every memorized poem is scanned. The texts are Stephen Fry's The Ode Less Travelled (practical, with daily exercises), Hollander's Rhyme's Reason (each form illustrated in itself) and Fussell's Poetic Meter and Poetic Form (the standard college text), with Saintsbury and Alden for historical depth.
objectives: Scan any line of accentual-syllabic English verse and name its meter
Identify and explain metrical substitution (initial trochee, feminine ending, spondee) and its expressive effect
Distinguish accentual-syllabic, accentual (Old English, Hopkins' sprung rhythm) and syllabic verse
Complete Fry's exercises in iambic pentameter (write 50+ correct lines)

coreTexts.title: The Ode Less Travelled: Unlocking the Poet Within
coreTexts.author: Stephen Fry

coreTexts.title: Rhyme's Reason: A Guide to English Verse
coreTexts.author: John Hollander

coreTexts.title: English Verse: Specimens Illustrating its Principles and History
coreTexts.author: Raymond Macdonald Alden

coreTexts.title: A History of English Prosody, Vol. 1
coreTexts.author: George Saintsbury

curriculumOptions.name: The Art of Poetry
curriculumOptions.notes: Christine Perrin's course on the elements of poetry (image, sound, meter, form) for middle and high school, with video lessons.

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry & Short Stories for the Logic Stage Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Introduces meter and poetic devices through the logic-stage anthology.

rows.historicalPrecedent: English schoolboys learned prosody first in Latin, through the rules of quantity in the Eton Latin Grammar and endless Latin verse composition (the "vulgus" at Eton and Rugby), and applied it to English afterward. Here English prosody comes first and runs parallel to Latin scansion (see the Latin track).
rows.notes: Saintsbury is exhaustive and opinionated, so use him for reference. Alden's anthology is a free set of examples for every meter and form.

rows.title: Poetic Forms & First Composition
rows.summary: Each traditional form is studied in its best examples and then written by the student. The sequence runs heroic couplet, quatrain and ballad stanza, tetrameter couplet, rhyme royal and ottava rima, Spenserian stanza, the sonnet (Petrarchan and Shakespearean), blank verse, villanelle and sestina. The weekly rhythm is read → scan → imitate → revise. The Oxford Book of English Verse serves as the source book.
objectives: Write a finished poem in each of eight forms, revised at least twice
Write two sonnets (one Petrarchan, one Shakespearean) with a true volta
Write 30 lines of blank verse on a narrative subject
Explain why a poet chose a given form, and the effect of the choice, for any studied poem

coreTexts.title: The Oxford Book of English Verse, 1250–1900
coreTexts.author: Arthur Quiller-Couch (ed.)

coreTexts.title: Rhyme's Reason: A Guide to English Verse
coreTexts.author: John Hollander

curriculumOptions.name: The Art of Poetry
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes writing exercises in the forms. Use it with Fry for composition.

curriculumOptions.name: Challenge III (Poetry & Shakespeare strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: Students assemble "a poetry anthology of their own work". A good co-op model for the portfolio.

curriculumOptions.name: The Harp and Laurel Wreath (rhetoric-stage section)
curriculumOptions.notes: The upper-level poems serve as models for imitation.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Writing verse was a normal school exercise until the 20th century. Eton, Winchester and Rugby boys wrote Latin elegiacs and hexameters weekly, and English verse exercises and prize poems were common (Tennyson won Cambridge's Chancellor's Medal for English verse in 1829). Franklin records in his Autobiography turning Spectator essays into verse and back into prose to enlarge his vocabulary.

rows.title: Major Poets I: Chaucer to Milton
rows.summary: Close study of the English poets from the Middle Ages to the Restoration: Chaucer's General Prologue, Shakespeare's Sonnets, Sidney, Donne's Songs and Holy Sonnets, Herbert's The Temple, Southwell, Marvell, and Milton's shorter poems (the Nativity Ode, Lycidas, the sonnets). The metaphysical conceit and the devotional lyric are the center of the course. The student writes imitations of Donne and Herbert.
objectives: Memorize 5 Shakespeare sonnets, 2 Holy Sonnets and 2 Herbert poems
Explicate a metaphysical conceit (e.g. Donne's compasses) in a 1,000-word essay
Scan the pentameter couplets of the General Prologue's opening (hear it read in Middle English; the student's own reading aloud in the original comes in old-english-05)
Write an imitation of a Herbert pattern poem or a Donne holy sonnet

coreTexts.title: A Defence of Poesie and Poems
coreTexts.author: Sir Philip Sidney

coreTexts.title: The Poems of John Donne, Vol. 1 (ed. Grierson)
coreTexts.author: John Donne

coreTexts.title: The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
coreTexts.author: George Herbert

coreTexts.title: The Poetical Works of Robert Southwell
coreTexts.author: St. Robert Southwell, S.J.

coreTexts.title: The Poetical Works of John Milton
coreTexts.author: John Milton

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry, Prose & Drama Book One: The Old English and Medieval Periods (set)
curriculumOptions.notes: The medieval anthology. Follow it with Poetry & Prose Book Two (Elizabethan to Neoclassical).

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry & Prose Book Two: Elizabethan to Neoclassical (set)
curriculumOptions.notes: Shakespeare, Donne, Herbert, Milton and others with guide.

curriculumOptions.name: English 12 (British Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic survey anthology covering Donne, Milton and Gray.

rows.notes: Catholic/Protestant note. This period's devotional poetry comes from both sides of the Reformation divide. Southwell was a Jesuit priest martyred at Tyburn in 1595 and canonized in 1970. Donne was born into a recusant Catholic family and became an Anglican dean. Herbert was a devout Anglican country parson, and Milton a Puritan. Crashaw (Anglican turned Catholic) can be added. The shared devotional tradition is itself a lesson. Chaucer here is studied only as the maker of the English pentameter couplet. The fuller reading of the Canterbury Tales is in literature-18, and the General Prologue in the original Middle English, read aloud and memorized, is in old-english-05.

rows.title: Translating Latin Verse into English
rows.summary: Verse translation and "imitation" in the Augustan manner. The student studies Dryden's Aeneid and Pope's Homer as models, and Johnson's London and Vanity of Human Wishes as imitations of Juvenal. They read Horace in Latin with Conington's verse translations, then produce their own English verse renderings of Horace's odes and passages of Virgil and Ovid, in heroic couplets, blank verse and stanzas. This joins the Latin track to the poetry track, and it is how English poets have always learned their craft.
objectives: Compare three translations of the same passage (e.g. Aeneid II or Iliad VI) for fidelity, meter and diction
Translate 6 Horace odes into rhymed English stanzas
Translate 50+ lines of Virgil into heroic couplets or blank verse
Write a Johnsonian "imitation" of a Latin satire applied to modern life

coreTexts.title: Horace: Odes and Epodes (Latin text, ed. Shorey & Laing)
coreTexts.author: Horace

coreTexts.title: The Odes and Carmen Saeculare of Horace (trans. John Conington)
coreTexts.author: Horace

coreTexts.title: The Vanity of Human Wishes (imitation of Juvenal X)
coreTexts.author: Samuel Johnson

curriculumOptions.name: Aeneid (Latin text and guides)
curriculumOptions.notes: MP's Latin Aeneid program supplies the source text and grammar support for translation.

curriculumOptions.name: Ancient Roman Literature 10
curriculumOptions.notes: The Roman literature course that pairs with the Latin reading.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Translating classical verse into English verse was the school exercise of the English poets. Dryden recalled translating a satire of Persius as a Westminster School exercise, and Pope fell in love with Homer as a boy through Ogilby's translation. Johnson's London (1738) and Vanity of Human Wishes (1749) are the model of "imitation", where the Latin poem is transposed into English circumstances.

rows.title: Major Poets II: Gray to Hopkins
rows.summary: English poetry from the mid-eighteenth century through the Victorians. The course reads Gray's Elegy; Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads and Wordsworth's sonnets and odes; Keats's Odes; Tennyson's In Memoriam; Browning's dramatic monologues; Christina Rossetti; Newman's Dream of Gerontius; and Gerard Manley Hopkins. The focus is the ode, the dramatic monologue and the elegy as forms the student will write in the capstone.
objectives: Memorize Gray's Elegy (or 60 lines of it), one Keats ode, and three Hopkins sonnets
Explicate one of Keats's odes stanza by stanza
Write a dramatic monologue in blank verse after Browning's "My Last Duchess" or "Andrea del Sarto"
Analyze Hopkins' sprung rhythm and inscape in a close reading

coreTexts.title: Select Poems of Thomas Gray (incl. Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard)
coreTexts.author: Thomas Gray

coreTexts.title: Lyrical Ballads, with Other Poems, 1800, Vol. 1
coreTexts.author: William Wordsworth & S. T. Coleridge

coreTexts.title: Goblin Market, The Prince's Progress, and Other Poems
coreTexts.author: Christina Rossetti

coreTexts.title: Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins (ed. Robert Bridges)
coreTexts.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins, S.J.

curriculumOptions.name: Poetry Book III: The Romantic to the Victorian Age (set)
curriculumOptions.notes: Anthology with guide covering the Romantics and Victorians.

curriculumOptions.name: British Literature Course Plan
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic survey including the Romantic and Victorian poets.

curriculumOptions.name: English 12 (British Literature)
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic survey anthology.

rows.notes: Catholic/Protestant note. Hopkins was an Anglican convert received into the Catholic Church by Newman, and he became a Jesuit. His poems were published posthumously in 1918 by his Anglican friend Robert Bridges. Keble (The Christian Year) and Rossetti represent the Anglican High Church. Newman's Gerontius (set by Elgar) is a Catholic poem of purgatory that Protestant readers may treat as a dramatic vision.

rows.title: Major Poets III: Frost, Yeats, Eliot & the Moderns
rows.summary: Twentieth-century poetry in English. The course reads Frost's early books, Yeats, Housman's A Shropshire Lad, Chesterton's "Lepanto" and ballads, Eliot's "Prufrock", The Waste Land and Four Quartets, and Kipling's verse. The question is how modern poets kept, broke or remade the traditional forms. Frost's blank verse and Yeats's stanzas become models, and Eliot's free verse is a problem to understand.
objectives: Memorize two Frost poems, one Yeats poem and one section of Four Quartets
Compare Frost's blank-verse dialogues ("Death of the Hired Man") with Browning's monologues
Write an essay on the religious turn in Eliot from The Waste Land to Four Quartets
Distinguish free verse from loosened accentual verse

curriculumOptions.name: Modern Era Literature 12
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes modern poetry within Kolbe's 12th-grade course.

curriculumOptions.name: Challenge III (Poetry & Shakespeare strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes "a book on poetry" and the student's own anthology.

rows.notes: Chesterton's "Lepanto" (1911) is collected in the 1915 Poems on Gutenberg and is a superb declamation piece. Mature content: a parent should read The Waste Land (the loveless seduction in section III) first and discuss it with the student; it is read with notes in literature-24.

rows.title: Verse Composition Capstone: Sonnet, Blank Verse & Ode
rows.summary: The capstone of poetic competence: a year-long workshop producing a finished portfolio of serious verse in the major forms of the English tradition. The portfolio holds a sonnet sequence, a long poem in blank verse, a Horatian and a Pindaric/irregular ode, a satire in heroic couplets, and verse translations from Latin. Each piece goes through drafts, critique and revision against the models from Milton, Wordsworth, Keats, Hopkins and Frost. The year ends with a public reading.
objectives: Complete a portfolio of 12 sonnets (including a linked sequence), 150+ lines of blank verse, two odes, a couplet satire, and 3 Latin translations
Critique a peer's poem in terms of meter, diction, image and form
Revise each poem at least three times, keeping drafts to show development
Give a public reading of the portfolio from memory
Submit work to at least one juried poetry competition or publication

coreTexts.title: The Poetical Works of John Milton (sonnets, Lycidas)
coreTexts.author: John Milton

coreTexts.title: The Oxford Book of English Verse, 1250–1900
coreTexts.author: Arthur Quiller-Couch (ed.)

curriculumOptions.name: The Art of Poetry
curriculumOptions.notes: Use it for its writing prompts. The portfolio standard here goes well beyond it.

curriculumOptions.name: Challenge III (Poetry & Shakespeare strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: Its own-anthology project is a ready co-op format for the capstone.

curriculumOptions.name: Scholastic Art & Writing Awards (Poetry category; Writing Portfolio for seniors)
curriculumOptions.notes: The oldest U.S. juried awards for young writers (since 1923). Open to students in grades 7–12, age 13 and up; homeschoolers enter through the regional program for their zip code. Poetry is its own category, formal verse included, and graduating seniors may submit a six-piece Writing Portfolio. Regional deadlines fall in December–January, and there is an entry fee (waivers available).

curriculumOptions.name: Dappled Things (Catholic literary journal; Jane Greer Memorial Poetry Contest)
curriculumOptions.notes: A Catholic "journal of ideas, art, and faith" (print and digital since 2005) that publishes poetry, fiction and essays. Every poem submitted in a year is also considered for its Jane Greer Memorial Poetry Contest. It has no separate student or young-writer contest; the student submits alongside adults, which suits a finished capstone portfolio.

rows.historicalPrecedent: English public schools and universities awarded prizes for original verse (Oxford's Newdigate Prize from 1806; Cambridge's Chancellor's Medal from 1813, won by Tennyson). Nineteenth-century educated men and women wrote occasional verse as a normal accomplishment. John Quincy Adams and Lincoln both wrote and published poems.

sources.label: Scholastic Awards: FAQ (eligibility, homeschoolers, fees)
Scholastic Awards: Categories (Poetry; Writing Portfolio)
Foyle Young Poets of the Year Award (Poetry Society, UK; ages 11–17, open worldwide, free)
Young Poets Network (Poetry Society, UK; free challenges for poets up to 25, worldwide)

rows.notes: This row carries the program's "poetic competence" goal. Work with a verse mentor or tutor, ideally one who writes metrical verse: meet every week or two to go over drafts line by line (meter, diction, image, form), and let the mentor choose which finished poems go out to competitions and journals. Poets associated with the classical-school world or with journals publishing formal verse can also critique portfolios. Outlets by stage: the Scholastic Awards (U.S., grades 7–12) and the Foyle Young Poets Award (worldwide, ages 11–17, one poem of up to 40 lines for international entrants) while the student is eligible; Young Poets Network challenges for practice; and Dappled Things as a first adult Catholic venue.

rows.title: Poetics Seminar: Aristotle to Eliot
rows.summary: A college seminar on what poetry is and what it is for. The course reads Aristotle's Poetics, Horace's Ars Poetica, Longinus On the Sublime, Sidney's Defence of Poesy, Pope's Essay on Criticism, Wordsworth's Preface to Lyrical Ballads, Shelley's Defence of Poetry, Eliot's "Tradition and the Individual Talent", and Lewis's An Experiment in Criticism. The student writes a defense of poetry of their own. Theory comes last, after the student has made poems.
objectives: Summarize and critique Aristotle's account of mimesis, plot, character and catharsis
Compare Sidney's and Shelley's defenses of poetry against Plato's charge
Evaluate Wordsworth's claim that poetry uses "the real language of men"
Write a 4,000-word "Defence of Poetry" of the student's own, citing the tradition

coreTexts.title: The Satires, Epistles, and Art of Poetry (trans. Conington)
coreTexts.author: Horace

coreTexts.title: A Defence of Poesie and Poems
coreTexts.author: Sir Philip Sidney

coreTexts.title: A Defence of Poetry and Other Essays
coreTexts.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

coreTexts.title: The Sacred Wood (incl. "Tradition and the Individual Talent")
coreTexts.author: T. S. Eliot

curriculumOptions.name: Aristotle's Poetics Study Guide Set
curriculumOptions.notes: Guided reading of the Poetics.

curriculumOptions.name: Great Books Reading List
curriculumOptions.notes: The Poetics is read in the St. John's freshman year alongside the tragedians.

curriculumOptions.name: Syllabus
curriculumOptions.notes: TAC reads Aristotle's Poetics in its seminar sequence, within a Thomist frame.

rows.notes: The 1800 Lyrical Ballads vol. 1 on Gutenberg (8905) carries the Preface. The expanded 1802 Preface (with "What is a Poet?") is worth locating in a modern edition. Plato's Ion and Republic X should be read first (see the philosophy track).

rows.title: Practical Life at Home: Chores and Household Help
rows.summary: Toddlers want to help, and a child-sized broom, pitcher, trowel and apron let them. Montessori "practical life" work (pouring, sweeping, washing vegetables, folding cloths, watering plants) builds fine-motor control, concentration and order. Real family chores build responsibility. By six a child can set the table, make his bed, help cook, weed, feed animals, and hand tools to a parent doing repairs.
objectives: Carry out daily self-care and tidying without prompting (dressing, bed, toys, dishes to the sink)
Help with food preparation (washing, stirring, spreading, cutting soft foods with a child-safe knife)
Care for a plant or pet on a daily schedule
Hold and pass common hand tools safely while helping an adult
rows.notes: Pay is not given for ordinary family chores, which are part of belonging to the household. Extra jobs can earn money (see economics-01).

rows.title: The Kitchen Garden
rows.summary: The child plants and keeps his own raised bed or plot through a full season. He starts seeds, plans the spacing, waters, weeds, composts, harvests, and saves seed. Like Jefferson, he keeps a garden book recording what was planted, when it came up, and when it was first ready for the table, and each year he compares results with the year before.
objectives: Plan a garden bed on graph paper with spacing and a planting calendar
Grow at least six vegetables and herbs from seed to harvest
Keep a dated garden journal of sowing, germination, harvest and weather
Build and turn a compost pile; save seed from one open-pollinated plant

curriculumOptions.name: Junior Master Gardener
curriculumOptions.notes: A youth gardening curriculum with certification levels; run through extension offices or at home.

curriculumOptions.name: 4-H (local club projects in gardening and plant science)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson kept his Garden Book for almost sixty years (1766–1824), recording plantings and first harvests at Shadwell and Monticello. In retirement he wrote to Charles Willson Peale (1811), "tho' an old man, I am but a young gardener."

sources.label: Jefferson to Charles Willson Peale, 20 Aug. 1811 (Founders Online)

rows.title: Cooking and Baking
rows.summary: A graded kitchen apprenticeship. It begins with knife safety, measuring and following a recipe (fractions in use), then moves to eggs, bread, soups, a roast, vegetables from the garden, preserving, and finally planning, budgeting and cooking a full family dinner. Historic American cookbooks are cooked from alongside modern ones; Mary Randolph's The Virginia House-Wife was written by the sister of Jefferson's son-in-law.
objectives: Use a chef's knife safely and master basic cuts
Measure accurately and double or halve a recipe
Bake a loaf of yeast bread and a pie from scratch
Can or preserve one garden crop safely
Plan, shop for within a budget, and cook a three-course dinner for the family

coreTexts.title: The Virginia House-Wife; or, Methodical Cook
coreTexts.author: Mary Randolph

curriculumOptions.name: Cooking Merit Badge
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes meal planning, nutrition and camp cooking requirements.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Fannie Farmer's cookbook grew out of the Boston Cooking School. It is often credited with bringing level, standardized measurements into American home cooking.

rows.title: Needle and Thread: Sewing, Mending and Knots
rows.summary: Every boy and girl should be able to mend his own clothes. The unit runs from threading a needle and the running, back and whip stitches, to sewing on buttons, hemming, darning a sock, patching jeans, and a first sewing-machine project such as an apron or tote bag. Essential knots (square knot, bowline, clove hitch, taut-line hitch, sheet bend) are learned alongside for camping and sailing.
objectives: Sew on a button, repair a seam, and hem a pair of trousers by hand
Darn a sock and patch a hole
Complete a simple machine-sewn project from a pattern
Tie and state the use of six essential knots from memory

rows.title: Sloyd: First Woodworking
rows.summary: Sloyd is the Scandinavian system of educational handwork. A graded series of useful wooden objects, each harder than the last (a plant label, a flower stick, a coat hanger, a cutting board, a spoon, a box), teaches knife, saw, plane and chisel skills, accurate measurement, and the habit of finishing work well. It was designed for children and uses real, sharp tools under close supervision.
objectives: Use a sloyd knife, crosscut and rip saws, block plane, chisel, brace and bit, and hand drill safely
Measure and mark to 1/16 inch and cut to a line
Complete a graded series of eight or more sloyd models
Sharpen a knife and a chisel on stones

coreTexts.title: The Teacher's Handbook of Slöjd, as Practised and Taught at Nääs
coreTexts.author: Otto Salomon

rows.historicalPrecedent: Otto Salomon's teacher-training school at Nääs, Sweden (from 1875), trained teachers from around the world. Sloyd spread into American schools in the 1880s–1890s, notably through Gustaf Larsson's Sloyd Training School in Boston.

rows.title: Typing and Computing Basics
rows.summary: Touch typing is the modern clerk's hand, and it should be learned properly once rather than badly forever. The student reaches 40 or more words per minute by touch. He learns file management, word processing and a spreadsheet (used for the garden and business ledgers), and the basics of online safety and privacy. A first taste of programming in Scratch leads into the Programming track.
objectives: Type 40+ words per minute by touch with 95% accuracy
Create, format and save documents and organize files in folders
Build a simple spreadsheet with formulas (a budget or garden log)
Explain basic rules of online safety, passwords and privacy
Complete a small Scratch project
rows.notes: Keep screen time purposeful and supervised. The early-development track's screen guidance still applies in spirit.

rows.title: Spencerian Penmanship and the Art of Correspondence
rows.summary: After ordinary cursive is mastered, the student learns the ornamental American hand, Spencerian script, from the Mott Media reprint copybooks. He then studies the eighteenth-century round hand (copperplate) from Bickham's Universal Penman. Fine penmanship is put to work in real letters: thank-you notes, letters to grandparents, business letters, and letters to a mentor. The models are Chesterfield's letters of advice to his son and Jefferson's to his nephew Peter Carr.
objectives: Write Spencerian lowercase and capitals legibly with correct slant and proportion
Write a page of copperplate with a pointed pen and ink
Write and mail at least one letter a month for a year (personal, business, and to a public official)
Know the conventions of heading, salutation, body, complimentary close and envelope address

coreTexts.title: Letters to His Son
coreTexts.author: Philip Dormer Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield

coreTexts.title: Thomas Jefferson to Peter Carr, 19 August 1785
coreTexts.author: Thomas Jefferson

curriculumOptions.name: Spencerian Penmanship Set (Theory Book and five copybooks)
curriculumOptions.notes: A faithful reprint of the nineteenth-century Spencerian system, suited to ages 9 and up.

curriculumOptions.name: IAMPETH (free lessons in Spencerian and engrosser's script)
curriculumOptions.publisher: International Association of Master Penmen, Engrossers and Teachers of Handwriting

rows.historicalPrecedent: Platt Rogers Spencer's system was the standard American business and school hand from the 1850s until the Palmer Method replaced it in the early twentieth century. Bickham's Universal Penman (1733–41) collected the round hands used by English and colonial clerks and merchants in the founders' generation.
rows.notes: Chesterfield's letters are excellent on manners, style and the use of time, but Samuel Johnson and others criticized some of their moral advice. Read them selectively and discuss.

rows.title: Animal Husbandry and the Small Farm
rows.summary: The student takes full responsibility for productive animals: a laying flock of hens, then rabbits, goats, a beehive or a 4-H market animal. He handles feeding, housing, health, breeding, butchering or sale, and keeps records of costs and production on the model of Jefferson's Farm Book. Rural families can add field crops and rotation. Town families can use 4-H, a neighbor's farm or a community garden.
objectives: Raise a laying flock (or equivalent) for a year, keeping records of feed, eggs and costs
Recognize common signs of illness and parasites and know when to call a veterinarian
Explain crop rotation, soil fertility and the farm year
Show an animal or project at a county fair or 4-H event

curriculumOptions.name: 4-H animal science projects
curriculumOptions.notes: The standard youth program for livestock projects, run through county extension offices.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Washington and Jefferson were serious experimental farmers who experimented with crop rotation, new plows and livestock breeding and corresponded about them.
rows.notes: Jefferson's Farm Book is also the record of the enslaved people who worked Monticello: their names, rations and assignments. Read it honestly as both an agricultural record and a primary source on slavery.

rows.title: Surveying, Map-Making and Orienteering
rows.summary: Washington's first profession, and a practical application of geometry and trigonometry. The student learns to use map and compass and competes in orienteering. He reads USGS topographic maps, then surveys a real field with a chain (a 66-foot Gunter's chain, or a tape), a compass or transit, and field notes, following Gibson's Treatise, the colonial surveyor's manual. He computes the area and draws a plat to scale, and compares it with a GPS survey and the county's recorded plat.
objectives: Take and follow bearings with a baseplate compass and complete an orienteering course
Read contour lines and plan a route on a topographic map
Run a closed traverse with chain and compass, keep field notes, and compute the error of closure
Compute the area of an irregular field in acres and draw a plat to scale
Explain Gunter's chain (66 feet, 100 links; 10 square chains = 1 acre) and the rectangular survey system
rows.historicalPrecedent: Washington studied surveying as a teenager, joined a Fairfax survey party in the Shenandoah in 1748, and in 1749, at seventeen, was commissioned by the College of William and Mary as surveyor of the new Culpeper County. He completed his first survey, a 400-acre tract, within two days. Jefferson's father Peter was a surveyor who helped draw the Fry–Jefferson map of Virginia (1751).

sources.label: Mount Vernon: Surveying (Digital Encyclopedia)
USGS: Topographic Maps

rows.title: Joinery and Carpentry
rows.summary: From sloyd to real furniture and building. The student learns to flatten and square stock by hand, then cut the classic joints: mortise and tenon, through and half-blind dovetails, rabbets and dados. He builds a tool chest, a bench or bookcase, and a Shaker-style table, and then joins a real carpentry project such as a shed, a deck or a church repair. The Joiner and Cabinet Maker (1839) follows a fictional English apprentice through his first projects and is the model.
objectives: Sharpen and set up a hand plane; flatten, joint and thickness a board by hand
Cut mortise-and-tenon and dovetail joints that fit off the saw
Build a dovetailed tool chest from a drawing
Frame a small structure (shed or playhouse) with a crew, including layout, squaring and roof pitch

curriculumOptions.name: The Joiner and Cabinet Maker (1839 text with modern project commentary)
curriculumOptions.notes: An 1839 apprentice's manual, reprinted with step-by-step modern builds of its three projects.

curriculumOptions.name: The Essential Woodworker (Robert Wearing)
curriculumOptions.notes: A clear English manual of hand-tool technique for the beginner.

rows.title: First Aid, CPR and Emergency Readiness
rows.summary: A citizen should be able to help in the first minutes of an emergency. The student earns a certification in first aid, CPR and AED use. He learns to control bleeding (tourniquet use), treat shock, splint fractures, and handle burns, choking, heat and cold injuries, and allergic reactions. He builds a home and car emergency kit and a family emergency plan. Wilderness first aid follows for older teens who camp and hunt.
objectives: Earn a current certification in first aid, CPR and AED (Red Cross or AHA)
Demonstrate bleeding control, including a tourniquet, and the recovery position
Assemble and maintain a home first-aid kit and a family emergency plan
Complete a wilderness first-aid course by age 16 if camping or hunting

rows.title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
rows.summary: The merchant's art since Venice. The student learns journal, ledger and trial balance by hand from the historical texts: Pacioli's 1494 treatise (in translation) and the nineteenth-century American bookkeeping manuals. He then keeps the books of his own enterprise and the family's accounts in a spreadsheet and in accounting software. The course ends with reading and preparing a balance sheet, an income statement and a cash-flow statement.
objectives: Record transactions in a journal, post to a ledger, and take a trial balance by hand
Explain debits, credits, assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses
Prepare a balance sheet and income statement for a small business
Keep the books of a real enterprise (his own or the family's) for at least six months

coreTexts.title: Ancient Double-Entry Bookkeeping: Lucas Pacioli's Treatise (1494), trans. J. B. Geijsbeek
coreTexts.author: Luca Pacioli

coreTexts.title: Duff's Book-Keeping by Single and Double Entry
coreTexts.author: P. Duff

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin's Autobiography praises the widow of his Charleston printing partner. Born and bred in Holland, "where... the knowledge of accounts makes a part of female education," she sent him clear accounts, ran the business profitably, and bought it for her son. Franklin draws the lesson that accounts should be taught to young women as well as young men.

sources.label: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Project Gutenberg)

rows.title: Running a Small Enterprise: Franklin's Apprenticeship and the Junto
rows.summary: The student starts and runs a real business for at least a year, such as lawn care, tutoring, woodworking commissions, eggs and produce, or web design. He writes a business plan, prices his work, finds customers, keeps double-entry books, files any required paperwork and taxes, and reports to a family board. He reads Franklin's Autobiography as the story of an apprentice who became a master, and he forms a Junto of peers that meets monthly to discuss its standing queries.
objectives: Write a one-page business plan with costs, pricing, market and break-even point
Operate a business for 12 months with books, invoices and a year-end profit and loss statement
Handle customers professionally (quotes, contracts, complaints, collections)
Found or join a peer Junto and lead at least one meeting using the standing queries

curriculumOptions.name: Junior Achievement (Company Program and entrepreneurship programs)
curriculumOptions.notes: Availability depends on local chapters and schools.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Franklin was bound apprentice at twelve to his brother James, a Boston printer, and left at seventeen. By twenty-two he had his own Philadelphia printing house. In 1727 he founded the Junto, a club of young tradesmen for "mutual improvement" that met weekly to debate set questions on morals, politics and natural philosophy. The Junto later gave rise to the Library Company and the American Philosophical Society.

rows.title: Celestial Navigation and Sailing
rows.summary: The student learns small-boat sailing (rigging, points of sail, tacking and jibing, capsize recovery, rules of the road) and coastal piloting with charts, then celestial navigation from Bowditch's American Practical Navigator. He learns sextant use, the noon sight for latitude, time and longitude, sight reduction with the Nautical Almanac and tables, and plotting a position. The navigation is practiced ashore with an artificial horizon and afloat where possible.
objectives: Earn a US Sailing small-boat certification (or the Small-Boat Sailing merit badge)
Plot a coastal course with dead reckoning and bearings on a paper chart
Take a noon sight with a sextant and compute latitude within 5 nautical miles
Reduce a star or sun sight and plot a line of position

coreTexts.title: The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), Pub. No. 9
coreTexts.author: Nathaniel Bowditch / National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency

curriculumOptions.name: US Sailing (youth and adult certification courses)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Nathaniel Bowditch of Salem left school at ten and was apprenticed to a ship chandler. He taught himself mathematics and Latin, corrected thousands of errors in the standard British navigation tables, and published The New American Practical Navigator (1802), still issued by the U.S. government. Midshipmen of the founding-era navies learned navigation at sea in their early teens.

rows.title: Architecture and Mechanical Drawing: Jefferson's Palladio
rows.summary: Jefferson taught himself architecture from Palladio and designed Monticello, the Virginia State Capitol and the University of Virginia. The student learns drafting by hand and then with CAD: orthographic projection, isometric views, sections, dimensioning and scale. He studies the classical orders from Palladio's Four Books and makes a measured drawing of a real building. His capstone is a set of drawings for a small building, which ideally he later builds (see practical-arts-10).
objectives: Draw orthographic, isometric and section views to scale by hand
Identify and draw the five classical orders with correct proportions
Produce a measured drawing of an existing building or room
Design a small building (shed, cabin or chapel) with plan, elevations and a materials list

coreTexts.title: The Four Books of Architecture (Isaac Ware trans.)
coreTexts.author: Andrea Palladio

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson owned several editions of Palladio and relied on it throughout his building life. He began Monticello in 1768 at twenty-five, redesigned it for decades, and planned the University of Virginia's "academical village" in his seventies.

sources.label: Monticello: A House and Home

rows.title: Home and Auto Mechanics, Driving and Field Skills
rows.summary: This course covers keeping a house and a car running and driving safely. Household repairs include plumbing (a faucet, a toilet, a clog), electrical work (a switch, an outlet, a fixture, done safely with the power off), patching drywall, painting, and caulking and weatherproofing. Automotive maintenance includes fluids, tires, brakes, a battery, belts and diagnosis with an OBD reader. The student completes supervised driving practice beyond the state minimum and earns a license. Firearm safety and marksmanship are standard and are taught in physical-training-07. Hunting is optional.
objectives: Fix a leaking faucet, clear a drain, replace an outlet or switch, and patch drywall
Change oil and a tire, check and top up fluids, and replace wiper blades and a battery
Log at least 100 hours of supervised driving across night, highway and bad-weather conditions
Earn a driver's license and maintain a clean record

curriculumOptions.name: Hunter education (state-approved online course plus field day)
curriculumOptions.notes: Required in most states before a first hunting license. See also Project Appleseed and NRA Eddie Eagle below.

curriculumOptions.name: Project Appleseed (optional; rifle marksmanship with Revolutionary War history)

sources.label: NHTSA: Teen Safe Driving
NRA Eddie Eagle GunSafe (gun-safety message for young children)

rows.notes: Firearm safety and marksmanship are standard (see physical-training-07). Hunting is optional and depends on family conviction and local law. Begin with the Eddie Eagle rule for young children (stop, don't touch, run away, tell a grown-up), then hunter education and supervised marksmanship. Keep firearms locked and unloaded when not in use.

rows.title: Public Service, Apprenticeship and Mentorship
rows.summary: The student serves the community and learns a profession under a master, as the founders did. Service means sustained volunteering (at least 100 hours a year) in a parish or civic organization, a hospital, a fire company, or Civil Air Patrol cadets. Apprenticeship means a structured, supervised placement with professionals in law, medicine, engineering, a skilled trade, business or government, where the student keeps a work journal, is evaluated, and asks for a letter of reference. Two placements in different fields are ideal.
objectives: Complete 100+ hours of documented community service per year with one organization
Complete at least one 6–12-week supervised placement with a professional mentor
Keep a daily work journal and write a reflective report on the profession
Earn a written evaluation and letter of reference from the mentor

curriculumOptions.name: Civil Air Patrol Cadet Program (ages 12–21)
curriculumOptions.publisher: Civil Air Patrol (U.S. Air Force Auxiliary)
curriculumOptions.notes: Leadership, aerospace education, emergency services and search-and-rescue.

curriculumOptions.name: Registered Apprenticeship finder
curriculumOptions.notes: For trades and technical fields; professional mentorships are usually arranged through family and parish networks.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Apprenticeship and reading in a practitioner's office were the normal routes into a profession in the eighteenth century. Franklin was apprenticed to a printer, Adams read law under James Putnam, Jefferson under George Wythe, and Hamilton clerked in a St. Croix trading house from his early teens. Washington held public office at seventeen as Culpeper County surveyor.

rows.title: College: Estate and Household Management
rows.summary: The capstone of the founder skills: managing a household, and eventually an estate, business or farm, as a steward. The course covers annual budgeting and capital planning, insurance, renting versus buying, property and maintenance schedules, hiring and managing help, contracts, and estate planning (wills, guardianship and trusts, with an attorney). It also covers hospitality and the duties of a householder to parish and neighborhood. The student reads Beecher and Beeton, the nineteenth century's comprehensive household manuals, alongside Washington's and Jefferson's farm and household records.
objectives: Prepare a full annual household budget and 10-year capital plan (roof, car, furnace)
Compare insurance options (health, auto, home or renter's, life, umbrella) and explain each
Draft a household maintenance calendar and inventory
Explain the basic instruments of estate planning and why each adult needs a will
Host a formal dinner for guests, planned, budgeted and cooked by the student
rows.notes: This row teaches general principles of household finance and management. It is not legal or financial advice; consult an attorney for wills and trusts and a qualified advisor for investments and insurance.

rows.title: Read-Aloud, Rhymes & Dialogic Reading
rows.summary: Daily read-aloud of good books, Mother Goose and memorized verse builds vocabulary, a sense of story and phonological awareness (rhyme, syllables, first sounds), which are the real foundations of reading. Dialogic reading, in which the adult asks the child questions and expands the answers, measurably boosts oral language.
objectives: Hear at least 20–30 minutes of read-aloud daily from quality picture books and verse
Recognize and produce rhymes; clap syllables; identify the first sound of a word
Retell a familiar story in sequence and answer "what/why" questions about it

sources.label: Reading Rockets: Dialogic Reading (Whitehurst)
National Reading Panel (NICHD, 2000)

rows.notes: This row overlaps with the early-development track. It is kept here as the literacy on-ramp.

rows.title: Pre-Reading: Phonemic Awareness, Letter Sounds & Letter Formation
rows.summary: When the child shows interest, play oral sound games (blending and segmenting spoken words), teach letter sounds rather than letter names first, and teach correct letter formation with a pencil or in sand. Keep sessions short and playful. The aim is readiness, not early reading for its own sake.
objectives: Blend spoken sounds into words (/c/-/a/-/t/ → cat) and segment simple words into sounds
Know the most common sound of every letter
Form lower-case letters correctly

coreTexts.title: The New England Primer (reprint of the earliest known edition)
coreTexts.author: ed. Paul Leicester Ford

curriculumOptions.name: Logic of English Foundations A
curriculumOptions.notes: Orton-Gillingham-based. Level A starts with phonemic awareness and handwriting for ages 4–7 and flows straight into reading.

curriculumOptions.name: Teach Your Child to Read in 100 Easy Lessons
curriculumOptions.notes: Direct Instruction (Engelmann), scripted 15–20 minute lessons. Effective for a ready 4–5-year-old, though it uses a special orthography at first.

sources.label: Neuman et al. (2014), Can babies learn to read? A randomized trial of baby media

rows.historicalPrecedent: Colonial children learned letters and syllables from the hornbook and then the New England Primer ("In Adam's fall / We sinned all"), usually at a dame school, often by age 4–6.
rows.notes: Evidence caveat. "Teach your baby to read" programs (Doman's How to Teach Your Baby to Read, the Your Baby Can Read videos) are not supported. In a randomized trial (Neuman et al., 2014), infants 9–18 months old who used a baby-reading program learned no more than controls, although parents believed they had. Reading instruction proper belongs at 4–6, when phonemic awareness is ready.

rows.title: Explicit Phonics I: Phonograms & Spelling-First Decoding
rows.summary: The child learns systematically the 70-odd phonograms (letters and letter teams and their sounds) and the rules of English spelling, writing each word from dictation before reading it. This spelling-first, Orton-Gillingham/Spalding approach produces readers who can decode, and spell, nearly any English word.
objectives: Say and write the common phonograms (sh, ch, th, ck, ai, ay, ee, igh, ow, ou…) with all their sounds
Read and spell one- and two-syllable words with blends, digraphs and silent-e
Read decodable sentences and short books aloud

curriculumOptions.name: Literacy Essentials: The Journey from Spelling to Reading
curriculumOptions.notes: Hillsdale's own K-2 literacy program for its classical charter schools. Spelling-first explicit phonics.

curriculumOptions.name: The Writing Road to Reading (Spalding Method)
curriculumOptions.notes: The original spelling-first program. Rigorous, with a steep teacher-learning curve; training is available.

curriculumOptions.name: Logic of English Foundations B–D
curriculumOptions.notes: Most parent-friendly of the three, with games and scripted lessons.

rows.title: Explicit Phonics II: Readers from the Classical & Catholic Traditions
rows.summary: The phonics sequence is completed (vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, multi-syllable words, common suffixes) while the child reads connected text daily from graded readers, including the McGuffey Primer and First Reader. Children in the Catholic programs read stories of saints and the Church year.
objectives: Decode multi-syllable words using syllable division and suffix rules
Read the McGuffey Primer and First Reader aloud with accuracy
Read about 60+ words per minute accurately in grade-1 text by the end of the year

curriculumOptions.name: First Start Reading (Books A–D)
curriculumOptions.notes: Gentle, inexpensive classical phonics with printing practice built in. Pairs with Memoria's readers.

curriculumOptions.name: Little Stories for Little Folks (Catholic phonics program)
curriculumOptions.notes: Phonics booklets with Catholic content. Warm and low-cost.

curriculumOptions.name: Seton Phonics (K–3)
curriculumOptions.notes: Traditional workbook phonics with Catholic content. Part of Seton's full grade-level program.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The McGuffey Readers (1836; revised 1879) sold over 100 million copies and taught most 19th-century American children to read, with graded lessons that also carried moral and religious instruction.

rows.title: Spelling Mastery: Webster's Blue-Back Speller & McGuffey's Speller
rows.summary: Spelling is consolidated through the old spellers' graded word columns, syllabication and accentuation, and weekly dictation. Webster's Blue-Back Speller, the most-used American schoolbook of the founding generation, is used alongside a modern spelling list sequence.
objectives: Spell the 1,000 most common English words correctly in dictation
Divide words into syllables and mark the accented syllable
Apply the major spelling rules (doubling, drop silent-e, y to i) automatically

curriculumOptions.name: Spalding spelling lists (The Writing Road to Reading)
curriculumOptions.notes: The Ayres-list sequence that continues the phonogram work of reading-phonics-03.

curriculumOptions.name: Memoria Press phonics and spelling
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical spelling workbooks that follow First Start Reading.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Webster's speller (1783) sold tens of millions of copies. With the New England Primer and the Bible it formed the basic literacy of the early Republic, and it was consciously designed to create a uniform American English.

rows.title: Fluent Oral Reading: McGuffey Second & Third Readers
rows.summary: Fluency (accuracy, rate and expression) is built through repeated oral reading of graded passages, as the 19th-century schools did with the McGuffey Readers. The child reads aloud daily to a parent and practises a passage until it is smooth and expressive.
objectives: Read grade-2 and grade-3 text aloud accurately with natural phrasing and expression
Reach roughly 90–110 words correct per minute on grade-level passages
Read a prepared poem or passage aloud to the family weekly

curriculumOptions.name: All About Reading (Levels 2–4)
curriculumOptions.notes: Orton-Gillingham-based modern alternative with built-in fluency sheets and lovely readers. The link is Level 1; later levels follow.

curriculumOptions.name: Memoria Press phonics & early-reading sequence (after First Start Reading)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical follow-on materials for grades 1–2. Choose from the category page by level.

sources.label: Reading Rockets: Hasbrouck–Tindal oral reading fluency norms (2017)

rows.title: Independent Reading: Speed, Silent Reading & Comprehension
rows.summary: The capstone of the track. The child moves from oral to fast silent reading, reads whole books independently for an hour or more a day, and proves comprehension through oral and written narration (Charlotte Mason), not worksheets. Reading then becomes the child's chief means of learning in every other subject.
objectives: Read silently at 150+ words per minute with full comprehension of grade-4 text
Read chapter books independently (e.g. McGuffey Fourth Reader level and real children's classics)
Narrate a chapter orally in sequence after one reading
Use a dictionary to look up unfamiliar words

coreTexts.title: Home Education (Vol. 1), on narration and reading
coreTexts.author: Charlotte M. Mason

coreTexts.title: McGuffey's Fifth and Sixth Eclectic Readers (look-ahead)
coreTexts.author: William Holmes McGuffey

curriculumOptions.name: Writing With Ease (narration and comprehension strand)
curriculumOptions.notes: Short daily passages from real books with scripted narration questions. Doubles as the start of grammar-composition-02.

curriculumOptions.name: Charlotte Mason narration (free, via Home Education)
curriculumOptions.notes: The child reads once, then tells back. No workbook is needed; the parent uses living books.

rows.historicalPrecedent: J.S. Mill's Autobiography records that he began Greek at three, read Aesop and Xenophon in Greek before eight, and read English histories for pleasure in early childhood. The McGuffey Fifth and Sixth Readers show that an ordinary 19th-century 10–12-year-old read Shakespeare, Irving and Webster's speeches, which is the literature track's starting line.

sources.label: J.S. Mill, Autobiography (Project Gutenberg)

rows.title: Recitation, Show-and-Tell & Memory Work
rows.summary: Young children build a store of memorized language (nursery rhymes, short poems, prayers, psalm verses) and practice speaking to a small audience. They tell about an object, retell a story in order, or "narrate" a read-aloud. This oral practice is the soil in which later composition and oratory grow.
objectives: Recite several short poems, rhymes and prayers from memory with expression
Stand, look at the listeners, and speak clearly for 30–60 seconds
Retell a familiar story with a beginning, middle and end
Listen politely and ask a question of another speaker

curriculumOptions.name: Linguistic Development through Poetry Memorization
curriculumOptions.notes: Ninety-six graded poems and speeches with recordings. Level 1 suits ages 4–7. It can be played in the car and at meals.

rows.notes: Keep it short and joyful: a weekly "family recital" where each child recites or shows something. Charlotte Mason–style narration (the child retells a passage after one hearing) is the simplest daily form.

rows.title: Recitation & Elocution I: Poems, Psalms and the Readers
rows.summary: Formal memorization and delivery of graded poems, Scripture passages and short prose selections, on the model of the McGuffey Eclectic Readers, which printed pronunciation and "articulation" exercises before each lesson. Children learn posture, breath, volume, pace and expression, and begin to narrate in writing.
objectives: Memorize and recite 10–20 poems and passages per year
Practice articulation drills and read aloud with proper phrasing and emphasis
Deliver a two-minute oral narration or report
Evaluate a sibling's recitation kindly using simple criteria (loud, clear, slow, expressive)

coreTexts.title: McGuffey's Eclectic Readers (First–Sixth), esp. the Sixth Reader's rules of elocution
coreTexts.author: William Holmes McGuffey

curriculumOptions.name: Linguistic Development through Poetry Memorization (Levels 2–3)
curriculumOptions.notes: A graded, review-driven memory system with poems and famous speeches.

rows.historicalPrecedent: American common schools of the 1800s drilled recitation and "declamation" from the McGuffey Readers, whose higher books open with rules of articulation, inflection and emphasis. Friday-afternoon declamations were a school tradition.

rows.title: Progymnasmata I: Fable, Narrative, Chreia & Maxim
rows.summary: These are the first graded exercises of the classical progymnasmata, the composition sequence handed down from Aesop-era schools through Aphthonius (4th century) to the Renaissance grammar schools. Students retell, condense, amplify and re-order fables and narratives, then develop a wise saying (chreia) or proverb (maxim) through the standard "heads of development".
objectives: Paraphrase and amplify a fable and state its moral
Retell a narrative from a different point of view or in a different order
Develop a chreia by praise, paraphrase, cause, contrary, analogy, example, testimony and epilogue
Copy and imitate model sentences (copia) to vary expression

coreTexts.title: Progymnasmata (Latin trans. by Rodolphus Agricola & J.M. Catanaeus)
coreTexts.author: Aphthonius of Antioch

curriculumOptions.name: Writing & Rhetoric Books 1–4 (Fable; Narrative I–II; Chreia & Proverb)
curriculumOptions.notes: Twelve-book progymnasmata series by Paul Kortepeter, starting in grade 3 or 4. It is gentle and well scaffolded, and each book is one semester.

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Composition I–III (Fable; Narrative; Chreia & Maxim)
curriculumOptions.notes: A more rigorous progymnasmata sequence (Fable at grade 4+, Narrative 5+, Chreia & Maxim 6+). Pairs naturally with Memoria Press Latin.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Aphthonius's Progymnasmata, in Latin translation, was a standard grammar-school text in 16th- and 17th-century England (the likely school exercises of Shakespeare and Milton), and Jesuit colleges used it too.

rows.title: Progymnasmata II: Refutation, Confirmation, Commonplace & Encomium
rows.summary: The middle exercises teach argument. Students refute or confirm a story as implausible, inconsistent or improper (refutation/confirmation); amplify the case against a vice or crime (commonplace); and praise or blame a person (encomium/invective). This is where logic and rhetoric meet, and the student's first persuasive essays and speeches appear.
objectives: Refute and confirm a narrative using the topics of clarity, plausibility, possibility, consistency and propriety
Write and deliver a commonplace against a vice
Compose an encomium of a historical or biblical figure by the standard heads (origin, upbringing, deeds, comparison)
Revise for arrangement (introduction, statement, proof, conclusion)

curriculumOptions.name: Writing & Rhetoric Books 5–7 (Refutation & Confirmation; Commonplace; Encomium & Vituperation)
curriculumOptions.notes: Continues the CAP series. Each book is a semester.

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Composition IV–VI (Refutation/Confirmation; Common Topic; Encomium, Invective & Comparison)
curriculumOptions.notes: A rigorous Memoria Press sequence with teacher guides and video.

rows.title: Declamation & Elocution: The 19th-Century Speaker's Training
rows.summary: On the model of 18th- and 19th-century schools, the student memorizes and declaims set pieces of oratory and poetry drawn from the standard "speakers" and readers, and studies voice, gesture, emphasis and pause. Thomas Sheridan's Lectures on Elocution (1762) and Lindley Murray's English Reader, the most widely used American school reader before McGuffey, supply both theory and repertoire.
objectives: Memorize and declaim at least one major speech excerpt per term (e.g. Henry, Webster, Lincoln)
Apply rules of emphasis, inflection and pause, and mark a text for delivery
Use gesture, eye contact and movement purposefully
Deliver a selection before an audience and take structured critique
