coreTexts.author: Lindley Murray

coreTexts.title: A Course of Lectures on Elocution
coreTexts.author: Thomas Sheridan

coreTexts.title: McGuffey's Sixth Eclectic Reader
coreTexts.author: William Holmes McGuffey (compiled with Alexander H. McGuffey)

curriculumOptions.name: Linguistic Development through Poetry Memorization (upper levels, famous speeches)
curriculumOptions.notes: Includes speeches suitable for declamation.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Declamation was a weekly exercise at Boston Latin, the academies, and the colleges. Harvard and Yale students declaimed in chapel, and Eton kept formal speech days. Murray's English Reader was one of the most widely used school readers in the early republic.

rows.title: Progymnasmata III: Comparison, Characterization, Description, Thesis & Law
rows.summary: The last progymnasmata. Students compare two persons or things; write in the voice of a historical or literary figure (characterization/ethopoeia); describe vividly (ekphrasis); argue a general question (thesis); and speak for or against a proposed law. The thesis and law exercises lead directly into full deliberative oratory and debate.
objectives: Write a comparison (syncrisis) of two statesmen or saints
Compose a speech in the character of a historical figure at a turning point
Argue a thesis ("Should a man marry?", "Is monarchy the best regime?") by the final headings
Draft and defend or attack a proposed law, using the topics of legality, justice, expediency and possibility

curriculumOptions.name: Writing & Rhetoric Books 8–11 (Comparison; Description & Impersonation; Thesis Parts 1–2)
curriculumOptions.notes: Completes the CAP series (it has no separate Law book; use Memoria Press IX or a tutor for the law exercise).

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Composition VII–IX (Characterization; Description; Thesis & Law)
curriculumOptions.notes: Completes the Memoria Press sequence.

rows.title: Classical Rhetoric I: Aristotle & the Five Canons
rows.summary: The student studies rhetoric as a theory. Aristotle's Rhetoric covers ethos, pathos and logos, the three genres, the topics, the enthymeme, and style and arrangement. The five canons (invention, arrangement, style, memory, delivery) organize the course. Corbett's Classical Rhetoric for the Modern Student is the standard modern bridge, and Kolln's Rhetorical Grammar teaches the rhetoric of the sentence.
objectives: Explain and apply ethos, pathos and logos to a speech
Distinguish deliberative, forensic and epideictic oratory and their ends
Use the common and special topics to invent arguments
Analyze figures of speech (schemes and tropes) and use several deliberately
Deliver a 5–7 minute deliberative speech built by the five canons

coreTexts.title: Classical Rhetoric for the Modern Student (4th ed.)
coreTexts.author: Edward P.J. Corbett & Robert J. Connors

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Rhetoric with Aristotle
curriculumOptions.notes: A guided study of Aristotle's Rhetoric in Memoria Press's high-school sequence.

curriculumOptions.name: Fitting Words — Classical Rhetoric for the Christian Student
curriculumOptions.notes: Thirty lessons organized by the five canons, drawing on Aristotle and the Ad Herennium, with model speeches from Scripture, Cicero, Henry and King.

curriculumOptions.name: Rhetoric Alive! Book 1 — Principles of Persuasion
curriculumOptions.notes: A lively modern introduction built on Aristotle. Pairs with CAP's Writing & Rhetoric.

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Logic and Rhetoric (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Ten 30-minute lectures by Benjamin Beier, modeled on Hillsdale's core course and covering the canons of rhetoric and great orators from Socrates to Churchill.

rows.notes: Kolln & Gray's Rhetorical Grammar (Pearson, https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/rhetorical-grammar-grammatical-choices-rhetorical-effects/P200000002254/9780137518265) works well alongside this course for sentence-level style.

rows.title: Great Speeches as Models: Demosthenes to King
rows.summary: Classical imitation (imitatio) means reading, analyzing, memorizing and imitating master speeches. The canon runs from Demosthenes' Philippics and Cicero's Catilinarians through Burke on conciliation with America, Patrick Henry, Webster's Reply to Hayne, Lincoln's Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural, and Churchill in 1940, to King's Letter from Birmingham Jail. Each speech is studied in its historical setting as an act of statesmanship.
objectives: Analyze each speech for situation, audience, purpose, arrangement and figures
Memorize and deliver at least four major passages across the unit
Write an imitation that uses a model's structure on a new subject
Compare the ancient and modern styles of deliberative eloquence

coreTexts.title: The Public Orations of Demosthenes, vol. 1 (Olynthiacs, Philippics)
coreTexts.author: Demosthenes (trans. A.W. Pickard-Cambridge)

coreTexts.title: Selections from the Speeches and Writings of Edmund Burke
coreTexts.author: Edmund Burke

coreTexts.title: Give Me Liberty or Give Me Death
coreTexts.author: Patrick Henry

coreTexts.title: The Great Speeches and Orations of Daniel Webster
coreTexts.author: Daniel Webster

coreTexts.title: We Shall Fight on the Beaches (1940) and The Sinews of Peace (1946)
coreTexts.author: Winston Churchill

rows.historicalPrecedent: Boys at the colonial colleges and the English public schools learned eloquence by translating and imitating Demosthenes and Cicero. In the 19th century American schoolbooks added Henry, Webster and Burke as declamation staples.
rows.notes: Cicero's Catilinarians are read in Latin in the Latin track and can be studied here in translation. Pair Lincoln with the Lincoln–Douglas debates in rhetoric-09.

rows.title: Debate: Lincoln–Douglas, Parliamentary & Mock Trial
rows.summary: Competitive and in-home debate trains the student to argue both sides, think on his feet, and cross-examine. The formats are Lincoln–Douglas value debate (one-on-one, modeled on the 1858 Senate debates), team parliamentary debate (impromptu), and mock trial or moot court (forensic rhetoric, rules of evidence, direct and cross-examination).
objectives: Research and brief both sides of a resolution with evidence
Construct a value/criterion case and rebuttals for Lincoln–Douglas debate
Cross-examine with short, leading questions
Argue impromptu in parliamentary format with 15–20 minutes of preparation
Play attorney and witness roles in a mock trial

curriculumOptions.name: Everyday Debate & Discussion
curriculumOptions.notes: An introduction to formal debate formats for home and classroom.

curriculumOptions.name: The Argument Builder
curriculumOptions.notes: Builds persuasive arguments with topics and evidence. It bridges logic and debate.

curriculumOptions.name: NCFCA homeschool speech & debate league
curriculumOptions.publisher: National Christian Forensics and Communications Association
curriculumOptions.notes: A national Christian homeschool league offering Lincoln–Douglas, team policy, parliamentary and individual speech events.

curriculumOptions.name: National Speech & Debate Association
curriculumOptions.notes: The main US high-school league, covering Lincoln–Douglas, Congressional debate and others.

rows.notes: Congressional debate (a model legislature) is excellent training for the future statesman. Mock trial connects to the civics-law track.

rows.title: Roman Rhetoric: Cicero, the Ad Herennium & Quintilian
rows.summary: This course reads the Roman systematizers who shaped 1,500 years of Western schooling. Students take the doctrine of invention and stasis from Cicero's De Inventione and the Rhetorica ad Herennium, the ideal of the philosopher-statesman-orator from De Oratore, and Quintilian's complete education of "the good man skilled in speaking", from the nursery to the forum.
objectives: Apply stasis theory (fact, definition, quality, procedure) to a legal or political case
Explain the six parts of an oration as taught in the Ad Herennium
Summarize Crassus's and Antonius's positions in De Oratore on the orator's education
Read Quintilian Books 1, 2, 10 and 12 and compare them with this program's own design
Use the memory palace (Ad Herennium III) to memorize a speech

coreTexts.title: De Inventione (On Rhetorical Invention), in The Orations of Marcus Tullius Cicero, vol. 4
coreTexts.author: Cicero (trans. C.D. Yonge)

coreTexts.title: De Oratore (in Cicero on Oratory and Orators)
coreTexts.author: Cicero (trans. J.S. Watson)

rows.historicalPrecedent: Harvard admission (1640s) required reading "Tully" (Cicero) ex tempore. Cicero and the Ad Herennium were the rhetoric of the medieval and Renaissance schools, and the Jesuit Ratio Studiorum (1599) built its rhetoric class on Cicero and Quintilian.
rows.notes: Harry Caplan's Loeb translation of the Ad Herennium (Harvard, 1954) is the standard English version. An accelerated Latin student should read De Oratore Book I in Latin.

rows.title: Founding-Era Rhetoric: Blair, Witherspoon, Campbell & Whately
rows.summary: The student reads the rhetorics that actually trained the founders and the 19th-century American statesmen. Hugh Blair's Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres (1783) was the most widely used rhetoric text in the United States c. 1790–1850. John Witherspoon's Lectures on Eloquence were delivered at Princeton to James Madison's generation. Campbell's Philosophy of Rhetoric (1776) and Whately's Elements of Rhetoric (1828) set out the new "psychological" rhetoric of evidence and persuasion.
objectives: Summarize Blair on taste, style (perspicuity, precision) and the eloquence of the bar, pulpit and assembly
Read Witherspoon's lectures on eloquence and relate them to Princeton's statesmen
Explain Campbell's four ends of speech (enlighten, please, move, persuade)
Explain Whately's burden of proof and presumption and apply them in debate
Write a critical review of a contemporary speech using Blair's criteria

coreTexts.title: Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres
coreTexts.author: Hugh Blair

coreTexts.title: Lectures on Eloquence (in The Works of John Witherspoon, vol. 7)
coreTexts.author: John Witherspoon

rows.historicalPrecedent: Witherspoon personally taught eloquence at the College of New Jersey (Princeton), where his students included Madison. Blair's Lectures ran to some 130 editions and became the rhetoric textbook of American colleges through the mid-19th century.
rows.notes: Richard Weaver's The Ethics of Rhetoric (1953; Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/68421) is an excellent 20th-century coda on rhetoric, truth and the Phaedrus.

rows.title: College Seminar: Oratory, Moot Court & the Rhetoric of Statesmanship
rows.summary: This is the capstone of the trivium. The student composes and delivers original speeches in all three genres before public audiences: a deliberative address on a live policy question, a forensic argument in moot court (appellate brief plus oral argument), and a commemorative (epideictic) oration. He critiques recorded speeches of statesmen and revisits Aristotle, Cicero and Quintilian with adult experience.
objectives: Write and argue a moot-court appellate brief before a panel
Deliver a 15-minute deliberative address from notes, then take hostile questions
Deliver a formal commemorative oration (e.g. for a national holiday or a funeral)
Critique speeches by the five canons in a written portfolio

curriculumOptions.name: Classical Logic and Rhetoric (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Use as a review. Hillsdale requires this as a core course of all undergraduates.

curriculumOptions.name: The Rhetoric Companion
curriculumOptions.notes: A rhetoric course in dialogue form from the classical Christian school movement. It can support the senior thesis and speech.

curriculumOptions.name: Rhetoric Alive! Senior Thesis
curriculumOptions.notes: Guides a senior thesis researched, written and defended orally.

rows.notes: Optional homiletics: a student preparing for ministry can add the art of preaching, beginning with Augustine's On Christian Doctrine, Book IV (New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/12024.htm), which is the first Christian rhetoric. Catholic and Protestant traditions differ on who preaches (the ordained homily within the Mass versus the central Protestant sermon), but both inherit Augustine's rhetoric.

rows.title: Human Nature Before Psychology: The Soul, the Passions, Habit and Memory
rows.summary: Psychology means "the account of the soul," and it had a long history before it had a laboratory. This unit reads short selections as a working anthropology for the rest of the track: Aristotle's On the Soul (the soul as the form of a living body, and its nutritive, sensitive and rational powers) and On Memory; Aquinas on the powers of the soul, the eleven passions, and habit as a "second nature"; and Augustine's meditation on the "fields and roomy chambers of memory" in Confessions X. The aim is a vocabulary (intellect, will, the passions, habit, memory, the imagination) against which each modern theory can later be tested. The philosophy track covers Aristotle and Aquinas as philosophers. This unit reads them as the first psychologists.
objectives: Explain Aristotle's definition of the soul and the hierarchy of vegetative, sensitive and rational powers
List Aquinas's eleven passions (concupiscible and irascible) and give an everyday example of each
Explain how habits are formed and lost according to ST I-II q.49–53, and compare with a modern account of habit
Summarize Augustine's account of memory and why he finds God "in" memory
Keep a two-week log of one's own passions and habits, classified in Thomist terms

coreTexts.title: On the Soul (De Anima), Books II–III
coreTexts.author: Aristotle

coreTexts.title: Summa Theologiae I q.75 and q.78 (the soul and its powers)
coreTexts.author: Thomas Aquinas

coreTexts.title: Summa Theologiae I-II q.22ff. (the passions) and q.49ff. (habits)
coreTexts.author: Thomas Aquinas

curriculumOptions.name: Aquinas 101: The Passions of the Soul (free video lessons)
curriculumOptions.notes: Short lectures by Dominican friars on the passions and the powers of the soul; free with registration.

curriculumOptions.name: Consciousness and Its Implications (Daniel N. Robinson)
curriculumOptions.notes: A philosopher-psychologist's history of the mind-body problem from the Greeks to neuroscience; sympathetic to Aristotle and Reid.

rows.historicalPrecedent: In the medieval universities Aristotle's De Anima was a set text of the arts course (it is named in the Paris arts-faculty statute of 1255). Every master of arts had therefore studied the powers of the soul before going on to theology, law or medicine.
rows.notes: Brennan's Thomistic Psychology (1941) is the classic attempt to set Aquinas's account beside the experimental psychology of its day, and is a useful teacher's reference. Protestant readers will find a parallel treatment of the "heart" and "affections" in Jonathan Edwards's Religious Affections. Keep the reading short. The full treatise on the passions belongs to theology-22 and philosophy-08.

rows.title: Introduction to Psychology: The Science of Mind and Behavior, from James and Wundt to AP
rows.summary: A full, college-level introductory psychology course in one year, taken at AP or CLEP level. It covers the biological bases of behavior, sensation and perception, learning (classical and operant conditioning), memory, cognition, motivation and emotion, development, personality, psychological disorders and treatment, and social psychology. The course is paired with the history of the field: the Scottish "mental philosophy" taught in American colleges, Wundt's laboratory at Leipzig (1879), and William James's Principles of Psychology (1890). James's chapters on habit, attention, memory and will are still among the best writing in psychology.
objectives: Master the content of a standard introductory text and sit the AP Psychology or CLEP Introductory Psychology exam
Explain classical and operant conditioning and the multi-store model of memory with experiments as evidence
Trace the history of psychology from Reid and the college "mental philosophy" through Wundt, James, behaviorism and the cognitive revolution
Read James's chapter "Habit" and compare it with Aquinas on habit (social-science-01)
Identify the view of the person assumed by each major school (behaviorist, psychoanalytic, humanistic, cognitive, evolutionary)

coreTexts.title: The Principles of Psychology, Vol. 1 (ch. IV Habit, IX The Stream of Thought, XI Attention, XVI Memory)
coreTexts.author: William James

links.label: Classics in the History of Psychology (York Univ.)

coreTexts.title: An Inquiry into the Human Mind, on the Principles of Common Sense (selections)
coreTexts.author: Thomas Reid

curriculumOptions.name: Psychology 2e (free textbook)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free, complete introductory text that follows the standard course sequence; enough for CLEP.

curriculumOptions.name: Myers' Psychology for the AP Course, 4th ed.
curriculumOptions.notes: The most widely used AP text, aligned to the current AP framework. Myers, a professing Christian, has also written on faith and psychology.

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Psychology, PSYC 110 (Paul Bloom)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free recorded Yale lecture course; lively and clear. Some lectures (on Freud, sex and evolution) need parental preview.

curriculumOptions.name: AP Psychology
curriculumOptions.notes: Course and exam description; five units from biological bases through mental and physical health.

curriculumOptions.name: CLEP Introductory Psychology
curriculumOptions.notes: A 90-minute exam for 3 semester hours of credit at many colleges; follows DSM-5 terminology.

curriculumOptions.name: Psychology classes for Catholic homeschoolers (live and recorded)
curriculumOptions.notes: Online psychology classes taught from a Catholic perspective; check the current catalog for level and schedule.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Before "psychology" was a separate science, American colleges taught "mental" or "intellectual philosophy" in the senior year, in the tradition of Thomas Reid and the Scottish common-sense school that Witherspoon brought to Princeton. Thomas Upham's Elements of Mental Philosophy (1831) was abridged "for academies and high schools"; Noah Porter taught The Elements of Intellectual Science at Yale; and James McCosh's Psychology: The Cognitive Powers (1886) was the Princeton text. William James, trained in this tradition and in German physiology, turned it into an experimental science.

sources.label: SEP: Scottish Philosophy in the 18th Century
SEP: Thomas Reid
Upham, Elements of Mental Philosophy, abridged for academies and high schools (Archive.org)
Porter, The Elements of Intellectual Science (Archive.org)
McCosh, Psychology: The Cognitive Powers (Archive.org)

rows.notes: Content cautions: standard texts treat sexuality, sexual orientation and gender under development and motivation, and treat human origins in evolutionary terms. Parents should preview those chapters and discuss them from Catholic teaching (Catechism 2331–2400) or their own tradition. Freud should be read critically; Paul Vitz's Sigmund Freud's Christian Unconscious and Psychology as Religion (see social-science-08) give a Christian critique. The textbooks' methodological naturalism is a working method, not a proof that there is no soul. Say so explicitly, and return to it in social-science-11.

rows.title: How to Read a Study: Research Methods, Statistics and the Replication Crisis
rows.summary: Before reading any more findings, the student learns how findings are made and how they fail. The unit covers experimental and correlational designs, random assignment and sampling, operational definitions, validity and reliability, confounds, effect sizes, p-values and confidence intervals, meta-analysis, and preregistration. It then reads the replication crisis in its primary sources: Ioannidis's "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False" (2005); "False-Positive Psychology" (2011) on "researcher degrees of freedom"; and the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 attempt to replicate 100 psychology studies, which reproduced significant results in only about a third to a half, depending on the criterion. The student ends by dissecting real studies and press reports of them.
objectives: Distinguish experiment, quasi-experiment, correlational study and case study, and what each can show
Explain why correlation does not establish causation, with confounding, reverse causation and selection effects
State correctly what a p-value is and is not, following the ASA's 2016 statement
Explain p-hacking, publication bias, small samples and low statistical power, and how preregistration addresses them
Summarize the main findings of Open Science Collaboration (2015) and Ioannidis (2005)
Write a one-page critical appraisal of a published study and of a news article that reports it

coreTexts.author: Open Science Collaboration

coreTexts.author: Stuart Ritchie

curriculumOptions.name: Research Methods in Psychology, 4th ed. (free open textbook)
curriculumOptions.notes: A clear, free first course in psychological research design, including the replication crisis.

curriculumOptions.name: Improving Your Statistical Inferences (Daniël Lakens)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free to audit; the best short course on p-values, effect sizes, power and open science. For strong 15–16-year-olds after mathematics-16.

curriculumOptions.name: Meaning from Data: Statistics Made Clear (Michael Starbird)
curriculumOptions.notes: A gentler lecture review of the statistics needed to read studies.

rows.notes: This unit depends on mathematics-16 (probability and statistics). It sets the habit for the rest of the track: for every finding, ask how large the effect is, how it was measured, whether it has replicated, and what else could explain it. Knowing the limits of a science is part of taking it seriously. This is not skepticism about science in general, and the student should also learn which findings have held up well (for example, the testing effect in social-science-05).

rows.title: Judgment and Decision: Heuristics, Biases and Their Critics (Kahneman and Gigerenzer)
rows.summary: Cognitive psychology's most influential program for a statesman or businessman is the study of judgment under uncertainty. The student reads Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 paper in Science and large parts of Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow: the two "systems," anchoring, availability, representativeness, base-rate neglect, overconfidence, loss aversion and framing. He then reads Gigerenzer's reply: simple heuristics are often "ecologically rational" and beat complex models in real environments, and many "biases" disappear when risks are stated as natural frequencies. The unit also reads Kahneman's own admission that the priming studies in his chapter 4 had not replicated.
objectives: Define and illustrate anchoring, availability, representativeness, base-rate neglect, framing and loss aversion
Solve base-rate problems (e.g. a medical screening test) in both probability and natural-frequency formats
State Gigerenzer's critique of the heuristics-and-biases program and assess where each side is strongest
Identify which findings in Thinking, Fast and Slow have replicated well and which have not
Compare the modern account of bias with the classical account of prudence, and of how passion clouds judgment
Keep a decision journal with predictions and confidence levels, and score it after three months

coreTexts.title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
coreTexts.author: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman

coreTexts.title: Risk Savvy: How to Make Good Decisions
coreTexts.author: Gerd Gigerenzer

curriculumOptions.name: Mindware: Critical Thinking for the Information Age (Richard Nisbett)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free to audit; statistical, causal and cost-benefit reasoning from a leading social psychologist.

curriculumOptions.name: Your Deceptive Mind: A Scientific Guide to Critical Thinking Skills (Steven Novella)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on perception, memory, bias and fallacies. Novella is a prominent scientific skeptic, and his asides on religion reflect that stance.

curriculumOptions.name: Harding Center for Risk Literacy (free fact boxes and tools)
curriculumOptions.notes: Gigerenzer's center; free "fact boxes" that show medical risks in natural frequencies, ideal for practice.

sources.label: Nature (2012): Nobel laureate challenges psychologists to clean up their act

rows.notes: Thinking, Fast and Slow is long, so assign Parts I–III and V in full and skim Part IV. Chapter 4 ("The Associative Machine") relies on behavioral-priming studies that have largely failed to replicate. Read it as a case study for social-science-03. Kahneman acknowledged the problem in his 2012 open letter and in later public comments. The unit pairs naturally with logic-02 on fallacies, since the fallacies catalog errors of argument and the bias literature catalogs errors of intuition.

rows.title: How Children Learn: Developmental and Educational Psychology
rows.summary: The student studies the science behind his own education. First come the classic theories of development: Piaget's stages and Vygotsky's "zone of proximal development" and scaffolding, with their later critics, together with Erikson and attachment research. Then comes the best-supported research in learning: retrieval practice (the testing effect), spacing, interleaving, worked examples, and the role of background knowledge, from Make It Stick, Willingham and the 2013 review by Dunlosky and colleagues. Ericsson's research on deliberate practice follows, with the meta-analysis that qualifies it. The student sees why recitation, memory work, narration and the commonplace book work, and designs his own study system.
objectives: Summarize Piaget's four stages and Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, and state one major criticism of each
Rank common study techniques by strength of evidence, following Dunlosky et al. (2013)
Explain retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving, and why re-reading and highlighting feel effective but are weak
Explain deliberate practice and assess how much of expert performance it accounts for (Macnamara et al., 2014)
Relate the research to classical methods (recitation, memoria, narration, copywork) and to William James's Talks to Teachers
Design, run and evaluate a spaced-retrieval study plan for one subject for a whole term

coreTexts.title: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning
coreTexts.author: Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III and Mark A. McDaniel

coreTexts.title: Why Don't Students Like School? (2nd ed.)
