coreTexts.author: L. S. Vygotsky

coreTexts.title: Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise
coreTexts.author: Anders Ericsson and Robert Pool

coreTexts.title: Talks to Teachers on Psychology; and to Students on Some of Life's Ideals
coreTexts.author: William James

curriculumOptions.name: Learning How to Learn (Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free to audit; one of the most popular online courses, a practical entry point before Make It Stick.

curriculumOptions.name: The Learning Scientists (free materials)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free posters, blog posts and podcasts by cognitive psychologists on the six evidence-based study strategies.

curriculumOptions.name: CLEP Human Growth and Development
curriculumOptions.notes: A lifespan developmental psychology exam for 3 credits; use OpenStax Psychology 2e plus a lifespan text.

curriculumOptions.name: CLEP Introduction to Educational Psychology
curriculumOptions.notes: Covers cognition, teaching methods, development and assessment.

sources.label: Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014), Deliberate Practice and Performance: A Meta-Analysis (DOI)
RetrievalPractice.org (Pooja K. Agarwal)

rows.historicalPrecedent: William James gave his Talks to Teachers to Cambridge schoolteachers in the 1890s. He warned that psychology is a science and teaching an art, and that "sciences never generate arts directly out of themselves." His chapters on habit, attention and memory are still a sound guide to the classroom.
rows.notes: This row ties the track to the program itself, and a good capstone is to have the student tutor a younger sibling using what he has learned. Piaget's stage theory is taught everywhere but is now considered too rigid. Children can often do more, earlier, than Piaget allowed, which suits an accelerated program. Theologically, the research on habit and practice fits the Aristotelian-Thomist account of virtue as a habit acquired by repeated acts.

rows.title: Moral and Social Psychology: Haidt, Obedience, Conformity and Persuasion
rows.summary: Social psychology studies how situations and groups shape what people do. The unit reads the classic experiments in the original papers: Asch on conformity (1956) and Milgram on obedience (1963). It then takes the Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) as a case study in how a famous study can fail: Le Texier's archival work (2019) shows that the guards were coached. Haidt's The Righteous Mind offers moral foundations theory and the "rider and elephant" model of intuition and reasoning. Cialdini's Influence catalogs the six (now seven) principles of persuasion, and the student learns to recognize them in advertising and politics. Throughout, the findings are set beside the classical account of virtue, which holds that character can resist situational pressure.
objectives: Describe the design and results of Asch's and Milgram's experiments and their later replications and critiques
Explain the methodological and ethical problems of the Stanford Prison Experiment, citing Le Texier (2019)
Summarize Haidt's six moral foundations and his claim that intuition comes first and strategic reasoning second
Identify Cialdini's principles of influence in five real advertisements or political appeals
Write an essay on the question "Does situationism refute virtue ethics?" drawing on Aristotle, Milgram and Haidt

coreTexts.title: Studies of Independence and Conformity: I. A Minority of One Against a Unanimous Majority
coreTexts.author: Solomon E. Asch

links.label: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology (DOI)

coreTexts.title: The Righteous Mind: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion
coreTexts.author: Jonathan Haidt

coreTexts.title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (new and expanded ed.)
coreTexts.author: Robert B. Cialdini

curriculumOptions.name: Social Psychology (Scott Plous)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free to audit; a well-produced survey including conformity, obedience, persuasion and prejudice.

curriculumOptions.name: Understanding the Mysteries of Human Behavior (Mark Leary)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures by a Duke social psychologist on self-control, emotion, stress, morality and group behavior.

curriculumOptions.name: Moral Foundations Theory (free questionnaires and readings)
curriculumOptions.notes: The student can take the Moral Foundations Questionnaire and compare results with a parent's.

rows.notes: Haidt writes as a secular evolutionary psychologist but treats religion as a real social good; his account of religion as a "hive switch" is functionalist and should be discussed. Christian readers will notice that his foundations of sanctity, loyalty and authority match themes of the older moral tradition. Milgram's and Zimbardo's films are distressing for some students. The honest lesson of the unit is double: situations are powerful, and the minority who resisted in Asch's and Milgram's experiments (and the rescuers and dissidents of the twentieth century; see history-26 and history-27) show that character still matters. Cialdini should be read with Aristotle's Rhetoric (rhetoric-07) as the ethics of persuasion.

rows.title: Sociology and the Social Order: Tocqueville, Durkheim, Weber, Nisbet and Putnam
rows.summary: Sociology studies the institutions between the individual and the state: family, church, town, association and class. The course reads its founders and its best American heirs. Tocqueville is read as a sociologist of mores and associations (Democracy in America, Volume 2). Durkheim's Suicide (1897) is the first great statistical study of society; it links suicide rates to social integration and religious community. Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905) argues that ideas and religion shape economic life. Nisbet's The Quest for Community (1953) argues that totalitarianism grows where the intermediate associations collapse. Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) and Coleman's 1988 paper on social capital measure that collapse and show how family and community shape children's success. Berger's Invitation to Sociology serves as a humane introduction.
objectives: Master the content of an introductory sociology text and optionally sit the CLEP Introductory Sociology exam
Summarize Tocqueville on associations, individualism and "self-interest rightly understood" as sociological claims
Explain Durkheim's types of suicide and his finding on religion and social integration, and evaluate his use of statistics
State Weber's thesis and at least two major criticisms of it (including Catholic ones)
Explain Nisbet's argument about community, the state and the intermediate associations
Define social capital (Coleman, Putnam) and assess the evidence for its decline since 1960
Write a research paper on the state of one mediating institution (parish, family, lodge, local club) in your own town

coreTexts.title: Democracy in America, Volume 2 (Part II, on individualism and associations)
coreTexts.author: Alexis de Tocqueville

coreTexts.title: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
coreTexts.author: Max Weber (trans. Talcott Parsons)

coreTexts.title: Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community (revised and updated)
coreTexts.author: Robert D. Putnam

coreTexts.title: Social Capital in the Creation of Human Capital
coreTexts.author: James S. Coleman

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Sociology 3e (free textbook)
curriculumOptions.notes: Free standard text for the survey half of the course. Its framing is conventionally progressive, so pair it with Nisbet and Berger.

curriculumOptions.name: CLEP Introductory Sociology
curriculumOptions.notes: One-semester equivalent covering institutions, social patterns and processes, stratification and the sociological perspective.

curriculumOptions.name: American Citizenship and Its Decline (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Complements the Tocqueville and Nisbet readings on self-government and the decline of civic life.

rows.notes: Content caution: Durkheim's Suicide is a statistical study, not a sensational one, but the topic calls for parental awareness; the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (see social-science-08) should be known. Weber's thesis is disputed. Catholic historians and economists (for example, those who stress the commercial economies of medieval Italy and Flanders) argue that capitalism long predates Calvinism, while Protestant readers often find in Weber a real insight about vocation. Read both sides. Catholic social teaching on subsidiarity (civics-law-15, economics-07) states in normative terms what Nisbet, Coleman and Putnam describe empirically; this course is the cross-reference, not the place to teach it.

rows.title: Personality, Mental Health and Meaning: The Big Five, Anxiety and Depression, Frankl and Christian Psychology
rows.summary: This unit covers what an educated adult, future parent and leader should know about personality and mental health. The Big Five model (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism) is the best-supported account of personality and predicts real outcomes. The student learns the signs, prevalence and evidence-based treatments of anxiety and depression, the research on resilience, and when and how to get help for oneself or a friend. Viktor Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning, written by a psychiatrist who survived Auschwitz, argues that the will to meaning is basic to man. Christian psychologists then show how the field can be integrated with a Christian anthropology: Paul Vitz's critique of "selfism," the Catholic Christian Meta-Model of the Person from Divine Mercy University, and Conrad Baars's work on affirmation.
objectives: Describe the Big Five traits, how they are measured, and what they predict; take an IPIP-based inventory and interpret it
Recognize the common signs of anxiety disorders and depression, and know the first steps to getting help, including 988
Summarize the evidence for cognitive behavioral therapy and for exercise, sleep and social connection in mental health
Explain Frankl's logotherapy and his three sources of meaning (work, love, and the attitude taken to unavoidable suffering)
Summarize Vitz's argument that popular psychology became a "religion of the self," and assess it
Explain the eleven dimensions of the person in the Catholic Christian Meta-Model and how it relates to secular therapy

coreTexts.title: Psychology as Religion: The Cult of Self-Worship (2nd ed.)
coreTexts.author: Paul C. Vitz

coreTexts.title: A Catholic Christian Meta-Model of the Person: Integration with Psychology and Mental Health Practice (selections)
coreTexts.author: Paul C. Vitz, William J. Nordling and Craig Steven Titus (eds.)

coreTexts.title: Born Only Once: The Miracle of Affirmation (3rd ed.)
coreTexts.author: Conrad W. Baars

curriculumOptions.name: Catholic Christian Meta-Model of the Person (overview and resources)
curriculumOptions.notes: The framework of the former Institute for the Psychological Sciences (IPS). A shorter "mini-version" of the book appeared in 2025.

curriculumOptions.name: Understanding the Mysteries of Human Behavior (Mark Leary)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on personality, emotion, stress and self-control; also used in social-science-06.

curriculumOptions.name: The Baars Institute
curriculumOptions.notes: Books and resources on Conrad Baars's Thomist psychiatry of the emotions and affirmation.

sources.label: NIMH: Depression
NIMH: Anxiety Disorders
988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
International Personality Item Pool (public-domain Big Five scales)

rows.notes: Content caution: this unit is not training in diagnosis, and students should be warned against self-diagnosis from checklists or social media. If a student recognizes himself or a friend in the material, the right step is a parent, a physician or a qualified counselor. Frankl describes the camps plainly; it is suitable for 16-year-olds, but some passages are harrowing. On the Christian perspective, Catholic integrationists (Vitz, the Divine Mercy University school, Baars) accept sound clinical science within a Thomist anthropology. Some Protestants take the same integrationist view, while the "biblical counseling" movement (after Jay Adams) is more skeptical of secular psychology. Present both fairly. Baars, a Buchenwald survivor like Frankl, worked from Aquinas's account of the emotions (social-science-01).

rows.title: Media, Technology and the Mind: Postman, Haidt and the Attention Economy
rows.summary: Every medium shapes the mind that uses it. Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985) argues that television turned public discourse into entertainment and weakened the "typographic mind" on which the founders' republic was built. Carr's The Shallows extends the argument to the internet and the research on attention and distraction. Haidt's The Anxious Generation (2024) argues that the move to smartphone- and social-media-based childhood after about 2012 caused a rise in adolescent anxiety and depression, and his critics argue that the data show only small correlations. The student weighs the evidence using the methods of social-science-03. Pieper's short essay on propaganda closes the unit, and the student then writes his own "rule of life" for technology.
objectives: Summarize Postman's argument about the "typographic mind" and apply it to a current medium
Summarize Haidt's four foundational reforms and the evidence he offers for them
Weigh Haidt's causal claims against his critics (Odgers; Orben and Przybylski) using the distinction between correlation and causation and the concept of effect size
Explain attention research on multitasking, notifications and deep reading
Explain Pieper's claim that the abuse of language for power is the root of propaganda
Write and keep for one term a personal technology rule, and report on it

coreTexts.title: Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business
coreTexts.author: Neil Postman

coreTexts.title: The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness
coreTexts.author: Jonathan Haidt

coreTexts.title: The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains
coreTexts.author: Nicholas Carr

coreTexts.title: Abuse of Language, Abuse of Power
coreTexts.author: Josef Pieper

coreTexts.title: The Tech-Wise Family: Everyday Steps for Putting Technology in Its Proper Place
coreTexts.author: Andy Crouch

curriculumOptions.name: Foundations of Humane Technology (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: A free course on persuasive design and the attention economy, from former technology-industry insiders.

curriculumOptions.name: The Anxious Generation movement (free resources for families and schools)
curriculumOptions.notes: Toolkits for the four reforms (no smartphones before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools, more free play).

sources.label: Odgers (2024), The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness? Nature
Orben and Przybylski (2019), The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use, Nature Human Behaviour

rows.notes: This unit continues the screen practices of early-development-07 and -15 at the level of argument, so that the student understands and owns his family's rules. The Haidt debate is a live scientific controversy and a good test of the methods unit. Present Odgers's and Orben's critiques fairly even if the family's practice follows Haidt. Postman wrote as a secular humanist from a Jewish background and drew on the Second Commandment for his argument about images. Crouch writes as an evangelical Protestant, and Pieper as a Catholic Thomist. Orwell's "Politics and the English Language" and 1984 (literature-25) make a good companion.

rows.title: Culture and Anthropology: Dawson, Evans-Pritchard and a Critical Introduction (optional)
rows.summary: An optional unit on culture as the anthropologist sees it. The student surveys cultural anthropology (kinship, ritual, exchange, fieldwork and ethnography) from a standard text, then reads three thinkers who studied culture from a Christian standpoint. Christopher Dawson argues that religion is the dynamic center of every culture. E. E. Evans-Pritchard, the Oxford anthropologist and Catholic convert, criticizes the Victorian theories that explained religion away. Mary Douglas, also Catholic, shows in Purity and Danger how the rules of clean and unclean express a whole social order, including a celebrated reading of Leviticus. The unit teaches the anthropologist's real virtue, which is to understand a people from the inside, while rejecting cultural relativism about truth and the good.
objectives: Define culture, ethnography, participant observation, kinship and ritual, and summarize one classic ethnography
Summarize Dawson's thesis that religion is the key to culture and test it against one non-Western case
Explain Evans-Pritchard's critique of intellectualist, emotionalist and sociological theories of religion
Explain Douglas's account of purity rules and her reading of the dietary laws of Leviticus
Distinguish methodological relativism (suspending judgment in order to understand) from moral relativism

coreTexts.title: Religion and the Rise of Western Culture
coreTexts.author: Christopher Dawson

coreTexts.title: Purity and Danger: An Analysis of Concepts of Pollution and Taboo
coreTexts.author: Mary Douglas

curriculumOptions.name: Introduction to Anthropology (free textbook)
curriculumOptions.notes: A free survey of all four fields; use the cultural-anthropology chapters. Its framing is contemporary-academic, so read it critically.

curriculumOptions.name: Understanding Peoples and Cultures of the World (Edward Fischer)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lecture survey of cultural anthropology by a Vanderbilt anthropologist, with applied examples.

rows.notes: This unit is optional. It suits a student headed toward diplomacy, missions, business abroad or the Spanish- and Chinese-language tracks. Dawson's The Making of Europe is read in history-19. This unit uses his more general Religion and the Rise of Western Culture (the 1948–49 Gifford Lectures). Content caution: ethnographies and anthropology texts describe sexual customs and initiation rites frankly, so preview the assigned chapters. Evans-Pritchard, Douglas and Victor Turner (another convert) are a notable Catholic presence in twentieth-century British anthropology and make good models for a Christian student.

rows.title: College Seminar: What Can Social Science Know? (Hayek, MacIntyre, Smith and the Person)
rows.summary: A capstone seminar on the philosophy of the social sciences. Hayek's The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) traces "scientism," the imitation of physics in the study of society, from Saint-Simon and Comte, and his Nobel lecture "The Pretence of Knowledge" (1974) states its practical danger. Chapter 8 of MacIntyre's After Virtue ("The Character of Generalizations in Social Science and Their Lack of Predictive Power") argues that systematic unpredictability is built into human affairs and that social science cannot supply the expertise that modern managers claim. Christian Smith's What Is a Person? proposes a critical-realist, personalist foundation for sociology. Gaudium et Spes (Part I, chapter 1) gives the Church's account of the human person, a text Karol Wojtyła helped draft and later cited constantly as John Paul II. The student ends by writing his own account of what the social sciences can and cannot know about a free, rational and embodied person.
objectives: Explain Hayek's distinction between the methods of the natural and the social sciences, and his critique of scientism
Summarize MacIntyre's four sources of systematic unpredictability and his critique of managerial expertise
Explain Smith's personalist and critical-realist alternative to both positivism and social constructionism
Summarize Gaudium et Spes 12–22 on the person as image of God, conscience, freedom and death
Evaluate one major finding from this track in the light of these readings, naming its assumptions about human nature
Write a 4,000-word seminar paper, "The Uses and Limits of Social Science for a Statesman"

coreTexts.title: The Counter-Revolution of Science: Studies on the Abuse of Reason
coreTexts.author: F. A. Hayek

coreTexts.title: The Pretence of Knowledge (Nobel Prize lecture)
coreTexts.author: F. A. Hayek

coreTexts.title: After Virtue, ch. 8: The Character of Generalizations in Social Science and Their Lack of Predictive Power
coreTexts.author: Alasdair MacIntyre

coreTexts.title: What Is a Person? Rethinking Humanity, Social Life, and the Moral Good from the Person Up
coreTexts.author: Christian Smith

coreTexts.title: Gaudium et Spes, Part I, ch. 1 (The Dignity of the Human Person)
coreTexts.author: Second Vatican Council

rows.historicalPrecedent: Hayek's essays first appeared in Economica in 1941–1944, while the planned economies of the war years seemed to vindicate social engineering. MacIntyre wrote chapter 8 as a former Marxist sociologist, against the claims to "managerial expertise" of the 1960s and 1970s.
rows.notes: This seminar should be run as a Socratic discussion on primary texts, as at St. John's or Thomas Aquinas College. No standard course exists. It overlaps philosophy-13 (MacIntyre) and economics-09 (Hayek's "The Use of Knowledge in Society"). Read only chapter 8 of After Virtue here and leave the rest to those rows. Christian Smith is a Catholic sociologist at Notre Dame. A Protestant counterpart is C. S. Lewis's The Abolition of Man (theology-18), which makes the same argument about the "conditioners" who would manage human nature. Natural-science-18 covers the philosophy of the natural sciences; this seminar is its social-science counterpart.

rows.title: By-Ear Spanish: Native-Speaker Caregivers & One Parent, One Language
rows.summary: The strongest predictor of early bilingual ability is the amount of live, interactive input a child hears in each language. Give Spanish a consistent human source from birth: a native-speaking parent, nanny, grandparent or au pair who speaks only Spanish to the child (One Parent, One Language), or a fixed "Spanish time or place" (minority-language-at-home).
objectives: Hear several hours a week of live, responsive Spanish from the same native speaker(s)
Understand everyday routines, commands and nursery rhymes in Spanish by age 2–3
Answer in Spanish (single words, then phrases) without being pressured to perform

coreTexts.title: Language Strategies for Bilingual Families: The One-Parent-One-Language Approach
coreTexts.author: Suzanne Barron-Hauwaert

sources.label: Kuhl, Tsao & Liu (2003), PNAS: live vs. recorded foreign-language exposure in infancy
Hoff et al. (2012), Dual language exposure and early bilingual development

rows.notes: Recorded audio and video alone do not produce phonetic learning in infants. In Kuhl's study, only live interaction did. Expect a bilingual child's vocabulary in each language to lag a monolingual child's for a while; combined vocabulary is normal. With three home languages (English, Spanish and Mandarin), assign each language to a fixed person or setting so the input stays consistent.

rows.title: Spanish Songs, Stories & Audio (with Screen Limits)
rows.summary: Enrich live input with Spanish nursery rhymes, songs, picture books read aloud, and a small amount of high-quality Spanish video watched together with an adult. Media supplements a human speaker and never replaces one. Before age 2, avoid screens except video chat with family.
objectives: Sing a repertoire of traditional Spanish children's songs and rhymes (e.g. "Los pollitos dicen")
Follow a Spanish picture book read aloud and retell it with pictures
Understand short Spanish cartoons or episodes watched with a parent (ages 3–6 only)

curriculumOptions.name: Canticos (bilingual nursery rhymes, books and videos)
curriculumOptions.notes: Bilingual English–Spanish songs and board books for ages 0–5. Use for singing together, not passive viewing.

curriculumOptions.name: Whistlefritz Spanish for Kids
curriculumOptions.notes: All-Spanish immersion videos and music for ages 2–8. Limit sessions and watch together.

curriculumOptions.name: Dreaming Spanish (Superbeginner videos)
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded comprehensible-input video. Good for ages 5+ and for parents learning alongside.

sources.label: AAP Council on Communications and Media (2016), Media and Young Minds

rows.notes: AAP guidance: no screen media before 18–24 months except video chat. From 2 to 5, at most about 1 hour a day of high-quality programming, watched together with an adult.

rows.title: Spanish I: Reading Spanish & First Grammar
rows.summary: Formal study begins. The child learns to read and spell Spanish (five pure vowels, regular grapheme–sound correspondences, accents and ñ), which transfers quickly from English phonics. They also begin grammar through chants and vocabulary on the classical model, in parallel with Latin.
objectives: Read aloud any Spanish text with correct pronunciation and stress, including accent rules
Chant present-tense conjugations of ser, estar, tener and regular -ar/-er/-ir verbs
Master about 300 high-frequency words and write simple dictated sentences

curriculumOptions.name: Spanish for Children Primer A
curriculumOptions.notes: Grammar-chant approach that parallels Latin for Children, with video and audio. Ideal for a child who already understands spoken Spanish.

curriculumOptions.name: Song School Spanish
curriculumOptions.notes: Gentler, song-based bridge for ages 5–7 if Primer A feels too heavy.

curriculumOptions.name: Madrigal's Magic Key to Spanish
curriculumOptions.notes: Classic cognate-based parent resource. Useful for a non-native parent teaching alongside.

rows.notes: A child who is already bilingual by ear should spend most of this year on literacy (reading real children's books in Spanish) and only lightly on grammar drills.

rows.title: Spanish II: Grammar & Comprehensible-Input Readers
rows.summary: Grammar continues through the preterite and imperfect, object pronouns and reflexives. Reading volume grows through short novels written in high-frequency vocabulary (comprehensible input) and public-domain graded readers from the early 1900s.
objectives: Narrate past events using preterite vs. imperfect correctly
Read four or more short Spanish novellas independently for pleasure
Write a half-page composition in Spanish without a dictionary

coreTexts.title: Spanish Tales for Beginners
coreTexts.author: E. C. Hills and Louise Reinhardt (eds.)

coreTexts.title: A First Spanish Reader
coreTexts.author: Erwin W. Roessler and Alfred Remy

curriculumOptions.name: Spanish for Children Primer B
curriculumOptions.notes: Continues Primer A with past tenses and more reading.

curriculumOptions.name: Fluency Matters comprehensible-input novels (e.g. Brandon Brown quiere un perro)
curriculumOptions.notes: Very-low-vocabulary novellas, levelled; read many of them quickly. Some later titles treat mature themes, so preview them.

curriculumOptions.name: Memoria Press modern languages
curriculumOptions.notes: Classical-school alternative sequence. Check the current Spanish offerings against your child's level.

rows.title: Spanish III: Full Program, Destinos & Conversation
rows.summary: A complete modern course covers the subjunctive, compound tenses and a wide vocabulary. It runs alongside Destinos, the 52-episode telenovela made for learners, set in Spain, Argentina, Puerto Rico and Mexico, and weekly conversation with a native speaker.
objectives: Use present and imperfect subjunctive in speech and writing
Follow Destinos episodes and summarize each one orally in Spanish
Hold a 20-minute conversation on everyday and school topics
Reach about ACTFL Intermediate-Mid in reading and speaking

coreTexts.title: Destinos: An Introduction to Spanish (video series)
coreTexts.author: WGBH / Annenberg

curriculumOptions.name: ¡Avancemos! Levels 1–2
curriculumOptions.notes: Standard U.S. school program with complete scope and sequence and workbooks. Communicative rather than classical.

curriculumOptions.name: Seton Spanish I
curriculumOptions.notes: Catholic high-school course that an accelerated 10–11-year-old can take early.

curriculumOptions.name: Dreaming Spanish (intermediate/advanced)
curriculumOptions.notes: Hours of graded listening that keep the spoken language growing.

rows.title: Graded Literature I: Lazarillo & Don Quijote (Adapted)
rows.summary: The first real literature, in adapted form. The picaresque Lazarillo de Tormes (1554) in a graded A2–B1 reader, then a school adaptation of Don Quijote. Students narrate, keep a vocabulary notebook, and memorize famous passages ("En un lugar de la Mancha…").
objectives: Read an adapted Lazarillo and an adapted Quijote in full, in Spanish
Narrate each tratado or chapter orally and in writing
Explain the picaresque and the chivalric romance that Cervantes parodies

coreTexts.title: Don Quijote de la Mancha: edición escolar (RAE, adapted by Arturo Pérez-Reverte)
coreTexts.author: Miguel de Cervantes

curriculumOptions.name: Lazarillo de Tormes (Lecturas graduadas, A2)
curriculumOptions.notes: Graded reader with audio and exercises.

curriculumOptions.name: Lazarillo de Tormes (Leer y aprender, A2)
curriculumOptions.notes: Alternative graded edition with audio.

curriculumOptions.name: Don Quijote (Colección Cucaña, adapted)
curriculumOptions.notes: Illustrated adaptation widely used in Spanish schools. Easier than the RAE school edition.

rows.historicalPrecedent: By John Quincy Adams's report, Jefferson taught himself Spanish on his 1784 Atlantic crossing with a grammar and a copy of Don Quixote. Franklin writes in his Autobiography that he acquired "as much of the Spanish as to read their books."

sources.label: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Project Gutenberg)

rows.title: Hispanic History from Primary Sources: Bernal Díaz & Las Casas
rows.summary: The conquest and evangelization of the Americas as told by participants. Students read Bernal Díaz del Castillo's eyewitness Historia verdadera of the conquest of Mexico and Bartolomé de las Casas's Brevísima relación, the Dominican friar's indictment of colonial cruelty. They read excerpts in Spanish and the whole in English.
objectives: Read selected chapters of Bernal Díaz and the Brevísima relación in the original Spanish
Compare the two witnesses on the same events and judge their reliability and purpose
Explain the Valladolid debate (1550–51) and the natural-law arguments of Las Casas and Vitoria

coreTexts.title: Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España
coreTexts.author: Bernal Díaz del Castillo

coreTexts.title: Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias
coreTexts.author: Bartolomé de las Casas

rows.historicalPrecedent: Jefferson to Peter Carr (10 August 1787) urged Spanish because "the ancient history of that part of America, too, is written in that language."

sources.label: Jefferson to Peter Carr, 10 Aug 1787 (Teaching American History)

rows.notes: The Brevísima was used in Protestant polemic (the "Black Legend"). Present Las Casas as a Catholic friar arguing from Catholic natural-law principles, and weigh his statistics critically.

rows.title: Golden Age Poetry & Lazarillo in the Original
rows.summary: Students read the unabridged Lazarillo de Tormes and an anthology of the Siglo de Oro: Garcilaso's sonnets and églogas, Fray Luis de León's odes, Lope de Vega, Góngora and Quevedo. They memorize and recite poems and learn Spanish metrics (endecasílabo, octosílabo, soneto, romance).
objectives: Read the original 1554 Lazarillo with a glossary
Memorize and recite at least ten Golden Age poems
Scan Spanish verse and identify sonnet, lira, romance and redondilla forms

coreTexts.title: Vida de Lazarillo de Tormes y de sus fortunas y adversidades
coreTexts.author: Anonymous

coreTexts.title: Historia de la vida del Buscón
coreTexts.author: Francisco de Quevedo

curriculumOptions.name: Spanish Poetry: A Dual-Language Anthology, 16th–20th Centuries (ed. Angel Flores)
curriculumOptions.notes: Inexpensive facing-page anthology running from Garcilaso to Lorca. It serves this row and spanish-11 and spanish-12.

rows.title: The Spanish Mystics: Teresa of Ávila & John of the Cross
rows.summary: Spanish prose and poetry at their spiritual summit. Students read Teresa of Ávila's Libro de la vida and selections from Las moradas (The Interior Castle), and John of the Cross's poems "Noche oscura", "Cántico espiritual" and "Llama de amor viva", with passages from his commentaries.
objectives: Read Teresa's Vida (selected chapters) and Las moradas I and VII in Spanish
Memorize "Noche oscura" and read it closely as poetry (his prose commentaries are read at college level in theology-24)
Write a short essay in Spanish on prayer as Teresa describes it

coreTexts.title: Poesías (Noche oscura, Cántico espiritual, Llama de amor viva)
coreTexts.author: San Juan de la Cruz

links.label: CCEL: Dark Night of the Soul (English)

rows.notes: Catholic–Protestant note: Catholics read Teresa and John as Doctors of the Church. Many Protestants value them as devotional classics, though traditionally with reservations about contemplative mysticism and monastic vows. The poems belong to the Spanish literary canon for every reader.

rows.title: Don Quijote in the Original
rows.summary: Students read the complete Don Quijote (Parts I and II) in Spanish, using the Instituto Cervantes's annotated online edition (Francisco Rico) and an English translation for difficult stretches. This is the defining achievement of the high-school Spanish track.
objectives: Read both parts of the Quijote in Spanish, about 20 pages a day
Keep a commonplace book of refranes (proverbs) and memorable passages
Discuss the novel's themes (madness and reason, fiction and reality, Christian charity, honor) in Spanish seminar

coreTexts.title: El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha
coreTexts.author: Miguel de Cervantes

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Quijote was the classic first long text for English-speaking learners of Spanish. Jefferson reportedly learned the language with it and a grammar (see spanish-06), and he recommended Spanish to his nephew in 1787.

rows.title: Calderón, Bécquer & Galdós: Drama, Romantic Lyric, the Novel
rows.summary: Three centuries in three authors. Calderón's La vida es sueño (1635) is the great Catholic philosophical drama of free will and grace. Bécquer's Rimas and Leyendas are the Spanish Romantic lyric. Galdós's Marianela or Doña Perfecta is the 19th-century realist novel, the latter a study of provincial religious conflict.
objectives: Read La vida es sueño in full and memorize Segismundo's soliloquy ("¿Qué es la vida? Un frenesí…")
Read and recite a selection of Bécquer's Rimas
Read one Galdós novel and write a Spanish essay comparing its view of faith and society with Calderón's
rows.notes: Doña Perfecta is anticlerical in tendency. Read it in dialogue with Calderón and discuss it rather than assigning it alone.

rows.title: Modern Masters: Unamuno, Neruda, Borges (AP Spanish Literature level)
rows.summary: The 20th century in Spain and Spanish America: Unamuno's San Manuel Bueno, mártir and essays on faith and doubt, selected poems from Neruda, and Borges's Ficciones. The course is framed by the College Board's AP Spanish Literature and Culture reading list, and the AP exam can serve as an external benchmark.
objectives: Read San Manuel Bueno, mártir and one Unamuno essay collection in Spanish
Analyze selected Neruda odes and Borges stories (e.g. "El Sur", "La muerte y la brújula")
Write timed literary-analysis essays in Spanish (AP format)

coreTexts.title: Abel Sánchez; Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho
coreTexts.author: Miguel de Unamuno

links.label: Project Gutenberg: Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho

coreTexts.title: Veinte poemas de amor y una canción desesperada (bilingual)
coreTexts.author: Pablo Neruda

curriculumOptions.name: AP Spanish Literature and Culture (course framework and reading list)
curriculumOptions.notes: Its required list overlaps this track (Lazarillo, Quijote, Garcilaso, Quevedo, Sor Juana, Bécquer, Unamuno, Borges, Neruda).

rows.notes: For Neruda, choose selections rather than whole books. The Canto general and the Odas elementales suit students better than all of the love poems. Neruda was a communist, which is itself worth discussing.

rows.title: College Spanish: The Hispanic Canon in the Original
rows.summary: A college-level seminar conducted entirely in Spanish, on longer and harder texts: complete Las moradas, Las Casas's Historia de las Indias, the full Bernal Díaz, Unamuno's Del sentimiento trágico de la vida, and self-chosen further reading (Sor Juana, Lope's comedias, Ortega y Gasset). Students write research essays in Spanish.
objectives: Read college-level Spanish prose and verse without translation aids
Write a 3,000-word research essay in Spanish on a Hispanic text or historical question
Discuss philosophical and theological texts orally in Spanish at an educated register

coreTexts.title: Del sentimiento trágico de la vida
coreTexts.author: Miguel de Unamuno

coreTexts.title: The Interior Castle (for comparison with the Spanish)
coreTexts.author: Teresa of Ávila

rows.notes: End-state check: the student can read a page of the Quijote, Calderón or Unamuno aloud, gloss it in Spanish, and discuss it with a native-speaking professor.

rows.title: Family Prayer & a Sacred Daily Rhythm
rows.summary: From infancy the child is prayed over and with: blessings at bedtime, grace at meals, the Sign of the Cross, short morning and night prayers, and Sunday Mass or worship as a fixed family habit. Toddlers memorize the Our Father, Hail Mary and Glory Be (or a Protestant equivalent such as the Lord's Prayer and the Doxology) by daily repetition. A home prayer corner with an icon, crucifix or Bible gives prayer a place.
objectives: Make the Sign of the Cross and fold hands for grace by age 2–3
Know the Our Father, Hail Mary and Glory Be (or equivalent) by heart by about 5
Attend weekly worship with the family and behave reverently for its length by about 6
Offer simple spontaneous prayers of thanks and petition

sources.label: Harvard T.H. Chan: Religious upbringing linked to better health and well-being (2018)
Chen & VanderWeele, American Journal of Epidemiology 187:11 (2018)

rows.notes: In a Harvard cohort study of more than 5,000 youth, those who attended services weekly or prayed daily as children and adolescents reported greater happiness and life satisfaction in their twenties and less depression and substance use. This is observational evidence, but it is large and carefully controlled. Children learn prayer chiefly by watching parents pray.

rows.title: Living the Liturgical Year at Home
rows.summary: The Church's calendar (Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, Pentecost, saints' feast days, name days and baptism anniversaries) gives young children a sensory, story-shaped experience of the faith. Families keep an Advent wreath and a Jesse tree, bless the home at Epiphany, keep Lenten sacrifices, and hold feast-day meals and celebrations.
objectives: Name the liturgical seasons and their colors
Take part in family customs for Advent, Christmas, Lent and Easter
Celebrate their baptism day and patron saint's feast
Connect each season with a Bible story (Annunciation, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, Pentecost)

coreTexts.title: Around the Year with the von Trapp Family
coreTexts.author: Maria Augusta von Trapp

curriculumOptions.name: Saints & Seasons of the Liturgical Year: A Hands-On Religion Resource
curriculumOptions.notes: Crafts, activities and stories keyed to the Church year for young children.

rows.notes: Liturgical Protestants (Anglican, Lutheran) keep much of the same calendar. Many evangelical churches keep only Christmas and Easter; the Advent wreath and Lenten customs are now widely shared.

rows.title: Bible Stories Read Aloud
rows.summary: Daily read-alouds from a good illustrated children's Bible give the child the whole storyline (Creation, Fall, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, the prophets, the life of Jesus, the early Church) and the images and names of Scripture that later literature and art assume. Children retell the stories and act them out.
objectives: Retell 30–50 major Bible stories in order
Name the main figures of the Old and New Testaments
Recite short memory verses (e.g. Psalm 23, John 3:16, the Beatitudes)
Connect Bible stories to the liturgical seasons
rows.notes: The Golden Children's Bible was approved by an interfaith (Protestant, Catholic and Jewish) board and is the Bible text of Memoria Press's Christian Studies. Lovasik's Catholic Picture Bible includes Catholic emphases (e.g. Mary, the Eucharist at the Last Supper).

rows.title: Saints' Stories & Heroes of the Faith
rows.summary: Short illustrated lives of the saints read on their feast days give young children heroes of courage, charity and purity: St. Francis, St. Nicholas, St. Patrick, St. Joan of Arc, St. Thérèse, St. George, and the child's own patron. Stories are told as true adventures and connected to virtues.
objectives: Know the story of their patron saint and 10–20 other saints
Name a virtue each saint shows
Ask a saint's intercession in prayer (Catholic practice)
rows.notes: Protestant families will omit intercession and emphasize the saints as "a great cloud of witnesses" (Hebrews 12:1). Missionary and Reformation-era biographies (Patrick, Augustine, Bunyan, Hudson Taylor) fill the same role.

rows.title: Catechesis of the Good Shepherd (Level I Atrium)
rows.summary: The Catechesis of the Good Shepherd was developed in Rome from 1954 by Scripture scholar Sofia Cavalletti and Montessori educator Gianna Gobbi. It offers children aged 3–6 a prepared "atrium" with hands-on materials for the parables (especially the Good Shepherd), the infancy narratives, and the gestures and objects of the Mass and Baptism. It emphasizes the child's own relationship with God, contemplation and wonder over instruction.
objectives: Work independently and reverently with atrium materials (Good Shepherd, altar, baptism)
Know the Good Shepherd parable and that "the sheep know his voice"
Name the articles and gestures of the Mass
Pray in silence and song for short periods

coreTexts.title: The Religious Potential of the Child: Experiencing Scripture and Liturgy with Young Children
coreTexts.author: Sofia Cavalletti

curriculumOptions.name: Catechesis of the Good Shepherd (find an atrium or train as a catechist)
curriculumOptions.notes: Parish- and school-based atria. Parents can take Level I formation to set up a home atrium. Episcopal and some other Protestant churches also use CGS.

sources.label: CGSUSA: Discover the Catechesis

rows.title: First Catechism & First Communion Preparation
rows.summary: This is formal catechesis for the age of reason (about 7). The child memorizes the basic questions and answers of the faith (God, creation, the Trinity, the Incarnation, sin, the commandments, the sacraments) and prepares for first Confession and first Holy Communion. The Baltimore Catechism's question-and-answer form suits the grammar stage's appetite for memorization.
objectives: Memorize the answers to the core catechism questions (Who made me? Why did God make me?)
Know the Ten Commandments, the Apostles' Creed and an Act of Contrition
Explain simply what happens in Baptism, Confession and the Eucharist
Prepare for and receive first Penance and first Holy Communion

coreTexts.title: St. Joseph First Communion Catechism (No. 0)
coreTexts.author: Confraternity of Christian Doctrine (rev. Baltimore Catechism)

coreTexts.title: A Catechism of Christian Doctrine, No. 1 (Baltimore Catechism)
coreTexts.author: Third Plenary Council of Baltimore

curriculumOptions.name: Faith and Life, Grades 1–2 (Our Heavenly Father; Jesus Our Life)
curriculumOptions.notes: A doctrinal text with fine classical art, with activity books and teacher guides. See the scope and sequence at https://loc.ignatius.com/faithandlife/scope.htm.

curriculumOptions.name: Preparing to Receive Jesus: A Hands-On Religion Resource
curriculumOptions.notes: A gentle, hands-on companion for first-sacraments preparation at home.

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Baltimore Catechism (1885) was the standard text of American Catholic schools until the late 1960s. Children memorized it question by question, much as colonial Protestant children memorized the New England Primer and the Westminster Shorter Catechism.
rows.notes: Protestant families would instead use a children's catechism (e.g. the Westminster Shorter Catechism or a Lutheran Small Catechism) and prepare for the Lord's Supper according to their church's practice. Many Protestant churches admit children to communion later, after profession of faith.

rows.title: Bible History I: Salvation History as Real History
rows.summary: This is a narrative survey of the Old and New Testaments taught as history: Creation to the Patriarchs, the Exodus and Conquest, Judges and Kings, Exile and Return, and the life of Christ and the early Church. The student memorizes a timeline, key places on a Bible map, and core passages, and learns to see the covenants as the Bible's unifying thread.
objectives: Place 40–60 Bible events and figures on a timeline and a map
Trace the covenants with Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and the New Covenant in Christ
Memorize Psalm 23, the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20), and the Beatitudes
Narrate a Bible story orally and in writing

curriculumOptions.name: Christian Studies I–III (with The Golden Children's Bible)
curriculumOptions.notes: A three-year reading course that teaches salvation history as real history, with timelines, maps and memory work. It is ecumenical and used by Catholic and Protestant families.

curriculumOptions.name: God's Great Covenant (Old Testament 1–2, New Testament 1–2)
curriculumOptions.notes: Bible-history curriculum organized around the covenants, for grades 3–6.

curriculumOptions.name: Faith and Life, Grade 3 onward
curriculumOptions.notes: The Catholic catechism series integrates Bible history. It can be paired with either option above.

rows.notes: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include the deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and parts of Esther and Daniel). Protestant Bibles omit them or print them as "Apocrypha". This row uses the Catholic canon and notes the difference without polemic.

rows.title: Baltimore Catechism No. 2 & Faith and Life (Grades 3–5 level)
rows.summary: This is the full intermediate catechism, taught in the Confirmation-class tradition: the Creed, the sacraments, the commandments and prayer, with definitions memorized precisely (grace, sin, virtue, sacrament) and explained with Scripture. It is paired with Faith and Life Grades 3–5, which present the same doctrine through narrative and art.
objectives: Memorize and explain the Baltimore No. 2 answers on the Creed, sacraments and commandments
Define sanctifying and actual grace, mortal and venial sin, and the theological and cardinal virtues
Know the seven sacraments, their matter, form and minister
Pray the Rosary and know its mysteries

coreTexts.title: A Catechism of Christian Doctrine, No. 2 (Baltimore Catechism)
coreTexts.author: Third Plenary Council of Baltimore

curriculumOptions.name: Faith and Life, Grades 3–5 (Our Life with Jesus; Jesus Our Guide; Credo—I Believe)
curriculumOptions.notes: The grade 5 volume walks through the Creed.

curriculumOptions.name: Our Lady of Victory School (traditional Catholic homeschool)
curriculumOptions.notes: A pre-Vatican II–style curriculum that relies heavily on the Baltimore series.

rows.title: Lives of the Saints & the Early Church for Young Readers
rows.summary: Chapter-book biographies of saints and heroes of Church history, from the martyrs of the catacombs to modern saints, read independently and narrated. Historical novels such as Wiseman's Fabiola (the Diocletian persecution) bring the early Church alive, and Butler's Lives is used for daily feast-day readings.
objectives: Read 8–12 saint biographies a year and narrate or write a report on each
Place the saints on the history timeline
Explain what martyrdom, sanctity and canonization mean
Read the feast-day entry from Butler's Lives on major feasts

coreTexts.title: The Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs, and Other Principal Saints
coreTexts.author: Alban Butler

coreTexts.title: Fabiola; or, The Church of the Catacombs
coreTexts.author: Cardinal Nicholas Wiseman

curriculumOptions.name: Vision Books (saints' biographies for ages 9–15)
curriculumOptions.notes: Classic 1950s–60s biographies, reprinted. Well written and historically careful.

curriculumOptions.name: Light to the Nations, Part 1: The History of Christian Civilization
curriculumOptions.notes: A Catholic-perspective history text for middle grades that pairs well with the biographies.

rows.title: The Pilgrim's Progress & Christian Allegory
rows.summary: Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress (1678), which for two centuries stood beside the Bible in English-speaking households, is read in full as a classic of Christian imagination. The student follows Christian's journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City and learns to read allegory.
objectives: Read the complete Part I and narrate its main episodes
Identify the allegorical meaning of key places and characters (Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, Giant Despair)
Memorize a passage (e.g. "Who would true valour see")
Compare Christian's journey with a saint's life read in theology-09

coreTexts.title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come
coreTexts.author: John Bunyan

curriculumOptions.name: Dangerous Journey: The Story of Pilgrim's Progress (for younger readers)
curriculumOptions.notes: A richly illustrated abridgment. It can be read aloud at 7–9, before the full text.

curriculumOptions.name: Pilgrim's Progress (Worldview Edition)
curriculumOptions.notes: The full text with a Reformed worldview guide.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Pilgrim's Progress stood beside the Bible in colonial and 19th-century American homes. Franklin records that it was among the first books he owned and loved as a boy.
rows.notes: Bunyan was a Puritan Baptist. Catholic readers will notice the book's Reformed account of conversion and assurance and its "Giant Pope"; both are worth discussing calmly. Its account of perseverance, temptation and grace is shared ground.

rows.title: Baltimore Catechism No. 3 & Faith and Life (Grades 6–8 level)
rows.summary: The advanced Baltimore Catechism, with fuller explanations and Scripture proofs, is paired with Faith and Life 6–8 (Following Christ; The Life of Grace; Our Life in the Church). It prepares the student for Confirmation and for apologetics: he learns not only what the Church teaches but where it is found in Scripture and Tradition.
objectives: Master the Baltimore No. 3 answers, including the scriptural references
Explain the four marks of the Church and apostolic succession
Explain grace, justification and merit in Catholic terms
Prepare for and receive Confirmation, choosing a saint's name with a written reason

coreTexts.title: A Catechism of Christian Doctrine, No. 3 (Baltimore Catechism)
coreTexts.author: Third Plenary Council of Baltimore

coreTexts.title: An Explanation of the Baltimore Catechism (Baltimore No. 4, teacher's reference)
coreTexts.author: Rev. Thomas L. Kinkead

curriculumOptions.name: Faith and Life, Grades 6–8
curriculumOptions.notes: Grade 8 covers the Church, and grade 7 covers grace and the sacraments.

curriculumOptions.name: Kolbe Academy religion courses
curriculumOptions.notes: A Jesuit Ratio-inspired Catholic homeschool program with Baltimore-based middle-school religion.

rows.notes: This is a natural place for a first comparative note. Catholics hold that justification infuses grace and makes one inwardly righteous, cooperating with faith and works done in grace. Lutheran and Reformed Protestants hold that justification is a forensic declaration received by faith alone, with good works following as fruit. The 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (Catholic–Lutheran) records significant convergence.

rows.title: Scripture II: The Gospels & Acts with a Study Bible
rows.summary: A close reading of Matthew, Mark, Luke, John and Acts in a modern Catholic translation, using the notes, essays and word studies of the Ignatius Catholic Study Bible (Hahn & Mitch). The student learns to read Scripture in context, use cross-references and commentary, and see how the Old Testament is fulfilled in the New.
objectives: Read all four Gospels and Acts in full
Compare the Synoptic Gospels in parallel passages and explain John's distinct purpose
Trace Old Testament fulfillment (Passover, manna, temple, David's kingdom) in the Gospels
Memorize the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), in sections

coreTexts.title: Ignatius Catholic Study Bible: New Testament (RSV-2CE)
coreTexts.author: Scott Hahn & Curtis Mitch

curriculumOptions.name: Ignatius Catholic Study Bible (Old and New Testaments)
curriculumOptions.publisher: St. Paul Center for Biblical Theology
curriculumOptions.notes: Scott Hahn's St. Paul Center also offers free and paid Bible studies and courses that can supplement this row.

curriculumOptions.name: Christian Studies (upper levels) / Gospel studies
curriculumOptions.notes: Memoria's sequence continues into New Testament study. It is ecumenical.

rows.title: Fr. Laux's Course in Religion (Doctrine, Sacraments, Morality, Apologetics)
rows.summary: Fr. John Laux's four-part high-school course (first published from 1928 and reprinted by TAN) is the pre-conciliar standard. It covers Chief Truths of the Faith, Mass and the Sacraments, Catholic Morality, and Catholic Apologetics, and has companion volumes on the Bible and Church History. It is clear, systematic and thorough, and it moves the student from catechism answers to reasoned theology.
objectives: Outline the proofs for God's existence and the credibility of revelation as Laux presents them
Explain the Mass as sacrifice and the theology of each sacrament
Apply the principles of Catholic morality (object, intention, circumstances; conscience)
Answer common objections to Catholic doctrine in writing

coreTexts.title: A Course in Religion for Catholic High Schools and Academies (Parts I–IV)
coreTexts.author: Rev. John Laux, M.A.

curriculumOptions.name: Fr. Laux's A Course in Religion Series (Set of 4)
curriculumOptions.notes: The core four-volume set. TAN Academy uses it in its high-school theology rotation.

curriculumOptions.name: Mother of Divine Grace School (high-school religion)
curriculumOptions.notes: A classical Catholic distance program whose high-school religion syllabi draw on Laux, Sheed and the Catechism.

rows.notes: Laux predates Vatican II. Use the Catechism of the Catholic Church (theology-21) to update points of emphasis (e.g. ecumenism, religious liberty), but the doctrinal core is unchanged.

rows.title: Apologetics I: Sheed, Kreeft, Karl Adam & Mere Christianity
rows.summary: This is the reasoned defense of the faith. Frank Sheed's Theology for Beginners gives the intellect a map of doctrine (God, Trinity, creation, fall, redemption, Church, sacraments, last things). Kreeft and Tacelli summarize the arguments for God, the soul, the resurrection and the Church. Karl Adam's Spirit of Catholicism explains the Church as a living whole. C.S. Lewis's Mere Christianity, the most widely read modern apologetic, gives the shared Christian ground of all traditions.
objectives: Explain the Trinity and the Incarnation accurately and without heresy
Present and defend three arguments for God's existence and the argument for the resurrection
Summarize Lewis's moral argument and his "liar, lunatic or Lord" trilemma, and evaluate them
Answer five common objections to Christianity in short essays

coreTexts.title: Handbook of Catholic Apologetics: Reasoned Answers to Questions of Faith
coreTexts.author: Peter Kreeft & Ronald K. Tacelli, S.J.

coreTexts.title: The God Delusion (elective, the opponent's case)
coreTexts.author: Richard Dawkins

coreTexts.title: The Last Superstition: A Refutation of the New Atheism (elective, response)
coreTexts.author: Edward Feser

coreTexts.title: Atheist Delusions: The Christian Revolution and Its Fashionable Enemies (elective, response)
coreTexts.author: David Bentley Hart

curriculumOptions.name: Handbook of Christian Apologetics (Kreeft & Tacelli, ecumenical edition)
curriculumOptions.notes: The earlier "mere Christian" edition, without the Catholic chapters. Used in Memoria's apologetics course.

curriculumOptions.name: C.S. Lewis on Christianity (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: A seven-lecture course tracing Lewis's path from skeptic to believer and his major apologetic works.

rows.notes: Lewis was an Anglican who deliberately avoided disputed questions ("mere" Christianity). Karl Adam's reputation is complicated by his early accommodation with National Socialism in 1933, which he later abandoned. Read his book for its theology and note the history honestly. The God Delusion is read critically, at the end of the course or up to 15, as the strongest popular statement of the opponent's case: the student summarizes Dawkins fairly (especially his "Ultimate Boeing 747" argument), then answers him from Kreeft and Tacelli, Feser's The Last Superstition (Aristotelian-Thomist philosophy: the Five Ways are not a "God of the gaps") and Hart's Atheist Delusions (the history the New Atheists get wrong). Feser writes polemically and with some sharp language; a parent should preview it.

rows.title: Scripture III: The Whole Canon, Covenant by Covenant
rows.summary: The student reads the whole Bible, most of it in a two-year plan, with study-Bible notes and Scott Hahn's covenantal framework: Pentateuch, historical books, wisdom literature and Psalms, prophets, Gospels, Pauline and Catholic epistles, and Revelation. He reads Scripture as the Church reads it, in the literal and spiritual senses (Catechism 115–119), and meets the major critical questions.
objectives: Complete a reading of the entire Bible
Explain the four senses of Scripture (literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical)
Outline each book of the Bible in one sentence and place it in salvation history
Read Romans and Hebrews closely, noting Catholic and Protestant readings
Read Dei Verbum (Vatican II) on revelation and inspiration

coreTexts.title: Dei Verbum (Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation)
coreTexts.author: Second Vatican Council

curriculumOptions.name: The Genesis Story / The Exodus Story / The David Story (free online courses)
curriculumOptions.notes: Literary-historical lectures on the Old Testament narratives. See also https://online.hillsdale.edu/courses/promo/exodus and https://online.hillsdale.edu/courses/promo/the-david-story.

curriculumOptions.name: St. Paul Center Bible studies
curriculumOptions.publisher: St. Paul Center for Biblical Theology
curriculumOptions.notes: Hahn's covenant-centered Bible studies.

rows.notes: Catholics read Scripture within Sacred Tradition and the Church's teaching office. Protestants hold sola scriptura, Scripture as the only infallible rule, usually read with the historic creeds. Both affirm divine inspiration. The King James Version (1611) should also be read for its literary and historical importance to English and American culture.

rows.title: The Church Fathers & Monastic Classics
rows.summary: The student reads the early Church in its own words. The Apostolic Fathers (Clement, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, the Didache) show the faith of the generation after the apostles. Augustine's Confessions, the first great autobiography, tells of a restless heart finding rest in God. The Rule of St. Benedict shows the ordered life of prayer and work that preserved Western civilization.
objectives: Identify in the Apostolic Fathers early witness to the Eucharist, the episcopate and Roman primacy
Read Confessions I–IX in full, and X–XIII in selection
Explain Augustine's account of evil as privation and of the restless heart
Summarize the Rule of St. Benedict on obedience, humility, prayer and work, and design a personal rule of life

coreTexts.title: The Writings of the Apostolic Fathers
coreTexts.author: Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, Hermas et al.

coreTexts.title: The Rule of St. Benedict (St. Benedict's Rule for Monasteries)
coreTexts.author: Benedict of Nursia

curriculumOptions.name: Early Christian Writings (Apostolic Fathers)
curriculumOptions.notes: Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, Barnabas and the Didache in a readable translation.

curriculumOptions.name: The Confessions (guided study)
curriculumOptions.notes: A high-school guide to the Confessions.

curriculumOptions.name: Ancient Christianity (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on how the Gospel spread through the Roman world, persecution, and early controversies.

rows.notes: Augustine is claimed by both traditions. The Reformers, especially Calvin and Luther, relied heavily on his theology of grace, and Catholics read him as a Doctor of the Church and a witness to sacramental and ecclesial faith.

rows.title: Spiritual Classics: Imitation, de Sales, Teresa, Thérèse
rows.summary: These are the great manuals of the interior life. The Imitation of Christ, perhaps the most widely read Christian devotional book after the Bible, teaches detachment and love of Christ. Francis de Sales's Introduction to the Devout Life shows holiness in lay life. Teresa of Ávila's Interior Castle maps the ascent of prayer. Thérèse of Lisieux's Story of a Soul teaches the "little way".
objectives: Read the Imitation Books I–II and keep a notebook of maxims
Follow de Sales's method of meditation for a month and write a reflection
Describe Teresa's seven mansions of the Interior Castle
Explain Thérèse's "little way" and why she was made a Doctor of the Church

coreTexts.title: The Story of a Soul (L'Histoire d'une Âme)
coreTexts.author: St. Thérèse of Lisieux

rows.notes: The Imitation has long been loved by Protestants too; John Wesley published an edition of it. Teresa is best read slowly with a spiritual director or mentor. John of the Cross's mystical theology is deliberately placed at college level (theology-24), because it assumes more spiritual and intellectual maturity.

rows.title: Modern Christian Letters: Newman, Chesterton & Lewis
rows.summary: Three great converts and men of letters defend the faith against modern unbelief. Newman's Apologia Pro Vita Sua is the history of his religious opinions from Anglicanism to Rome. Chesterton's Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man argue with paradox and history. Lewis's Screwtape Letters and The Great Divorce are imaginative works on temptation and on heaven and hell, and The Abolition of Man defends objective value and natural law in education.
objectives: Trace Newman's development and his idea that "to live is to change"
Summarize Chesterton's "Ethics of Elfland" and "The Paradoxes of Christianity"
Explain Lewis's "Tao" and "men without chests" and apply them to modern education
Write a Screwtape-style letter on a modern temptation

curriculumOptions.name: An Introduction to C.S. Lewis: Writings and Significance (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on Lewis's fiction and nonfiction.

curriculumOptions.name: Orthodoxy (guided study)
curriculumOptions.notes: A high-school guide to Chesterton's Orthodoxy.

rows.notes: Newman and Chesterton converted from Anglicanism to Catholicism, while Lewis remained an Anglican. The Great Divorce's purgatory-like "refrigerium" is Lewis's imaginative device, but Lewis did personally believe in purgatory, which surprises many Protestant readers.

rows.title: Comparative Theology: The Protestant Classics Read with Charity
rows.summary: The founders' America was overwhelmingly Protestant, and a statesman must understand its theology from the inside. The student reads the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647) alongside the Baltimore Catechism, selections from Calvin's Institutes (Book I on the knowledge of God, Book III on faith and justification), several of John Wesley's standard sermons, and Bonhoeffer's Cost of Discipleship on "cheap" and "costly" grace. He also reads Pascal's Pensées, the work of a Catholic layman close to the Jansenist movement.
objectives: Compare the Westminster Shorter and Baltimore Catechisms answer by answer on God, man, sin, grace, sacraments and the Church
Summarize Calvin on the knowledge of God and self, and on justification by faith
Explain Wesley's teaching on assurance and Christian perfection
Explain Bonhoeffer's distinction between cheap and costly grace and relate it to his martyrdom
State Pascal's wager and his "reasons of the heart", and note where Jansenism diverged from Catholic teaching
Write a comparative essay that states each side in terms its own adherents would accept

coreTexts.title: Sermons on Several Occasions (the standard sermons)
coreTexts.author: John Wesley

curriculumOptions.name: Calvin's Institutes (Books I–IV) and A Study Guide to Calvin's Institutes
curriculumOptions.notes: A Reformed publisher's guide, useful for hearing Calvin read sympathetically by his heirs.

curriculumOptions.name: Theology 101: The Western Theological Tradition (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: A survey of the Western theological tradition from a Protestant-founded, nondenominational college.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Colonial New England children memorized the Westminster Shorter Catechism, printed in the New England Primer. The colonial colleges (Harvard, Yale, Princeton) were founded largely to train Reformed ministers, and Witherspoon, a Presbyterian minister, signed the Declaration.
rows.notes: The aim is understanding, not controversy. Read each author as his own tradition reads him. Neutral notes: Calvin's doctrine of predestination and of the Eucharist differs from both Catholic and Lutheran teaching; Wesley was an Anglican priest whose followers became the Methodists; Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran pastor executed by the Nazis in 1945. Pascal remained a Catholic, and his Pensées are admired by Catholics and Protestants alike, though several Jansenist propositions associated with his Port-Royal friends were condemned by Rome.

rows.title: Liturgy, Moral Theology & Catholic Social Teaching
rows.summary: The course has three parts. Liturgy: Guardini's and Ratzinger's Spirit of the Liturgy and Vatican II's Sacrosanctum Concilium on worship as the Church's summit and source. Moral theology: the virtues, natural law, conscience and the moral act, from Aquinas through Veritatis Splendor. Catholic social teaching: the encyclical tradition from Rerum Novarum (1891) on labor and property, through Quadragesimo Anno (subsidiarity), to Centesimus Annus (the free economy within a moral and juridical framework). The statesman needs all three.
objectives: Explain the Mass as sacrifice and as the "source and summit" of Christian life
Define natural law and the principle of double effect, and apply them to cases
State the principles of CST (human dignity, common good, subsidiarity, solidarity, private property)
Compare Catholic social teaching with the American founding's view of property and limited government
Write a policy memo on a current issue using the Compendium of the Social Doctrine

coreTexts.title: The Spirit of the Liturgy (Commemorative Edition, with Guardini's work of the same title)
coreTexts.author: Joseph Ratzinger & Romano Guardini

coreTexts.title: Moral Theology: A Complete Course Based on St. Thomas Aquinas
coreTexts.author: Charles J. Callan & John A. McHugh, O.P.

coreTexts.title: Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church
coreTexts.author: Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace

rows.notes: Protestant social thought offers parallels worth noting: Abraham Kuyper's "sphere sovereignty" is close to subsidiarity. Liturgical practice differs widely, from Anglican and Lutheran liturgy to free-church worship, and the student should attend and describe services of at least two other traditions respectfully.

rows.title: The Catechism of the Catholic Church & the Roman Catechism
rows.summary: The capstone of high-school catechesis is a complete reading of the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992/1997), in its four pillars (Creed, Sacraments, Life in Christ, Prayer), set beside its model, the Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent (1566). Frank Sheed's Theology and Sanity serves as a companion that turns doctrine into a way of seeing reality.
objectives: Read the entire Catechism of the Catholic Church over a year, with a written summary of each part
Compare the CCC and the Roman Catechism on the Creed and sacraments
Use the CCC's footnotes to trace a doctrine to Scripture, the Fathers and councils
Explain Sheed's claim that theology is necessary for sanity, that is, for seeing what is there

coreTexts.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church (2nd ed.)
coreTexts.author: Catholic Church

coreTexts.title: The Catechism of the Council of Trent (Roman Catechism)
coreTexts.author: Council of Trent (trans. McHugh & Callan)

rows.historicalPrecedent: The Roman Catechism, compiled under St. Charles Borromeo, was the reference for parish preaching from the 16th to the 20th century. Leo XIII recommended it, with the Summa, to all seminarians.

rows.title: College Seminar: St. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae)
rows.summary: This is a Thomas Aquinas College–style tutorial in the Summa Theologiae, read article by article (objections, sed contra, respondeo, replies). It covers sacred doctrine (I q.1), the existence and nature of God and the five ways (I qq.2–13), the Trinity (I qq.27–43), man and happiness (I-II qq.1–5), the treatise on law (I-II qq.90–97, including natural law), and Christ and the sacraments (III, selections). Kreeft's Summa of the Summa supplies notes for self-study.
objectives: Read and present a Summa article in its full scholastic structure
Defend and respond to objections to the five ways
Explain eternal, natural, human and divine law and their relation (I-II q.91)
Apply natural-law reasoning to a constitutional or legislative question
Explain the doctrine of the Trinity using Aquinas's terms (procession, relation, person)

coreTexts.title: Summa Theologiae
coreTexts.author: Thomas Aquinas (trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province)

links.label: New Advent: the five ways (I q.2)
New Advent: the essence of law (I-II q.90)
New Advent: the natural law (I-II q.94)

curriculumOptions.name: Thomas Aquinas College senior theology tutorial
curriculumOptions.notes: The model for this seminar, covering the Summa on sacred doctrine, God, the Trinity, law, the sacraments and Christ's Passion. See the full syllabus at https://www.thomasaquinas.edu/a-liberating-education/syllabus.

curriculumOptions.name: Theology 101: The Western Theological Tradition (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: A broader survey that places Aquinas in the tradition.

rows.historicalPrecedent: Leo XIII's Aeterni Patris (1879) restored Aquinas as the Church's common doctor for philosophy and theology. The Jesuit Ratio Studiorum (1599) had already made him the standard in theology.
rows.notes: Protestant readers note that Aquinas's natural-law teaching was widely received by Reformed and Anglican scholastics (e.g. Richard Hooker), and through them it reached the founding-era idea of natural law.

rows.title: College Seminar: Church History & the Development of Doctrine
rows.summary: This seminar covers the history of the Church from Pentecost to the present through primary sources and the question of doctrinal development. It reads Eusebius's Church History (the first), the ecumenical councils and creeds, the Reformation and Counter-Reformation in their own words, and Newman's Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, whose tests for a true development are the key to reading the whole story. Warren Carroll's History of Christendom supplies the narrative.
objectives: Read Eusebius Books I–III and VIII–X and assess him as a historian
Summarize the first seven ecumenical councils and the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed
Read Luther's 95 Theses and Trent's Decree on Justification side by side
State and apply Newman's seven notes of genuine development
Write a research paper on one council or reform movement from primary sources

coreTexts.title: An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine
coreTexts.author: John Henry Newman

coreTexts.title: The Founding of Christendom (A History of Christendom, vol. 1)
coreTexts.author: Warren H. Carroll

curriculumOptions.name: The History of the Church (Eusebius) with guide
curriculumOptions.notes: Eusebius in the Penguin translation with a study guide.

curriculumOptions.name: Ancient Christianity (free online course)
curriculumOptions.notes: Lectures on the early Church in the Roman world.

curriculumOptions.name: Fr. Laux's Church History
curriculumOptions.notes: The companion volume to Laux's Course in Religion. A clear one-volume Catholic narrative.

rows.notes: Where the traditions differ (the papacy, the Reformation, the councils after 1054), the seminar presents the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant accounts in their own words. The Reformers saw themselves as recovering the early Church; Newman's development thesis is the Catholic answer. Protestant historians such as Philip Schaff (History of the Christian Church) and Jaroslav Pelikan (a Lutheran who later became Orthodox) are valuable counterweights.

rows.title: College Seminar: Mystical Theology of St. John of the Cross
rows.summary: This is a slow, guided reading of the Carmelite Doctor of the Church. The Ascent of Mount Carmel and the Dark Night of the Soul give his account of the active and passive purifications of sense and spirit, and the poems ("Noche oscura", "Cántico espiritual", "Llama de amor viva") are the summit of Spanish mystical verse. It is read after the Aquinas seminar so that the student can connect mystical theology with Thomist teaching on grace, the virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
objectives: Read the Ascent of Mount Carmel Book I and the Dark Night Books I–II in full
Explain the active and passive nights of sense and spirit, and why John counsels detachment
Relate John's teaching to Aquinas on the theological virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit
Write a seminar paper on the relation of the poem "Noche oscura" to its prose commentary
rows.notes: Moved here from the age-14 spiritual classics unit by family decision, because John's mystical theology assumes spiritual maturity. The Spanish track reads his poems as literature at 13–14 (spanish-09). Read with a spiritual director or mentor. Protestant readers have also valued John (e.g. in the Anglican and Wesleyan traditions of spiritual reading), though his Carmelite and sacramental framework is distinctly Catholic.

rows.title: Daily Spiritual Reading: O'Sullivan, St. Alphonsus & Lectio with a Parent
rows.summary: Spiritual reading is a daily habit, not a course. For 10–15 minutes a day, ideally with a parent, the student reads a few pages of a devotional book slowly, in the manner of lectio divina: read, pause on a phrase, turn it into a short prayer, and carry one resolution into the day. The first books are short, warm and practical: Fr. Paul O'Sullivan on prayer, the Mass and the Holy Spirit, and St. Alphonsus Liguori on accepting God's will in every event. The habit leads into the great spiritual classics at 14 (theology-17).
objectives: Keep 10–15 minutes of spiritual reading five or more days a week, most days with a parent
Keep a small notebook of one sentence or resolution per reading
Explain in his own words the meaning of the Our Father, the Hail Mary and the Mass from O'Sullivan
Explain St. Alphonsus's teaching that uniformity with God's will is the summit of holiness, with an example from his own life

coreTexts.title: How to Be Happy, How to Be Holy
coreTexts.author: Fr. Paul O'Sullivan, O.P.

coreTexts.title: The Holy Ghost, Our Greatest Friend: He Who Loves Us Best
coreTexts.author: Fr. Paul O'Sullivan, O.P.

coreTexts.title: Chicken Soup for the Soul (elective)
coreTexts.author: Jack Canfield and Mark Victor Hansen (eds.)

coreTexts.title: Chicken Soup for the Christian Soul (elective)
coreTexts.author: Jack Canfield, Mark Victor Hansen, Patty Aubery and Nancy Mitchell (eds.)

rows.notes: This is a standing daily practice that runs alongside the catechism and Scripture courses, not a separate subject. The three TAN books are core. The Chicken Soup books are light inspirational reading, not spiritual reading in the traditional sense: short true stories of kindness, courage and hope, good for a tired evening, a sick day or reading aloud as a family. Chicken Soup for the Christian Soul is ecumenical rather than Catholic in its stories. The TAN books are old-fashioned in tone ("Holy Ghost" is the older name for the Holy Spirit) and full of anecdotes from the saints, which children tend to love. From 14 the same daily slot moves on to the Imitation of Christ and de Sales (theology-17).
